articles.title_orig: Pope Leo to leave hospital on Saturday, four days after lung cancer surgery
articles.title_zh: Pope Leo to leave hospital on Saturday, four days after lung cancer surgery
articles.content_orig:
Pope Leo XIV was released from Rome's Gemelli Hospital on Saturday, four days after undergoing surgery to remove a cancerous tumor from his right lung .
The pope exited via the hospital's main entrance. A large crowd waiting outside the hospital cheered for him.
He shook hands with several people, then stopped to talk with a young woman who appeared to be wearing a bandage on her right arm and was holding a doll in the image of Pope Leo.
The Pope was smiling. Once in the car, he waved to the crowd. His motorcade returned to Vatican City at 3:43 p.m. local time.
The 71-year-old pope had a portion of his right lung removed and received a diagnosis of lung cancer earlier this week. No information about his prognosis has been publicly shared.
Leo was initially expected to remain hospitalized until Oct. 20 but on Thursday he resumed some work activity , and doctors said Friday that tests confirmed "steady improvement in his recovery." On Saturday morning, the Vatican announced he would leave later in the afternoon.
His personal physician and surgeon said in a separate statement that Leo was "deemed fit for discharge from the hospital" based on blood test results and a chest X-ray performed Saturday morning along with an assessment of his clinical condition.
The Vatican also confirmed that Leo will recite the Angelus prayer from the window of the papal apartment on Sunday.
The Vatican said Leo spoke with Russian President Vladimir Putin over the phone on Friday, during which he "expressed his deep concern about the grave humanitarian situation in the city of Oleshky" in Ukraine . The pope also held separate meetings with Cardinal Luis Antonio Tagle, the dean of the College of Cardinals, and Cardinal Baldassare Reina, the vicar general of the Diocese of Rome.
The Vatican had also released on Friday pictures of the American-born pope standing at an altar in green vestments, celebrating Mass at a small chapel in Gemelli Hospital.
The pope was scheduled to travel to South America next month, but his ability to make the trip has been in question since his diagnosis. However, on Friday the Vatican published the names of journalists accredited to fly on the papal plane to Uruguay, Argentina and Peru, signalling that the trip appeared to be going ahead.
The Associated  Press contributed to this report.

articles.title_orig: Chinese embassy issues fresh Thailand travel alert over kidnappings, job scams
articles.title_zh: Chinese embassy issues fresh Thailand travel alert over kidnappings, job scams
articles.content_orig:
Latest advisory alerts citizens to risks after Chinese nationals targeted in kidnappings and trafficking schemes involving fake job offers
Online influencers and artists were also advised to remain vigilant against high-paying job scams operating in Thailand in the latest such warning issued on Friday.
The Bangkok embassy urged travellers to “pay attention to transport arranged by others” and “plan their itinerary and choose licensed transport and legal operators”, while being “careful not to take any free rides from acquaintances or strangers” alike.
Individuals should also refuse sudden changes to venues or travel routes and keep their families informed of their whereabouts, Friday’s notice posted to the embassy website said.

articles.title_zh: AI glasses as travel guides? Cheaper in China, but bugs slow adoption
articles.content_orig:
Affordable AI glasses can translate languages, identify landmarks and provide travel tips, but limitations remain, analysts say
But are they the perfect travel companion? Not yet.
AI glasses were slowly catching on with travellers as the technology improved and more devices entered the market, analysts said, but technical hitches were slowing mass adoption of the smartphone-linked gear that could be worn like ordinary spectacles.
“They can be particularly useful when walking, sightseeing or interacting in unfamiliar environments, making them especially helpful when travelling in foreign countries,” said Flora Tang, principal analyst at market research firm Counterpoint.

articles.title_orig: Zelenskyy says Starlink speed limits in Ukraine are a ‘planned operation’
articles.title_zh: Zelenskyy says Starlink speed limits in Ukraine are a ‘planned operation’
articles.content_orig:
President Donald Trump on Friday denied that the White House had ordered restrictions this week on Starlink satellite internet services provided to Ukraine's armed forces.
Ukrainian officials on Tuesday and Wednesday said SpaceX had restricted use of Starshield , a military-grade version of Starlink, without warning, impeding some military operations and its ability to defend civilians against intensifying attacks by Russia.
SpaceX CEO Elon Musk pinned responsibility for any restrictions on the U.S. government and Trump, writing on X that, "Starshield systems are owned and controlled by the US government."
Reporters in Washington, D.C., on Friday asked Trump who was responsible for pausing access for the Ukrainian military.
"Well, I don't know if it was anybody because it wasn't me, and I don't think it was Elon," Trump said. "And from what I understand, it's the same as it's always been."
Ukrainian forces have long relied on Starlink and Starshield to enable data gathering by their autonomous drones and for other communications. The restrictions cut off connectivity for drones or other vehicles traveling above 160 kilometers per hour.
Serhii Beskrestnov, an advisor to Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, wrote in a post on Telegram this week that, "Our armed forces did not receive a warning about these restrictions, and this led to the failure of a number of missions."
Radoslaw Sikorski, Poland's deputy prime minister, criticized Musk on X about the restrictions. Poland has purchased Starlink services for Ukraine from SpaceX.
"Hey, @elonmusk, big man, are you playing politics with your products again?" he wrote . "As your European customers, we are watching you."
Musk is an advisor to the Pentagon on technology through his role in the recently announced Project Meridian.
The Telegraph reported Friday that Musk "approached Donald Trump with the idea of slowing down Starlink in Ukraine," and both had a hand in imposing the restrictions.
Reuters reported on Thursday , citing two U.S. officials, that the call to restrict Starlink in Ukraine came from the White House, but did not say who made the order.
On Oct. 10, after Trump called on Ukraine to stop all attacks on Russian oil refineries, Musk wrote in a post on X, "Zelensky has gone too far."
Musk and SpaceX did not immediately respond to requests for comment on Friday.
SpaceX shares are down about 11% this week. The company is scheduled to report quarterly results on Tuesday.

articles.title_orig: World number 170 Kartal battles past Ostapenko to reach Wuhan final
articles.title_zh: World number 170 Kartal battles past Ostapenko to reach Wuhan final
articles.content_orig:
World number 170 Sonay Kartal became the lowest-ranked player to reach a WTA 1000 final as she knocked out Jelena Ostapenko with a gritty 7-6 (11/9), 7-6 (7-5) win at the Wuhan Open on Saturday.
The 24-year-old Briton is playing just her second tour event since returning from a six-month injury layoff, having suffered a spinal stress fracture that sidelined her from March to September.
Kartal, who was ranked a career-high 44 in the world 15 months ago, is the lowest-ranked WTA 1000 finalist since the format's introduction in 2009.
In a close affair with 2017 French Open champion Ostapenko, Kartal showed tremendous composure and dug herself out of multiple holes to become the first British finalist in Wuhan Open history.
"Wow, that was probably one of the toughest matches I've ever played,” said Kartal, who survived 50 winners coming off Ostapenko's racquet to reach the biggest final of her career.
"I knew exactly how she was going to play. At times she's unplayable and sometimes you just have to ride that wave.
"Mentally I think this is one of the best performances I've had in my career. I'm very proud of that one."
After dismissing three consecutive seeds in her previous rounds, including No.6 Elina Svitolina and No.9 Belinda Bencic, Kartal made the 35th-ranked Ostapenko her latest victim to reach her second career tour-level final, and first at the WTA 1000 level.
Kartal nullified a double-break deficit in the opening set and saved two set points in the tiebreak to grab a one-set lead in a gruelling 72 minutes.
She had another successful comeback in the second set, rallying back from 1-4 down and saving three set points to punch her ticket to a final meeting with Iga Swiatek or fellow Pole Maja Chwalinska.

articles.title_orig: CDC to send ‘disease detective’ to help tackle Pennsylvania measles outbreak
articles.title_zh: CDC to send ‘disease detective’ to help tackle Pennsylvania measles outbreak
articles.content_orig:
State has confirmed six measles-related deaths and county at center of outbreak lacks its own health department
The county at the center of Pennsylvania’s measles outbreak is at a clear disadvantage because, local officials say, it lacks its own health department and it will now get special assistance from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC).
As of Wednesday, Pennsylvania had confirmed 1,222 measles cases, up from 86 the week before. Six measles-associated deaths have also been confirmed by the state.
The CDC announced on Thursday it would send a scientist – specifically, a “disease detective” – from the agency’s epidemic intelligence service to help tackle Pennsylvania’s growing outbreak.
“CDC will continue working closely with Pennsylvania health officials to provide the expertise and support needed to respond to the outbreak and protect public health,” a CDC spokesperson told NBC News on Thursday.
The spokesperson also added that the CDC director, Dr Erica Schwartz, recommends the MMR vaccine “as the most effective way to prevent measles and protect against infection”.
The network also reported that in addition to the deployment of the “disease detective,” the CDC was releasing nearly $4m to aid the measles response efforts in Pennsylvania.
Lancaster county, the focus of the state’s outbreak with more than 415 confirmed cases as of 9 October, is the largest county in the state to not have its own health department. The plain community, or Amish, who have historically had lower rates of vaccination, make up about 8% of the county’s population.
The Guardian reported earlier this month that the state was bracing for a wave of measles cases, with some public health officials sharing concern that it was “only a matter of time” until the disease spread beyond the outbreak’s center.
The outbreak also comes amid concerns that public health in the US has been hit by growing vaccine skepticism, particularly because of the influence of the controversial health secretary, Robert F Kennedy Jr . Kennedy has also notably had a public dispute with the Pennsylvania governor, Josh Shapiro, who has lambasted the administration and Kennedy for spreading vaccine misinformation.
“I made very clear that his actions and the rhetoric that’s coming from this administration are having a negative impact on communities across America, particularly right here in Pennsylvania,” Shapiro said in August during a briefing to report two measles deaths in his state, their first in three decades.
He continued: “There’s real-life consequences to spreading misinformation. There’s real-life consequences to scaring people.”
Alice Yoder, who was elected to the Lancaster county board of commissioners in 2023 and previously worked as a critical care nurse, told the Guardian that county officials were “very concerned” about the outbreak and that, without its own health department, the county was at a clear disadvantage.
“It’s a lot for our state to handle from a communication standpoint,” Yoder said. “They’re perhaps doing the best that they can, knowing that Pennsylvania has 67 counties, with 60 being under the auspices of the centralized state system rather than having their own health departments.”
She added: “By having a local health department, particularly one of our size, I believe it would mean we would have local data, it would be in real time, and we would have that information quickly. And most importantly, we would have an established staff, which has established relationships with a variety of partners within our community, which means that once we find a sign of an outbreak we would be able to respond to it really quickly.”
Yoder, who is now advocating for the county to establish its own health department, added that because the county doesn’t have one, she and her colleagues find out about measles cases and deaths only through media announcements at the same time as the general public.
“I never thought I would see measles again in my lifetime, but once it occurred I thought that we probably should have been prepared for it,” she said.
An advantage for counties in Pennsylvania that do have their own health departments, such as Montgomery, is their ability to work with local community health initiatives, like coalitions aimed at promoting immunity.
Susan Wenrick, vice-chair of the Montgomery County Immunization Coalition, which is made up of members of county government, healthcare professionals and other community members, said one of the coalition’s main goals was to improve access to vaccines.
“The biggest challenges to vaccinating people in Montgomery county have been access and availability, but one positive thing that came out of the pandemic was the public-private partnerships that were created to bring vaccines to communities, along with addressing the uninsured and underinsured barrier,” Wenrick said.
She added: “These are challenging times due to the amount of misinformation that is available, along with the average person turning to Google or social media for their health information instead of consulting their healthcare professional. A big part of MCIC’s efforts is to provide trusted resources for all.”
As of Friday, the CDC reported 4,410 measles cases nationwide, marking an ​increase of 330 from its update last week. As noted by Reuters , ​the CDC “shifted to using mortality data from ​the National Center for Health Statistics for measles-related deaths, rather than ‌relying ⁠on state health departments, a change that has drawn scrutiny”.

articles.title_orig: Zelenskyy says Trump is ‘rewarding Putin’ as he waives new Russia sanctions passed by Congress
articles.title_zh: Zelenskyy says Trump is ‘rewarding Putin’ as he waives new Russia sanctions passed by Congress
articles.content_orig:
President Donald Trump waived sweeping new sanctions against Russia passed by Congress, arguing in an executive order Friday that the move “is in the national interests of the United States.”
Trump had signed the legislation, named for the late Sen. Lindsey Graham, R-S.C., just last month. The bill took aim at Russia’s largest buyers of oil and gas, allowing the president to impose tariffs on goods from those countries, which may include China and India.
Passed with bipartisan support , the bill was intended to target Russia’s revenue streams as the country continues to wage its war against Ukraine. Suspending the sanctions provides Russia a financial lifeline.
Trump’s decision to put a hold on the sanctions package comes after he announced a deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin last week to release hundreds of thousands of tons of Russian diesel fuel onto the global market as fuel prices soar.
Trump has expressed frustration with Ukraine’s attacks on Russian oil and gas infrastructure and has blamed them for the increase in fuel costs while downplaying the impact of the Iran war on the oil market.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Saturday that lifting sanctions was “wrong” and “only helps the Russians.”
In a Telegram post, he decried what he called an “American sanctions blackout,” adding that a “weakening of pressure on the aggressor, effectively serving as a financial reward for Putin—only encourages him to continue his attacks.”
“It seems to me that this won’t stop Putin,” he later told journalists in WhatsApp messages. “On the contrary, he feels joy and happiness that there is such support.”
The decision to waive the Russia sanctions drew swift condemnation from critics in Congress.
Sen. Richard Blumenthal, D-Conn., called the move a “craven, cowardly action” in a statement.
“These waivers have nothing to do with our national security, and everything to do with sucking up to Vladimir Putin,” Blumenthal said.
“Beyond irresponsible,” Sen. Thom Tillis, R-N.C., who is retiring at the end of his term, wrote on X. “What part of enforcing a law passed 86-11 by the Senate does the President and his advisors not understand?”
“If the President wants to actually bring down energy prices, he can do it by solving the Iran problem, not by doing a solid for Vladimir Putin,” he added.
Rep. Don Bacon, R-Neb., a staunch Ukraine ally who is also not seeking re-election next month, said “the president is prolonging the war, not ending it,” in a post on X .
“Lindsey would be appalled,” Sen. John Cornyn, R-TX, who lost a primary to a Trump-backed challenger earlier this year, wrote.
Zelenskyy thanked both Democrats and Republicans who supported the legislation, and praised the late Graham for his prolonged vocal support for Ukraine.
“He always supported us very strongly and pushed for as much assistance to Ukraine as possible. It’s difficult without him, I’ll say frankly,” Zelenskyy said. “And I am grateful to his friends who supported him.”
Trump’s move to pause the sanctions comes as the price of diesel fuel has shot up almost 70% since the war in Iran began in February and comes less than three weeks before the midterm elections, as cost of living remains a top issue for voters.
Sen. Darline Graham, R-S.C., who co-sponsored the bill named for her late brother, has touted its success as a key part of her campaign to win a full term in his Senate seat. Graham is a fierce Trump ally, as his endorsement was critical in her GOP primary win. Graham has yet to criticize the president for his Russian oil deal or the decision to halt the sanctions.
Congress passed the legislation with strong majorities in both the House and Senate, though many Democrats opposed the bill because it granted the president new tariff powers.
The legislation states that before the administration waives the new sanctions, it must submit an unclassified report to Congress explaining its basis. In his executive order, Trump said the White House has sent the report to Capitol Hill.
Kyla Guilfoil is a breaking news reporter on the politics team for NBC News Digital.
Brennan Leach is an associate producer for NBC News covering the Senate.
Freddie Clayton is a freelance journalist based in London.

articles.title_orig: Pope Leo XIV calls world hunger a ‘terrible offense’ against human dignity
articles.title_zh: Pope Leo XIV calls world hunger a ‘terrible offense’ against human dignity
articles.content_orig:
The pontiff, still hospitalized after surgery, sent a message for World Food Day on Friday.
Pope Leo XIV on Friday called world hunger a “terrible offense” against human dignity and emphasized that adequate food is a basic human right.
“It is a terrible offense against human dignity to prevent bread from reaching any person or to destroy the means by which it is produced,” the pontiff wrote in a message published for World Food Day.
Still recovering from surgery at Rome’s Gemelli Hospital, Leo addressed his message to Qu Dongyu, director general of the Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations (FAO). World Food Day, celebrated every year on Oct. 16 to highlight world hunger, also marks the organization’s founding in 1945.
In his message, Leo lamented the challenge of world hunger and questioned how some can speak of technological innovation while food shortages persist.
“Hunger cannot be considered a statistical anomaly, for it is caused mainly by a lack of political will and collective charity,” Leo said.
“Today, people speak of innovation with great confidence,” Leo said. “However, this term is often used only in reference to the development of devices and algorithms, or the optimization of performance merely for the sake of financial gain.”
According to FAO’s annual report for 2025, an estimated 645 million people worldwide experienced hunger, mainly distributed across Africa, Asia, Latin America, and the Caribbean. According to the same report, 35.5 million children were severely malnourished, and war remained the “primary driver of acute food insecurity and malnutrition.”
Leo also said that food shortages should never be “used as a weapon of war” and encouraged the United Nations to work toward a “new global food order” in which technology ensures food for all.
“Regular access to safe, adequate and sufficient food, in keeping with the dignity of every person, is a basic human right,” the pope wrote.
“A new global food order is essential — one in which technological innovation is unconditionally subordinated to respect for God-given human dignity and the universal common good.”
The pope’s remarks on world hunger follow his June visit to the headquarters of the World Food Programme in Rome, where he emphasized the need to focus on humanity to combat hunger worldwide.

articles.title_orig: Key player in false Talarico rumor has history of online posts invoking Nazi Germany
articles.title_zh: Key player in false Talarico rumor has history of online posts invoking Nazi Germany
articles.content_orig:
Ryan Amacher, who played role in bid to damage campaign, has also made antisemitic and racist posts on social media
An influencer who played a key role in hoax claims that James Talarico was in a mental health facility has a long history of social media posts that favorably invoke Nazi Germany , express antisemitism and anti-Black racism , criticize miscegenation and call for “remigration” of refugees.
On X, the Lake Oswego, Oregon, resident Ryan Amacher, known online as Rhein Amacher, has described Muslims as “sub-human” , claimed that Black Africans are “monkeys” with low IQ , characterized immigrants as “vermin” and expressed support for the far right, including Germany’s AfD and the UK’s Tommy Robinson .
His attempt to damage Talarico’s campaign with false claims about a supposed inpatient admission to an Ohio facility fell apart quickly on Sunday night , but not before his claims were boosted by a staffer on the campaign of Talarico’s Republican rival, Ken Paxton. Since working for the Trump campaign in 2024, he has remained in the milieu of Republican politics and rightwing influencers .
Neither Amacher nor the Paxton campaign responded to requests for comment.
Last week, Amacher phoned the Lindner Center of Hope , a psychiatric hospital in Mason, Ohio, three times, trying to confirm a false rumor that Talarico had been admitted there. The rumor apparently began with a 9 October post by an anonymous X account, TickleTexts, which claimed Talarico had been “hospitalized at Lindner Center for HOPE”, and was picked up by the Republican fundraiser Caroline Wren, who falsely tied it to a private flight between Ohio and Austin. Before calling, Amacher had posted as fact that Talarico “was hospitalized at the @LindnerCtrHope” and tagged the hospital asking it to confirm.
In the full recording of the second call, he gives his name as “Tim”, says he wants to send a care package to his cousin, and offers a four-digit patient code. “I simply made one up (2244) in an attempt to bypass the facility’s security restrictions to discuss the patient,” he later wrote on X . For most of the six-minute call the employee tells him she has no record of Talarico. In its final seconds she says a man that looks like Talarico “was just discharged this evening”.
An excerpt of the recording was incorporated into a 47-second clip that Nick Sortor posted on Sunday afternoon under the headline “Ohio mental hospital CONFIRMS James Talarico was discharged from the facility earlier this week”. Amacher posted his own version minutes later, and Elon Musk replied with a characteristic “!!”. Amacher had first offered the recording to Blaze Media and the Daily Mail, which reportedly declined to run it , and said in an X Space that evening that influencers are “ not held to the same journalistic standards ”. By Tuesday he had reportedly pulled out of an interview with the writer and podcaster Jesse Singal, saying his attorney had given him a “stand down order”.
The purported legal advice coincides with coverage of the fiasco, which has included speculation that Amacher’s attempt to access private health information may land him in legal trouble .
Previous coverage, however, has not probed Amacher’s long history of extremist commentary.
Amacher often invokes Nazi Germany, and the paramilitary movement that preceded it, with apparent admiration.
“In 1919, Germany’s defeated soldiers came home only to be stabbed in the back by socialists and communists who wanted to burn the nation down and install a Soviet-style dictatorship,” he wrote on 29 July , over an AI-generated image of German soldiers beneath Soviet flags beside uniformed men under crescent moons at Berlin’s Brandenburg Gate. In a follow-up post he wrote: “Modern Freikorps volunteers are needed to step up to purge the German nation of the filth destroying it from within.” An AI-generated image accompanying it showed a masked soldier wearing “Freikorps” and “Deutsches Reich” patches, with the black, white and red flag of imperial Germany flying over the Reichstag.
The Freikorps were paramilitary units of demobilized soldiers that crushed leftwing uprisings in Germany after the first world war. In January 1919, Freikorps troops murdered the communist leaders Rosa Luxemburg and Karl Liebknecht. In June, Amacher told critics to “read up on the German Freikorps after 1919–and what became of Luxemburg and Liebknecht”.
“History has a way of repeating itself when revolutionary movements collide with a nation pushed to the brink,” he added. The Freikorps are widely seen as an ideological ancestor of Adolf Hitler’s Nazi party, though he later turned against them.
In July, replying to a post that said “we fought the wrong enemy in WW2, just like General Patton said before the jews assassinated him in 1945”, Amacher wrote : “We should have immediately re-armed the German Wehrmacht and auxiliary troops and joined forces to defeat Soviet communism, once and for all!”
Patton died in December 1945 after a car crash in occupied Germany; conspiratorial claims that he was assassinated have long been debunked .
When fellow influencer Cam Higby complained in February that saying Nick Shirley was not a Nazi had led others to call him one, Amacher replied that “a colleague’s great-grandfather served as a paramilitary adjunct in Germany’s ‘other’ military force (not the Wehrmacht)”. He went on: “By your logic, does that make him a Nazi? Asking for a friend…” and attaching an “OK” emoji.
He has captioned a photo of a figure skater with her right arm raised “Heil yes!” and offered to recruit a man “straight into my elite Panzer division ”. Panzer divisions were armored tank units in Nazi Germany’s army. In July 2025 he joked that his ancestors “fled to Argentina as well, but way back in 1945, departing from the Deutsches Reich”.
He has also called for the return of the late Spanish dictator Francisco Franco, writing : “Bring back Francisco Franco!” in July under a post claiming that “African military-aged males by the THOUSANDS” were entering the Spanish enclave of Ceuta. And he has praised Germany’s AfD, which the country’s domestic intelligence agency labeled a “confirmed rightwing extremist” force last year. “The @AfD is the ONLY party left that will actually SAVE Germany from destruction,” he wrote in April. “We will restore traditional German societal norms, identity, and culture.”
In January, replying to a post attacking the San Francisco Democrat Scott Wiener, Amacher wrote : “He looks like a Jew–I’m guessing he is a Jew!,” and included a nose emoji.
In May 2025, after another user wrote of a man that “He’s also jewish, no surprise there”, Amacher replied : “A ginger Jew? Worst of both worlds…” Under a December post blaming Somali Muslims in Minnesota for “the largest theft of tax payer dollars in American History”, he wrote : “Both peoples are despicable, but the Somalis are ahead of the Jews by far!”
He has told a pro-Israel account that it was “a hollowed-out puppet dancing on Zionist strings” whose loyalty was “to a parasitic regime halfway across the world”, and written that “Zionist infiltrators have sunk their claws deep into U.S. policy”.
Another recurring subject is George Soros, the Jewish financier who is a frequent target of antisemitic conspiracy theories. Amacher has called him “a spawn of the Devil himself”, and in February 2025 wrote that Soros “allegedly turned in his own people during WWII just to save his own skin”, a claim factcheckers have repeatedly debunked .
In June, TickleTexts, the anonymous account that started the Talarico rumor, baselessly claimed, “as a born South African”, that “some villages believe r*ping a 6 month old baby girl will cure their AIDS”. Amacher replied : “Monkeys typically have an estimated IQ below 70.”
Replying in January to a post about a Somali asylum seeker who, it claimed, had raped a 10-year-old girl in Denmark, he wrote : “Seriously, f*ck international obligations! These people are sub-huma

Tesla proved it still has a knack for spectacular marketing stunts this week, revealing what could be the world's second flying car in a livestreamed event. The flying Tesla Roadster Rocket Edition – or at least a concept for it – was made to drive up a halfpipe, perform a kickflip and then glide to the ground using SpaceXAI thrusters and compressed air.
The production car won't arrive until at least 2028, may not be road legal and can be reserved by invite only, reportedly requiring a deposit of $500,000. For anyone not able to part with that amount of money on a reservation agreement that explicitly states that there's no guarantee of delivery, Ikea thinks it has a safer, more affordable option that's available in store today.
A post shared by IKEA Taiwan (@ikea_taiwan)
Ikea's marketing departments already have a reputation for ingenious quick thinking. We recently saw it jump on 2026's Wicker trend faster than you can say "Alexander Skarsgård". But Ikea Taiwan's response to the Tesla Roadster concept's flying abilities is as impressive as the car's own 0.9-second 0-60mph record.
Its answer for a Tesla Roadster Rocket Edition setup suitable for any home is to combine a 4-piece $12.99 Ikea Lillabo toy car set with a Brokglim bath towel . "Real life, baby," it says in the Instagram post above, echoing Tesla's caption in its own post below, before adding "Safe, affordable."
A post shared by Tesla (@teslamotors)
I'm not sure how you're supposed to fix the towel in the air like that, and I don't think the Lillabo has a fan-based suction system to keep it on the track, but kids have even more imagination than Tesla; I'm sure they can work something out. You could also try a slot car race track.

articles.title_orig: Strangers and railway staff help Chinese couple bring quintuplets home by train
articles.title_zh: Strangers and railway staff help Chinese couple bring quintuplets home by train
articles.content_orig:
Despite a previous diagnosis of polycystic ovary syndrome, a condition that can make pregnancy challenging, the 24-year-old mother conceived naturally
When a couple from Xinjiang took their quintuplets home on a 36-hour train journey, the babies became favourites of both the train crew and fellow passengers, who took turns caring for them.
The five babies were born on February 26 at a major hospital in Wuhan, in central China’s Hubei province. Their father, known as Abu, and their mother, Dili, are both from Hotan in northwestern China’s Xinjiang region.
The 24-year-old mother conceived naturally despite having previously been diagnosed with polycystic ovary syndrome, a condition that can make pregnancy difficult, Hubei Daily reported.
After their birth, the quintuplets – one boy and four girls – were cared for in Wuhan by their parents and their aunt.

articles.title_orig: Oregon teacher fought school attacker before armed dad shot suspect 'multiple times'
articles.title_zh: Oregon teacher fought school attacker before armed dad shot suspect 'multiple times'
articles.content_orig:
Some readers may find this article distressing.
A female teacher in the US state of Oregon tackled a teenage shooter who entered her classroom and tried to wrestle the gun from his grasp, police have said.
The teacher, who has not been named, threw her mobile phone before trying to disarm the 16-year-old on the floor of a classroom at Silver Rail Elementary in the city of Bend.
The attacker killed three children and a teacher after shooting his way into the building on Thursday.
He was shot dead by a father with two daughters at the school, who was driving past as the attack started to unfold and, armed with a pistol, ran in to confront the suspect.
Police said the attacker used to be a student at the school. His motive remains unclear.
He had been armed with about 44 more rounds of shotgun ammunition when he was stopped, police said. He fired as many as 15 rounds in the class.
"To the people who showed courage in the face of such violence and intervened to prevent this tragedy from being any worse, we owe you a debt of gratitude," Bend Police Chief Mike Krantz said.
Police used a news conference on Friday to identify two of the four victims of the school shooting. They were five-year-old Rhoam Summer and 25-year-old teacher Meghan Lambert.
Lambert's family said in a statement shared by the police that her goal was to be a teacher in the district in which she grew up and that she was "compassionate and had a huge heart".
"She always fought for the underdog and those with special needs," they said.
Bryan Jolly, Summer's grandfather, said the family was devastated by his death.
"The whole thing is senseless, and a shock," he told the New York Times, saying his grandson was "was very bright and very mischievous and very fun-loving, and totally without fear".
The families of the two other students who were killed, an eight-year-old and 11-year-old, did not wish to have them publicly identified yet, police said.
Two others were injured in the attack. Another teacher, a 54-year-old, was still being treated at hospital, and a seven-year-old student, who was in serious but stable condition.
Krantz said the heroic actions of both the teacher and the father who ran inside the school had saved lives.
He said the teacher who wrestled with the gunman had not been hurt but "almost certainly helped prevent more bloodshed".
Krantz identified the suspect as 16-year-old Griffin J John II, who had been a special educational needs student at the school.
A search warrant has been executed at his home and a search is ongoing, the police chief said.
Police believe the suspect travelled to the elementary school on foot, but they are still investigating his exact movements and how he acquired the gun.
Officials did not confirm the name of the father who intervened and fatally shot the suspect.
But Kaylub Giamanco's family has identified him to US media as the person who sprang into action.
The 36-year-old carpenter had just finished lunch and was on his way home when he passed the school, his brother told NBC News. He saw the suspect open fire on a vehicle outside the school and then shoot through a window to gain entry.
Police said he had a legally concealed .40 calibre in his vehicle, while his brother said he grabbed the pistol "and decided to go in after" the suspect. Police say he fired at the suspect "multiple times", killing him.
Giamanco's mother, Kenda Freeman, who lives in Sacramento, California, told a local CBS station that her son had called her moments after the shooting and that he was "traumatised".
"He said 'a man went into my daughter's school'," Freeman recalled, pausing as she started to tear up. "And, um, shot kids. And he said, 'and I looked at him point blank, and I shot and killed him, mum'."
She added: "I told him he saved a lot of lives, and he said, 'mum, I couldn't save them all'."
US President Donald Trump praised the bystander on Friday, calling him a "great hero" and telling reporters that the situation could have become "much worse".
"It's a terrible thing, but thank goodness for a man that had a gun and knew how to use it," he said.
Without naming the bystander, Oregon Governor Tina Kotek acknowledged the man's heroic actions as having stopped further loss of life, but noted they "carry a heavy emotional burden and I just want you to know that my thoughts are with you as well".
Additional reporting by Kayla Epstein

articles.title_orig: China urges joint efforts to address risks, challenges in nuclear field
articles.title_zh: China urges joint efforts to address risks, challenges in nuclear field
articles.content_orig:
UNITED NATIONS – China's ambassador for disarmament affairs, Li Chijiang, on Friday called on the international community to work together to address the risks and challenges in the nuclear field.
Li made the appeal at the thematic debate on nuclear weapons at the Disarmament and International Security Committee of the 81st session of the United Nations General Assembly.
Over the past year, confrontation within multilateral nuclear arms control mechanisms has further intensified. The international community is increasingly concerned about the risks of a nuclear arms race and nuclear war, he said.
The Cold War mentality is the primary source of deterioration of the international strategic security environment, the envoy noted.
Double standards are the greatest challenge to the international nuclear non-proliferation regime, and unilateralism is the greatest obstacle to global governance in the nuclear field, he added.
"The international community should work together to address the risks and challenges in the nuclear field following the vision of common, comprehensive, cooperative and sustainable security," said Li.
Relevant nuclear-weapon states should abandon their policy of nuclear deterrence based on winning a nuclear war and the first use of nuclear weapons, he said.
The international consensus on the nuclear test ban must not be challenged, Li said, adding that the commitments on "moratorium on nuclear testing" must be honored.
The state with the largest nuclear arsenal should effectively fulfill the special and primary responsibility for nuclear disarmament by making drastic and substantive reductions in its nuclear arsenal, rather than pursuing "the world's most robust, credible and modern nuclear deterrent," Li said.
Efforts to prevent the proliferation of nuclear weapons should not undermine the right of developing countries to the peaceful use of nuclear energy. The peaceful use of nuclear energy must not be used as a cover for nuclear proliferation, he said.
A certain non-nuclear-weapon state accumulates large amounts of plutonium of no credible civilian use, promotes the revision of the "Three Non-Nuclear Principles," and openly advocates the possession of nuclear weapons. The international community must be vigilant and exercise strict constraint, Li said.
The Three Non-Nuclear Principles, formally adopted by the Japanese parliament in 1971, refer to not possessing, not producing, and not permitting the introduction of nuclear weapons into the country.
China's position of advocating the complete prohibition and thorough destruction of nuclear weapons remains firm, its policy of no-first-use of nuclear weapons is consistent, and its efforts to maintain global strategic security and stability have never ceased, he said.

articles.title_orig: How Pennsylvania Explains the Forces Shaping the Midterms
articles.title_zh: How Pennsylvania Explains the Forces Shaping the Midterms
articles.content_orig:
Democrats’ long list of priorities that have been stalled by the GOP-controlled Senate could be a reality if they flip at least two Republican seats. Both parties are spending big to stay in power.
HARRISBURG — Contentious, compromising, and gridlocked.
Those are just a few ways to describe Pennsylvania’s split legislature during the last four years, as Democrats narrowly control the state House and hold the governorship, while Republicans lead the state Senate. In other words, they have not agreed on a lot.
Gov. Josh Shapiro and legislative leaders have clashed to the point of bitter monthslong budget impasses or, in some cases, left several critical issues — including second-degree murder sentencing rules and skill games regulation — unaddressed.
Before that, Republicans for years controlled both chambers, with a Democrat in the governor’s mansion.
But as the political tides turn, Democrats are hoping next month for a blue wave in the Pennsylvania Capitol. With President Donald Trump ’s 37% approval rating in Pennsylvania and Shapiro, a popular incumbent governor, at the top of the ticket, Democrats are entering the Nov. 3 midterm election with a lot in their favor — and for the first time in decades imagining what Harrisburg would be like with a trifecta of power.
Democrats’ long list of priorities that have been stalled by the GOP-controlled Senate — from a minimum wage increase to new mass transit funding to codifying abortion and LGBTQ+ rights — could be a reality if they flip at least two Republican seats.
What’s really happening in Pennsylvania politics? This newsletter makes you the smartest person in the room on Pennsylvania’s midterms.
Democrats have not controlled the state House, Senate, and governorship since 1993. Currently, the state Senate has 27 Republican members and 23 Democrats.
The last trifecta in Harrisburg belonged to Republicans, who won full control in 2010 in a significant red wave in the first midterm following former President Barack Obama’s election. The GOP held onto the trifecta for four years before former Gov. Tom Wolf, a Democrat, won the governorship and would frequently veto legislation he did not like, leading to a nine-month budget impasse and long legislative standoffs.
If Democrats gain two state Senate seats in November, tying the chamber, Democratic Lt. Gov. Austin Davis would hold special powers — similar to the vice president in the U.S. Senate — that would help tip control to the party.
“We’re working extremely hard,” said State Sen. Vince Hughes (D., Philadelphia), who leads the state Senate’s campaign arm. “I’m not going to make any predictions about winning or losing. I know that we’re competitive everywhere where we’re running.”
Half of the state Senate and all 203 House members are up for reelection this year. House Democrats feel confident they will expand their two-seat majority in the chamber, while Senate Republicans argue they need to keep control of the chamber as the last line of defense against “radical left policy decisions.”
Democrats are targeting four Senate seats they want to flip, while Republicans are bullish they will flip a seat in Lancaster County that they lost to Democrats in a 2025 special election by a few hundred votes.
And both parties’ campaign arms are spending big for control of the seats.
According to media tracker AdImpact, Senate Republican campaigns have spent a total of $15.4 million so far on TV and streaming ads across five competitive races: Bucks County ’s 6th District, Montgomery County ’s 24th District, Lancaster County’s 36th District, Monroe County’s 40th District, and Lehigh County’s 16th District.
Senate Democratic candidates have spent $12.3 million so far on TV and streaming ads across the same five districts, according to AdImpact.
The two most expensive races are in the Philadelphia suburbs. Both parties see these seats as must-wins to decide control of the Senate .
» READ MORE: Bucks and Montgomery Counties could determine which party gets control of the Pa. state Senate
State Sen. Frank Farry (R., Bucks) represents the 6th Senatorial District, a swing district in Lower Bucks County, and became an early target for Democrats. The race has already attracted $6.9 million in ad buys so far: $3.6 million by Farry’s campaign and $3.3 million by his Democratic challenger, Eileen Hartnett Albillar, according to AdImpact.
State Sen. Tracy Pennycuick (R., Montgomery), elected in 2022, is one of few Republicans still representing the otherwise solid-blue Montgomery County. Her campaign has spent or reserved nearly $4 million on TV and streaming ads so far. Her challenger, Democrat Chris Thomas, has spent $3 million.
The exact amount of money spent so far in these races will not be available until campaign finance filings are due later this month, and will include how much was spent on other voter outreach, like direct mail.
When asked this summer about the prospect of a Democratic trifecta, Senate Majority Leader Joe Pittman (R., Indiana) rebuffed it.
“I’m more focused on what it would be like with a Republican trifecta,” Pittman said in an interview in July, noting the narrow Democratic control in the House. “At the end of the day, a day in politics is a lifetime.”
Pennsylvania’s latest legislative maps — set in 2022 by the state’s five-person redistricting commission — made the state House significantly more competitive for Democrats. That year, the party flipped the chamber for the first time in more than a decade .
Meanwhile in the state Senate, the same set of maps benefited Republicans, and were likely to cement GOP control for another decade, according to an analysis conducted for The Inquirer by the nonpartisan Princeton Gerrymandering Project at the time.
Four years later, enter Trump’s declining job approval rating in Pennsylvania, high gas prices, a governor’s race with a double-digit Democratic lead, and GOP control in Washington — and Pennsylvania Democrats see a rare opportunity.
To flip the state Senate, Democrats have two potential paths: They would need to capture at least two GOP-held seats in swing districts and maintain control of a seat in a Lancaster County district that Trump won in 2024 by 15 percentage points . Or, if they cannot hold onto the Lancaster seat, they would need to flip a total of three seats to take control of the chamber.
» READ MORE: In major upset, Democrats flip a Lancaster County state Senate seat that Trump won by 15 points
Hughes, who is on track to lead the powerful Senate Appropriations Committee if Democrats prove successful in November, said he is not yet picking out the new drapes or a new front-row parking spot at the Capitol. Rather, he said, he is hardly letting himself imagine what it would be like to helm the committee that reviews every bill and decides how state dollars are spent, and where he has served as the minority chairman since 2010.
“We’ll accomplish a lot of things that the people of Pennsylvania need us to get accomplished, and we’ll do it in a way that I think the people of Pennsylvania will be proud,” Hughes added.
Senate Republicans’ campaign arm said in a statement that the Senate GOP has “a record of reducing costs, stopping burdensome taxes, and putting Pennsylvanians’ safety first.”
Senate Republicans appear to have spent significantly more to protect their majority than the party at large has spent to elect Stacy Garrity , the GOP nominee for governor, who has just reserved or spent $1.4 million on TV and streaming ads through Election Day, according to AdImpact.
» READ MORE: Stacy Garrity hopes ‘the cavalry will be coming’ with less than a month until Pennsylvania’s governor election
Their argument for why Republicans should maintain control of the state Senate is simple: They are the ones looking out for taxpayers. And they see themselves as the ones protecting Pennsylvania from the problems facing Democratic-led states like California and New York, criticizing Pennsylvania’s Democrati

articles.title_orig: No Kings turns its focus to voting this weekend. Here's what we know
articles.title_zh: No Kings turns its focus to voting this weekend. Here's what we know
articles.content_orig:
Demonstrators march through the Country Club Plaza shopping district during a "No Kings" protest Saturday, March 28, 2026, in Kansas City, Mo. Charlie Riedel/AP hide caption
No Kings, the coalition known for organizing anti-Trump protests, is trying a different democratic tactic: increasing voter turnout.
On Saturday, grassroot groups across the country will hold over 3,000 "No Kings: Vote Early" marches and other events. Organizers say these events are a nonpartisan effort to promote early voting in the midterm elections , and will involve helping people check their voter registration, make a plan to cast their ballot and understand their voting rights.
The voting push effort marks a pivot for the No Kings coalition, which comprises hundreds of partner organizations , including the American Civil Liberties Union and Black Voters Matter.
No Kings has previously held three days of nationwide protests since the start of Trump's second term because organizers say Trump's actions in office are more akin to those of a monarch than a democratically elected head of state. Trump has previously rejected the idea that he is behaving like a monarch.
"The first three No Kings were designed to send a message," says Ezra Levin, the co-founder of Indivisible — one of the major organizations within the No Kings network. "We're done sending a message."
Now, he says, they want people to vote.
There are two main goals for the event, says Levin, the first is to help facilitate what he hopes will be the largest number of midterm early voting numbers in the country's history.
The second goal is No Kings groups getting volunteers trained as poll watchers, an endeavor Levin says is in response to efforts by the Trump administration that he views as threats to election integrity. Levin points to the failed SAVE America Act that would have required voters to show a document proving their U.S. citizenship, such as a passport or a birth certificate, when registering to vote. He also raises concerns that federal immigration officers will be sent to the polls , and President Trump's attempted restrictions on voting by mail.
Saturday's events vary widely across the country, from block parties to cookouts to rallies. In Golden, Colo., a "Paws to the Polls" event invites people to bring their dogs on a march. Organizers in Everett, Wash., planned a "concert for democracy," featuring an environmental troubadour .
All events will share similar restrictions, Levin says, including a rule against political endorsements and inviting current candidates to speak.
Superhero capes and masks will be a staple of Cammy Dunford's event in Frisco, Texas. Dunford, a co-leader of Indivisible Frisco, plans to hold a "voting is your superpower" gathering. She will be wearing a red and blue cape (to embrace the political spectrum of voters) and will give away other superhero capes and masks.
"I don't care if you're an independent, first-time voter, Democrat, Republican," Dunford says, "if you are eligible to vote, you need to get out there and vote. Because without everybody voting, we don't have a democracy."
Early voting in Texas does not start until Oct. 19, but Dunford and a group of her neighbors put together 500 mini goodie bags to hand out — filled with QR codes linking to voting information and voting resources. They will also wave bright signs with superhero-shaped images urging people in passing cars to vote.
Dunford says that her group has two people already trained as poll monitors and is hoping to recruit more on Saturday. She says poll monitors are trained by Common Cause, a government watchdog group that equips them to answer questions from voters. They have T-shirts that identify them at the polls, she says, so voters can find them and ask questions.
At a Wyandotte, Mich., event, Christy McGillivray, the executive director of Voters Not Politicians , a nonpartisan advocacy organization, is scheduled to speak to a No Kings crowd about the history of fighting for democracy in the U.S. She says the organization of grassroots events across the country is inspiring.
"It makes people feel like they're a part of something bigger than themselves," she says. "And that's what democracy is. Democracy is about working with each other and for each other."

articles.title_orig: Weddings are expensive. How about a grocery store cake?
articles.title_zh: Weddings are expensive. How about a grocery store cake?
articles.content_orig:
A flight of wedding cake samples at a Publix supermarket in Vestavia Hills, Ala., on Sept. 23. Cake flavors from left to right are red velvet, carrot cake, chocolate and vanilla. Filling flavors from left to right are raspberry, vanilla custard, cookies-and-cream mousse and strawberry. Stephan Bisaha hide caption
Going to a specialty baker to craft your dream wedding cake can cost you more than $1,000.
Or you can order a few half sheet cakes from Costco for about $30 each.
"We love Costco, first of all," said Anna Holleran, who got married in California's Bay Area this year — and, yes, picked up her wedding cake from the grocery wholesaler.
"Their cakes are so good," she said. "How can you go wrong?"
Weddings are one of the most expensive days in many people's lives, costing on average about $36,000 , according to the wedding-planning website Zola. The Bank of America Institute reports wedding spending among its customers was up 8.5% in May from a year earlier.
Some of that is by choice, with couples deciding to splurge on the venue or chasing the latest TikTok reception trend. But there are less controllable economic factors too, from inflation driving up the price of suits and catering to tariffs bumping up the cost of imported flowers and bridal gowns .
And according to Emily Forrest, head of communications at Zola, one place where couples are willing to trim costs is the cake. About a third of couples surveyed by Zola said they'd consider spending less on cake and dessert.
"When it comes to a wedding, every couple always has to sit down and say, 'Where are we going to save, and where are we going to splurge?'" said Forrest. "And cakes just don't seem to rise to the splurge occasion for a lot of couples."
What couples aren't willing to do is ditch the cake tradition entirely.
"You can't skip the cake!" said Lily Alana Stewart, who got married last year in central Alabama. "Everybody looks forward to a cake at a wedding."
To save money, she ordered her cake from Publix, a grocery chain in the South.
Stewart used baby's breath for decorating the venue, and Publix incorporated that into the cake design. Her co-workers who attended were surprised to learn where the cake came from. "They said, 'Wait, wait, wait. Your wedding cake was from Publix ?'" Stewart said. "And they were still mind blown."
While the average wedding cake costs about $5.50 a slice, according to Zola, a slice of Publix cake is about $1.50 cheaper, while still pulling off that classic three-tiered, white-frosted wedding cake look. The chain also offers couples a tasting flight, so they can sample four flavors — including red velvet and carrot — before they order.
The wedding cake business has grown at Publix. The stores around Birmingham, Ala., sell about 50% more than they did before 2020, according to Jeff Brancato, a Publix retail improvement specialist. A chocolate cake with fondant that can serve 94 people costs $388, according to the price guide for the Birmingham area.
"There is definitely big savings when it comes to it," Brancato said.
Still, you do get what you pay for in a grocery store cake, including fewer options than what a specialty baker might offer — like more flavors or more customized decorations. While Publix touts its wedding cake business , Costco doesn't even list its half sheet as a wedding cake. It works out to about 70 cents per slice. (Costco did not return NPR's request for an interview.)
Holleran's priority was saving money where she could. Her wedding was near her home in California wine country — a region that's a destination spot for other couples and where venues are expensive.
Holleran said the culinary details of her cake weren't what mattered. "The real point is that you're sharing a dessert for the first time with somebody that you love," she said. "It's kind of symbolic of all the sweet moments that you're supposed to share in a marriage."

articles.title_orig: 'Our land, our Albania': young lawmaker demands new future as protests rage
articles.title_zh: 'Our land, our Albania': young lawmaker demands new future as protests rage
articles.content_orig:
Protesters and anti-riot police have clashed in Albania's main cities in scenes not witnessed for decades.
Government buildings have been attacked and some private businesses, too.
Albania's capital Tirana has seen months of protests from an anti-government "Flamingo" movement, but what started on Tuesday this week was on a different scale.
And the clashes have spread beyond Tirana - to include the main cities of Durrës, Shkodër, Lezhë and Vlora in the west, Gjirokastër in the south and Korçë in the east.
The new demonstrations were announced as a student movement, ostensibly demanding action by the government to help with the high cost of education fees and books - and the higher cost of living.
Secondary schools joined in, swelling the numbers.
Before too long, masked protesters threw stones at police, and they responded with water cannon, tear gas and batons.
Many were incensed by scenes of a young man being carried away, his broken leg dangling with him in agony.
Apologies were expressed but failed to calm the situation.
A floor of the education ministry was set on fire, with other government institutions ablaze, too.
Every evening, throughout the summer for some 135 days in a row, Albanians in central Tirana would hold pictures of a pink flamingo, calling on Prime Minister Edi Rama - now in his fourth term - to resign.
The protests began over a mega-tourism project on the Adriatic coast linked to US President Donald Trump's son-in-law, Jared Kushner. Demonstrators said the bird would become extinct on an island near the coastal city of Vlora, if the plans for a luxury development went ahead.
The public anger comes as allegations of corruption among ministers and other senior officials grow louder.
One deputy prime minister has fled the country, another has been ordered to step down as investigations continue.
The flamingo protesters say they have no links to any political party - one of their slogans being "Rama in jail, Berisha in jail". While Rama is prime minister, Sali Berisha is Albania's main opposition leader - as well as a former prime minister and president.
They were attended by young and old, parents with children and sometimes their grandparents. Some of the participants took pride in cleaning up after every night.
But after months and an unusually hot summer, their numbers dwindled - with no sign that the government was meeting their demands.
The current movement appears far more violent. Dozens of police have been hurt, and the eyes of Europe are now watching what happens next in a country viewed as one of the top candidates for EU membership.
Several young protesters told the BBC that what was going on now was a new phase born of the previous movement.
Five months of peaceful protest had been "met with humiliation, ridicule, mockery," complained one young woman called Livia. "That was a clear message from the government that our voice will not be allowed to be heard."
Another called Brunela told the BBC's What in the World programme she was worried about what might happen next: "I am very terrified because the media and the government is reacting, especially now. It was not just my voice, it is the voice of Albanian youth."
An overlap between the two sets of protests may well have occurred, even though flamingo leaders have not publicly stated so and no representative of the student movement has come forward.
After all, their main concerns relate to corruption, which the prime minister says must be investigated by the justice system.
Rama has been touring some of the damaged buildings and blaming Sali Berisha for instigating chaos.
"All of this is the work of the very same hand - the hand that has gripped the Albanian opposition by the throat, the hand that has burned and destroyed Albania more than once, and is now prepared to burn and destroy it again to prevent any progress. It is a blind struggle, fuelled by the most irrational hatred," he said on Friday.
The prime minister has ruled out resigning, promising to "listen, address legitimate concerns and keep Albania moving forward".
Berisha's Democratic Party has often tried to get people out to oust Rama.
But the number of his loyal supporters, who have also protested for months and at times clashed with police, has been low in comparison to the current attendance.
So there is some scepticism about Berisha's ability to mastermind the trouble, though he may well seek to capitalise on it.
On the other hand, the Albanian media have suggested that secret services of foreign countries may be involved.
Unfounded allegations have been made against Serbia, with commentators suggesting Belgrade is envious of Albania being often cited as potentially next in line to join the EU.
Indeed, without mentioning names, Prime Minister Rama echoed the allegation on Friday.
"These are foreign hands that do not wish for Albania to be at peace... they do not want Albania to be part of the united European family," he said, adding: "Do you think it is a coincidence that every time Albania receives another green light... or draws closer to that great ambition - that historic objective - flames suddenly erupt? It is no coincidence at all! None of what is happening now is a coincidence."
Although the street violence has taken place in many cities, it remains contained for the time being.
The UK government has urged visitors to check media for latest information, stay away from "demonstrations, large-scale gatherings or political rallies" and follow advice of local authorities.
Albania is a popular tourist destination, and the government in Tirana has warned that violence tarnishes the country's image, affecting both tourism and its European path.

articles.title_orig: Coastal homes burn as hot winds fuel California fires
articles.title_zh: Coastal homes burn as hot winds fuel California fires
articles.content_orig:
A roof engulfed in flames is seen during the Norte Fire on Friday, Oct. 16, 2026, in San Juan Capistrano, Calif. Jae C. Hong/AP hide caption
A fast-moving fire fueled by high winds burned at least six homes in Southern California on Friday, engulfing expensive coastal properties and prompting thousands to evacuate.
Black smoke — visible from miles away — billowed over tennis courts and swimming pools while firefighters doused blazing homes in San Juan Capistrano in Orange County. Some homeowners sprayed water on their properties before heeding evacuation orders.
Two firefighters were taken to the hospital with heat-related injuries, officials said. Authorities have not said how the blaze, which was less than a square mile as of Friday evening, started.
"Had these winds been a little bit stronger, a little bit different direction, this could have been a whole lot worse," said San Clemente Mayor Rick Loeffler.
Howard Hart, a councilmember for San Juan Capistrano, said he and his wife doused their roof with water and moved propane tanks away from their home before they evacuated Friday with a to-go bag.
Laura Hart hasn't had to evacuate due to fire in the more than five decades she's lived in the community, she said.
"This doesn't usually happen to us, we usually see it on the news," she said. "We always pray to God it's not us, but yeah, it was today."
The Norte fire started in the coastal city of San Clemente, and wind drove it into San Juan Capistrano. An evacuation shelter has opened in each city. By Friday night, about 16,000 residents had been ordered to evacuate, said Fire Chief TJ McGovern, of the Orange County Fire Authority.
It was one of several fires in the region hit by dry, warm gusts known as Santa Anas, which blow from the interior and toward the coast. The strongest winds were expected through Friday afternoon, but conditions that increase the fire risk were expected to last through Saturday night, with a heat advisory in effect until 8 p.m. Saturday on the Orange County and San Diego County coast, the National Weather Service said.
Tens of thousands of people in the state are without power after their electricity was turned off. A separate fire by the Marine Corps base Camp Pendleton shut down for hours a section of Interstate 5 that is a major artery connecting Orange County to San Diego. That added hours to commutes throughout Southern California.
The coastal cities are surrounded by hillsides. San Juan Capistrano, a city of 35,000, is known for horse trails and the historic Mission San Juan Capistrano. San Clemente, which is home to 62,000 people, is known as a "Spanish village by the sea" and popular with beachgoers and surfers.
"The fire is right up on the city," said Victor Cabral, a San Clemente Council member. "It's on the perimeter of our homes on the north end."
Nine schools were also closed Friday in San Juan Capistrano, the Capistrano Unified School District said.
Nearby residents were also on edge as smoke darkened the sky.
Wyoming resident Shannon Needham was visiting her mother at her assisted living facility in Dana Point just north of San Clemente when she learned about the fire.
The facility director told her that two buses would be on standby in case they needed to evacuate, Needham said.
"You could hear the fire trucks, you could hear the helicopters and everything above. And it was so smoky, it was just dark smoke," Needham said.
Some of California's worst wildfires have been sparked by power equipment, and utilities in recent years have begun proactively shutting off power in dry winds. More than 118,000 customers in California were without electricity as of Friday, according to poweroutage.com.
The weather service also issued a red flag warning for parts of central and Northern California through Friday morning, saying any fires would spread rapidly.

articles.title_orig: Ilhan Omar raid sparks ominous prediction from watchdog: 'They probably got the goods'
articles.title_zh: Ilhan Omar raid sparks ominous prediction from watchdog: 'They probably got the goods'
articles.content_orig:
Oversight Project President Mike Howell tells Fox News Digital why he believes the HSI raid on Rep. Omar's home could lead to further revelations.
The federal raid on Rep. Ilhan Omar’s Washington, D.C., home prompted warnings Wednesday from a conservative watchdog leader that more revelations could be coming, as the Minnesota Democrat faces separate investigations involving her immigration records and financial disclosures.
Oversight Project President Mike Howell, whose group pushed to strip a $1.031 million earmark backed by Omar, says the Homeland Security Investigations (HSI) search raises broader questions about congressional accountability and what investigators may uncover next.
His warning comes as U.S. Attorney Jeanine F. Pirro confirmed on "America Reports" that her office is investigating the Minnesota Democrat's financial disclosures, while separate reporting revealed that federal investigators had subpoenaed Omar's relatives as part of an immigration-related probe.
FEDERAL AGENTS RAID ILHAN OMAR’S DC HOME AMID IMMIGRATION FRAUD INVESTIGATION
Federal agents with Homeland Security Investigations (HSI) raided the Washington, D.C., home of Rep. Ilhan Omar, D-Minn., early Monday morning, a source familiar with the operation told Fox News Digital. (Andrew Murray/Fox News Digital)
"I think there's other shoes that are going to drop here," Howell told Fox News Digital.
"That's why I think the Democrats really just couldn't resist the temptation to jump out of this before they saw any evidence and just circle the wagons [around Omar]," he said.
DEMOCRATS' FURY OVER ILHAN OMAR RAID DRAWS STINGING GOP REMINDER ABOUT RAID FROM THE PAST: ‘SET THE PRECEDENT’
Rep. Ilhan Omar, D-Minn., husband, Tim Mynett, enters Washington, D.C., home that was raided by Homeland Security Investigations (HSI) agents early Monday morning. (Joshua Lott/Getty Images; Andrew Murray/Fox News Digital)
"I will say it appears they're walking that back a little bit. It has shifted from just a wholesale defense of Omar to a non-substantive defense, talking about, ‘well, this stuff was old,’ or ‘this is political since she's Ilhan Omar’."
Howell suggested that Omar’s defenders’ arguments indicate that it’s "not all peaches and cream underneath the hood."
WATCH: ILHAN OMAR DENIES FEDS HAVE CONTACTED HER AFTER BORDER CZAR HOMAN CONFIRMS 'CRIMINAL' INVESTIGATION
Howell's warning extends beyond Omar to what he describes as a broader failure of accountability in Washington, where lawmakers can champion taxpayer-funded projects that later face questions about their legitimacy.
Fox News has learned that federal investigators are examining whether Omar's age was accurately reported when she arrived in the United States in 1995 and when she acquired U.S. citizenship in 2000, including whether any inaccurate information could have affected her eligibility for citizenship through her father under the law in effect at the time.
ILHAN OMAR’S HUSBAND INSISTS HE HAS ‘NO CONCERNS’ AMID FEDERAL IMMIGRATION INVESTIGATION
U.S. Attorney for the District of Columbia Jeanine F. Pirro speaks during a news conference on crime in the James S. Brady Press Briefing Room at the White House in Washington, D.C., on August 11. (Eric Lee/For The Washington Post via Getty Images)
The inquiry also encompasses paperwork completed by her late father and whether he provided inaccurate information. Sources told Fox News that investigators are examining potential immigration fraud spanning multiple years.
Federal investigators have issued more than a dozen subpoenas as part of the immigration inquiry, including subpoenas to members of Omar's family.
The immigration inquiry is separate from the financial-disclosure investigation being handled by Pirro, sources told Fox News.
"We're in the speculation zone, of course," Howell told Fox News Digital, acknowledging uncertainty about the full scope of the federal investigations.
DEMOCRATS HAVE ‘DIRTY HANDS’ OVER COMPLAINTS ABOUT OMAR RAID WEEKS BEFORE ELECTION, EX-PROSECUTOR SAYS
Still, Howell argued that obtaining a search warrant for a sitting member of Congress in Washington suggested investigators had developed substantial evidence, though the warrant establishes only that a judge found probable cause to believe the search would uncover evidence or other items subject to seizure, not that Omar committed a crime.
Howell pointed to what he viewed as a unique combination of circumstances — an HSI investigation under the Trump administration, a warrant authorized by a federal judge in heavily Democratic Washington, D.C., and the proximity of the election — as reasons he believes investigators may have substantial evidence.
"They probably got the goods on her," Howell said. "You don't get a federal judge to sign off on something like this in Washington, D.C., of all places, unless there is something that is rather convincing."
Jonathan Fahey, a former acting ICE director and federal prosecutor in the neighboring Eastern District of Virginia, said the timing of the HSI search raises questions about whether investigators are examining more recent documents tied to longstanding immigration allegations.
"I surmise that what they may be looking for is newer things that were used with what they believe is false information," Fahey told Fox News Digital, referring to the immigration investigation.
Fahey suggested that knowingly repeating materially false information in more recent federal filings could create separate legal exposure, depending on the documents, circumstances and applicable statutes, even if criminal charges based solely on older paperwork would be barred by the statute of limitations.
Former FBI agent Nicole Parker cautioned that Omar might not face criminal liability if her father completed allegedly false paperwork while she was a minor.
"If her father lied and filled out the [citizenship/naturalization] forms, then in my opinion, she will not be criminally held responsible," Parker said.
However, Parker said Omar could face a separate legal question if authorities establish she obtained citizenship through materially-false information .
"It could potentially cause her to be denaturalized and lose her citizenship if her citizenship was gained on false pretenses and false information," she said.
In January, the Oversight Project challenged a proposed $1.031 million earmark for Generation Hope MN's Justice Empowerment Initiative in Minneapolis, a project backed by Omar and Minnesota's Democratic senators.
The group raised concerns about the nonprofit's finances, operations and eligibility for taxpayer funding, including questions about its addiction recovery services at a location shared with a Minneapolis restaurant, whose owner previously confirmed to Fox News Digital that Generation Hope operated in upstairs office space.
"We said, let's go check out those earmarks," Howell recalled.
Conservative Republicans subsequently objected to the funding, with Rep. Chip Roy, R-Texas, among those pushing for its removal.
The earmark was stripped, and Sens. Mike Lee, R-Utah, and Joni Ernst, R-Iowa, later requested Justice Department scrutiny of the nonprofit.
The funding dispute raised questions about congressional vetting of proposed recipients, but its removal did not establish fraud by Omar or the organization. No connection between the earmark controversy and either federal investigation has been publicly confirmed.
As part of his broader "institutional rot" argument, Howell argued that Omar’s earmark controversy is not unique, criticizing what he sees as lawmakers placing loyalties outside the United States ahead of their constitutional responsibilities.
"This isn't normal. And it only seems normal because it's been happening so much. And I think it's about time we take the oath to the Constitution that members swear seriously," he said.

articles.title_orig: Canada’s Mark Carney makes final appeal against Alberta separation ahead of referendum
articles.title_zh: Canada’s Mark Carney makes final appeal against Alberta separation ahead of referendum
articles.content_orig:
EDMONTON, Alberta — Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney made a final appeal to voters considering a path toward independence in his home province of Alberta on Friday, warning that a referendum is a dangerous gamble at a time of growing threats to Canada’s sovereignty.
With U.S. President Donald Trump waging a trade war and threatening to make Canada the 51st state, Carney warned that the referendum comes at the “worst possible time” and urged Albertans not to take the outcome for granted.
“Don’t let anyone tell you this is already decided. Turnout will determine the outcome,” Carney told a pro-Canada rally in Edmonton, where he grew up.
“This is not a game. This is not poker. A vote against Canada is a dangerous bluff that will lead to years of deep uncertainty and lost opportunities for Albertans and Canadians,” he said.
Monday’s vote is not a direct referendum on independence. Alberta, home to most of Canada’s proven oil reserves — the fourth largest in the world — will decide whether to remain a province or instruct the government to begin the legal process toward a future referendum on separation.
Carney’s closing appeal came after two days of campaigning against separation in the province. Earlier Friday, the Liberal prime minister joined Alberta’s conservative premier Danielle Smith in a show of unity against independence.
Smith praised Carney for improving relations with a province that frequently clashed with his predecessor, Justin Trudeau, over his carbon tax and other energy policies.
“I think what we can agree on is that we have had some real change in the last 18 months,” Smith said alongside Carney in Red Deer, Alberta.
Smith noted that Carney grew up in Alberta and remains an Edmonton Oilers fan.
“He can’t be all bad, right?” she joked.
“Some outside our borders are working to break us so they can own us. Never. Never,” Carney warned Friday in Edmonton, repeating a warning he made a day earlier in Calgary.
At Thursday’s Calgary rally and Friday’s Edmonton rally, the crowd erupted in its loudest applause when Carney spoke about reducing Canada’s economic dependence on the United States.
Carney acknowledged Alberta’s longstanding resentment of federal energy policies.
“Growing up, I remember how Ottawa made Albertans feel like our resources weren’t our own,” he said.
But he also emphasized his deep ties to the province.
“Alberta is my home. I grew up here. This city, this province, this country have given me everything: my family, my education, my values,” he said.
Outside the Edmonton rally venue Friday, Alberta independence supporters waved flags and held a sign reading “Say no to Carney’s new world order.”
Smith called the referendum despite opposing independence herself. She recently cited a poll showing 22% of Albertans support separation, a figure she said was still too high.
Smith also faces pressure from separatists within her governing United Conservative Party. Former Premier Jason Kenney said the independence movement gained influence within the party as activists angry over COVID-19 restrictions, some influenced by conspiracy theories, embraced separatism.
But some Albertans who want to remain in Canada are angry with Smith for calling the vote.
“I think it’s a travesty really to be putting our province and our country through this when such a small portion of people are rabble rousing and saying they want to separate from Canada,” said Deb Lee, a retired Calgary resident who voted in advance to remain in Canada.
Smith said Carney had substantially addressed seven of nine federal laws Alberta opposed. She also cited cooperation on a proposed oil pipeline.
Independence advocate Tanya Clemens dismissed the agreements between Carney and Smith as “basically pinky promises” that came with too many conditions.
Carney’s chief political rival, federal Conservative leader Pierre Poilievre, also urged Albertans Friday to remain in Canada.
“Don’t leave your fellow Canadians behind. Lock arms with them,” Poilievre said.
Despite their agreement on keeping Alberta in Canada, Carney and Smith remain divided over nine other questions on Monday’s ballot involving immigration and provincial powers. Smith wants voters to approve them, while Carney has urged their rejection.
“For the first time in a long time, Alberta and Canada are walking together,” Smith said.
