articles.title_orig: How many people in the world identify with a particular religion?
articles.title_zh: How many people in the world identify with a particular religion?
articles.content_orig:
Religious compositions vary a lot from country to country.
In my own country , the United Kingdom, Christianity is the most popular, and following no religion is becoming increasingly common, particularly among young people. But I struggle to get a sense of how these differences stack up globally.
The Pew Research Center publishes estimates of religious affiliation across the world. You can see the global breakdown in the chart for 2020 (the most recent year available). It shows the number of people who identify with each religion. Pew counts people by the religion they report, regardless of their beliefs or practices.
You can see that Christians are the largest group, with 2.3 billion people, followed by Muslims, with 2 billion. People with no religious affiliation come close behind.
Those not affiliated with any religion are among the largest groups in the world. But this undersells religion’s reach: when we add up all religious groups, most people in the world — around three in four — identify with a religion. Those with no religious affiliation are still a minority.
According to the latest data from the World Health Organization, the global death rate from malaria has almost halved since the year 2000.
The chart above puts this recent progress into a larger historical perspective. It combines the latest estimates from the WHO and the Institute for Health Metrics and Evaluation with those for the 20th century published by the late malaria researcher Richard Carter. Since 1900, the global death rate has declined by 96%. If it were still as high as it was then, around 16 million people would die from malaria every year instead of 610,000.
Behind this long-run decline is a shift in the distribution of the burden of malaria. In the first half of the 20th century, most malaria victims died in the Asian tropics. It was the substantial progress there — as well as in the Mediterranean and in the Americas — that made this vast improvement in human health possible.
Today, more than 9 out of 10 malaria deaths occur in Africa. This means that the recent progress shown in the chart is, above all, Africa’s progress.
Hannah Ritchie and Pablo Arriagada
China is often the poster child for rapid reductions in poverty, and for good reason. In the early 1980s, over 90% of its population lived in extreme poverty, but by the early 2020s, that number had dropped to nearly zero.
Some might assume that China is the only reason why global extreme poverty has declined. But that’s wrong : many countries have seen dramatic reductions in poverty, too. Indonesia is one clear example; it’s shown alongside China on the chart.
In 1984, 86% of Indonesians lived on less than $3 per day. By 2025, this had fallen to less than 4%. While it didn’t quite match China’s decline, it has still been impressive. The number of people living in extreme poverty has fallen from 140 million to about 10 million.
Note that the international poverty line is extremely low, defined as people living on less than $3 per day. But Indonesia has also made progress when measuring higher poverty lines .
Many of us will have seen the stark images of plastic in the ocean: bottles and wrappers clumped together, or rubbish trapped along the coastline. But how much of the world’s plastic waste ends up in the ocean?
In 2020, Gapminder asked people in Sweden, Norway, Finland, Denmark, and the UK this question. They had three options to choose from:
Almost nine in ten people picked B or C, thinking it was more than one-third.
The correct answer was A: around 0.5% of plastic waste ends up in the ocean.
The chart shows how the OECD gets to this number. Globally, we produce around 350 million tonnes of plastic waste a year. Most of this is managed responsibly, either in secure landfills, through recycling, or incineration. But around one-quarter of it is mismanaged or littered.
From there, a decreasing fraction of plastic waste leaks to the environment, then into rivers and coastlines, and finally into the ocean. Around 1.7 million tonnes end up there: around 0.5% of what was generated in the first place.
People tend to think that most of our plastic ends up there, but only a tiny percentage does. This should make plastic pollution an easier problem to solve: we already know how to manage most of it well. The challenge is to ensure that all plastic is handled this way.
The new Living Planet Index report has just been published. It estimates an average decline of 73% in studied wildlife populations since 1970. You can see this in the chart.
Every two years, it hits the headlines, and I always have mixed feelings about it.
I love that biodiversity loss gets its rare spot in the limelight. It’s a problem that I think doesn’t get enough attention. The trouble is that journalists often report it incorrectly: either as the number of animals or wildlife lost, the number of species in decline, or the number that have gone extinct.
But it tells us none of that.
It examines changes across nearly 36,000 animal populations and reports the average change. This gets even more complicated because it’s based on a geometric mean, and populations get weighted differently in the final index.
When we look a bit deeper, we see that not all populations are doing poorly. As shown in the chart, around half have declined, while the other half have either increased in abundance or remained stable.
As I explained in a previous article , being able to identify which of these populations is doing particularly badly is crucial if we’re to focus our conservation efforts on where they’re needed most.
In 1950, almost one in four children worldwide died before their fifth birthday. In Africa, one in three children died.
The chart shows the change since then. In every region, the mortality rate of children has declined.
In Africa and Oceania, the child mortality rate declined 5-fold, in Asia 10-fold, and in Europe about 27-fold.
Progress was not always steady. The sharp spike in Asia around 1960 was due to the “Great Leap Forward” famine in Mao’s China, the deadliest famine in recorded history.
And the progress is far from finished. The global average has declined to 3.5%, but this still means that about 4.7 million children younger than five years died in 2025 — 13,000 children every single day.
Globally, electricity generation per person has grown by more than 50% this century.
In the United Kingdom, things have moved in the opposite direction. Its generation per person peaked in 2003 and has fallen by more than a third since then.
You can see this in the chart, which shows generation per person since 1920. Today, levels are back to where they were in the late 1960s.
Some of that decline is a change in electricity imports, rather than demand: net imports have increased from 1% of electricity demand in 2010 to 9% in 2025. But it’s still true that the UK consumes much less electricity than it used to.
The most common explanation is deindustrialization: as the economy shifted from manufacturing to services, electricity demand fell. That’s part of the explanation, but far from all of it.
Sectoral data from the International Energy Agency confirms that electricity consumption in industry has fallen by one-quarter since 2005 (more if we calculate this per person). But residential and commercial electricity use has fallen by just as much.
Deindustrialization has reduced demand, but improvements in energy efficiency — such as the shift from incandescent to LED lightbulbs and the introduction of efficiency standards for appliances — have played an important role too.

articles.title_orig: Evacuation orders issued as wildfire burns in Orange County, California - ABC News
articles.title_zh: Evacuation orders issued as wildfire burns in Orange County, California - ABC News
articles.source: Breaking News, Latest News and Videos
articles.content_orig:
The Norte Fire has damaged or destroyed multiple homes, officials said.
Evacuation orders have been issued for parts of Orange County, California, as firefighters work through the night to contain a fast-spreading fire.
There are some 4,600 hundreds and nearly 16,000 people, in the evacuation zone , according to officials with the Orange County Fire Authority.
The Norte Fire ignited midday Friday in San Clemente and has burned at least 465 acres so far, according to fire officials.
"Due to weather and topography, this fire moved fast," Orange County Fire Authority Fire Chief T.J. McGovern said at a news conference Friday evening, calling the wind "relentless."
The vegetation fire threatened multiple structures, with at least six homes damaged or destroyed so far, officials said. No residents have been injured but two firefighters have been hurt, fire officials said.
"Crews are aggressively attacking the fire from the ground and air. Please continue to avoid the area," the Orange County Fire Authority said.
Several schools in the area were dismissed early on Friday due to the fire "out of an abundance of caution," Capistrano Unified school officials said.
The fire comes amid critical fire weather conditions in the region, including strong Santa Ana winds and high heat.
Red flag warnings are in effect for Los Angeles and Ventura counties and the Antelope Valley foothills through Saturday night.
This fire is burning about 20 miles north of the Henderson Fire at Camp Pendleton in San Diego County, which has burned 2,079 acres.
Some 400 firefighters were working to contain the fire with another 400 en route, officials said.
This is a developing story. Please check back for updates.

articles.title_orig: Malibu wildfire rages, triggering evacuations in Southern California
articles.title_zh: Malibu wildfire rages, triggering evacuations in Southern California
articles.content_orig:
The California Department of Forestry and Fire Protection was busy Friday tracking multiple fires across the state Friday, and the weather will provide little relief over the weekend.
Critical fire conditions are expected to persist as a threatening combination of strong Santa Ana winds, low humidity and dry vegetation will make it more difficult to contain wildfires in the region, Los Angeles County officials said Friday.
In San Diego County, the day-old, 2,080-acre Henderson Fire was burning at Marine Corps Base Camp Pendleton, and, just north of the base, in San Juan Capistrano, was the 465-acre Norte Fire.
A blaze in Malibu known as the Bryson Fire has triggered evacuations in the famed Southern California beach community. It was at 146 acres and was 17% contained Friday evening.
Firefighters worked overnight to suppress the fire, said Lindsey P. Horvath, supervisor of the Los Angeles County’s third district.
“It is still red flag alert,” Horvath said in a news conference Friday morning, adding that such conditions are expected to last at least until Saturday night. “Be vigilant and be prepared.”
Flames from the Henderson Fire at Camp Pendleton on Friday licked the northbound shoulder of Interstate 5 , the main artery between the state’s two largest cities, Los Angeles and San Diego, and prompted the California Highway Patrol to shut it down for more than four hours.
Amtrak’s Pacific Surfliner line between the two cities announced a track closure and warned its customers of “significant delays and/or cancellations” on Friday.
Neighborhoods near Calle Delgado in San Juan Capistrano faced mandatory evacuation orders as the separate-but-nearby Norte fire “continues to grow,” the Orange County Fire Authority said on Friday afternoon.
An estimated 16,000 residents were subjected to mandatory evacuation orders, Orange County Fire Authority Chief TJ McGovern said at an evening news conference about the Norte Fire.
Among them was U.S. Rep. Mike Levin, D-Calif., who said he had to abandon his longtime home in San Juan Capistrano. He thanked firefighters for keeping it standing.
“You saved our entire neighborhood today,” Levin said at the news conference.
Two of the estimated 400 firefighters assigned to the Norte Fire were stabilized at a hospital after sustaining unspecified injuries battling the blaze, McGovern said.
At least six homes have been damaged or destroyed since the fire was reported about 11:30 a.m., he said.
Gov. Gavin Newsom’s office said the state secured a grant from the Federal Emergency Management Agency to help fund the firefight in Orange County. Firefighters and equipment were staged in the county Thursday in anticipation of Friday’s fire weather, it said.
The governor’s office blamed “a significant wind event” for imperiling Southern California communities and fanning the Norte Fire, which is also beset by low humidity and summer-like temperatures.
It warned residents that utilities may shut off power as a precaution intended to avoid live lines sparking wildfires
Federal forecasters said the Norte Fire was thriving in 96-degree temperatures, with offshore winds clocking speeds as great as 30 mph.
The Bryson Fire began just before 5 p.m. Thursday on Encinal Canyon Road’s rugged terrain in the Santa Monica Mountains.
No fatalities and no structure losses or damages have been reported as of Friday morning. Los Angeles County Fire Chief Anthony Marrone said he estimates that more than a hundred structures in the general area of the Bryson Fire are threatened.
At least one firefighter had minor injuries from working to contain the fire Thursday night. That person was transported to a hospital and is expected to recover, Marrone said.
Evacuation orders for the Encinal, Trancas and Zuna Canyon areas have been issued, meaning residents must leave immediately as they face an immediate threat to life and property because of the Bryson Fire .
Over 400 firefighters are continuing to work on containing the Bryson Fire alongside more than 75 “ground and aerial resources,” Marrone said.
Winds from up to 35 mph are expected to heighten fire weather threats in the area, according to the National Weather Service, with gusts forecast to reach up to 70 mph.
These conditions could potentially help spark new fires or allow existing fires to rapidly spread. The risk for fires will be highest on Friday for western Los Angeles County, Ventura County and southeastern Santa Barbara County.
“As wildfires continue to burn faster and push deeper into our built environment, I urge residents to continue to monitor high-risk weather conditions,” Marrone said.
Hours before the Bryson Fire began Thursday, another wildfire erupted in the city of Azusa, located north of Los Angeles.
The Peak Fire burned 43 acres on Thursday and briefly prompted evacuation orders for a neighborhood in the foothills of the San Gabriel mountains. Forward progress on the blaze had been stopped by Thursday night after firefighter managed to contain 41% of it.
Nicole Acevedo is a news reporter for NBC News.
Dennis Romero is a breaking news reporter for NBC News Digital.

articles.title_orig: Verizon Will Charge $10 a Month for iPhone Handoff
articles.title_zh: Verizon Will Charge $10 a Month for iPhone Handoff
articles.content_orig:
Verizon plans to charge customers $10 per month for the iPhone Handoff feature that Apple added in iOS 27 . iPhone Handoff allows one phone number to be shared across two separate iPhones.
Pricing was included in Verizon's iPhone Duo announcement today , with the carrier confirming iPhone Handoff will work with the iPhone Duo and the iPhone 18 Pro models.
Verizon will support iPhone Handoff, giving customers the flexibility to use a single Verizon phone number seamlessly across two compatible iPhone models. Whether using the pocketable iPhone Duo on the go or iPhone 18 Pro for work, customers can switch active status between devices at any time while keeping full access to Verizon's 5G network. iPhone Handoff will be available from Verizon for $10/month on compatible iPhones models running iOS 27.
With iPhone Handoff, users can switch between a main iPhone and a companion iPhone at will, though a phone number can only be active on one iPhone at a time. Verizon says support is "coming soon," and Apple previously said Verizon would adopt the feature before the end of the year.
U.S. carrier T-Mobile already supports iPhone Handoff, but charges just $5 per month for the feature. AT&T, the third major U.S. carrier, recently suggested it has no imminent plans to support iPhone Handoff.
U.K. carrier EE also said this week that it will soon support iPhone Handoff. Customers who have EE's Full Works Plus plan will get iPhone Handoff free, while other EE users can get it for £5 per month.
Deutsche Telekom in Germany is the only other carrier that's added iPhone Handoff support so far. It costs €6.95 per month, but the carrier includes it for free in the MagentaMobil L and XL plans.

articles.title_orig: HP Googlebook 14 Review: Great laptop, shame about the OS
articles.title_zh: HP Googlebook 14 Review: Great laptop, shame about the OS
articles.content_orig:
HP’s first crack at a Googlebook laptop is a winner, or at least as much of one as the platform allows. While Googlebook as an operating system leaves a lot to be desired, the HP Googlebook 14 checks every single box for a fantastic laptop.
Kicking things off with the hardware, HP really has built a very good laptop here.
The design is subtle at a glance, but I appreciate the sharp corners of the underside where the feet hold the laptop up for air circulation. There’s a decent-sized gap in the back for airflow as well which almost feels like a handle when you’re carrying the closed laptop. It’s a far cry from something as flat and edgeless as a MacBook Air, but I’ve really come to like it while using the HP Googlebook 14.
The machine is just 10.9mm thick, and weighs in at 2.74lbs (despite an error that doubles the weight on HP’s website). The aluminum build is sturdy with minimal flex in the deck, and it mostly passes the one-handed opening test.
The keyboard has been a tremendous highlight. Despite the thin design, there’s a ton of travel in this keyboard and it’s wildly comfortable to type on. The keys have a satisfying clack without being too loud to be used in public spaces, and the spacing is great, while the backlight is also perfectly pleasant. It took just a few minutes to feel completely at home typing, though Googlebook’s keyboard shortcuts do take a moment to settle into. The top row of function keys are simple and straightforward for the most part, but the window fullscreen toggle (F4) and screenshot tool (F5) both need better iconography — the screenshot key is incredibly vague.
The trackpad is also quite good. While I still struggle with Google’s premium push on Googlebook’s first wave, I’m glad that haptic trackpads were mandated, though HP’s implementation feels just a tiny bit hollow. The placement of the trackpad going right up to the spacebar might prove troublesome for some users, but I never ran into any issues in my testing period.
As for the display, the 14-inch OLED panel is gorgeous. It’s crisp and colorful, and just bright enough. I’d love if it were a bit brighter for outdoor usage, but it’s perfectly acceptable as long as you’re not in direct sunlight.
Battery life is good enough, though not quite at the level of something like a MacBook Air. That’s a bit of a tough pill to swallow given Googlebook OS’ inherent limitations, but this is a far cry from the dark days of laptop battery life and easily on par with a Snapdragon-powered Windows machine. Standby time is good, and it’s actually quite nice having Android’s typical battery usage stats at the ready. Windows is far behind in this regard. Charging has been very quick and I commend HP for including a charger that feels like it belongs in this decade, though I typically stuck with whatever USB-C chargers I had at the ready both in at-home use and on a recent trip.
Performance on the Snapdragon X Elite with 16GB of RAM is unsurprisingly excellent. Seeing as Googlebook is built on Android, it’s a clear formula for a speedy machine. While I’ve absolutely run into my fair share of hiccups here or there, boot times are near-instant, and the overall performance is impossible to complain about.
HP Googlebook 14 has every piece of a great laptop, but sadly it all comes down to the software, and Googlebook is a drag on this machine.
Our Abner Li has already delivered a pretty in-depth review of Googlebook OS as a whole, so this is basically my own personal addendum on that.
My view of Googlebook is that, frankly, it seems a bit pointless in this day and age. Google has rebuilt ChromeOS on top of a new foundation that, yes, presents more possibility for the future, but also fixes virtually none of the existing problems. Like ChromeOS, Googlebook has an incredibly limited library of desktop-class software, even more so given that Linux support has regressed tremendously. One could point at obvious examples like the Adobe suite here, but it really comes down to the niche apps and tools that have been built out for Windows, macOS, and Linux for decades now. That’s an impossible task for any new platform to deal with, but Googlebook feels as though it is actively ignoring that clear gap in functionality. As mentioned, Linux app support has been largely decimated, which was a major boon to the app situation on ChromeOS. There’s also no way to emulate apps for other platforms here, which would be another good way to meet the needs of users not satisfied by what can be found on the Play Store or the web. Google literally has the tools to do this and, yet, none of them can be found here.
In launching this platform, Google’s repeated line about who this is for is “it’s a laptop for Android users.” I’m absolutely sick of hearing that. It’s utterly meaningless.
In a smartphone-dominated society, smartphones are the tentpole. Yes, you want integration between devices, but you’re not buying a laptop for smartphone integration. You buy a laptop to do the things that your phone can’t, and Googlebook can’t really do much more than your phone, at least not yet.
HP did a great job building out a very good laptop for Googlebook. The hardware is just let down by the software. You’d have a much better time using this laptop with Windows or even Linux compared to Googlebook right now. Especially at a time when the cost of laptops continues to skyrocket, I cannot recommend that anyone invests $1,200 into a Googlebook when you can get a Windows laptop, or even a MacBook, for the same price, if not less. There’s simply no reason to get less functionality for the same price. Fast-forward to when Googlebook is available on less expensive hardware and it might be a different story, but right now, eh .

articles.title_orig: Stock Market Today: Nasdaq Faces Weekly Loss on Tech Stock Slump — Live Updates
articles.title_zh: Stock Market Today: Nasdaq Faces Weekly Loss on Tech Stock Slump — Live Updates
articles.content_orig:
Stocks slid on Friday as traders notched a mostly losing week amid a shift away from tech and artificial intelligence-related names as well as a rise in oil prices.
The S&P 500 lost 1.09% and ended at 7,659.44, while the Nasdaq Composite shed 2.14% to close at 26,140.03. Both indexes ended the session below their 50-day moving averages. The Dow Jones Industrial Average fell 175.28 points, or 0.34%, to 52,002.41. The sell-off sent the Cboe Volatility Index (VIX) above 22 for the first time in four months .
Chipmakers were lower again. The VanEck Semiconductor ETF (SMH) lost 3%, led by declines in Micron Technology , Advanced Micro Devices and Sandisk . Semiconductors have struggled this week amid jitters about competition from China . The SMH slid 10% week to date for its biggest weekly decline since April 2025.
Those declines, coupled with drops in other stocks linked to AI, dragged the S&P 500 to a losing week. The benchmark index fell about 2% this week, while the Nasdaq shed more than 4% for its worst week since June. The Dow, on the other hand, advanced 0.7% on the week.
Investors have also grown concerned that tech companies are borrowing too much for the AI buildout . Shares of neoclouds like CoreWeave , which has seen its total debt rise to more than $51 billion , were down nearly 12%, bringing the stock's week-to-date losses to 25%.
"The question is: Is this a systemic issue?" said Michael Rosen, Angeles' chief investment officer. "Obviously, increased debt issuance is something to observe and continue to watch and be concerned about if it continues to get to levels of excessiveness. But we're not remotely close to that right now."
Other areas of the market such as energy saw gains Friday, with stocks like Chevron helping to keep the Dow's losses in check. Oil prices moved higher amid rising tensions between the U.S. and Iran as well as between Russian and Ukraine. West Texas Intermediate crude futures increased 3.51% to settle at $101.41 per barrel, while Brent crude futures advanced 3.72% to $109.86.
Simultaneously, investors have been grappling with hotter-than-expected inflation data, which has been exacerbated by elevated energy prices in the wake of the U.S.-Iran war. Wholesale inflation this week saw its biggest gain since 2022 , while consumer inflation remained well above the Federal Reserve's target of 2%.
Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh spoke at an IMF event in Bangkok overnight. And while he didn't comment on whether the Fed would raise rates before year-end, traders took that as a sign that the central bank will hold policy steady later this month. The CME Group's FedWatch tool points to an 82% chance the Fed keeps its overnight rate unchanged at its Oct. 27-28 meeting.
The three leading U.S. indexes ended Friday's session with losses.
The S&P 500 dropped 1.09% to finish at 7,659.44, while the Nasdaq Composite lost 2.14% to 26,140.03. The Dow Jones Industrial Average shed 175.28 points, or 0.34%, to 52,002.41.
As the market sell-off intensified Friday afternoon, the Cboe Volatility Index (VIX) rose to levels it last closed at four months ago.
The VIX rose to 21.32, as of 3:10 p.m., rising more than 4.8 points on the session. It's on pace for its highest close since June 10, when it closed at 22.22.
Typically, when the VIX is above 20 that indicates greater fear in the market. The index last closed above that level on July 29 , when markets fell after the Federal Reserve kept interest rates steady at its meeting that month. The next day , stocks rose, and the day marked a bottom in a market where many AI-related stocks had been selling off in the previous month .
The Nasdaq Composite was down about 2.5% in afternoon trading on Friday, bringing its loss on the week to almost 5%.
With that move, the tech-heavy index on pace for its worst weekly performance since the week ended April 4, 2025, when the index recorded a roughly 10% drop.
Communication services and information technology led the S&P 500 lower on Friday.
The two sectors were down 2.7% and 2.4%, respectively, becoming the two biggest laggards among the 11 S&P 500 sectors. Consumer discretionary followed behind them, falling 1.5%.
However, a look beneath the surface showed that the S&P 500 — which was last down 1.3% — was more evenly split despite the losses at the index level. There were about 280 losers in the index and 222 gainers.
In total, five out of the 11 S&P 500 sectors were in positive territory, led by energy with its 2.1% gain and utilities with its rise of 1.2%.
— Sean Conlon and Sarah Min
U.S. crude oil prices rose sharply Friday as Iran escalated its attacks in the Strait of Hormuz this week and Ukraine vowed to keep striking Russian refineries.
U.S. West Texas Intermediate futures were up 2.9% to $100.78 per barrel. Brent crude, the international benchmark, was 3.3% higher at $109.37 per barrel. Read more .
Here are the stocks making moves in midday trading:
Early in the "SaaSpocalypse" that roiled software companies this year, Manish Gupta, a portfolio manager at First Eagle Investments, added to Workday as he parsed through the wreckage for some bargains.
In recent months, that bet has paid off for the value investor. After falling about 40% in the first quarter of 2026, during which the enterprise software stock at various points was trading at not even three times revenue, the stock went on to surge more than 55% in the third. It's also outperforming this week, rising more than 2% amid a broader tech sell-off as investors exit for safer assets.

articles.title_orig: DHS Secretary Mullin calls Ilhan Omar probe a "strong case," says agents executed multiple search warrants
articles.title_zh: DHS Secretary Mullin calls Ilhan Omar probe a "strong case," says agents executed multiple search warrants
articles.content_orig:
Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said federal agents executed multiple search warrants on the same day they searched Democratic Rep. Ilhan Omar's Washington home. While appearing on a podcast Friday, Mullin described the ongoing investigation as a "strong case" while suggesting cases of coordinated immigration fraud could be prosecuted under federal racketeering laws.
In an interview with Andrew Kolvet, who hosts the "Charlie Kirk Show," Mullin volunteered that multiple warrants had been served on Monday, adding that a judge had authorized the enforcement action and that investigators expected to present their case to a grand jury.
Omar has not been charged with a crime. She has called the investigation politically motivated.
"She wasn't – or it wasn't the only place we served the warrant," Mullin said, referencing the D.C. residence of the Minnesota congresswoman. "There was multiple other warrants served on that same day."
"We had a judge sign it, and we expect to be able to take the case to a grand jury," Mullin said, revealing new details about the scope of the operation. "But I will tell you, we wouldn't move forward, and President Trump didn't want to move forward either, unless we knew that it couldn't be politically driven. Now they want to try making it political driven. This individual wants to try making it about themselves. This was about enforcing once again our nation's laws, and it's a strong case."
President Trump previously stated he didn't know anything about the investigation, which is being handled by DHS' Homeland Security Investigations division and the Justice Department. Asked about the Omar probe on Monday, Mr. Trump told reporters: "I think she's a terrible person, but that's really up to the DOJ."
Mullin's remarks came amid a federal investigation into possible fraud involving immigration documents submitted by Omar's family decades ago. The documents in question date back to Omar's childhood, involving paperwork completed by her late father when she was a child, CBS News reported earlier this week . Multiple relatives of Omar received grand jury subpoenas as part of the investigation, and the lawmaker's personal cellphone was taken by DHS, sources told CBS News.
During the interview, Kolvet also asked Mullin about a hypothetical scenario involving a former foreign warlord who entered the United States as a refugee with his daughter. Mullin did not establish that the circumstances applied to Omar's family. But the DHS secretary did use the hypothetical to suggest that those who submit fraudulent immigration documents and enable others to enter the country under the same purported scheme could very well be prosecuted under U.S. law.
Such conduct, he said, could potentially constitute a violation of the Racketeer Influenced and Corrupt Organizations Act, or RICO, a federal law used to prosecute organized criminal enterprises.
"If someone … fills out their paperwork illegally, and they claim that they are this person and this is their background, and then underneath that individual, a lot of other people come in. And I'm just saying hypothetically across a whole bunch of cases that's out there, then that can be considered a RICO case, right?" the DHS secretary offered. "Because there was conspiracy to deceive the American government, and therefore everything else that came in with it could then be looked at [part of] the same case."
Mullin suggested that a racketeering prosecution could allow investigators to examine conduct extending back decades, arguing that statutes of limitations generally would not apply to such cases.
Under federal law, criminal RICO prosecutions are generally subject to a five-year statute of limitations, although in certain cases prosecutors can incorporate older acts into a timely prosecution involving an ongoing criminal enterprise or conspiracy.
In Grunewald v. United States, the Supreme Court held in 1957 that prosecutors cannot indefinitely extend a conspiracy simply because perpetrators covered it up after it ended.
Mullin did not explicitly indicate that prosecutors were pursuing RICO charges against Omar. But his remarks did suggest investigators are considering whether alleged immigration violations could be examined as part of a broader conspiracy rather than simply as isolated offenses. He said Homeland Security Investigations (HSI) agents had worked closely with the Justice Department to build out the case.
It is unusual for federal officials to speak openly about ongoing criminal investigations beyond confirming that a court-authorized search was conducted, in part due to due process protections and grand jury secrecy rules.
CBS News has reached out to Omar's attorney for comment.
Earlier this week, Omar — a staunch Trump critic who has drawn the president's ire for years — denied all wrongdoing and said she "will not be silenced."
"Make no mistake: this is an attempt to target political enemies and weaponize federal law enforcement," she wrote on X . "For ten years, Trump has targeted me with baseless lies and smear campaigns. This is just the latest escalation in his campaign of political intimidation."
Sarah N. Lynch contributed to this report.

articles.title_orig: Pope pictured for first time since surgery and cancer diagnosis
articles.title_zh: Pope pictured for first time since surgery and cancer diagnosis
articles.content_orig:
Pope Leo XIV has been pictured celebrating Mass from hospital, in the first images of him released by the Vatican since he underwent lung surgery.
The 71-year-old pontiff was diagnosed with lung cancer after the operation, which the Vatican said had been "successful" and proceeded without complications, at Rome's Gemelli Hospital on Tuesday afternoon.
The images shared on Friday showed the Chicago-born Pope wearing green vestments while standing behind a makeshift altar on the tenth floor of the hospital.
The head of the Roman Catholic Church "celebrated with the medical and nursing staff" and thanked workers for their service, the Vatican press office said.
Also on Friday, the Pope phoned Russian President Vladimir Putin from hospital to urge a ceasefire in the Russian-occupied Ukrainian city of Oleshky, where access to food and water has been cut off for thousands .
"The fact that he accepted the call and spoke with the Pope may, I hope, be a sign that the Pope's request will indeed be carried out," said Cardinal Pietro Parolin, the Vatican's secretary of state.
Without mentioning a ceasefire, the Kremlin said: "The Vatican's intention to help create the conditions necessary to ensure the safety of the town's population and to organise vital supplies has been supported."
It added: "It has been agreed to co-operate on this matter."
The UN high commissioner for human rights, Volker Turk, made a similar plea to address what he described as a "desperate" situation in Oleshky.
The Pope's doctors said on Friday that tests had shown "a steady improvement in his general condition" since his surgery.
His doctors said that a chest X-ray indicated "good recovery of the operated lung".
The whole lower lobe of the Pope's right lung was removed "to ensure the procedure was radical", the Vatican said following the surgery.
"After the operation, the Pope awoke normally and returned after a brief period of observation to his room," it said earlier, before he spent a "peaceful night" at the hospital.
The pontiff first announced that he would be having the operation during his weekly Sunday prayers, telling the crowd in St Peter's Square that doctors had found a "well-contained" nodule on his lung "at an early stage" and advised him to have it removed.
Nodules are quite common and not necessarily cancerous, but after it was examined the medical team confirmed it was, "as suspected by pre-operative tests", the Vatican said. He was diagnosed with lung adenocarcinoma.
The Vatican has stressed that the Pope had shown no symptoms of infection or illness prior to the procedure.
Additional reporting by Joel Guinto

articles.title_orig: Astronomer leads global team on NASA mission to create unprecedented view of the early universe
articles.title_zh: Astronomer leads global team on NASA mission to create unprecedented view of the early universe
articles.content_orig:
The Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope blog is NASA's hub for the mission's launch updates, where all are invited for behind-the-scenes looks on Roman's road to launch and beyond. This flagship mission’s vast, deep surveys will help astronomers explore dark matter, dark energy, exoplanets, and almost anything from our own solar system to galaxies at the edge of the observable universe. Follow along to join in on the excitement!
NASA’s Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope team completed a marathon of activities to fine-tune the observatory’s vision and prepare the primary instrument for routine use.
“All of Roman’s sweeping surveys will rely on the Wide Field Instrument,” said Dave Hickey, a Wide Field Instrument systems engineer at NASA’s Goddard Space Flight Center in Greenbelt, Maryland. “Many of the mission’s primary goals, like studying dark matter and dark energy, wouldn’t be possible without it, so it’s both exciting and a huge relief to see that it’s working well!”
Since the Wide Field Instrument was activated in September , the Roman team has been running it through a series of tests to exercise its components both individually and together. They started by checking out the 18 sticky note-sized detectors and all of their electronics before moving to the element wheel, a mechanism containing filters and other tools to pass specific wavelengths of light to the detectors and disperse light into its individual colors.
Then engineers turned on all of the internal LEDs in the calibration system, which are like precisely dimmable lights of various colors engineers control from the ground. These components are designed to measure how the detectors respond to different light levels and correct for any variations in their sensitivity.
The team tested the alignment mechanism, then deployed it to its predicted best focus position from the out-of-focus position it was stowed in for launch. Finally, engineers put the thermal system through its paces, ensuring it will keep the instrument’s various components at the proper temperatures.
“Calibrating an instrument is like tuning a piano or guitar before a concert,” said Maxime Rizzo, a Wide Field Instrument systems engineer at NASA Goddard. “You adjust everything until it’s just how you want it and then leave the settings alone so it performs consistently while you use it.”
Meanwhile, another team worked on sharpening the telescope’s focus.
“The telescope’s performance was excellent even before we began adjusting the alignment of all the mirrors and other optics, thanks to exceptional preparatory work done on the ground prior to launch,” said Matthew Bolcar, Roman’s optical systems lead at NASA Goddard. “All of the testing and modeling work done at Goddard and by contractors at L3Harris and BAE Space and Mission Systems left only small corrections for us to make to bring everything into near-perfect alignment.”
That precision is significant because it’s difficult to anticipate exactly how things will shift during launch and in space. Roman launched on Aug. 30 .
“Our ground testing couldn’t exactly reproduce the environment Roman would experience in space, such as the absence of gravity,” Bolcar said. “And there are also slight differences in temperature variations and moisture content. Despite those challenges, the recent assessments showed that our ground testing was excellent, with both instruments either matching or exceeding the performance we had predicted.”
When cosmic light enters the telescope, it bounces around between mirrors and other optics in a carefully choreographed way. Everything must be extremely precisely aligned to focus the light and direct it to Roman’s two instruments.
Since the optics were already arranged near perfectly, the team only had to make miniscule adjustments.
“We moved the secondary mirror by about one-sixteenth of the diameter of a human hair,” said Alden Jurling, a senior optical engineer working on Roman at NASA Goddard. “This adjustment nudged the height of the secondary mirror above the primary. If we scale that height up to the height of the empire state building, the change in height is a little bit less than you would get by stacking a single U.S. penny on top of the tip of the tower.”
This microscopic modification could have a big impact on the mission’s science.
Initially, the Coronagraph Instrument’s images were slightly out of focus, though not to the degree the team had anticipated, which was relatively simple to correct. Now the instrument’s performance meets the team’s high expectations. The Coronagraph Instrument team will continue to calibrate its camera settings and determine the best settings for its deformable mirrors before they attempt to demonstrate its light-blocking capabilities in the coming weeks.
After fine-tuning the Coronagraph Instrument’s focus, the team moved on to the Wide Field Instrument to make another round of adjustments.
Now, the Wide Field Instrument’s performance is nearly 30% better than the Roman team predicted. The requirement for image quality was set at about 90 nanometers RMS (Root Mean Square), which means the optics only deviate from absolute perfection by 90 nanometers — that’s around 1,000 times thinner than a human hair.
The team did even better: After applying corrections, the Wide Field Instrument’s optics have an error of just 63 nanometers RMS.
“All of the images from Roman’s cosmic surveys will be even sharper than we expected,” Jurling said. “It’s a great outcome from years of careful modeling, precision metrology, and testing.”

articles.title_orig: Apple’s updated App Store rules go after ‘nudify’ AI apps
articles.title_zh: Apple’s updated App Store rules go after ‘nudify’ AI apps
articles.content_orig:
The terms more explicitly ban apps that create ‘nonconsensual intimate imagery.’﻿
The terms more explicitly ban apps that create ‘nonconsensual intimate imagery.’﻿
Apple’s App Store rules now more explicitly ban so-called “nudify” apps that generate intimate images of people without their consent using AI tools.
The rule changes follow significant criticism toward Apple after X users used Grok earlier this year to make nonconsensual, sexualized deepfakes, including minors . Apple didn’t pull X or Grok from the App Store, though it told senators that it threatened to yank Grok . At Apple’s WWDC event in June, protestors also called on Apple to “remove Grok, X, and all nudify technology from the App Store,” and in July, a San Francisco city attorney ordered Apple to remove 13 “nudify” apps, which it said it did .
As part of updates announced Friday , Apple says that developers “must proactively prevent and remove” nonconsensual, sexual images as part of its content moderation requirements for App Store apps. Developers who “fail to implement adequate safeguards” or “don’t remedy violations after notice” may be removed from the App Store. Apple also clarified a rule that bars “bait-and-switch” apps, or apps that add or change features, including “nudification,” after they have been approved.
Apple’s rules also more clearly spell out that any apps that “facilitate human trafficking or the exploitation of children” will be pulled from the App Store and “blocked from alternative distribution.”

Police say a 16-year-old former student carried out the attack that killed three children and a teacher in a special needs classroom.
• Community in mourning: Police say a 16-year-old gunman killed three children and a teacher Thursday at Silver Rail Elementary School in Bend, Oregon. Another child and teacher were hospitalized. All the victims were shot in one special needs classroom , police said.
• Heroic actions: A father of two students saw the gunman and followed him into the school, fatally shooting him to stop the attack, officials said. Police commended the man’s heroism and the actions of a teacher who tackled the shooter and fought to disarm him.
• What we know about the shooter: The teen previously attended special needs classes at Silver Rail, according to investigators. Authorities have searched the gunman’s home but a potential motive remains under investigation. “I’m so sorry,” the boy’s mother told CNN .
• Grim total: This is the 36th shooting on K-12 school grounds across the United States this year, according to a CNN data analysis.
A 7-year-old girl and a 54-year-old teacher are receiving treatment at local hospitals after being critically injured at the school shooting in Bend, Oregon, police said today.
The child, who has not been identified, had received first aid at the scene and is now in “serious but stable condition” at Oregon Health & Science University Hospital, Bend Police Chief Mike Krantz said at a news conference today.
The educational assistant in the special education department, identified as Becky Drury , suffered “serious but non-life-threatening injuries” and is being hospitalized at St. Charles Bend, Krantz said.
Three children and a teacher were killed in the shooting Thursday, according to authorities.
Megan Lambert, a 25-year-old teacher who was killed in the Silver Rail Elementary School shooting yesterday, “loved those children” and being an educator, her family said in a statement.
“Her goal was to be an educator and teach in the school district she loved growing up in,” the family said in a statement read at a news conference today.
The family described her as a “compassionate” person with a “huge heart” who “always fought for the underdog and those with special needs.”
Lambert was an Oregon native who grew up in Bend, graduated from Mountain View High School in 2019 and from Boise State in 2023, her family said. She also traveled to Barcelona, Spain, for an English teacher training school. She was a substitute teacher at Silver Rail before becoming a full-time teacher there.
“She loved Silver Rail; this was her dream job,” the family said.
Lambert was passionate about sports and had been a volleyball coach, her family said. She turned down pay her first season as a coach to help families who couldn’t afford to participate.
Lambert’s family says she was “funny and opinionated, and she lit up the room.”
Police and school officials just gave an update on the latest information from their investigation into the shooting at Silver Rail Elementary School, which left at least three kids and one teacher dead.
Big questions still remain, including any potential motive.
CNN’s Emma Tucker, Maria Aguilar Prieto, Andi Babineau, Dalia Faheid and John Miller contributed reporting.
The teenager who opened fire at Silver Rail Elementary School on Thursday, killing three students and a teacher inside a single classroom, has been identified as Griffin J. John II, Bend Police Chief Mike Krantz announced at a news conference Friday.
The shooter used a Maverick 88 pump-action 12-gauge shotgun in the attack, Krantz said. The gun had been purchased by his mother, a senior law enforcement official briefed on the investigation told CNN earlier Friday.
He had about 44 remaining rounds of 12-gage ammunition, Krantz said.
The shooter had approached the campus, dropped the shotgun over a fence, then climbed over and forced his way into the building, opening fire inside the classroom, according to Krantz.
The shooter’s mother spoke to CNN off camera from her balcony, but would not comment on how her son got access to the weapon. Investigators say that is still under investigation.
“I miss my boy. I’m so sorry,” the woman said as she cried and smoked a cigarette.
And in a message to the families of those killed, she said, “I’m so sorry, I wish I could have done something. I’m sorry for their loss.”
The shooter’s parents were interviewed on Thursday and were cooperative with investigators, the official told CNN earlier Friday. The teen had attended the elementary school, though no clear motive for the shooting has been uncovered, authorities said Friday.
The shooter was previously a special needs student at the school and the shooting occurred in the special needs classroom, Bend-La Pine Schools Superintendent Steven Cook said. During the pandemic, his mother spoke with CNN affiliate KTVZ about how she hopes the in-person classes for special needs kids will resume. The program is described as being for kids with “intensive behavioral and social skills challenges.”
CNN has reached out to the program for comment.
A search warrant was executed on the shooter’s home Thursday, with investigators recovering computers and other electronic devices. Additional warrants have been obtained to retrieve data from the devices, according to the source.
CNN’s Nick Watt and Norma Galeana contributed reporting.
The teacher who was shot and injured at Silver Rail Elementary in Bend, Oregon, yesterday has been identified as Becky Drury, 54, an educational assistant in the special education department, family spokesperson Zack Hall said.
“We are incredibly grateful for the outpouring of support, prayers, and well-wishes following yesterday’s tragedy at Silver Rail Elementary,” Drury’s husband, Will Drury, said in a statement.
The family asked for privacy and is declining interviews at this time, according to the statement and the family spokesperson.
“We ask that you continue to hold everyone affected by this tragedy in your thoughts,” the statement concluded.
It is not yet clear why the shooter was able to bypass security measures at Silver Rail Elementary School before the deadly shooting, the district’s superintendent said.
Bend-La Pine Schools Superintendent Steven Cook told reporters he couldn’t say “with confidence” how the gunman got through the doors, but the district is going to do “a lot of reviewing of our procedures.”
All schools in the Bend-La Pine Schools district are equipped with “secure vestibules” at the entrance of each of its buildings and a classroom door locking system, according to the school district’s website .
But Chief Mike Krantz of the Bend Police Department said during today’s news conference that the shooter was able to breach the building by shooting multiple rounds into glass panes in an external set of double doors.

articles.title_orig: Oregon school shooter identified, used shotgun bought by mother, sources say
articles.title_zh: Oregon school shooter identified, used shotgun bought by mother, sources say
articles.content_orig:
The 16-year-old gunman who shot and killed three children and one 25-year-old teacher at Silver Rail Elementary School in Bend, Oregon, on Thursday has been identified as Griffin J. John II, Bend's police chief announced in a news conference Friday.
Authorities said he was shot and killed by a bystander at the school. The suspect was a former student of Silver Rail Elementary, police said.
The attacker used a shotgun purchased by his mother, law enforcement sources told CBS News. Bend Police Chief Mike Krantz said Friday that a Maverick 88 pump-action 12-gauge shotgun was located near the suspect, as well as a backpack. Krantz said that three types of ammunition were used in the shooting: birdshot, buckshot and slugs.
The suspect fired as many as 15 rounds during the shooting, Krantz said Friday, and another 44 remaining rounds of ammunition were located at the scene.
A motive for the attack has not been provided. Bend-La Pine Schools Superintendent Steven Cook said in Friday's news conference that the classroom where the shooting occurred was a special needs classroom, and he disclosed that the suspect had been a special needs student at that school.
In 2020, the suspect's mother, Shauntai Nickerson, spoke to a local television station about her then-10-year-old son, who she said had special needs and struggled to learn from home during the pandemic.
Krantz said the suspect approached the fence of the school on foot, threw the shotgun over the fence, and then climbed it himself.
When he was confronted by a man who was passing in a pickup truck, he fired on the truck, striking it at least three times, Krantz said. That driver then drove on and made the initial 911 call.
It was at that time that the bystander who would later kill the suspect, a 36-year-old man whose children attend the school, witnessed that shooting and drove into the school parking lot.
Krantz said that the suspect forced his way into the school by firing several rounds into the glass panes of a set of double doors. He then went directly into the classroom immediately to the left of those doors, where he opened fire.
"All of the victims were shot in that classroom," Krantz said.
Krantz told reporters Friday that the bystander, who was identified by his family as Kaylub Giamanco, took from his vehicle a .40-caliber pistol which he legally owned, and entered the school and classroom where the shooting was taking place.
"As he made entry through the forced open doors, he heard shooting and saw a teacher involved in a physical altercation with the suspect," Krantz said. "He then went to the classroom where the struggle was underway and fired his weapon, striking the suspect multiple times."
Krantz also praised the "heroic actions" of the teacher who engaged the suspect in the physical struggle, saying she "threw her cellphone at the suspect and then tackled him and fought to take the firearm from him."
That teacher, who was not hurt, "almost certainly helped prevent more bloodshed," Krantz said.
Law enforcement sources told CBS News that investigators are combing through his computer, phone, social media, search history and other online activity. They are probing whether the shooter may have been obsessed with violence, including prior mass shootings. The sources emphasized that the investigators are in the preliminary stages of their investigation.
The children killed in the shooting were ages 5, 8 and 11, Krantz said. The 5-year-old victim was identified by police and her family as Rhoam Summer. Bend police identified the 25-year-old teacher killed as Meghan Lambert. The families of the two other children have not made their names public, Bend police said.
Two others — a 7-year-old girl and a 54-year-old teacher — were wounded. The 7-year-old girl was being treated at Oregon Health & Science University in Portland, where she was in serious but stable condition, Krantz said Friday. The teacher, identified to CBS News by her family as Becky Drury, suffered serious but non-life-threatening injuries, Krantz said. She was being treated at St. Charles Medical Center.
The family of Giamanco, a Bend resident with two daughters who attend Silver Rail Elementary School, issued a statement Friday, in which they said Giamanco "is not seeking recognition, but instead wishes to express his gratitude to the first responders, school personnel, and community for the outpouring of love and support."
Police said they responded within minutes to the 911 calls from the school and found the deceased shooter and other victims inside.
Rhona  Tarrant contributed to this report.

CoreWeave (CRWV) stock plunged 12% on Oct. 16, putting the AI infrastructure company on track to finish the week down 25% as concerns over AI funding continued to weigh on market sentiment.
Earlier this week, Bloomberg reported a sharp rise in CoreWeave's bond yields, raising questions about whether the company can generate enough cash flow to support its rapid expansion.
CoreWeave's bond yields climbed to around 15%, while the cost of insuring its five-year debt against default rose by as much as 74.5 basis points to 1,194.5 basis points, an all-time intraday high, according to Bloomberg. That could mean odds of more than 60% that CoreWeave would default sometime in the next five years.
CoreWeave has been spending heavily on data centers and Nvidia (NVDA) chips to meet soaring demand for AI computing power.
The company has secured major contracts with AI developers and technology companies, but building the infrastructure needed to fulfill those agreements requires substantial upfront investment.
The Friday, Oct. 16, decline came after CoreWeave stock rebounded the prior day, following comments from Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang that helped ease some concerns.
"CoreWeave's strength is improving every day," Huang said at a Bloomberg event in Stockholm. "I'm optimistic. Their cost of capital is actually decreasing."
Nvidia holds roughly 47.2 million shares of CoreWeave, representing about a 10% stake in the company. CoreWeave is also a major customer of Nvidia's chips.
However, Huang's reassurance failed to sustain the rebound.
Peer Nebius (NBIS), another company investing heavily in AI computing infrastructure, dropped about 12% on Oct. 16 and was also headed for weekly losses. Nvidia also invests in Nebius.
Also read: Dell stock price tumbles 6.8% after epic 271% run
In August, CoreWeave reported second-quarter results that topped Wall Street expectations.
The company posted an adjusted loss of $1.03 per share, narrower than the $1.20 loss analysts expected. Revenue came in at $2.58 billion, up 112% from a year earlier and above the $2.56 billion estimated by Wall Street.
For the third quarter, CoreWeave guided for revenue of $3.4 billion to $3.6 billion, implying 158% growth at the midpoint. Analysts surveyed had expected $3.43 billion, CNBC reported.
CoreWeave also reported a revenue backlog of more than $100 billion. That means it hasn't earned that money yet.
Despite the recent sell-off, Cantor Fitzgerald analyst Brett Knoblauch believes investors are focusing too heavily on CoreWeave's debt and overlooking its improving business fundamentals.
In a research note, Knoblauch said CoreWeave's debt-yield spike reflects concerns about financing massive AI capital expenditures rather than weakening demand, according to StockTwits , citing The Fly.
Also read: Micron stock tumbles despite analyst calls semiconductor sell-off
Knoblauch said demand remains strong, with nearly all of CoreWeave's 2027 capacity already sold and Nvidia providing a backstop for unsold capacity. He also pointed to improving economics, including rising revenue per megawatt and contribution margins, which have shortened the payback period for AI chips to 2-2.5 years.
Knoblauch believes improving unit economics and asset-backed financing can help CoreWeave sustain its rapid growth, despite concerns about borrowing costs.
Cantor Fitzgerald maintained its overweight rating and $176 price target on CoreWeave shares, recommending that investors buy the dip.
CoreWeave stock trades at around $61 as of writing.

articles.title_orig: How China Has Quietly Taken a Lead in International Agency Staffing
articles.title_zh: How China Has Quietly Taken a Lead in International Agency Staffing
articles.content_orig:
The front of the World Health Organization building in Geneva, Switzerland, on December 3, 2019. China has sought to staff the middle ranks of the international civil service, write Mike  Kuiken and Leland Miller. (Shutterstock/Diego Grandi)
Since 2020, the US-China Economic and Security Review Commission has published a ledger of Chinese citizens holding senior positions across the international system, agency by agency, and the April 2026 edition lists five at the International Seabed Authority (ISA), an institution few Americans have even heard of. Under the World Health Organization ( WHO ), which everyone has heard of, it lists none.
Earlier this month, Beijing nominated Song Li, a National Health Commission official who has spent years on WHO technical committees, for the post of WHO director-general. This leadership contest is only one part of China ’s effort to shape international institutions. Across international institutions, Beijing is seeking to fill middle- and senior-level posts where officials (whose tenures often outlast leadership terms) draft standards, interpret procedures, process applications, and shape the choices that reach leadership for approval. Washington counts Beijing’s people at the top. The more consequential question is who holds the pen underneath.
In Kingston, Jamaica, the official who runs the office that processes applications to mine the deep ocean floor is Yongsheng Cai , a former Chinese foreign ministry official. He sits at the International Seabed Authority , which regulates mining on the half of the planet’s seabed that lies beyond any nation’s jurisdiction, and applications to explore and eventually extract the metals that go into electric-vehicle batteries cross his desk before they reach anyone else. He is one of five Beijing-aligned appointees in senior staff and oversight posts at the authority, and none of them arrived there by accident.
For years Washington has measured Chinese influence by the top jobs, and by that measure Beijing peaked in 2020 , when Chinese officials ran four United Nations agencies at once: food and agriculture, telecommunications, civil aviation, and industrial development. By 2023 , they had left three of those four top jobs, with only Qu Dongyu winning a second term at the Food and Agriculture Organization. Beijing’s candidate also lost the 2020 race for the World Intellectual Property Organization leadership. At Interpol, China’s candidate, Meng Hongwei, won the presidency in 2016; Beijing summoned him home two years later and imprisoned him (his resignation letter arrived from custody).
That run of departures may seem like proof that Beijing is in retreat. But it obscures an influence strategy that has been underway beneath the agency heads. Beijing’s influence in that layer persists through leadership changes, even as its WHO bid signals renewed ambition for the top jobs—just when Washington has walked away from the table.
Plenty of serious people in Washington, in both parties, regard these institutions as sluggish, politically captured, and venues for anti-American speeches. They are not wrong. However, the institutions exist anyway, and they decide who mines the seabed, who gets which radio frequencies, and how international trademark-registration systems operate, whether or not the United States is in the room. Every American city has a zoning board that will rule on the building next door whether or not you show up, and the people who do show up write the rules.
In intellectual property, Binying Wang , the Chinese nominee who lost the 2020 contest for Director General of the World Intellectual Property Organization (WIPO), remained deputy director general for its brands and designs sector for years afterward. WIPO’s current leadership listing identifies her successor as Shen Changyu , who ran China’s patent and trademark office for 12 years. The individual has changed; Chinese representation in the portfolio that administers the international trademark and design-registration systems has continued.
In civilian technology, the Standardization Administration of China serves as the secretariat for 95 Technical Committees and subcommittees of the International Organization for Standardization, including the one drafting global standards for brain-computer interfaces. These systems connect brain activity to computers. Technical standards bodies may sound obscure, but the point is simple: standards built around a country’s existing technologies can give its companies a head start, leaving competitors to adapt their products.
The International Telecommunication Union ( ITU ) coordinates international use of the electromagnetic spectrum, the radio waves that carry everything from cell signals to satellite internet, and the Commission’s April 2026 ledger lists no Chinese citizen in its General Secretariat, which again looks like a retreat until you check the layer below. Witnesses at the Commission’s April 2025 hearing on China’s space program cited Chinese filings covering more than 74,000 low-earth-orbit satellites. Every one of those filings has to clear the union’s coordination rules, which are written by consensus at its conferences and interpreted by a twelve-member board, so whoever controls the room and the board controls the orbits. They described Beijing’s practice of flooding union and World Radiocommunication Conference sessions with enough personnel to overwhelm consensus.
For the telecommunications union’s elections in Doha this November, Beijing has nominated Cheng Jianjun , an executive vice president of China Mobile, for another term on the 12-member Radio Regulations Board , which interprets the Radio Regulations and handles associated disputes. A government able to send more people than anyone else to handle problems such as these does not especially need the secretary-general’s office.
The private sector needs the tools to defend itself from unconventional drone or cyber threats.
Foreign and malign actors constantly exploit weak ownership reporting requirements to launder money throughout the United States.
The frozen conflict in Cyprus is a major roadblock to integrating one of NATO’s most powerful militaries into European defense initiatives.
The International Monetary Fund’s ( IMF ) general counsel is Yan Liu , a Chinese citizen. Her department helps shape the IMF’s sovereign debt policies and supports the Common Framework and the Global Sovereign Debt Roundtable , processes where China’s role as a major creditor is consequential. China is the largest bilateral lender to the developing world and has a well-documented record of lending on secret terms in Zambia, Sri Lanka, and across the countries that have joined the Belt and Road Initiative . When those debts come up for restructuring, her office writes the IMF’s positions, a proximity to the referee no other creditor would be allowed.
A recent Center for Global Development study found that China’s formal voting power in these institutions still lags compared to the size of its economy, which is true. Yet that’s beside the point, because Beijing’s strategy isn’t to outvote anyone so much as staff the offices that write the rules the votes are about.
Congress rightly saw this problem coming years ago and wrote remedies into the CHIPS and Science Act of 2022 , including a binding duty for the National Institute of Standards and Technology ( NIST ) to coordinate American participation in international standards bodies, and a pilot grant program to pay for the people who would do it. Congress gave the duty to NIST because setting standards is what NIST exists to do, and has done for the United States and much of the world since Congress created it in 1901.
Four years on, Congress should ask what that mandate has delivered: how many American experts are participating, which committees they lead, and where gaps remain. NIST announced a $15 million, five-year cooperative agreement with ASTM International in O

articles.title_orig: On World Food Day, We Must Take Real Action on Global Malnutrition Crises
articles.title_zh: On World Food Day, We Must Take Real Action on Global Malnutrition Crises
articles.content_orig:
Save the Children Renews Call for Global Food Security Strategy
FAIRFIELD, Conn. (Oct. 16, 2026) — This World Food Day, Save the Children is calling for renewed action to ensure every child has access to the food and nutrition they need to survive, learn and thrive. Whether they face acute malnutrition in a humanitarian crisis or rely on nutrition programs here in the United States, children need consistent access to healthy food to reach their full potential.
As more than 43 million children across the globe suffer from severe malnutrition, [1] Save Children is also reiterating its call for the U. S. government to release its overdue Global Food Security Strategy.
The Global Food Security Act requires a new Global Food Security Strategy every four years. The strategy due in 2026 is yet to be released. At a time when hunger is worsening in many parts of the world and a “Super” El Niño is expected to worsen hunger and malnutrition in many parts of the world, the strategy can help guide U.S. efforts to identify emerging crises and support early and effective action – before children face serious health complications.
In an op-ed published by The Hill earlier this month, Save the Children President and CEO Janti Soeripto wrote : “The new Global Food Security Strategy should be built on a clear picture of where hunger is worsening, who is most vulnerable and which interventions stop a crisis before it becomes a catastrophe. It should treat early warning, early financing and early action as inseparable, strengthening tools like the Famine Early Warning Systems Network with better technology, nutrition data and information from frontline workers and communities.”
This year’s El Niño weather event – predicted to be one of the strongest in decades – is expected to deepen hunger and malnutrition further, because of dangerous droughts, crop failures, flooding and livestock losses.
Children in Somalia, Yemen and other countries facing conflict, extreme weather and economic instability need urgent support to prevent hunger from becoming a catastrophe.
World Food Day is also a reminder that child hunger remains a challenge in the United States . Federal nutrition programs, including the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP), Child and Adult Care Food Program and school meals, help millions of children access healthy food and support their learning and development. Children cannot reach their full potential when they are hungry.
While acute malnutrition is both treatable and preventable, prevention requires sustained investment in nutrition, health systems, resilient food systems and early action before crises escalate.
Save the Children supports policies that reduce child hunger, improve nutrition and strengthen food security for children and families in the U.S. and around the world. Investing in children’s nutrition is one of the most effective ways to improve health, education outcomes and long-term opportunity.
In its programmatic work, Save the Children takes a comprehensive approach, investing in prevention, treating malnutrition and strengthening health systems while delivering food to children in need.
This World Food Day, Save the Children urges policymakers to prioritize actions that prevent hunger, protect children’s nutrition and help to build a future in which every child has the opportunity to grow up healthy and thrive.
[1] Levels and Trends in Child Malnutrition. Joint Child Malnutrition Estimates: Key findings of the 2025 edition; May 2025. UNICEF/WHO/World Bank Group/JME-Brochure-UNSDG-regions-2025-v23.pdf
Save the Children believes every child deserves a future. Since our founding more than 100 years ago, we've been advocating for the rights of children worldwide. In the United States and around the world , we give children a healthy start in life, the opportunity to learn and protection from harm. We do whatever it takes for children – every day and in times of crisis – transforming the future we share. Our results , financial statements and charity ratings reaffirm that Save the Children is a charity you can trust. Follow us on Facebook , Instagram , LinkedIn , X and YouTube .

articles.title_orig: Pour One Out for the Leap Second
articles.title_zh: Pour One Out for the Leap Second
articles.content_orig:
Leap seconds have driven a raging debate in the metrological community for three decades. Now, that argument has been put to rest: The leap second is officially dead.
Doing away with an obscure metric the average person has been blissfully unaware of may seem like a novelty, but killing the leap second has major ramifications for technology you rely on every day. It also helps stave off what could’ve been a dangerous moment in time: The possibility of the world’s first negative leap second.
The International Bureau of Weights and Measurements (known by its French acronym BIPM) on Thursday said that in May 2027 it would stop issuing leap seconds, 32 of which have been added since 1972 to adjust what’s known as Coordinated Universal Time (UTC).
The world implemented the leap second in 1972 due to a growing gap between time measured with atomic clocks and time based on the Earth’s rotation. The reason for the discrepancy? The latter is slowing down due in large part to tidal friction caused by the moon and Earth’s rotation not lining up. The molten core of the Earth as well as oceans and the atmosphere also affect the spin rate.
Leap seconds are a way to keep atomic-clock-driven UTC in line with astronomically kept Universal Time (UT1). Think of it like adding a little extra track for a train to keep running exactly parallel with another one. Rather than happening on a set interval—like a leap year—BIPM uses the average of hundreds of atomic clocks around the world and compares their time calculations to astronomical time to determine when a leap second is necessary. The most recent one was added in 2016.
Of course, adding track is no small effort, and it may seem like a lot of hassle for a measly second. But UTC is vital for all sorts of technology given the number of APIs and databases that rely on it. Introducing a leap second helped keep UTC and UT1 aligned, but it also wrought havoc on various systems running on UTC and forced companies to figure out how to deal with them when they were added every few years.
A number of tech companies like Google and Meta use “a ‘smear’ method of dealing with leap seconds,” Judah Levine, a fellow at the US National Institute of Standards and Technology, writes in an email. In essence, they spread a leap second out over the course of a day or so in tiny increments. But leap seconds have thrown off other systems ; the airline Qantas, for example, saw its booking system borked by a leap second in 2012 .
Adding a leap second is hard enough as it is. But the odds of having to add a negative leap second have been rising in part because Earth has picked up rotational speed in recent years due to climate change. (There’s always a climate angle.) Melting ice has caused a shift in the planet’s gravity so extreme that a negative leap second may have been required as soon as 2029, according to a 2024 Nature study . Part of the calculus of ditching the leap second altogether was that going negative isn’t worth the risk.
“There are continuing problems with positive leap seconds even after 50 years, and the concern was that the negative leap second would be much more serious because its effects had never been tested,” Levine says.
BIPM time department director Patrizia Tavella confirmed those concerns in an email to WIRED. “The probability of a negative leap second convinced us [to] set the application date in 2027,” she wrote, adding that there was added urgency following tests by an industry standards group that “showed several failures with a negative leap.”
Tavella says the group is waiting until May 20 2027 to implement it because it's the anniversary of 1875 signing of the Metre Convention, creating BIPM, as well as Metrology Day. In other words, it’s the perfect time to mark the passing of time—or more accurately, the lack thereof.
The death of the leap second makes life easier for everyone now. “The nice fact is that we have nothing to do!” Tavella says. “Just continue to accumulate second[s] and ‘normal’ minutes of 60 seconds.”
Levine concurs, writing that “life will have one less hassle.”
But kicking the can on adding leap seconds doesn’t mean atomic time and astronomical time won’t continue to drift apart. That’s why BIPM also agreed to create a leap hour. Given how long it takes leap seconds to add up, a leap hour is millennia away. (There are, after all, 3,600 seconds in an hour.)
“We do not speak of leap hour yet,” Tavella says. “If systems rely on UTC, they have nothing to do. If they rely on UT1, they have to be able to use the information UT1-UTC which, in [the] future, will be larger than 1 second.”
In other words, not our problem, and good luck to future generations!
