articles.title_orig: Troy Jackson tells Susan Collins to ‘shut up’ during final Maine Senate debate
articles.title_zh: Troy Jackson tells Susan Collins to ‘shut up’ during final Maine Senate debate
articles.content_orig:
It was likely their final face-to-face showdown in a race with potentially major national implications.
Over the hour, Republican U.S. Sen. Susan Collins and Democrat Troy Jackson disparaged each other's records, portrayed the other as beholden to political interests far from Maine and drew laughs from the audience with their sharp barbs. At one point, Jackson even told Collins to "shut up" after she quipped that a protester obviously came from his camp.
But they occasionally agreed on issues, such as about the pernicious effects of the "dark money" that is pouring into Maine to attack and prop up both candidates.
Here are a few key takeaways from Thursday night's debate co-sponsored by Maine Public, NEWS CENTER Maine and the Portland Press Herald.
As he'd done throughout their three previous joint appearances, Jackson sought to portray Collins — a 30-year Senate veteran — as a key cog in a Republican majority in Congress that he says refuses to stand up to what he believes is a dangerous president.
"They will not stop Donald Trump and I do think our democracy is risk," Jackson said before accusing Trump of trying to suppress the vote in November. "Donald Trump is trying every trick in the book to keep power. And we've already seen what he will do on Jan. 6 when he led an insurrection."
And he repeated one of his favorite statistics — that Collins allegedly votes with Trump 96% of the time.
"The reality is that 100% of the time, when Donald Trump needs her, Susan Collins is going to be there," said Jackson, a professional logger and former Maine Senate president who entered the race in July after former Democratic nominee Graham Platner withdrew. "The votes that she throws away are managed votes that she already knows the outcome."
As she's done in previous debates, Collins accused Jackson of cherry-picking a number from a study that only examined about one-third of the votes that have been taken. The real figure, she said, is about 72%. And Collins, who chairs the powerful Senate Appropriations Committee, pointed to years of analysis consistently showing her the most or one of the most bipartisan senators from either party.
"He is going to be an automatic vote for the Democratic position no matter what," Collins said of Jackson. "We have lost a lot of the centrists and one of the reasons is we need people who will work across party lines."
It's probably a safe assumption that both candidates have wanted to say this to the other at some point (or lots of times) during the three previous tense debates. But it took an unexpected disruption to bring it out.
The brief scene began when an audience member began shouting at Collins about the environmental impact of data centers as she started answering a question on an entirely different topic.
"So this is obviously one of Troy's supporters," Collins said, leaning slightly into the microphone.
"Oh shut up," Jackson shot back. "I did not ... I don't even know that kid."
"Oh right," Collins said sarcastically.
Just before Collins' initial remark, Jackson had been frowning and shaking his head in the direction of the protester. And from the audio and video, it seems like Jackson's "oh shut up" was more flippant than mean-spirited. The two rivals even seemed to exchange snarky smiles before the debate quickly resumed without future disruption.
Not surprisingly, the Senate Leadership Fund — one of the super PACs spending millions of dollars to support Collins — called attention to Jackson's statement in an email blast.
The protester was later identified as Henry Elgie, a 19-year-old Bowdoin College student. A press release from the Sunrise Movement — a self-described "youth movement to stop climate change and create millions of jobs in the process" — said that Elgie was part of a pattern of students confronting politicians on the campaign trail.
Despite this being the fourth debate, the two panelists — Maine Public chief political correspondent Steve Mistler and NEWS CENTER Maine host and political reporter Phil Hirschkorn — managed to get the candidates to weigh in on some new issues.
In some cases, they almost agreed.
Both Jackson and Collins said they were opposed to so-called "dark money," which is when political donors hide their contributions by giving to organizations that don't have to disclose their sources, such as politically active 501(c)(4) nonprofits. According to Mistler, Collins and Jackson have benefited from at least $75 million in dark money spending so far.
Collins said she has supported sweeping campaign finance reforms in the past that did not pass constitutional muster.
"I still think that there are reforms that could be made, and one of them is full disclosure of everyone who is contributing," Collins said.
"I'm 100% for overturning Citizens United," Jackson said, referring to the Supreme Court decision that opened the door to unlimited spending on campaigns and, by extension, the creation of super PACs. "I mean, billionaires have bought Congress and everyday people can't afford to buy them back."
On the issue of guns, Collins reiterated that she would support a ban on so-called bump stocks that allow semi-automatic guns to function more like a machine gun and would support "reasonable" limits on magazine capacity. She also said would be "open" to increasing the age to purchase an assault weapon from 18 to 21.
Jackson said he opposes increasing the minimum age. But unlike Collins, he would support a ban on the purchase of assault weapons — but would not support taking them away from people who already own them.
But the rivals disagreed sharply on whether the Supreme Court should be expanded.
Some progressives are pushing to add justices to counteract the court's 6-3 conservative majority. Jackson supports the idea and also called for term limits on justices and ethics reforms.
"We have the best Supreme Court that money can buy right now and I think that has to be turned over," Jackson said.
But Collins said adding justices would amount to political interference.
"It's inconsistent with the whole idea of the Supreme Court being insulated from politics ... that would make it a total political body," Collins said.
The last time Congress added seats to the Supreme Court was in 1869.

articles.title_orig: Trump hits Georgia to rally Republicans despite party divisions in battleground state
articles.title_zh: Trump hits Georgia to rally Republicans despite party divisions in battleground state
articles.content_orig:
The unpopular president is rallying to support Republican nominees ahead of midterms
Sign up for the Breaking News US email
Donald Trump’s speech to a small crowd of supporters in Dalton, Georgia, was just disrupted by protesters holding up signs against Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE), who were forced out of the crowd by Trump supporters, including a man wearing a yellow Gadsden flag as a cape.
Two of the signs denounced the idea of sending ICE officer to the polls on election day, which the administration has refused to rule out.
After he began speaking again, Trump praised “the woman in the yellow cape”.
“She went up there, ripped them out of their seats and threw them the hell out of here. Where’s the woman with the yellow cape, then? She was great,” Trump said.
As Donald Trump continues to rail against senator Jon Ossoff at his rally in Georgia, it is worth noting that Ossoff, the Democratic incumbent and a fierce Trump critic, said on Thursday that he would be “delighted for the president to come every day between now and the election”.
Speaking on MS Now, Ossoff said Trump was welcome to campaign against him in Georgia because “the public is turning against this administration.”
“They see, on the one hand, the total incompetence,” Ossoff continued. “The nation plunged recklessly into a war that they don’t know how to win or to end, a global energy crisis, record high diesel prices, record high prices for healthcare.”
“It costs more today than ever before in our country’s history to fill up your truck, to stock your fridge, to power your home,” the Democratic senator continued. “And then everybody can see that at the same time, the first families raking in billions of dollars from all over the world. The president’s adorning his office in gold. People are fed up and they’ve had enough.”
Donald Trump’s remarks to supporters in Georgia are mainly a rehash of previous speeches, filled with false claims we have debunked repeatedly, suggesting that the president is not a regular reader of the Guardian.
“Less than two years ago, our country was dead. Now we have the hottest country anywhere in the world,” Trump said, before claiming, as he has in the past, that this was an observation made to him by the Saudi king during his visit to that country last year.
“So that statement was true. The king of Saudi Arabia, when I was over there, he said, ‘A short time ago, you had – you were a laughingstock’ – meaning our country was a laughingstock, all the way, all the way around the world, everybody was laughing at the USA,” Trump said. “‘And in a very short period of time, you made it the hottest country,’” the president continued, attributing this remark to the Saudi king.
As the Guardian has reported previously, Trump did not meet the Saudi king, who is elderly and not often seen in public, during his visit last year. Instead, he was hosted by the Saudi crown prince, Mohammed bin Salman. There is also no evidence that the Saudi prince made this statement to Trump, but there is video of Trump making a version of that claim to Prince Mohammed during an address to a US-Saudi investment event in Riyadh on 13 May 2025.
“The days of economic misery under the last administration are rapidly giving way to the greatest economy in the history of the world,” Trump said before directly addressing the crown prince in the audience. “We are rocking. The United States is the hottest country, with the exception of your country, I have to say, right? … No Mohammed… You’re hotter. At least as long as I’m up here, you’re hotter. But groceries, gasoline, energy and all other prices are down with no inflation. We have no inflation.”
Two weeks after his return to the US, Trump began saying that this observation had been made not by him, but to him. “I went to Saudi Arabia,” Trump told reporters in the Oval Office on 28 May 2025. “The king told me, he said, ‘you got the hottest com-’ we have the hottest country in the world right now.,” Trump said. “Six months ago this country was stone cold dead. We had a dead country.”
As he repeated the story, again and again, Trump began to also attribute his own claim, that the US was “dead” under Joe Biden, to the Saudi king as well. In remarks at the Nato summit in the Hague in June 2025, Trump insisted that the Saudi king had told him: “A year ago, your country was dead. You had a deadhead running it. You had a country that was dead”.
Since then, Trump has repeated the tale dozens of times.
Speaking in Georgia, Donald Trump is spending most of his time defending his record as president, rather than discussing Republican candidates at the rally who are up for election next month.
Much of what he said was simply not true.
To take one example, the president repeated an entirely imaginary story he has repeated frequently in recent weeks, about how he was supposedly blamed for high prices by reporters on the second day of his term, in January 2025.
“When I came in, it was January 20th. I came in and on January 21st I had a news conference and some of those same people were at the news conference and they were screaming at me. I was only there for less than one day, substantially less than one day. And I’m having a news conference. I thought it would be a victorious conference. I thought the fake news would be saying, ‘Oh, sir, what a great race you ran,’” Trump said.
“My first news conference, January 21st. So I take office on the 20th. I figured maybe I won’t have a news conference. So the next day I have a news conference and I’m waiting for accolades from the press. And they said, what about the cost of eggs? What about the cost of beef?” Trump claimed.
In fact, a review of the transcript from that news conference reveals that no such exchange took place on 21 January 2025, when he was mainly pressed on the pardons he signed the day before for Capitol rioters convicted of violence against police officers on January 6 2021, in support of his attempt to stay in power despite losing the 2020 election.
Donald Trump’s speech to a small crowd of supporters in Dalton, Georgia, was just disrupted by protesters holding up signs against Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE), who were forced out of the crowd by Trump supporters, including a man wearing a yellow Gadsden flag as a cape.
Two of the signs denounced the idea of sending ICE officer to the polls on election day, which the administration has refused to rule out.
After he began speaking again, Trump praised “the woman in the yellow cape”.
“She went up there, ripped them out of their seats and threw them the hell out of here. Where’s the woman with the yellow cape, then? She was great,” Trump said.
As he has in the past, Donald Trump just bragged to supporters in Georgia about what he called his key role in helping to defeat Democrat Jon Ossoff in a 2017 special election for a Georgia House seat, but made no mention at all of the fact that he also campaigned hard against Ossoff in the 2020 Georgia Senate race that Ossoff won, when he defeated the Trump-backed Republican David Perdue.
“Ossoff was leading by a lot and they called me in to help. It was a special election,” Trump recalled. “And I came in and I held a massive rally for the person, very nice woman. And we ended up beating Ossoff. So I beat him. And that was in 2017. I beat him once and now we’re going to beat him more importantly a second time.”
Trump failed to mention that the second time he campaigned against Ossoff was at a rally in Valdosta, Georgia, on 5 December 2020 – ahead of the runoff election Ossoff won in January 2021.
That rally was supposed to encourage Georgia Republicans to vote for Perdue, and a second Republican Senate candidate, Kelly Loeffler, but Trump devoted most of his speech to complaining about his loss in the 2020 presidential election and giving voters the idea that the elections were “rigged” against Republicans.

articles.title_orig: Presidential adviser says Ukraine is in talks to lift speed limit on military satellite network
articles.title_zh: Presidential adviser says Ukraine is in talks to lift speed limit on military satellite network
articles.content_orig:
President Donald Trump on Friday denied that the White House had ordered restrictions this week on Starlink satellite internet services provided to Ukraine's armed forces.
Ukrainian officials on Tuesday and Wednesday said SpaceX had restricted use of Starshield , a military-grade version of Starlink, without warning, impeding some military operations and its ability to defend civilians against intensifying attacks by Russia.
SpaceX CEO Elon Musk pinned responsibility for any restrictions on the U.S. government and Trump, writing on X that, "Starshield systems are owned and controlled by the US government."
Reporters in Washington, D.C., on Friday asked Trump who was responsible for pausing access for the Ukrainian military.
"Well, I don't know if it was anybody because it wasn't me, and I don't think it was Elon," Trump said. "And from what I understand, it's the same as it's always been."
Ukrainian forces have long relied on Starlink and Starshield to enable data gathering by their autonomous drones and for other communications. The restrictions cut off connectivity for drones or other vehicles traveling above 160 kilometers per hour.
Serhii Beskrestnov, an advisor to Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, wrote in a post on Telegram this week that, "Our armed forces did not receive a warning about these restrictions, and this led to the failure of a number of missions."
Radoslaw Sikorski, Poland's deputy prime minister, criticized Musk on X about the restrictions. Poland has purchased Starlink services for Ukraine from SpaceX.
"Hey, @elonmusk, big man, are you playing politics with your products again?" he wrote . "As your European customers, we are watching you."
Musk is an advisor to the Pentagon on technology through his role in the recently announced Project Meridian.
The Telegraph reported Friday that Musk "approached Donald Trump with the idea of slowing down Starlink in Ukraine," and both had a hand in imposing the restrictions.
Reuters reported on Thursday , citing two U.S. officials, that the call to restrict Starlink in Ukraine came from the White House, but did not say who made the order.
On Oct. 10, after Trump called on Ukraine to stop all attacks on Russian oil refineries, Musk wrote in a post on X, "Zelensky has gone too far."
Musk and SpaceX did not immediately respond to requests for comment on Friday.
SpaceX shares are down about 11% this week. The company is scheduled to report quarterly results on Tuesday.

articles.title_orig: Man Charged in Fatal Fentanyl Overdose and Rape of FIT Student
articles.title_zh: Man Charged in Fatal Fentanyl Overdose and Rape of FIT Student
articles.content_orig:
The suspect is accused of waiting 45 minutes before seeking help.
NEW YORK (WABC) -- Two teens are facing federal charges this week accusing them of supplying the fentanyl that killed one New York City college student and poisoned a second.
According to the newly unsealed indictment, Moises Freire, 19, brought fentanyl he obtained from Brian Peralta, 18, to the victims' undergraduate residence hall at Fashion Institute of Technology on March 18.
Officials said Freire falsely claimed the drug did not contain fentanyl and was "pure cocaine."
Freire encouraged the victims to ingest the substance and almost immediately both women lost consciousness, prosecutors said.
While the victims were incapacitated, Freire allegedly raped Annabel Richter in her FIT dorm room. Authorities say he then took photos of her that he sent to friends.
He waited 45 minutes before seeking help from campus security, to whom he claimed the two undergraduates had simply consumed too much alcohol.
Campus security responded and administered emergency aid, including Narcan. Both victims were transported to hospitals in Manhattan.
Toxicology results later confirmed that both women had ingested fentanyl and no cocaine.
The second victim regained consciousness after life‑saving treatment.
Richter remained in critical condition and eventually died from complications of acute fentanyl intoxication.
"This case alleges not only the deadly distribution of fentanyl to two young women but also the sexual assault of a victim rendered defenseless by that poisoning," said U.S. Attorney Jamie McDonald. "We will work tirelessly to hold accountable those who endanger young people living and learning on our campuses."
Christopher Roberts, the head of the Drug Enforcement Administration New York Task Force Division, said the allegations were "beyond disturbing and include a cruel deception and unimaginable assault."
"College should be a place where young people can learn, grow, and pursue their dreams, not a place where predators exploit their vulnerability," Roberts said. "Every student deserves to feel safe, whether walking across campus, sitting in a classroom, or inside their own dorm room."
Freire and Peralta, both from Queens, are charged with conspiracy to distribute a controlled substance resulting in death. They face at least 20 years in prison if convicted. Freire is also charged with distributing a controlled substance with the intent to commit rape.
(The Associated Press and ABC News contributed to this report.)

articles.title_orig: Apple blames ‘extraordinary’ demand as foldable iPhones sell out
articles.title_zh: Apple blames ‘extraordinary’ demand as foldable iPhones sell out
articles.content_orig:
Apple 's iPhone Duo , its most expensive iPhone ever, went up for preorder Friday, with launch-day pickup inventory selling out and some online delivery estimates already slipping into late January.
The company said in a statement that the preorder demand was "nothing short of extraordinary."
"We are working hard to get this revolutionary new product into customers' hands as quickly as possible, and we will continue accepting orders online," Apple said.
Apple's first foldable phone starts at $1,999 and passes $3,000 at the 2TB storage tier. It is the biggest change to the physical design of the iPhone in years and establishes an entirely new price point above the Pro and Pro Max.
The early rush offers a first glimpse at the demand behind Apple's bet: Whether a dramatic new design can persuade customers to spend more and push the iPhone even further as a status symbol.
But analysts who spoke with CNBC said Apple's bet is not that foldables suddenly become a mass-market product. It is that a relatively small group of its highest-spending customers can become significantly more valuable.
Foldables are expected to make up just over 2% of global smartphone units this year but nearly 7% of industry revenue, according to IDC. By 2030, IDC expects the category to account for 10% of smartphone revenue while still representing only about 3% of units.
That gap between volume and value is central to Apple's opportunity.
"Duo is fast becoming an aspirational foldable," IDC's Nabila Popal told CNBC, comparing its appeal with Apple's broader position as an aspirational smartphone brand.
Popal, global senior research director for the Consumer Device Team at IDC, said the technology itself is not necessarily the breakthrough. Foldable Android phones have existed for years. What's new is Apple bringing that form factor to the enormous base of consumers already invested in the iPhone ecosystem.
Apple itself has been exploring the form factor for more than a decade. In 2011, Ternus and five other Apple engineers filed a patent application for foldable electronic devices, according to a recent Time profile.
"It's not that it's a breakthrough or new technology, but it's from Apple," Popal said.
The Duo could also prove more accessible than some industry watchers had anticipated.
Anshel Sag, an analyst at Moor Insights who attended Apple's launch event, said many expected the foldable iPhone to start between $2,400 and $2,500.
Apple coming in at $1,999, Sag said, suggests the company "wants a lot of share."
Sag expects the Duo to become "very much a status symbol" during the holiday season and potentially into next year.
That status appeal could be reinforced by scarcity.
Counterpoint Research Director Tarun Pathak told CNBC the firm expects initial demand to exceed supply.
Apple has an installed base of roughly 1.4 billion iPhones, he noted, meaning even a small percentage of early adopters could overwhelm the roughly 6 million or fewer units Counterpoint expects to be available in the near term.
IDC also expects supply to be constrained initially because of the complexity of the device and Apple's manufacturing and quality standards.
"Exclusivity is part of the current appeal," Popal said.
And Apple has made explicit luxury plays before.
When the first Apple Watch launched, the company offered the 18-karat gold Edition starting at $10,000. Apple also formed a long-running partnership with Hermès around premium watch bands and designs.
That push came during the tenure of Angela Ahrendts, the former Burberry CEO who joined Apple in 2014 to lead retail and online stores, as the company experimented with bringing more of the language and presentation of luxury fashion into its stores and products.
The Duo takes that idea into Apple's largest product business.
IDC expects Apple to ship roughly 7 million units this year, or roughly 3% of Apple's total shipments in 2026. Popal, the IDC analyst, forecasts Duo shipments could grow another 70% next year. That would give Apple roughly 40% of the global foldable market and would make it the category's largest player, surpassing Samsung and Huawei.
According to her forecast, Apple could ship as many Duos in the next six months as the previous category leaders did in all of 2025.
But the more important number for Apple may not be units.
A large share of Duo customers are expected to be existing iPhone owners, analysts said, including consumers who otherwise might have purchased a Pro Max and are now trading up to a device costing hundreds of dollars more.
Others could add the Duo as a second smartphone, with Apple's ecosystem allowing users to move relatively seamlessly between it and their primary iPhone.
Popal said that migration from roughly $1,200 premium iPhones to a device starting at nearly $2,000 should provide a "healthy boost" to Apple's revenue even if overall volumes remain relatively small.
JPMorgan reached a similar conclusion.
The bank expects the Duo to have a disproportionate impact on iPhone revenue because of its much higher average selling price, even as overall iPhone shipments are expected to remain roughly flat next year.
JPMorgan said the iPhone 18 cycle is increasingly likely to be driven by price and product mix rather than unit growth.
D.A. Davidson analyst Gil Luria said Apple needs the Duo to succeed as it comes up against a difficult set of earnings comps with its strongest upgrade cycle in years.
"Without an uplift from Duo, they may experience some pretty pedestrian revenue growth," Luria told CNBC.
The device gives Apple several ways to generate that uplift, he added.
It raises the company's average selling price by capturing die-hard Apple customers who might otherwise have bought a Pro Max. It could bring in some consumers who previously bought folding Android phones because Apple did not offer one. And it could create a halo around the rest of the iPhone lineup.
Luria said some consumers will visit Apple stores specifically to see the Duo, "but probably walk out with an iPhone or iPhone Pro at half the price."
That means the Duo can potentially help Apple even when someone decides not to buy it.
Lead times for the iPhone 18 Pro have softened in several markets compared with the prior cycle, while the more expensive Pro Max has held up better, according to JPMorgan's tracking.
Morgan Stanley has separately said its supply-chain checks are consistent with unusually early component order reductions for the Pro and Pro Max, though the firm has not yet seen evidence that those adjustments have translated into cuts to finished iPhone production.
That puts more pressure on the Duo to pull buyers toward the very top of Apple's lineup.
Apple's move toward a more expensive iPhone comes as the economics of the broader smartphone market become increasingly difficult.
Consumers are already holding on to phones for longer, and global smartphone growth is slowing.
Wayne Lam, an analyst at TechInsights, said moving the iPhone further upmarket gives Apple another way to protect the revenue generated by its most important product.
"Given that the iPhone is almost 20 years old, there really isn't anywhere else to head to, given Apple's market position," Lam told CNBC.
With smartphone sales expected to slow, he said, "moving upmarket allows Apple to maintain the all-important iPhone revenues they report every quarter."
Lam described the Duo as an aspirational or luxury product rather than something designed for the average consumer.
But unlike Apple's Vision products, he believes the foldable phone has a path toward becoming a larger category over time, particularly as artificial intelligence changes how consumers interact with their devices.
The trade-off is that pushing prices higher could also make consumers wait longer to upgrade.
Higher iPhone prices could stretch already-long upgrade cycles even further, Lam said, creating what he described as a potential negative feedback loop: devices become more expensive, c

articles.title_orig: Oil hits $110 per barrel for first time since May
articles.title_zh: Oil hits $110 per barrel for first time since May
articles.content_orig:
Crude oil prices rose sharply Friday as Iran escalated attacks in the Strait of Hormuz, Houthi militants fired missiles at Saudi Arabia and Ukraine vowed to keep striking Russian refineries.
Brent futures hit a session high of $110 per barrel for the first time since May before easing slightly to close at $109.86, a gain of 3.7%.
U.S. West Texas Intermediate rose 3.5% to settle at $101.41 per barrel. WTI added more than 10% this week while Brent advanced nearly 5%.
Saudi Arabia intercepted several missiles fired over the Red Sea on Friday, including one that was heading toward the oil export terminal Yanbu, a military spokesman said. Three drones were also destroyed in the kingdom's Riyadh and southern regions, the military said.
Iran-allied Houthi militants in Yemen have repeatedly fired at Saudi Arabia this week. Oil giant Aramco came under attack when one of its administrative buildings in Dhahran was hit Tuesday, the kingdom's energy ministry said .
The Houthis attacked Riyadh's international airport on Oct. 10, killing 12 and injuring more than 300.
In the Strait of Hormuz, at least nine tankers and cargo ships have come under attack since Sunday as Iran tries to choke off oil exports through the waterway. Iran sank the container ship GFS Pride on Wednesday, U.S. Central Command said. The crew of the Singapore-registered ship was safely evacuated, according to Singapore's maritime authority.
The attacks have left three seafarers injured and two missing this week, according to the International Maritime Organization .
Crude exports through Hormuz have pulled back after touching prewar levels in September. Shipments  stood at 9.4 million barrels per day for the week ended Wednesday, about 70% of the average before the Iran war, according to data provided by the energy researcher Kpler.
Meanwhile, the " energy ceasefire " that President Donald Trump tried to broker between Ukraine and Russia has quickly unraveled. The Kremlin continued attacking Ukrainian infrastructure despite the supposed truce. President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Kyiv would resume strikes on Russian refineries in retaliation.
Diesel prices have surged this year due to Ukraine's attacks on Russian refineries and Iranian strikes on energy infrastructure in the Middle East. The fuel cost an average of $6.33 a gallon in the U.S. Friday, more than 70% above the same period last year, according to AAA data.
U.S. crude oil prices were also driven higher by a big decline of more than 8 million barrels for the week ended Oct. 9 in commercial inventories due to production shut-ins on the Gulf Coast from Hurricane Isaias, according to the Energy Information Administration.

articles.title_orig: Airline High School students run their own store to build real-world business skills
articles.title_zh: Airline High School students run their own store to build real-world business skills
articles.content_orig:
BOSSIER PARISH, La. (KSLA) - Airline High School students are getting a hands-on lesson in business through the Viking Exchange, a student-run store designed to help prepare them for the workforce and life after graduation.
The store sells concessions, school supplies, and Airline spirit gear to the school’s approximately 1,700 students. But the program goes beyond selling products. Students manage inventory, place orders, provide customer service, maintain the store and handle the daily responsibilities of running a business.
Brad Winstead, an Airline teacher and coach, serves as the school advisor and sponsor. He says the program was created to give students practical experience they can use on a resume and in future careers.
“It’s practical education and instruction,” Winstead said. “What’s taught in the abstract and the principles of business classes—inventory, receiving, the inventory accounting process, workplace safety—those things, which in a traditional classroom setting are taught in the abstract, this allows us to teach it in three dimensions.”
The Viking Exchange proposal is aligned with customer service and business-of-retail credentials from the National Retail Federation. Students can earn experience with customer interaction, inventory control, workplace safety and business operations.
Winstead said students also learn the small details that matter in a professional setting, including how to present themselves while serving customers.
The store is managed by students, with school staff providing guidance. Maxwell Moore serves as the Viking Exchange store manager. He said the experience can give students an advantage when they begin looking for jobs.
“This is a great opportunity for everybody to gain business experience,” Moore said. “Whenever they want to get in the workforce, they can join the business industry.”
Moore said he earned the manager position by working consistently, showing leadership, helping with inventory and making sure the store is clean and organized—even coming in on weekends when needed.
He plans to study kinesiology and hopes to eventually open his own physical therapy business. Moore said the program is helping him develop skills he can use as a future business owner.
“My path right now is kinesiology and hopefully starting my own business in kinesiology one day and helping my own physical therapy business because I want to help people,” Moore said.
Winstead believes more schools could benefit from similar programs. He said students who gain hands-on experience at a younger age may be better prepared for employment, college, trade school or entrepreneurship.
The Viking Exchange was supported by Red River Credit Union. Winstead said the partnership helped make the program possible and aligned with the credit union’s interest in supporting student education.

articles.title_orig: Wall Street ends down sharply, worries about AI trade and high oil prices weigh
articles.title_zh: Wall Street ends down sharply, worries about AI trade and high oil prices weigh
articles.content_orig:
Stocks slid on Friday as traders notched a mostly losing week amid a shift away from tech and artificial intelligence-related names as well as a rise in oil prices.
The S&P 500 lost 1.09% and ended at 7,659.44, while the Nasdaq Composite shed 2.14% to close at 26,140.03. Both indexes ended the session below their 50-day moving averages. The Dow Jones Industrial Average fell 175.28 points, or 0.34%, to 52,002.41. The sell-off sent the Cboe Volatility Index (VIX) above 22 for the first time in four months .
Chipmakers were lower again. The VanEck Semiconductor ETF (SMH) lost 3%, led by declines in Micron Technology , Advanced Micro Devices and Sandisk . Semiconductors have struggled this week amid jitters about competition from China . The SMH slid 10% week to date for its biggest weekly decline since April 2025.
Those declines, coupled with drops in other stocks linked to AI, dragged the S&P 500 to a losing week. The benchmark index fell about 2% this week, while the Nasdaq shed more than 4% for its worst week since June. The Dow, on the other hand, advanced 0.7% on the week.
Investors have also grown concerned that tech companies are borrowing too much for the AI buildout . Shares of neoclouds like CoreWeave , which has seen its total debt rise to more than $51 billion , were down nearly 12%, bringing the stock's week-to-date losses to 25%.
"The question is: Is this a systemic issue?" said Michael Rosen, Angeles' chief investment officer. "Obviously, increased debt issuance is something to observe and continue to watch and be concerned about if it continues to get to levels of excessiveness. But we're not remotely close to that right now."
Other areas of the market such as energy saw gains Friday, with stocks like Chevron helping to keep the Dow's losses in check. Oil prices moved higher amid rising tensions between the U.S. and Iran as well as between Russian and Ukraine. West Texas Intermediate crude futures increased 3.51% to settle at $101.41 per barrel, while Brent crude futures advanced 3.72% to $109.86.
Simultaneously, investors have been grappling with hotter-than-expected inflation data, which has been exacerbated by elevated energy prices in the wake of the U.S.-Iran war. Wholesale inflation this week saw its biggest gain since 2022 , while consumer inflation remained well above the Federal Reserve's target of 2%.
Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh spoke at an IMF event in Bangkok overnight. And while he didn't comment on whether the Fed would raise rates before year-end, traders took that as a sign that the central bank will hold policy steady later this month. The CME Group's FedWatch tool points to an 82% chance the Fed keeps its overnight rate unchanged at its Oct. 27-28 meeting.
The three leading U.S. indexes ended Friday's session with losses.
The S&P 500 dropped 1.09% to finish at 7,659.44, while the Nasdaq Composite lost 2.14% to 26,140.03. The Dow Jones Industrial Average shed 175.28 points, or 0.34%, to 52,002.41.
As the market sell-off intensified Friday afternoon, the Cboe Volatility Index (VIX) rose to levels it last closed at four months ago.
The VIX rose to 21.32, as of 3:10 p.m., rising more than 4.8 points on the session. It's on pace for its highest close since June 10, when it closed at 22.22.
Typically, when the VIX is above 20 that indicates greater fear in the market. The index last closed above that level on July 29 , when markets fell after the Federal Reserve kept interest rates steady at its meeting that month. The next day , stocks rose, and the day marked a bottom in a market where many AI-related stocks had been selling off in the previous month .
The Nasdaq Composite was down about 2.5% in afternoon trading on Friday, bringing its loss on the week to almost 5%.
With that move, the tech-heavy index on pace for its worst weekly performance since the week ended April 4, 2025, when the index recorded a roughly 10% drop.
Communication services and information technology led the S&P 500 lower on Friday.
The two sectors were down 2.7% and 2.4%, respectively, becoming the two biggest laggards among the 11 S&P 500 sectors. Consumer discretionary followed behind them, falling 1.5%.
However, a look beneath the surface showed that the S&P 500 — which was last down 1.3% — was more evenly split despite the losses at the index level. There were about 280 losers in the index and 222 gainers.
In total, five out of the 11 S&P 500 sectors were in positive territory, led by energy with its 2.1% gain and utilities with its rise of 1.2%.
— Sean Conlon and Sarah Min

Flu season in the U.S. typically starts around late October or early November and peaks between December and February. But new data reveals that the current flu season is starting slightly earlier than normal .
According to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) , around 3.4% of respiratory samples tested for flu came back positive for the week of Sept. 26. That's around seven times the rate compared with the same week in 2025 .
The positive tests are coming mainly from Western states, including California, Washington and Arizona. Regardless of where you're located in the U.S., though, most people are recommended to get their annual flu shot in September or October, and the same goes for this flu season.
The annual flu shot is the best way to prevent hospitalization and death from seasonal influenza. Nearly everyone ages 6 months and older is recommended to get a flu vaccine, and older adults have several special options, including a high-dose shot, a vaccine containing an extra immune-stimulating ingredient called an adjuvant, and a brand-new mRNA vaccine .
Given that flu season is off to an earlier start this year, our latest poll asks whether you plan to get vaccinated or have gotten vaccinated already. Tell us your thoughts in the comments below.
Kenna Hughes-Castleberry is the Content Manager at Live Science. Formerly, she was the Content Manager at Space.com and before that the Science Communicator at JILA, a physics research institute. Kenna is also a book author, with her upcoming book 'Octopus X' scheduled for release in spring of 2027. Her beats include physics, health, environmental science, technology, AI, animal intelligence, corvids, and cephalopods.

articles.title_orig: Farm animals: The hidden victims of climate change
articles.title_zh: Farm animals: The hidden victims of climate change
articles.content_orig:
Last month, the United Nations made a startling announcement: Within the next few years, the planet is expected to heat up by more than 1.5 degrees C (2.7 F) compared to pre-industrial levels. This means governments around the world failed to meet the goal of the Paris Agreement, which was designed to reduce the anticipated impact of climate change.
Animal agriculture is a major contributor to this current crisis, but the animals stuck within this industry are also among its most vulnerable victims.
In 2018, Hurricane Florence hit North Carolina—one of the top animal agricultural states in the United States. Researchers found the storm was larger and produced significantly more rainfall because of climate change. Over 3 million chickens and 5,500 pigs died from the flooding, according to state government estimates.
As Kelly Guerin-Buckley documented the fallout, the word that came to mind was “apocalyptic.” Traveling by boat through the flooding with nonprofit We Animals, she saw hundreds of floating dead chickens before she even found her first barn. Later, she documented pigs who’d survived the devastation wandering a flooded highway.
Jo-Anne McArthur/We Animals
“The animals who are strategically hidden away, warehoused in CAFOs [concentrated animal feeding operations], were now washed up, dead and alive…where we could see their faces,” Guerin-Buckley, now a video producer with Humane World for Animals, wrote about her experience .
Earlier this year, countries across Europe were hit with five heat waves over four months . In a region known for mild summers and a lack of air conditioning, temperatures soared so high that highway and train tracks buckled.
An estimated 30,000 people died. On farms, animals died in massive numbers. An estimated 2.5 to 3 million birds bred for their meat died in France alone. Services that remove dead animals were so busy that some farms were left with piles of carcasses rotting in the sun, according to reporting from The New York Times .
In between these two tragedies were numerous other extreme weather events, including Zambia’s worst flooding in over 50 years in 2023 and the 2025 Los Angeles wildfires. But experts warn the worst is yet to come.
“This summer’s scorching heat, raging wildfires and deadly floods are a warning of what lies ahead,” U.N. Secretary-General António Guterres said in a press release about the new climate projections.
The impact may reach such a degree that even using heat-resilient species such as goats may prove inadequate, as future climates in large regions such as Africa will exceed the upper-temperature threshold (29 to 30 degrees C) for all common grazing species.”
Chaohui Li, et al. in a 2026 Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences study
Many of the species people use for farming are already biologically prone to heat stress. Chickens and pigs cannot sweat to cool themselves off. Because cows use so much energy to process their highly fibrous diet, their internal temperature often ramps up.
Add in more than a century of selective breeding to make farm animals produce a massive amount of “product” incredibly quickly and the risks grow exponentially. “Particularly with chickens who are bred for meat production. They grow so fast that they go from hatching to market weight in just six weeks,” says Sara Shields, our managing director of global farm animal welfare . “There's a trade-off between putting all of their genetic energy into growth versus health.”
Living conditions can also put animals at high risk too. Most cows used for beef production spend their final months on feedlots—facilities where bovines rapidly gain weight before slaughter. The animals are usually kept in outdoor dirt plots with little to no shade. Inside barns, conditions can be similarly risky.
“High stocking densities can reduce airflow, while concrete flooring prevents animals from engaging in instinctive behaviors that help regulate body temperature, such as pigs cooling themselves in mud wallows or cattle seeking relief in ponds and shaded areas,” says Dr. Jan Raines, managing director of veterinary medicine at our sanctuary, Black Beauty Ranch .
In Latin America, Mexico and Southeast Asia, the open-sided barns commonly used provide little protection from sweltering temperatures or floods.
There is no clear estimate on how many farm animals are killed by extreme weather a year. In fact, there does not appear to be a single country government that tracks farmed animal deaths from heat stress and extreme weather. The closest estimate comes from a 2025 report by Compassion in World Farming that found 14.8 million farm animals were killed during just 11 extreme weather events.
Even if global numbers were available, they wouldn’t show the full picture, as heat stress weakens animals’ immune systems, putting them at higher risk of dying from other diseases.
died from heat stress en route to slaughterhouses during the UK’s record-hot 2025 summer compared to the previous year’s summer, according to an analysis by Carbon Brief .
in the UK will experience at least 15 additional heat wave days by 2050, according to a 2026 study in Nature .
Much of the current discourse about how extreme weather impacts animal agriculture revolves around the economic losses farmers face. Significantly less attention is given to the welfare of the animals themselves.
In addition to increased risks of death from heat and other diseases, heat-stressed animals often lose weight, produce less milk and are more likely to miscarry. This means that, in some cases, more animals likely need to be used to get the same amount of “product.”
When disasters do occur, it’s nearly impossible—and incredibly expensive—to evacuate the huge number of animals kept on factory farms . Countless animals are simply left to die from the elements or from trampling one another in a panic.
There does not appear to be a single country that mandates farmers to create proactive evacuation plans for their animals. In the U.S., for instance, farmers are eligible for compensation for animals lost during extreme weather. Because of this, animal welfare experts argue there’s little incentive for them to implement costly measures to try saving their animals.
Without regulations in place, the level of preparedness varies widely from farm to farm. “Some farmers care very deeply about this and they're very concerned and they have great emergency management plans,” says Shields. “Others simply do not.”
Shatabdi Chakrabarti/We Animals Media
Over and over, experts have been warning that climate change will seriously disrupt our global food system .
In addition to directly harming animals, climate change is making it harder to grow the crops needed to feed the 97.6 billion land animals used globally for food each year. Farm animals who live on pastures and graze their food are not exempt from the harms.
A 2026 study in Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences found that by 2100, suitable grazing areas for farmed animals could shrink by up to 50%, displacing 1.4 billion farm animals and creating “substantial declines in grazing suitability across entire continents.”
Animal agriculture also uses massive amounts of water to grow feed, provide drinking water to farm animals and cool them down on hot days. Earlier this year, the U.N. announced the world had moved past a water crisis and into a “global water bankruptcy.”
“If something happens in the supply chain for either the feed or the water, that can have devastating effects on the animals,” Shields with Humane World for Animals says. “With climate change, I think those types of situations could become more common.”
Humane World for Animals is calling for an array of changes to address this growing threat. Our UK team is asking the British government to track and publish heat-related farm animal deaths and include farm animals in climate adaptation planning as sentient beings, not just economic units.

articles.title_orig: Family of US man who died on Six Flags ride question if death was preventable
articles.title_zh: Family of US man who died on Six Flags ride question if death was preventable
articles.content_orig:
Hassan Jihad Ibn Kariem died after reportedly ‘passing out’ and falling off Goliath rollercoaster in Georgia
The family of a man who was ejected from a rollercoaster at a Six Flags amusement park in Georgia and died has publicly questioned whether the death could have been prevented.
Hassan Jihad Ibn Kariem was riding the Goliath rollercoaster at Six Flags Over Georgia near Atlanta alongside his niece during a family trip to celebrate her birthday when he was thrown from the ride. His niece witnessed her uncle’s death, a relative told the Atlanta ABC News affiliate WSB-TV .
“A large part of me does believe, you know, it was a freak accident, but the other part of me questions … could this have been prevented?” Joshua Nelson, Kariem’s brother-in-law, told the outlet.
Nelson, whose daughter was seated beside Kariem, shared her account of the terrifying moments leading up to her uncle’s death.
“She said he fainted, or passed – her words were ‘he passed out,’” Nelson said. “And then they went up and down, up and down, up and down – and she said it went up again and his latch, I guess, snapped or came loose and he fell,” Nelson remarked.
During the celebratory family outing, Kariem had expressed his excitement about riding the Goliath, which was one of his favorite attractions, according to Nelson.
Nelson said that he hoped Kariem did not experience pain during his final moments.
Kariem was an educator and a father to a 10-year-old daughter. According to Atlanta public schools, Kariem started his career at Wesley International Academy as a technology teacher before being promoted to an information technology manager.
Georgia authorities as of Friday were still investigating the circumstances of Kariem’s death at Six Flags Over Georgia, which opened its gates Friday evening for the first time since the incident. Cobb county police department’s major crimes unit has launched an investigation.
Since Kariem’s death, Six Flags temporarily closed nine rollercoasters across six amusement parks around the US.
Deaths such as Kariem’s are rare. But his death has prompted some to call for federal oversight of amusement parks, which in the US has been left to individual states, as the New York Times reported .

articles.title_orig: Tech stocks tumble as AI debt fears rattle Wall Street
articles.title_zh: Tech stocks tumble as AI debt fears rattle Wall Street
articles.content_orig:
Financial markets slumped on Friday as investors bailed on technology stocks amid concerns that companies exposed to artificial intelligence are starting to wobble.
The tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite tumbled 573 points, or 2.1%, to end at 26,140, closing out its worst week since June. The broader S&P 500 and blue-chip Dow Industrial Average sank 1.1% and 0.3%, respectively.
Chipmakers and other tech companies have been under pressure this week as investors worry about the heavy borrowing associated with the emergence of AI and the rapid buildout of thousands of data centers required to provide computing power for AI models.
So-called neocloud companies like CoreWeave, which provide the brute computing power AI models need to function, were particularly hard hit. That's because they are financing much of their capital expenditures through debt and equity issuance rather than cash flow, raising investor concerns about mounting debt, market analyst Adam Crisafulli, head of Vital Knowledge, told CBS News.
Shares of CoreWeave slid nearly 12% on Friday and dropped roughly 24% this week as investors nervously eye its mounting debt. Micron Technology fell 5.6%, Advanced Micro Devices dropped 6%, Broadcom was down 4.5% and Intel lost 5.8%.
Elsewhere on Wall Street, Tesla shares fell 2.1% after the electric vehicle company unveiled a new Roadster sports car that appears capable of thrusting itself into the air.
The downturn on Friday came amid concern about whether the AI company Anthropic, soon set to go public, will be able to maintain its revenue momentum, Crisafulli said in a note to investors. Anthropic investors are now considering valuing the company at $1.5 trillion, down from the original target of $2 trillion, Reuters reported on Thursday.
Also rattling investors this week were fresh signs that U.S. inflation is increasing and moving further away from the Federal Reserve's 2% annual target.
Yields on the 10-year U.S. Treasury bonds — a key benchmark for mortgages, credit cards and other loans — held steady at 5.1% on Friday. Earlier this month, bond yields surged to their highest level in more than two decades amid concerns over inflation and rising U.S. government debt.
The hot inflation readings this week could spur the Federal Reserve to raise interest rates at its next meeting on Oct. 28-29, according to some economists. For now, most Wall Street traders expect the central bank to keep its short-term rate unchanged, but the odds of a rate hike at the Fed's December meeting have jumped to 74.3% from 50.2% a month ago, according to CME FedWatch, which tracks Fed funds futures prices.
On Friday, Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh offered no hints about potential interest rate policy moves while attending a meeting of financial leaders in Bangkok. The Fed hiked rates at its last meeting in September, bringing the federal funds rate to between 3.75% and 4% — its highest level since December 2025.
The Associated  Press contributed to this report.

articles.title_orig: X suspends 13,000 accounts linked to China, Russia and Iran - VOA
articles.title_zh: X suspends 13,000 accounts linked to China, Russia and Iran - VOA
articles.content_orig:
Editor's note: this story was translated from the original VOA Mandarin article.
Social media platform X says it has suspended more than 13,000 accounts involved in suspected foreign influence operations linked to China, Russia and Iran that targeted U.S. political discourse ahead of the November 3 midterm elections. In a statement posted on October 14, the platform said the networks used inauthentic accounts to post and amplify political content targeting candidates and public figures across the political spectrum. X said its safety team uses a variety of detection methods to identify and address activity that violates the platform's rules, building on security measures that operate around the clock throughout the year. “Free speech is the bedrock of a functioning democracy, and we are proud that X is the global town square where these debates happen,” the social media platform said. “Our job is to keep that conversation authentic, open, and safe.” X said its authenticity policy plays a key role in efforts to combat spam networks and influence operations that use coordinated inauthentic behavior to undermine the integrity of the platform. The company did not publicly provide evidence supporting its findings or specifying how many of the suspended accounts were linked to each country. X also highlighted what it calls its civic integrity policy, which addresses misleading content that could affect participation in elections or other civic processes. The policy covers information that could confuse voters about how, when or where to participate, as well as content intended to discourage participation. The platform said users can report potentially misleading content under the “Civic Integrity” category in its in-app reporting system. The company said its efforts to address election-related violations would continue through Election Day and beyond. X is not the only platform to raise concerns about alleged Chinese influence operations.
On June 10, OpenAI said it had disrupted two online influence operations linked to China. The operations used ChatGPT to generate social media posts, comments and images in an apparent effort to shape U.S. debates over artificial intelligence, data centers, tariffs and technology policy. OpenAI said in its report that the accounts used its models to support covert influence operations while concealing their origins and intentions. However, the company said the operations appeared to have limited impact, with no evidence that the content generated substantial authentic engagement or spread widely beyond the accounts involved. President Donald Trump also has accused China of attempting to interfere in U.S. elections. In a prime-time address in July, Trump warned that U.S. election infrastructure was vulnerable to foreign attacks, and he specifically accused China of trying to interfere in the 2020 presidential election. He did not provide evidence, though, that the election had been disrupted or that votes had been incorrectly counted. Despite his warnings, the president did not publicly raise the issue of alleged Chinese election interference during Chinese President Xi Jinping's visit to Washington last month.

articles.title_orig: El-Sayed responds after Vance calls him a "weasel" as Michigan Senate race grows contentious
articles.title_zh: El-Sayed responds after Vance calls him a "weasel" as Michigan Senate race grows contentious
articles.content_orig:
Marquette, Michigan – After being called a "weasel" who should "shut his mouth" by Vice President JD Vance, Michigan Democratic Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed said he was something else instead.
"No, no, no. What you're talking about is a f****** Wolverine. You could take your Buckeye and go shove it somewhere else," El-Sayed, a Michigan alumnus, told a crowd of over 1,300 in the Upper Peninsula of the state. Vance was previously Ohio's senator and is an Ohio State University graduate.
Vance, President Trump and Republicans have sought to portray El-Sayed, an epidemiologist who has led city and county health departments in Michigan, as an Islamic extremist. Late Thursday night, Mr. Trump in a Truth Social video accused El-Sayed of being a "Muslim radical" and a "Muslim Brotherhood Member," though there is no evidence for either claim.
During his own rally in Monroe on Thursday, Vance criticized El-Sayed's past critical comments about America's history, and said "it's clear – Abdul doesn't love this community, Democrat or Republican."
"He wants to litigate ancient grievances with your tax dollars, and he wants to use the grievances of faraway lands to punish you. Well, I say, on November the third, send a message to Abdul El-Sayed: Punish him, don't send him to Washington D.C," Vance told the crowd.
Vance and El-Sayed have traded jabs before. After an El-Sayed post questioned whether Vance's grandfather would have accepted second lady Usha Vance, an Indian-American, Vance called him "very, very evil."
In response to Vance's latest comments, El-Sayed said the remarks were intended "to raise questions about my commitment to America."
"I got a front-row seat to what my life might have been had I not been born in America. So don't lecture me about America," El-Sayed countered, in reference to trips he has taken to Egypt.
"In America, we don't discriminate against people for who they love, how they identify, how they pray, the color of their skin. We believe in an America big enough for all of us. So don't you dare come from Ohio to lecture me about America. You don't know a damn thing about America," he added.
Holding the Michigan Senate seat is critical to Democrats' efforts to flip control of the U.S. Senate into their hands in November. But the race has turned especially contentious this month.
At a campaign stop in Iron Mountain on Thursday, El-Sayed said the race could go down "as one of the ugliest campaigns in modern history," a reference to Republican claims that El-Sayed has ties to foreign terrorist groups.
The claims in part stem from old social media posts made by his half-sister, first reported by the conservative outlet The Washington Free Beacon , when she wrote about their mother's activism in the Muslim Brotherhood during college in the 1970s.
In 2012, after a Muslim Brotherhood candidate won the presidential race in Egypt, she wrote that her family "has long been MB" but added that she has "always felt that it has navigated the political sphere poorly/destructively."
El-Sayed has denied any ties to the Islamist organization and has criticized the attacks as being tied to his Muslim faith. He said after his parents divorced, he was raised by his father and stepmother in Michigan and did not see his mother for years and did not talk with her about any activism in the 1970s.
"My mom and my sister are not running for office. I'm running for office. Judge me by my actions and my work, but please do not assume that because I might pray differently than anybody who's ever held this office, that somehow I am not deeply committed to this Constitution," he added.
Islamophobic rhetoric on the campaign trail, including claims that El-Sayed himself is a terrorist, has increased in recent weeks. Far-right instigator Jake Lang and others held signs that read "Abdul = Terrorist In A Suit" at the protest of an El-Sayed event last weekend. The Rogers campaign condemned Lang's appearance and said it has no affiliation with him.
Republican protesters also showed up outside the first two stops of El-Sayed's tour on Thursday. They held signs with messages criticizing his "Medicare for All" platform, declaring "The United States Will Always Be A Christian Nation" and urging voters to "Keep Terror Out Of Congress."
On the campaign trail with Rogers last weekend, Republican Sen. John Kennedy of Louisiana quipped that El-Sayed "sleeps in a Bin Laden jersey."
Asked by CBS News Thursday if he thinks El-Sayed is a terrorist, Rogers replied, "Look at the data. It's pretty clear."
But speaking to reporters in Detroit on Friday about the recent focus on El-Sayed's religion in the Senate race, Rogers said the race "has never been about how you pray."
"You get to pray any way you want, and I passionately believe that. It is about your ideology and how you think. We can't let this be a campaign deciding to hunker down because they say it's Islamophobic or racist, or fill-in-the-blank," he said, according to Fox 2 Detroit .
The Upper Peninsula of Michigan accounts for just 3% of the state's total population, and Republicans have easily won the area since 2016. Mr. Trump won all but one of the area's 15 counties in 2024.
El-Sayed took his campaign bus there anyway, and brought Democratic Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez of New York with him as he tried to appeal to disaffected Republican and independent voters frustrated with the economy and the Iran War.
At packed stops, Ocasio-Cortez addressed the GOP attack ads and mailers targeting El-Sayed, and said they were trying to create a "caricature of him, so that you close your ears before you even hear what this man has to say."
Independent voter John Haigh says he's backing El-Sayed, and said the higher grocery, gas and diesel prices are a reason more conservative-leaning voters in the area are considering El-Sayed.
"You should always be looking at the other side and hearing what they have to say, not just negative ads," Haigh told CBS News at the Iron Mountain event.
About an hour away, in the small town of Escanaba, Republican voter Al Hansen said he likes El-Sayed's ideas on affordability. But Hansen is still backing Rogers, in part because he's skeptical of the feasibility of a government-run healthcare plan and the barrage of TV ads have not convinced him.
"How are you gonna do it? Of course, in a 30-second commercial they don't have time to explain that. It's very hard," Hansen conceded when spoke with CBS News at a coffee shop nearby El-Sayed's event.
Republican groups have spent over $119.2 million on TV ads in Michigan, compared to $86.6 million for Democratic groups, according to advertisement tracking firm AdImpact.
Last weekend in Highland, Michigan, Rogers dismissed El-Sayed's attempts to whittle away at his GOP base of support. He then pointed to his own wooing of typically Democratic enclaves in the Detroit metro area – with heavily Jewish and Black populations whom El-Sayed's primary opponent, Rep. Haley Stevens , won decisively.
"He really needs to shore up his base down here. That tells me they are desperate," Rogers told reporters. He claimed their internal polling shows they will get between 60% to 70% of Jewish Democratic voters who have been critical of El-Sayed's positions in opposition against the U.S.' relationship with Israel.
El-Sayed and his campaign have pointed to conversations he's had with the Jewish community, and support from Democratic statewide Jewish politicians, like Michigan Attorney General Dana Nessel and Sen. Elissa Slotkin.
Rogers has also targeted the Black vote in Detroit through appearances at churches and closed door conversations. He argues his education and housing plans appeal to Detroit voters, and that he is finding a "whole new coalition that's coming to us."
"Some of those areas in Detroit feel pretty neglected. They haven't had people down and around paying attention to them," Rogers told CBS News at Vance's rally Thursday. He added, "We even went into a church the other d

articles.title_orig: With Tesla Roadster debut, Elon Musk shows "flying cars are real"
articles.title_zh: With Tesla Roadster debut, Elon Musk shows "flying cars are real"
articles.content_orig:
Tesla CEO Elon Musk unveiled what he described as a "flying" car, equipped with thrusters, during a livestreamed event at his SpaceX rocket company's facility on Thursday.
Technical and regulatory challenges have so far prevented the much-hyped flying car sector from getting off the ground.
Musk revealed Tesla 's new Roadster sports car during a launch event at a SpaceX test facility in Texas.
During the demo, which was livestreamed on Tesla's X account, the car launched from a ramp that curled over so the vehicle was upside down, appearing to defy gravity by clinging to the surface before flying off the end, and then rolled over 180 degrees midair to land on its wheels.
"Flying cars are real," Musk said during the event, adding that the vehicle's "success is not guaranteed" but "it will probably work."
Musk said the car was equipped with "ultra high-pressure air tanks" to propel itself into the air .
The tech billionaire described the development as "what happens when you have a collaboration with the world's best car company and the world's best rocket company," referring to Tesla and SpaceX.
The vehicle would go into production in 2028, he said. Prices were not announced.
Tesla's website notes that the planned flying model is not approved for public road use.
Would-be buyers can place a reservation online, with a $5,000 deposit, for a non-flying model of the Roadster. A limited-edition Thrust model is also promised online but cannot be reserved. Tesla's website says the Rocket model, with its "full flight system," will be offered by invitation only.
"The Roadster will not move the volume or revenue needle, with production likely limited, and investors should not model it as a growth driver," Wall Street analyst Dan Ives of Yorkville Ives said in a research note. "What it does is restore the brand halo at the top of the market and put a spotlight on the engineering stack a week before the FY3Q26 print on October 21st."
It wasn't immediately clear what government agency would have oversight of the vehicle , CBS News senior transportation and national correspondent Kris Van Cleave reports. A senior U.S. Transportation Department official expressed some skepticism to CBS News that the vehicle will actually be able to take off, but acknowledged there wasn't a clear answer.
The National Highway Traffic Safety Administration typically has regulatory oversight of vehicles but delegates safety certification to the automaker. NHTSA didn't immediately respond to CBS News' request for comment.
The Federal Aviation Administration told CBS News the vehicle doesn't meet the agency's definition of an aircraft.
The concept of flying cars has been around almost as long as motor vehicles themselves, with American aviation pioneer Glenn Curtiss debuting the first flying car prototype in 1917. But successful designs have been pursued more seriously only in recent years as electric motors and high-performance batteries have advanced.
Ives said the Roadster shows how Tesla and SpaceX can collaborate. The new vehicle "puts the Tesla and SpaceX relationship on the table in a tangible way, with propulsion, pressure-vessel, and control hardware developed at the rocket company sitting on a Tesla product, which in our view strengthens the case for the two companies operating as one engineering platform over time," he said.
Musk — a major GOP political donor known for an often close but sometimes tumultuous relationship with President Trump — has thrust his companies to the forefront of several major industries, and he continues pushing into new ones.
SpaceX announced a week ago that it had agreed to buy licenses for radio airwaves that will enable its Starlink Mobile satellite business to provide cellular service inside buildings, a move the company said would allow it to "become a major mobile carrier in the U.S."
"This is the last critical piece of the spectrum puzzle needed for SpaceX to provide complete phone coverage in America," Musk said in an Oct. 8 social media post .

articles.title_orig: Trump denies limiting Ukraine access to Starlink network
articles.title_zh: Trump denies limiting Ukraine access to Starlink network
articles.content_orig:
US President Donald Trump has denied limiting Ukraine's access to Starlink's sister internet network Starshield after it restricted drone speed, hampering Kyiv's ability to protect itself from Russian attacks.
"It wasn't me and I don't think it was [Starlink owner] Elon [Musk]," Trump said, hours after Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said speed had yet to be restored.
Musk himself suggested the US government might have been behind the restrictions, while Reuters news agency reported on Thursday that the order had come from inside the White House.
Ukraine was hit by several deadly strikes on Tuesday after the network slowdown.
Starlink is a civilian-use high-speed internet network operated by Musk's SpaceX. Starshield - which relies on Starlink- is its military-grade sister service that was designed for the Pentagon.
The US had previously warned it could withhold sharing intelligence, crucial for Kyiv's defences, if Ukraine did not stop hitting Russian oil refineries.
Tension has been brewing between Washington and Kyiv for days over a recent controversial diesel deal between Russia and the US.
Zelensky - angered by the deal - resumed targeting Russian oil refineries this week in a move criticised by Trump three days after he announced a ceasefire on energy infrastructure. Kyiv said it would stop the strikes if Russia did the same but Moscow  never confirmed the ceasefire and continued its attacks.
"If I don't stand up to this... who else will?" Zelensky asked EU leaders at a summit on Friday.
Trump had also said that Zelensky was "more difficult to deal with than [Russian President Vladimir] Putin".
But speaking to reporters as he left the White House on Friday, the US president said he had a good relationship with his Ukrainian counterpart.
Asked about Starshield, he said he was "not sure" it "ever came down".
Musk earlier explained that Starshield was managed by the US government, and that the Pentagon could have been responsible.
In its report about the alleged order regarding Starshield, Reuters quoted two US officials and a Western official briefed on the matter.
The US government has allowed Ukraine to use Starlink and Starshield in its defence against Russia. Musk cut Moscow's access to the service in February, giving Kyiv an advantage in the conflict.
On Tuesday night, Starlink restricted speed limits to 100mph (160km/h), meaning any weapons that travelled faster than that lost connectivity to the network.
Some 600,000 in Ukraine were left without power as communications and energy facilities used by Ukraine's military were also hit in the deadly attacks.
A bipartisan group of US senators has signed a letter demanding an investigation into the disruptions to the network.
"Restrictions reportedly degraded Ukraine's ability to conduct defensive operations against Russian drone and missile attacks on civilian infrastructure," the letter read.
On Friday, French President Emmanuel Macron vowed that EU states would not abandon Ukraine.
Speaking at the end of the two-day summit in Brussels attended by Zelensky, Macron said it was Europe's job to hold the line in the face of some people's "ambiguities". That was apparently a reference to signs of wavering US support for Ukraine.
Funding for Ukraine and helping it get through another freezing winter - its fifth since Russia's full-scale invasion in 2022 - topped the summit's agenda.
The war will cost €155bn (£131bn; $174bn) next year, Zelensky told the European Council, with at least €70bn needed to come from the EU for defence and weapons.
Macron said Europe was working to help Ukraine with its satellite and early warning systems, and Ukraine's friends would look at its request for further aid.
