articles.title_orig: Trouble: buyers would rather wait for Chinese EVs than buy Western ones
articles.title_zh: Trouble: buyers would rather wait for Chinese EVs than buy Western ones
articles.content_orig:
Canadian EV customers are delaying buying decisions while they wait for more Chinese EVs to reach their shores, according to a new survey, suggesting widespread awareness of China’s EV dominance is causing EV buyers to ignore Western automakers’ offerings entirely.
The survey was commissioned by Clean Energy Canada , and shows that Canadian interest in EVs is slowly ticking up, with nearly half of them inclined, likely or certain to buy an EV as their next vehicle.
But more interestingly, among potential EV buyers, there’s one big stumbling block: China.
Originally, Canada had the same tariff on Chinese EVs that the USA had, a 100% tariff implemented ( unwisely ) by President Biden. As trade partners with the US and with a heavily intermeshed auto industry (given Detroit is literally a stone’s throw away from Canada), Canada thought it would be wise to maintain a united front on auto tariffs.
But then, idiocy happened . The squatter in the US White House put tariffs on Canada leading to immediate job losses , and repeatedly threatened its sovereignty. Now, the US’ relationship with Canada is strained, and Canada is looking towards the rest of the world for allies.
At the same time, China saw an opportunity, and decided to put a tariff on Canadian canola . This was a big deal for farmers in the center of the country, and led to the somewhat unexpected effect of the most conservative, oil-loving Canadian provinces lobbying the Canadian government to drop tariffs on Chinese EVs and allow them into the country, in exchange for China dropping canola tariffs.
Now, China and Canada have an agreement which will allow 49,000 Chinese EVs into the country per year, and the first have started to arrive .
But so far, there aren’t actually a ton of Chinese EV models available in Canada yet. Companies are spinning up their distribution networks, but everything is still in progress. Canada is actually nowhere near selling out this year’s 49k quota, with only about 16k Chinese EVs imported total.
Some brands, like Tesla, have already hit their quota allocation , because they already had distribution networks built up. Other brands are lagging. So there aren’t that many models available, and more are expected to hit shores next year.
This has led to a situation where Canadian buyers know that a wave of high-tech, new, reasonably priced EVs are just around the corner (although they are perhaps overestimating how cheap those EVs will be, as prices will be higher in Canada than in China). And where the type of cars they currently have access to in North America are largely from Western brands that have spent this year lobbying against EVs and canceling models . Or, perhaps worse, brands that are associated with the US, which are subject to significantly more negative public opinion in Canada than ever before.
So, Canadian EV buyers don’t want to buy American cars, and know Chinese EVs are coming, and are higher tech and cheaper than European and Japanese EVs.
This all led to the interesting survey result in question. Of the 48% of Canadians surveyed who said they were likely to buy an EV for their next vehicle, 42% said they wanted to “wait for more Chinese EVs to become available.”
So, these are Canadians who already want an EV, and are ready to buy one – at least the next time they buy a car. But instead of getting one, at a time when gas prices are at historic highs (due to, uh, the same aforementioned idiocy), they’re waiting until they see more Chinese cars.
This is a massive condemnation of everything the West has to offer in the electric space right now. In the past, it was thought that Western buyers might be skeptical of Chinese brands, thinking them to be lower quality, as has been the stereotype in the West for a long time.
But now, that dynamic has flipped on its head – Canadians are refusing the options available to them now, and waiting for Chinese options to become available, expecting them to be superior than the traditional options that have been available to them.
And given that it’s taking time for Chinese brands to establish their networks and ship cars Canada, that means a lot of Canadian buyers are twiddling their thumbs right now.
It’s an interesting situation, given most other countries already have access to Chinese EVs, and they’re selling well in those countries. And it perhaps offers us a view to what might happen to the US auto industry, if there’s ever a sniff that Chinese EVs might come here (which, inevitably, in the long term, I am sure they will).
With US automakers so far behind on electrification, and constantly lobbying to fall even further behind , it doesn’t feel like the gap is going to get any smaller. Eventually, Americans will see that the rest of the world, including their two closest neighbors, are getting access to cheap, efficient EVs that don’t give them the anxiety of supporting the most evil industry in the history of the world to fuel. Eventually, they’ll get tired of spending so much for so little , when everyone else gets great cars for cheap.
They're avoiding AMERICAN product, just like whisky. If they do need a new car they'll probably wait until Trump is out of office to see if we become friendly and rational again if a Canadian product isn't suitable.  And I don't believe there are any Canadian EVs.
There are a few moves within American automakers to try to compete , but it remains to be seen if that’s too little or too late. China has released literally thousands of new EV models, with cutthroat competition driving prices down and quality up.
We do not see that sort of competition happening in the US, especially after republicans sent so many EV jobs to China . And being given the safety blanket of tariffs won’t encourage harsher competition , it will just lull automakers into a false sense of security . The only way to catch a moving target that’s in front of you is to move faster than them, and US automakers simply are not doing that right now.
But US consumers will figure it out eventually. And Canada’s EV buyers are a signal of what’s to come.

articles.title_orig: Stock Market Today: Dow, S&P 500 and Nasdaq sink to session lows as tech rout continues and oil prices surge
articles.title_zh: Stock Market Today: Dow, S&P 500 and Nasdaq sink to session lows as tech rout continues and oil prices surge
articles.content_orig:
Stocks slid on Friday as traders notched a mostly losing week amid a shift away from tech and artificial intelligence-related names as well as a rise in oil prices.
The S&P 500 lost 1.09% and ended at 7,659.44, while the Nasdaq Composite shed 2.14% to close at 26,140.03. Both indexes ended the session below their 50-day moving averages. The Dow Jones Industrial Average fell 175.28 points, or 0.34%, to 52,002.41. The sell-off sent the Cboe Volatility Index (VIX) above 22 for the first time in four months .
Chipmakers were lower again. The VanEck Semiconductor ETF (SMH) lost 3%, led by declines in Micron Technology , Advanced Micro Devices and Sandisk . Semiconductors have struggled this week amid jitters about competition from China . The SMH slid 10% week to date for its biggest weekly decline since April 2025.
Those declines, coupled with drops in other stocks linked to AI, dragged the S&P 500 to a losing week. The benchmark index fell about 2% this week, while the Nasdaq shed more than 4% for its worst week since June. The Dow, on the other hand, advanced 0.7% on the week.
Investors have also grown concerned that tech companies are borrowing too much for the AI buildout . Shares of neoclouds like CoreWeave , which has seen its total debt rise to more than $51 billion , were down nearly 12%, bringing the stock's week-to-date losses to 25%.
"The question is: Is this a systemic issue?" said Michael Rosen, Angeles' chief investment officer. "Obviously, increased debt issuance is something to observe and continue to watch and be concerned about if it continues to get to levels of excessiveness. But we're not remotely close to that right now."
Other areas of the market such as energy saw gains Friday, with stocks like Chevron helping to keep the Dow's losses in check. Oil prices moved higher amid rising tensions between the U.S. and Iran as well as between Russian and Ukraine. West Texas Intermediate crude futures increased 3.51% to settle at $101.41 per barrel, while Brent crude futures advanced 3.72% to $109.86.
Simultaneously, investors have been grappling with hotter-than-expected inflation data, which has been exacerbated by elevated energy prices in the wake of the U.S.-Iran war. Wholesale inflation this week saw its biggest gain since 2022 , while consumer inflation remained well above the Federal Reserve's target of 2%.
Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh spoke at an IMF event in Bangkok overnight. And while he didn't comment on whether the Fed would raise rates before year-end, traders took that as a sign that the central bank will hold policy steady later this month. The CME Group's FedWatch tool points to an 82% chance the Fed keeps its overnight rate unchanged at its Oct. 27-28 meeting.
The three leading U.S. indexes ended Friday's session with losses.
The S&P 500 dropped 1.09% to finish at 7,659.44, while the Nasdaq Composite lost 2.14% to 26,140.03. The Dow Jones Industrial Average shed 175.28 points, or 0.34%, to 52,002.41.
As the market sell-off intensified Friday afternoon, the Cboe Volatility Index (VIX) rose to levels it last closed at four months ago.
The VIX rose to 21.32, as of 3:10 p.m., rising more than 4.8 points on the session. It's on pace for its highest close since June 10, when it closed at 22.22.
Typically, when the VIX is above 20 that indicates greater fear in the market. The index last closed above that level on July 29 , when markets fell after the Federal Reserve kept interest rates steady at its meeting that month. The next day , stocks rose, and the day marked a bottom in a market where many AI-related stocks had been selling off in the previous month .
The Nasdaq Composite was down about 2.5% in afternoon trading on Friday, bringing its loss on the week to almost 5%.
With that move, the tech-heavy index on pace for its worst weekly performance since the week ended April 4, 2025, when the index recorded a roughly 10% drop.
Communication services and information technology led the S&P 500 lower on Friday.
The two sectors were down 2.7% and 2.4%, respectively, becoming the two biggest laggards among the 11 S&P 500 sectors. Consumer discretionary followed behind them, falling 1.5%.
However, a look beneath the surface showed that the S&P 500 — which was last down 1.3% — was more evenly split despite the losses at the index level. There were about 280 losers in the index and 222 gainers.
In total, five out of the 11 S&P 500 sectors were in positive territory, led by energy with its 2.1% gain and utilities with its rise of 1.2%.
— Sean Conlon and Sarah Min
U.S. crude oil prices rose sharply Friday as Iran escalated its attacks in the Strait of Hormuz this week and Ukraine vowed to keep striking Russian refineries.
U.S. West Texas Intermediate futures were up 2.9% to $100.78 per barrel. Brent crude, the international benchmark, was 3.3% higher at $109.37 per barrel. Read more .

In recent months, that bet has paid off for the value investor. After falling about 40% in the first quarter of 2026, during which the enterprise software stock at various points was trading at not even three times revenue, the stock went on to surge more than 55% in the third. It's also outperforming this week, rising more than 2% amid a broader tech sell-off as investors exit for safer assets.

articles.title_orig: The Rupturing Trump-Zelensky Relationship Stands to Hurt Ukraine and Its European Allies
articles.title_zh: The Rupturing Trump-Zelensky Relationship Stands to Hurt Ukraine and Its European Allies
articles.content_orig:
President Donald Trump has labeled Ukraine’s resumption of strikes on Russian oil refineries a “disgrace,” the latest salvo in his campaign to pressure the U.S. ally over rising gas prices that could cost Republicans in next month’s midterm elections .
Kyiv said Thursday that it would no longer abide by Trump’s “energy ceasefire,” citing Russia’s refusal to halt its own attacks on Ukraine’s power grid. President Volodymyr Zelenskyy angrily accused the U.S. of costing civilian lives by striking deals with Moscow and withdrawing support that is crucial to Kyiv’s defense against the invasion launched by President Vladimir Putin.
Ukrainian officials had raised alarm after gaps in intelligence sharing left Kyiv vulnerable to Russian attacks and restrictions on the Starlink satellite service disrupted military operations.  Zelenskyy said Friday that the technology was still not fully restored.
With Ukraine defying his demands to halt strikes, Trump responded late Thursday.
“If you tell me that Zelenskyy is again shooting at refineries, all he’s doing is making the world oil price higher,” Trump told Newsmax’s Rob Finnerty. “I think that’s a disgrace. There’s plenty of other targets; they don’t have to hit,” Trump said.
“Zelenskyy is not a good guy for us to deal with” on the war, he said, adding that “I think they actually both would like to see it end, but I think I find Zelenskyy to be more difficult to deal with than Putin.”
As his clash escalated with Trump, Zelenskyy was in Brussels on Friday to shore up support from European allies, whom he called “real leaders” as they gathered for a crucial summit.
Ukraine hit a Russian oil refinery Thursday after Zelenskyy said he was “done” with the truce, which Trump had announced to the apparent surprise of both sides in the war. Neither Moscow nor Kyiv reported any new strikes on Russian refineries Friday.
Trump has sought to blame Ukraine’s strikes for destabilizing the price of diesel globally, despite the impact of his own war with Iran .
But this campaign of attacks deep inside enemy territory has given Ukraine crucial leverage, sparking a major fuel crisis inside Russia .
Kyiv hoped this would give it a stronger hand at the negotiating table, but as Washington pushes for an end to the conflict it has taken a series of steps that have caused surprise and alarm among Ukraine and its backers in Europe.
Last week, Trump announced a deal to buy diesel from Russia, an apparent attempt to relieve pressure at the pump for American consumers ahead of the midterm elections but which reversed years of U.S. policy. Trump then called for Kyiv to stop all strikes on Russian oil infrastructure and said Zelenskyy had to be replaced as Ukraine’s leader.
It comes amid mounting questions about whether the U.S. is still sharing critical military intelligence with Ukraine after a pair of major strikes earlier this week that Kyiv said came without a usual advance warning from its partners.
Ukraine also reported a slowing down of the Starlink satellite terminals , which are critical for its army’s communications, drone missions and aerial defenses.
Kyiv said that Starshield, the military version of the technology that is used by Ukraine’s troops, had been limited without any warning.
SpaceX chief Elon Musk, the billionaire Trump ally, said that such decisions were up to the U.S. military and ultimately Trump.
After repeated requests for comment about Musk’s statement, a senior U.S. official told NBC News that “no such request was ever made by the president.” Trump has also denied restricting military intelligence for Ukraine.
Kyiv said Thursday the Starshield service was being restored, but the episode only added to the mounting suspicion in Ukraine that the U.S. was willing to cut it off from battlefield support in order to exert pressure for a peace deal. Asked about the service on Friday, Zelenskyy said that issues were ongoing. “Has the speed been fully restored to what it was? No. Is the speed returning? Yes,” he told reporters in Brussels.
European and Ukrainian officials told NBC News they believed that the moves, coming only days after Trump eased sanctions on Russia’s diesel exports and railed against Zelenskyy, were most likely aimed at pressuring Kyiv into making concessions at the negotiating table amid the stalemate in peace talks.
The Kremlin agreed with Trump on Friday, with spokesman Dmitry Peskov saying it was clear that “Zelenskyy doesn’t want to take responsibility and move toward a peaceful resolution.”
Russia has always stated it’s open to a peace settlement but only on its own hard-line terms, which would see Ukraine ceding significant territory.
Yuliya Talmazan is a reporter for NBC News Digital, based in London.

articles.title_orig: Police assess Palestine Action post by national security adviser's wife
articles.title_zh: Police assess Palestine Action post by national security adviser's wife
articles.content_orig:
Police are assessing a social media post by the wife of the government's national security adviser Jonathan Powell which referenced Palestine Action, a group labelled a terrorist organisation by the Home Office.
Sarah Helm wrote on the social media site X: "God help us authors who support Palestine and Palestine Action."
She was responding to a discussion on Sky News about the author Sally Rooney, whose novels will not be supplied to booksellers in the UK following her announcement that she intends to use her royalties to support Palestine Action.
A No 10 spokeswoman said Helm was "an individual who does not represent the government in any capacity". The BBC has attempted to contact Helm for comment.
On Friday, a Metropolitan Police spokesperson said: "We have been made aware of an X post on Thursday, 15 October referencing Palestine Action.
"It is in the process of being assessed to determine whether any further police investigation may be required."
Reform UK MP Danny Kruger has written to the prime minister raising concerns about Helm's post.
The Campaign Against Antisemitism said the post was "gobsmacking".
"Spouses are entitled to independent views, but plainly Mr Powell, who leads on our country's national security and has been intricately involved in our Middle East diplomacy, must publicly denounce this rhetoric if he is to continue in post," the group said.
However, Green Party leader Zack Polanski said: "Sarah Helm is speaking absolute common sense and should be commended for her bravery."
He called for Palestine Action to be de-proscribed "immediately", calling its official labelling as a terror group "ludicrous and authoritarian".
Helm is an author and journalist, who has previously worked at the Sunday Times and as a foreign correspondent for the Independent.
Palestine Action describes itself as a "direct action movement" that uses "disruptive tactics".
Earlier this year, four of the group's activists were jailed after causing £1.2m of damage at a UK site of an Israel-based defence firm.
In 2025, the UK government proscribed Palestine Action as a terrorist group, saying it would not "tolerate" organisations that put the UK's national security at risk.
The proscription made it a criminal offence to belong to or support Palestine Action, punishable by up to 14 years in prison.
The government's decision triggered a wave of protests, which saw an estimated 3,700 people arrested in the UK for publicly expressing their support for the group.
Around 2,500 have been charged, but the cases have not gone to trial as a legal challenge to the proscription is due to be heard in the Supreme Court next month.
Powell began his government career as a diplomat but later served as an adviser in Tony Blair's government, where he was credited with negotiating a peace deal in Northern Ireland.
In 2024, Sir Keir Starmer appointed him as national security adviser, a position he retained when Andy Burnham became prime minister.

articles.title_orig: Designing for world in flux
articles.title_zh: Designing for world in flux
articles.content_orig:
At Harvard’s Graduate School of Design, students are often hoping to make structures and innovations that last.
But the current era has been marked by relatively rapid environmental, social, political, and technological shifts across the globe. Designers are increasingly being asked to make things that can be adaptable, accessible, and economical.
Enter “ Infrastructure in a Time of Flux: Methods, Conditions, and Situations ,” the School’s fall exhibit on display in the Druker Design Gallery through December. The show spotlights architectural, engineering, urban planning, and design innovations focused on building for a world in transition.
“I think there’s an interesting tension between these two words,” said Rahul Mehrotra , professor of urban design and planning and co-curator along with Dan Borelli , GSD exhibitions director. “Infrastructure is generally understood as a stable framework within which life happens, but flux suggests almost the opposite. Flux implies movement, change, uncertainty, transformation. So what happens to our understanding of infrastructure when permanence can no longer be assumed as the fundamental condition of the city?”
Mehrotra said he was inspired in part by his home city of Mumbai, where the Hindu Kumbh Mela festival brings millions of people into a camp created just for the celebration. The festival grounds are dismantled just as quickly as they are constructed — a temporary city within a city.
“Millions of people arrive, infrastructures are assembled — roads, bridges, sanitation, electricity, water, housing, markets, security systems — all come together,” Mehrotra said. “It has all the attributes of a regular city, and then after a relatively short period — 55 days — it takes only three or four weeks to assemble it and takes 10 days to disassemble it. The land returns to another condition.”
He’s also drawn inspiration from artists, including Christo and Jeanne-Claude, who made their mark creating large-scale temporary installations across the globe. The exhibition features stills of their work, including the iconic 1985 covering of the Pont Neuf in Paris.
“[Christo] would always say permanence is the enemy of freedom,” said Vladimir Yavachev, director of operations at the Christo and Jeanne-Claude Foundation. “You can pick up and go at any time. You don’t have to be dependent.”
In addition to exploring impermanence , the exhibition is an examination of feasibility, highlighting techniques, materials, and practices that balance efficacy with affordability and efficiency.
Some examples include scaffolding in New York City that allows construction to take place without interrupting pedestrian traffic, and plastic housing for Ethiopia’s Kobe Refugee Camp, where there are about 37,000 people .
“Some of the examples in the exhibition are speculative, artistic, and even dreamy. Others are scrappy, ad hoc, and poignant. Some harken back to very old traditions. Other others are futuristic,” said Sarah Whiting , GSD dean and Josep Lluís Sert Professor of Architecture. “Every example offers fodder for thinking and acting. We have nine different degree programs here at the GSD, ranging from urban design to design engineering to ecologies, architecture, and more. And I think every one of them is reflected by the work displayed in the exhibition out there.”
Some methods embrace geometry and dynamic movement to create lightweight and affordable structures and infrastructure.
One example are space frames — truss lattices of interlocking geometric patterns like you might see in an airplane hangar — which distribute load evenly across structures and eliminate need for permanent load bearing beams or columns.
Another involves folded structures, often done with stiff plastic, that transform flexible materials into sturdy shapes .
Scholars say designers often face projects that require them to consider questions like: How do people actually access different resources? Would they be willing to travel for certain things? How far? What occupied the site before and what connotations does that space hold? How much buy-in exists from stakeholders?
“People move, economies change, buildings are adapted, spaces are occupied differently, new meanings are attached to old places,” Mehrotra said. “The city is constantly being adjusted.”
And sometimes design is only intended to be temporary for celebrations, religious gatherings, nomadic groups, disaster victims, and military refugees.
During Italy’s Feast of the Redeemer, a temporary pontoon bridge brings visitors and pilgrims to the Church of the Most Holy Redeemer, commonly known as Il Redentore. At Burning Man, a temporary city in the desert makes sure festival-goers have access to food, water, and bathrooms.
“Reversibility is not just about whether we can take something apart. It is about how we think. It asks whether the things we build can anticipate change. Can they be adapted? Can they be moved? Can they be reused? Can they be dismantled? Can they leave something behind, or perhaps leave almost nothing behind?” Mehrotra said.
A symposium will be held on Nov. 12 and 13 bringing together designers, architects, humanitarian workers, and historians to reflect on the exhibition’s three themes and interrogate the Kumbh Mela festival as a case study.

articles.title_orig: “Against Tech Oligarchy”: Inside the Worker Resistance in the World’s Most Powerful Industry - Democracy Now!
articles.title_zh: “Against Tech Oligarchy”: Inside the Worker Resistance in the World’s Most Powerful Industry - Democracy Now!
articles.content_orig:
Sign up for Democracy Now!'s Daily Digest to get our latest headlines and stories delivered to your inbox every day.
Longtime tech worker organizers Clarissa Redwine and JS Tan’s new book, Against Tech Oligarchy: Worker Resistance in the World’s Most Powerful Industry , draws on the authors’ experiences at major tech companies to chronicle the rise and fall of the tech worker movement, its early victories, and the repression and slide to corporate control that followed.
“Over the course of the 2010s, what we saw was that the tech industry wasn’t quite the industry that it had promised to its workers and to the public. Rather than making the world more open, more democratic, we saw it really be the culprit of misinformation,” says Tan, who was pushed out of Microsoft after raising objections to the company’s ties to fossil fuel companies.
Silicon Valley’s slide to the right was influenced by corporate backlash to labor’s demands, explains Redwine, who was fired from Kickstarter for union organizing. She says she hopes to inspire a new generation of tech workers to organize “within these tech oligarchs’ own empires, to stand up and push back.”
AMY GOODMAN : This is Democracy Now! , democracynow.org, The War and Peace Report . I’m Amy Goodman.
If you work in the tech industry, your boss might not want you to tune in to our next segment. It’s about a remarkable new book called Against Tech Oligarchy: Worker Resistance in the World’s Most Powerful Industry . It’s written by longtime tech worker organizers Clarissa Redwine and JS Tan. Drawing on their own experience organizing at high-tech companies, they chronicle the rise of the tech worker movement, its early victories, and the challenges it faces today as tech titans consolidate their economic and political power, while tech workers face mass layoffs.
Clarissa Redwine helped unionize Kickstarter, where she was fired amidst a union-busting campaign before workers went on to win union recognition. JS Tan is a former Microsoft software engineer who publicly challenged Microsoft’s work with the Pentagon, with ICE and with fossil fuel companies, including its use of cloud and AI technologies to help Chevron expand oil extraction.
Their new book comes as tech companies embrace artificial intelligence, workplace surveillance and increased automation. At Meta, for example, a new initiative will collect workers’ mouse movements, keystrokes and some screenshots to help train AI models to replace them in the future. In response, Meta workers reached out to United Tech and Allied Workers, a branch of the Communication Workers Union, to discuss unionization efforts and how best to resist.
Clarissa Redwine and JS Tan join us now.
We welcome you both to Democracy Now! It’s great to have you with us. Clarissa, let’s start with you. First of all, explain what Kickstarter is and how you got the experience you did, and then how you tried to unionize your workplace, though it ultimately did get unionized.
CLARISSA REDWINE : Yes, it did. Yeah. So, I joined the tech industry in a moment where there was a lot of optimism for what tech could do for society. And Kickstarter was especially idealistic, where the reason the platform exists is to give communities a tool for bringing projects to life, cultural projects, but also technology. And, you know, in 2016, when I joined, there was a moment where tech management and workers felt aligned and united against the Trump administration. But as the years went by, we saw, over and over, tech companies capitulating, becoming complicit in the rise of the alt-right. And there came a moment at Kickstarter where we had the same experience.
So, there was a moment where Breitbart wrote an article saying that a Kickstarter project was inciting violence. This project was a comic book called Always Punch Nazis , which they did not like. And management decided, rather than stand up to Breitbart and this push from the alt-right, that they would cancel the project. And I and my co-workers demanded that we keep this project on the site. And that moment of collective action was transformative for myself, but also my co-workers, where we saw the promise of collective action. And after that, we decided we wanted structural power in the workplace. We wanted lasting change. And we fought for a union, and we won.
AMY GOODMAN : And talk about where you went in that struggle.
CLARISSA REDWINE : Yeah, so, I was part of the core organizing group at Kickstarter, and when management was attempting to bust the union, they decided to fire a third of our organizing committee in the same week. And unfortunately, I was first to go. But it was all completely worth it. And the reason that Kickstarter is such a bright spot in the tech worker movement is because it showed tech workers across the industry that it was possible to win a union. And ever since, I’ve been organizing and building worker power.
AMY GOODMAN : And, JS Tan, talk about your experience at Microsoft.
JS TAN : Yeah, you know, so, I started in the tech industry in the mid-2010s, and my first job out of college was at Microsoft. And, you know, I think it was around that time where this idea that the tech sector, you know, with the rise of the internet especially, was going to be this place that could really push for a more open society, a more connected society, and even a more democratic society. And so, coming out of college, you know, myself and a lot of us coming out of these CS departments had these ideas that joining the tech industry and building these internet platforms would allow us to do just that. And so, that’s what happened to me when I went to Microsoft.
But, you know, I think over the course of the 2010s, what we saw was that the tech industry wasn’t quite — you know, wasn’t quite the industry that it had sort of promised to its workers and to the public, right? You know, rather than making the world more open, more democratic, we saw it really be the culprit of misinformation. You know, when I started at Microsoft, they were starting to get involved with military contracts with the Pentagon. And, you know, in particular at Microsoft, at that time when I was working there, there was this really strong messaging push from the bosses that Microsoft was going to be this place of — that was really going to push the agenda of sustainability and green technology. But, you know, from the inside, it was clear to me and many of my co-workers that, actually, they were collaborating with the oil and gas companies and, in many cases, helping them intensify the drilling that these companies were doing.
AMY GOODMAN : And how did they respond to those inside raising objections?
JS TAN : Yeah, I mean, compared to some of the other companies, they were a little bit more tactful and not sort of just outright firing a lot of the organizers. But in my case, you know, I had gone to Kazakhstan and had had sort of seen up close how Chevron wanted to use Microsoft cloud and AI technologies to drill and to extract even more oil. And, you know, I came back to the U.S. and wrote about it all in an essay, and that ended up getting me in some trouble, where I ended up getting pushed out of the company.
AMY GOODMAN : And what do you do now?
JS TAN : Well, now I’m a — I’m a graduate student at MIT , and I continue, with Clarissa, to continue to organize in the tech worker movement.
AMY GOODMAN : So, this latest news that we just included in the lede about Meta, Clarissa, a new initiative collecting workers’ mouse movements, keystrokes and some screenshots to help train AI models to replace them in the future, especially for the Luddites among us, if you can explain what exactly that means?
CLARISSA REDWINE : Yes, absolutely. So, you know, if you think about how a company operates, management is always trying to cut costs, cut corners. And the management at Meta saw that they had this very valuable resource, which was their employees and the work that their employ

articles.title_orig: U.S. Budget Deficit Nears $2 Trillion, a Reality Check for Trump’s Cost Cutting
articles.title_zh: U.S. Budget Deficit Nears $2 Trillion, a Reality Check for Trump’s Cost Cutting
articles.content_orig:
The federal budget deficit rose to nearly $2 trillion for the past fiscal year, which ended September 30, the Treasury Department reported Friday.
It was the largest annual deficit since 2021, during the height of the pandemic, when the federal government doled out support to keep the economy and Americans afloat.
This past fiscal year’s deficit was 12% higher than the prior year’s $1.78 trillion gap.
Net interest payments on the public debt topped $1 trillion for the first time, driven up in part by the nation’s skyrocketing debt levels and higher interest rates. The United States spent more on interest than on any category other than Social Security and Medicare.
The deficit also grew because the Trump administration had to issue refunds after the Supreme Court found that certain global tariffs it imposed violated federal law . The Treasury Department estimates that about $145 billion in tariff refunds was issued in the last fiscal year.
Although the economy is in relatively good shape, the nation’s fiscal health has worsened in recent years with neither Republicans nor Democrats on Capitol Hill willing to fully address the issue.
“Today’s deficit figures cap off a remarkably dismal year for our fiscal health,” Maya MacGuineas, president of the Committee for a Responsible Federal Budget, said in a statement. “Fiscal discipline requires finding something both achievable and aggressive … Tough choices will be needed to get there, and we’re running out of time to make them.”
Federal budget deficit climbs to $2 trillion as fiscal jitters multiply
The US debt hit a record $40 trillion in August, a grim milestone that will have consequences for Americans, businesses and the government for years to come. Yet the “big, beautiful bill” that President Donald Trump and congressional Republicans enacted last year is expected to add trillions more to the national debt over a decade as its generous tax breaks outweigh the package’s spending cuts.
The nation’s growing financial woes, along with rising corporate debt supply and expectations for higher Federal Reserve interest rates, have sparked turmoil in bond markets in recent months. Investors are increasingly jittery, which has sent rates on US debt soaring: The yield on the 10-year Treasury note recently hit its highest level since 2002. That has also led to higher mortgage rates, making it even more difficult to buy and sell homes.
With rising deficits, the government has to issue more bonds to fund its spending. Yields on bonds have soared this year as investors demand more compensation to hold US debt. That raises the government’s cost of borrowing, exacerbating concerns about the mounting debt burden.
The average weighted interest rate of the debt outstanding was 3.53% at the end of the fiscal year, up from 3.36% at the end of the prior fiscal year, according to the Treasury Department.
Meanwhile, the deficit as a share the nation’s economy was more than 6% in the last fiscal year, according to Treasury’s rough estimate. That’s more than twice Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent’s goal.
The Republicans’ sweeping tax cuts are also starting to have an effect. Although many businesses are raking in higher profits, gross corporate tax revenue declined by $43 billion, or 9%.
The “big, beautiful bill” allowed companies to take larger deductions for certain investments. Most of the “big, beautiful bill’s” historic cuts – notably to Medicaid – don’t start kicking in until next year.
At the same time, Social Security benefits are becoming more costly as the nation ages, which also contributed to the widening gap between revenue and spending.
Lawmakers will likely have another chance to address the nation’s fiscal problems next year, when the US is once again expected to hit the debt ceiling .
CNN’s John Towfighi contributed to this report.

articles.title_orig: Pope Asks Putin for a Cease-Fire for a Ukrainian City Under Siege
articles.title_zh: Pope Asks Putin for a Cease-Fire for a Ukrainian City Under Siege
articles.content_orig:
Pope Leo spoke with Russian President Vladimir Putin from hospital on Friday, just days after his lung cancer surgery, and expressed his concern about the “grave humanitarian situation” in a Russian-occupied Ukrainian city.
During the call, the Vatican said Leo expressed “deep concern” about the conditions in Oleshky, a Russian-occupied Ukrainian city in the Kherson region where Ukrainian authorities say around 2,000 civilians remain and supply routes for food and medicine are blocked.
Leo, to whom Ukrainians have appealed for help, called for a local ceasefire to allow for civilians to be safely evacuated and aid to be delivered.
Putin “supported” the Vatican’s intention to help alleviate the dire humanitarian situation, the Kremlin said in a statement. Ukraine has accused Russia of “deliberately creating a humanitarian catastrophe” in Oleshky.
Cardinal Pietro Parolin, the Holy See secretary of state, told reporters he hoped Putin would act on the pope’s requests.
“I hope that faced with a request from the Holy Father, … President Putin agrees to implement what the Pope asked of him,” Parolin said.
The pope’s call with Putin, only the second in Leo’s papacy, offers another indication that he is returning to work after undergoing lung cancer surgery on Tuesday.
Leo led Mass at midday on Friday with off-duty medical and nursing staff from the Gemelli Hospital present as the Vatican said he showed “steady improvement” after having part of his lung removed earlier in the week. Pictures of the pontiff showed him standing up and celebrating mass in the hospital’s makeshift chapel.
The pope thanked staff for their work caring for him and others who are sick during his homily, the Vatican said.
The Mass took place in a room on the 10th floor of the hospital where a suite of rooms is set aside for any time a pope is admitted for medical treatment.
The Vatican also said that Pope Leo will recite the traditional Angelus prayers on Sunday in what will be his first public appearance since his treatment.
US President Donald Trump said he had spoken to the pope’s brother and asked him to pass along a message wishing Leo well.
“We wished him the best. I spoke to his brother… and I said please extend my best wishes,” Trump said.
In the latest update from the Vatican, the press office said Leo underwent blood tests and a chest X-ray on Friday morning.
The pontiff is continuing his respiratory physiotherapy sessions, doctors involved in his treatment said, adding that his  recovery allows him to carry out normal daily activities independently.
The 71-year-old is completely autonomous now in movement and breathing, the Vatican added.
Post-operative test results to confirm whether the pope is completely cancer-free and what, if any, treatment is needed have not been released yet.
The news of the pope’s diagnosis has been received with shock inside the Vatican, with Leo known as someone as physically active and seen to be in good health.
The pope’s engagements have been canceled until October 20 and it is not clear whether his planned trip to Latin America from November 6-17 will take place.
The Vatican, however, is continuing with preparations for the visit and on Friday posted the list of journalists traveling with the pope to report on the trip.
This story has been updated.
CNN’s Svitlana Vlasova, Issy Ronald and Sharon Braithwaite contributed reporting.

articles.title_orig: 'Taking action to protect the natural world': Conservation officials celebrate protection of 465 acres in Heath, Colrain
articles.title_zh: 'Taking action to protect the natural world': Conservation officials celebrate protection of 465 acres in Heath, Colrain
articles.content_orig:
HEATH — State and local conservation officials celebrated the protection of 465 acres in Heath and Colrain in a ceremony at Franklin Land Trust’s Branch View Barn on Thursday.
The land will be open to the public as the Stone Mountain Wildlife Management Area, and the conservation effort was financially supported by the Massachusetts Audubon Society’s 30×30 Catalyst Fund , marking a big step toward a regional goal of conserving a contiguous 5,400 acres of land by June 2027 through continued public-private partnerships.
“This permanent protection of nearly 500 acres here in Heath and in Colrain is really a tremendous accomplishment, and one that will have lasting benefits for wildlife habitat and for people for generations to come,” MassWildlife Director Eve Schlüter said.
Per information boards displayed at the event, this newly established wildlife management area helps protect wildlife, including rare and endangered animal species, and their habitats, while also boosting water-quality protection and opportunities for outdoor recreation. The MassWildlife website explains that wildlife management areas are free and open to the public for a variety of outdoor recreational purposes, like walking, hiking, fishing, trapping, hunting and wildlife viewing.
The Stone Mountain Wildlife Management Area joins several other protected landscapes in Franklin County, including MassWildlife’s Spur Brook Wildlife Management Area in Colrain, the Hinsdale Brook Wildlife Management Area in Shelburne, and the Zoar Wildlife Management Area in Charlemont and Rowe.
Although not in attendance for the celebration, Gov. Maura Healey said in a statement that Massachusetts is “home to some of the most beautiful natural landscapes in the country,” and that there is a responsibility to protect this land.
“We’re protecting clean water, preserving wildlife habitats and creating more opportunities for people to enjoy the outdoors,” Healey said. “We’re grateful to our local and conservation partners for helping us protect these special places for generations to come.”
In addition to the Stone Mountain Wildlife Management Area, Franklin Land Trust completed its purchase of 47 acres of land at the former Branch View Farm property in May, bringing the total to 512 acres of contiguous protected land in Heath and Colrain.
Franklin Land Trust Executive Director Mary Lynn Sabourin said that with more than 500 acres conserved within the last year, this brings the goal of hitting 5,400 acres of protected land closer to reality. The land trust is in the process of securing an additional 800 acres by next summer.
“We look forward to continuing to collaborate with local landowners, and many of you … to protect this additional 800 acres by June of 2027, with funding support from [the Executive Office of Energy and Environmental Affairs’] Landscape Partnership Grant, Mass Audubon’s Catalyst Fund and the Kestrel Land Trust,” Sabourin told attendees, eliciting cheers.
Speakers noted that the partnerships between the public agencies — the Department of Fish and Game, MassWildlife and the Executive Office of Energy and Environmental Affairs — alongside Mass Audubon and Franklin Land Trust made the Stone Mountain Wildlife Management Area possible.
Tom O’Shea, commissioner of the Department of Fish and Game, explained that the state has a goal of protecting 30% of all state land and water by 2030, and that public agencies partnering with private organizations and landowners is what will make this goal possible.
“This is going to get us on the way there, and we want to make sure to include these sort of large landscapes that provide really important migration corridors,” O’Shea said.
The 30×30 Catalyst Fund was designed to help bolster that movement toward the state’s 2030 conservation goal, with a $25 million seed investment by the Natick software company MathWorks supporting the fund.
David O’Neill, president and CEO of Mass Audubon, spoke to how land conservation efforts are like a “puzzle,” with protected land not always being contiguous. To put the pieces together, O’Neill said it requires “all of us working together, hand-in-glove.”
O’Neill added that the reason for a pre-acquisition of the property by Mass Audubon came from the loss of federal support. According to a July 2025 statement from Mass Audubon, the Trump administration stripped the organization of its largest federal grant for $25 million, impacting the protection of 10,000 acres of forests and wetland in the Connecticut River Valley.
“That’s not right, and that’s what we’re facing today,” he said. “We all have to step up. We can complain about that or we can just take action, and what we’re about is taking action to protect the natural world.”
Despite that challenge, O’Neill said these hurdles to conservation work can be overcome, and that the 30×30 Catalyst Fund is making that possible.
“I hope you feel like this is like one team working together to do something that we couldn’t otherwise do on our own,” O’Neill said.
Erin-Leigh Hoffman is the Montague, Gill, and Erving beat reporter. She joined the Recorder in June 2024 after graduating from Marist College. She can be reached at ehoffman@recorder.com, or 413-930-4231. More by Erin-Leigh Hoffman

articles.title_orig: China plans to tighten export controls on open-weight models and 23 key AI technologies
articles.title_zh: China plans to tighten export controls on open-weight models and 23 key AI technologies
articles.content_orig:
China's commerce and science ministries have released a draft update to the nation's list of banned and restricted export technologies.
The catalog targets 23 key AI technologies across large models, agents, compute clusters, and data processing. AI tools that can write or alter malware on their own to attack critical infrastructure, the military, or government agencies face a total export ban. Certain AI tools for finding software vulnerabilities won't be banned outright, though they will face new export limits.
Large AI models also face export controls in two cases. The first covers models trained on China's "important data" (as defined by the country's Data Security Law and related rules) that offer services based on it. Lawfully public data is exempt. Tiny amounts of up to 0.1 percent are also allowed if the data was cleaned beforehand, never shows up in AI outputs, and doesn't substantially boost the model's R&D capacity for core tech in that field.
The second case covers the core technologies behind large models, including weights, checkpoints, source code, architecture, and training or inference methods. These controls kick in once a model hits 10^26 FLOPs of training compute, has at least 2 trillion parameters, or ranks in the global top 10. Export officials determine that top-10 status using public rankings from major domestic and foreign evaluators or industry platforms, looking at overall performance, specific tasks, safety, or global usage numbers.
"This move does not mean 'China is shutting down open-weight models,' but it does indicate the Chinese government establishing the optionality to shut down future open-weight models at will," writes Dean W. Ball , head of strategic futures at OpenAI. Ball adds that Beijing's framework is a "mirror image" of the model-weight export controls the US government has already put in place.
This will likely push US companies that rely on open-weight AI to double down on domestic models instead of Chinese alternatives. Europe is in a much tougher spot. The EU has been banking on running open-weight models in domestic clouds to stay independent, alongside companies that want to host closed top-tier models on local servers. That sovereignty strategy falls apart when all the best open models come from the US or China and can get cut off by export controls at any time. At least AI tech that is already public through open-source releases or research papers skips these new rules entirely.
To avoid choking off its domestic open-source boom, China is introducing a fast-track process at the same time. Publishing restricted AI tech and weights as open source qualifies for "automatic licensing." The same goes for Chinese firms that run their own data centers abroad, tape out chips overseas, conduct research with foreign partners, or help set international standards. Under the ministry's rules, eligible exports are cleared the moment a company files the paperwork.
Using restricted models through API calls, apps, websites, SaaS tools, or lightweight versions on local devices stays free of these export controls. Installing restricted AI tech on local servers abroad, however, requires a standard export license. Companies can still use the streamlined process if the software runs on their own overseas cloud.
Beijing also pledges to back AI development in the Global South and ease exports for capacity building, tech sharing, and joint rulemaking within the World Artificial Intelligence Cooperation Organization , a bloc China launched to counter Western AI bodies. Until the final rules take effect, companies must register affected exports through the commerce ministry's portal.

Katie Zacharia was “let go” as White House press secretary on Friday, a White House official said, five days into a tenure dominated by questions over her claimed legal career in China, where she said she had passed a bar exam.
Her exit came on the same day Beijing invited her to visit China more often, responding to her remark that the country “doesn’t even have proper toilets”.

articles.title_zh: Stanford Just Figured Out How to Lead Dying Coral Reefs to a ‘Fast and Full Recovery’
articles.content_orig:
Stanford Doerr School of Sustainability
The Stanford Doerr School of Sustainability educates the next generation of leaders to solve our greatest sustainability challenges. Through degree programs spanning engineering, Earth system and planetary science, energy science, social sciences, geophysics, and oceans, students learn, research, and collaborate both on campus and at field sites around the world.
Scholars at the Stanford Doerr School of Sustainability focus on discovery and applied research essential for understanding our world and ensuring a thriving future. Through dedicated funding opportunities and access to cutting-edge facilities, including Hopkins Marine Station on Monterey Bay and the O'Donohue Family Stanford Educational Farm, they pursue bold ideas and turn science into real-world impact.
The Stanford Doerr School of Sustainability launched in 2022 as Stanford's first new school in 75 years, bringing together disciplines to advance the long-term prosperity of humanity and the planet. From making electricity affordable and sustainable for all to designing cities where people and nature thrive, our scholars collaborate across Stanford and the world to build a better future.
To shape a more sustainable world, the Stanford Doerr School of Sustainability extends learning opportunities and collaboration to students, scholars, solvers, and scalers across the globe. Opportunities include Executive Education, the Sustainability Forum, the Global Sustainability Challenge, Sustainability Undergraduate Research in Geoscience and Engineering, K-12 outreach, and Art and Sustainability.
Discover the latest research and insights shaping the future of sustainability. From groundbreaking research and inspiring milestones, to global forums that bring scholars, students, and leaders together, the Stanford Doerr School of Sustainability is a catalyst for innovation, turning bold ideas into lasting impact.
The Stanford Doerr School of Sustainability advances knowledge, solutions, and impact through research and education, creating a thriving, enduring future for humanity and the planet. Its seven departments, two institutes, and Sustainability Accelerator work in concert. Institutes spark innovative environmental and energy research across disciplines, and the Accelerator turns research into scalable technology and policy solutions for urgent global challenges.
Bleached corals can fully recover within a few weeks through brief contact with healthy corals, opening new possibilities for restoration.
10-14-2026 • Coastal ecosystems , Marine conservation , Marine biology
For the first time, scientists have observed bleached corals on the brink of death fully recover through brief contact with healthy clones.
Ghostly white corals returned to full health in a laboratory setting within seven weeks, the fastest documented recovery to date, according to a study published Oct. 14 in Science Advances . The findings could inspire the development of new methods to rapidly restore corals, which, by some estimates , could disappear within a few decades as climate change drives more frequent and intense marine heat waves .
When waters warm, corals expel colorful, beneficial algae that live in their tissues and provide the energy that corals need to grow. The loss of their algae partners leaves corals pale, starving, and vulnerable to the invasion of harmful algae. If corals survive these bleaching events, it can take months to years for them to fully recover.
“While bleached corals may be dying, they are not dead yet,” said lead author Danny Collins , an oceans PhD student at the Stanford Doerr School of Sustainability . “The question we wanted to answer is, once a coral has bleached, what can we do?”
All corals are animals. Across most species, individual corals multiply by producing clones that grow together to form vast, reef-building colonies of the same genetic makeup.
In 2025, study coauthor Steve Palumbi , the Jane and Marshall Steel, Jr. Professor in Marine Sciences, observed something curious about coral biology in his research lab. Two coral fragments – one bleached, one healthy – sampled from the same colony had tipped over in a tank and were now touching. Where they made contact, color returned to the bleached fragment, signaling the return of beneficial algae.
Around the time of this observation, Collins was considering the origins of coral disease, particularly the transmission of bacteria lurking on plastic debris that settles onto corals.
“Harmful bacteria enter corals through physical contact,” said Collins, who is also a Knight-Hennessy Scholar . “We were curious about what would happen if we used contact to reintroduce something good – the beneficial algae from healthy corals.”
Collins set up a simple experiment. He assembled 10 pairs of coral fragments – one bleached, one healthy – from the same animal. He arranged five pairs close enough to touch, and left gaps of just a few millimeters between the remaining pairs. The bleached fragments in touching pairs fully recovered within seven weeks, while those without contact died.
“Genetically identical corals recognize one another when they come into contact,” said Palumbi, who is a professor of oceans in the Doerr School of Sustainability and of biology in the School of Humanities and Sciences . “Their tissues fuse if they are from the same clone. We see something similar in humans. Organ transplants are often successful if the donor is your identical twin.”
Collins and team used a powerful microscope to discover that microscopic channels in coral tissues align shortly after contact, creating a pathway for transport between corals. Beneficial algae and the nutrients they produce then flow through these channels. The team observed that beneficial algae moved from healthy to bleached fragments within three days of contact.
The team also tested how different contact durations influenced recovery rates. They separated coral pairs at varying time intervals and found that after one week of contact, and in some cases after just five days, bleached fragments received enough beneficial algae to complete recovery on their own.
After separation, recovery took just seven weeks, matching the recovery time of coral pairs left in continuous contact. This led the team to realize that algae replicating within the bleached fragment, rather than traveling from the healthy fragment, primarily drove continued recovery.
“Once beneficial algae enter bleached corals, they don’t just spread out,” said Palumbi. “They flood in and start dividing at the fastest rates seen in corals.”
During the second week of contact with healthy corals, algae within bleached fragments doubled every four days, roughly ten times faster than the rate observed in wild corals.
For several decades, researchers have raced to develop tools and approaches that can protect corals from bleaching, disease outbreaks, and increasingly acidic waters, among other threats. Solutions include selectively breeding heat-tolerant corals , cultivating coral nurseries to restore degraded reefs , and even transplanting coral microbiomes.
“Bleached corals are often considered a lost cause because recovery after a heatwave is very slow, if it happens at all,” said Fiorenza Micheli , the David and Lucile Packard Professor in Marine Science and a faculty advisor of Collins. “We hope this new research will inspire solutions that keep corals healthy long enough to enable full recovery after heat waves through slower processes such as growth, reproduction, and recruitment of new colonies.”
The study team cautions that while the healing potential of physical contact is promising, many questions still remain. The approach requires a genetically identical, healthy copy of every bleached coral, which is not feasible at the scale needed to restore reefs.

articles.title_orig: US records 4,410 measles cases as outbreak grows
articles.title_zh: US records 4,410 measles cases as outbreak grows
articles.content_orig:
The United States Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) has recorded 4,410 measles cases so far in 2026, an increase of 330 in a week, and has dispatched an investigator to the state of Pennsylvania to help contain the country’s largest outbreak.
CDC figures also show 451 measles-related hospitalisations nationwide this year. Children and teenagers aged five to 19 account for 42 percent of cases, followed by adults aged 20 and older, who make up 41 percent. Seventeen percent of cases were among children under the age of five.
Pennsylvania reported 1,222 cases across 42 counties as of Wednesday, including 86 new infections since October 9, according to the state health department. The outbreak has led to 225 hospitalisations and five confirmed measles-associated deaths. State officials are actively investigating a sixth reported death.
The CDC is sending a so-called “disease detective” from its Epidemic Intelligence Service to work with state health officials on the Pennsylvania outbreak. The deployment follows Pennsylvania’s request for federal assistance, known as an Epi-Aid .
Pennsylvania has expanded vaccination efforts in affected communities. State health centre staff have administered more than 5,900 measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) vaccine doses at 202 pop-up clinics since the outbreak began in late April.
New York Governor Kathy Hochul declared a statewide disaster emergency on October 5 as measles cases rose in nearby Pennsylvania. The order is effective until November 4 and expands the number of healthcare professionals authorised to administer vaccines and allows nurses greater flexibility to order measles testing.
Measles vaccination coverage among US kindergarteners fell from 95.2 percent in the 2019–2020 school year to 92.4 percent in 2025–2026, according to data from the CDC. The agency estimates that about 280,000 kindergarteners are at risk because of gaps in vaccination coverage.

articles.title_orig: Cumulus Media Emerges From Chapter 11 Again
articles.title_zh: Cumulus Media Emerges From Chapter 11 Again
articles.content_orig:
Update your browser to view this website correctly. Update my browser now
Home › News and Business › Headlines
Cumulus Media Inc. announced on Friday that it has completed financial restructuring and emerged from the Chapter 11 reorganization process.
It has a new board and is now privately owned, but its management team will stay in place, including President/CEO Mary Berner.
The company had received the necessary approvals earlier from the bankruptcy court and, in August, from the Federal Communications Commission.
This is the second time the company has gone through a Chapter 11 process in nine years. In 2018 it concluded a reorganization to alleviate $1 billion in debt.
This latest restructuring stripped away another $550 million owed. Cumulus says the process was completed on an accelerated timeline without disruption to its normal business.
Berner has led the company since 2015. In a statement she said, “I am grateful to our lenders and noteholders for their collaboration throughout this process, and to our employees, vendors, affiliates, customers, and partners for their continued trust and support.”
The company emerges with a significantly stronger balance sheet, Berner said.
“We are more committed than ever to providing engaging content across our national footprint, serving as a lifeline and voice for the local communities we serve, driving meaningful growth for our advertising partners, and delivering value for our new shareholders.”
The company also owns Westwood One and the Cumulus Podcast Network.
Atlanta-based Cumulus had 2,862 employees, 2,078 of them full-time, at the end of 2025.
It has 377 radio stations in 84 U.S. markets. That number has dropped since the beginning of the Chapter 11 process. According to our previous reporting, the company owned 393 stations earlier this year.
Cumulus has surrendered the licenses of some AM stations, including KZAC in San Francisco .
But it has also been selling some FMs. In May, Cumulus said it planned to sell WWFF in Huntsville, Ala., WWFN in Florence, S.C., and a translator in Atlanta to Radio Training Network for $2.45 million. In August it sold KKEG in Bentonville, Ark., and WIXV in Savannah, Ga., also to RTN, for $2.05 million. The transactions are subject to regulatory approval.
Among commercial U.S. radio companies, though, it still holds the No. 2 slot for the number of radio stations owned, after iHeartMedia.
Cumulus and certain of its subsidiaries commenced the prepackaged Chapter 11 process in United States Bankruptcy Court for the Southern District of Texas on March 4.
The process involved a comprehensive restructuring support agreement with a group of its lenders.
Cumulus says it canceled 100% of its existing funded indebtedness in exchange for 100% of the reorganized equity and $50 million of new convertible notes issued to former lenders.
It said it also amended and restated its asset-based revolving credit facility to provide continued liquidity.

articles.title_orig: FIT student dies after being drugged and raped on Manhattan campus: officials
articles.title_zh: FIT student dies after being drugged and raped on Manhattan campus: officials
articles.content_orig:
The suspect is accused of waiting 45 minutes before seeking help.
NEW YORK (WABC) -- Two teens are facing federal charges this week accusing them of supplying the fentanyl that killed one New York City college student and poisoned a second.
According to the newly unsealed indictment, Moises Freire, 19, brought fentanyl he obtained from Brian Peralta, 18, to the victims' undergraduate residence hall at Fashion Institute of Technology on March 18.
Officials said Freire falsely claimed the drug did not contain fentanyl and was "pure cocaine."
Freire encouraged the victims to ingest the substance and almost immediately both women lost consciousness, prosecutors said.
While the victims were incapacitated, Freire allegedly raped Annabel Richter in her FIT dorm room. Authorities say he then took photos of her that he sent to friends.
He waited 45 minutes before seeking help from campus security, to whom he claimed the two undergraduates had simply consumed too much alcohol.
Campus security responded and administered emergency aid, including Narcan. Both victims were transported to hospitals in Manhattan.
Toxicology results later confirmed that both women had ingested fentanyl and no cocaine.
The second victim regained consciousness after life‑saving treatment.
Richter remained in critical condition and eventually died from complications of acute fentanyl intoxication.
"This case alleges not only the deadly distribution of fentanyl to two young women but also the sexual assault of a victim rendered defenseless by that poisoning," said U.S. Attorney Jamie McDonald. "We will work tirelessly to hold accountable those who endanger young people living and learning on our campuses."
Christopher Roberts, the head of the Drug Enforcement Administration New York Task Force Division, said the allegations were "beyond disturbing and include a cruel deception and unimaginable assault."
"College should be a place where young people can learn, grow, and pursue their dreams, not a place where predators exploit their vulnerability," Roberts said. "Every student deserves to feel safe, whether walking across campus, sitting in a classroom, or inside their own dorm room."
Freire and Peralta, both from Queens, are charged with conspiracy to distribute a controlled substance resulting in death. They face at least 20 years in prison if convicted. Freire is also charged with distributing a controlled substance with the intent to commit rape.
(The Associated Press and ABC News contributed to this report.)

articles.title_orig: Hot flashes, night sweats, insomnia – OB-GYNS set new rules for menopause treatment
articles.title_zh: Hot flashes, night sweats, insomnia – OB-GYNS set new rules for menopause treatment
articles.content_orig:
For the first time since 2014, the American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists has updated its guidelines for the treatment of symptoms commonly associated with menopause. BSIP/Universal Images Group/Getty Images hide caption
For stories on the science of healthy living, subscribe to NPR's Health newsletter.
For the first time since 2014, the American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists has updated its guidelines for the treatment of symptoms commonly associated with menopause. The doctor's group, known as ACOG, recommends hormone replacement therapy alongside certain antidepressants, nonhormonal medicines, and other treatments to address symptoms like hot flashes, insomnia and mood swings.
"What's changing is the breadth of options that we now have … And the benefit of that is that we are better equipped to be able to take an individualized approach for patients," said Catherine Cansino, MD, MPH, an obstetrician/gynecologist, chair of ACOG's Committee on Clinical Practice Guidelines and co-author of the new guidance.
The guidance, released Thursday, focuses on specific menopausal symptoms and underscores that the safety of hormone replacement therapy is now "well-established," Cansino said.
In 2002, the Women's Health Initiative suggested that hormone replacement therapy increased the risk of heart disease, breast cancer, stroke and pulmonary embolism.
However, as researchers revisited that data years later, they noticed certain limitations, (including that a majority of participants were 60 years or older) making it difficult to generalize the findings to younger women experiencing menopause or perimenopause.
With more and better quality studies, physicians are able to review the evidence and make better-informed recommendations, Cansino said.
"Hormone therapy is probably the best option for symptomatic, newly menopausal women within 10 years of the final menstrual period or before the age of 60," said Robert Kauffman, MD, MSCP, a co-author of the guidelines, during a press briefing on Thursday.
In addition to hormone replacement therapy, the guidelines highlight new nonhormonal options for treating menopausal symptoms, including the drug fezolinetant, brand name Veozah, which the Food and Drug Administration approved to treat hot flashes in 2023 and elinzanetant, brand name Lynkuet, which was approved in 2025.
"What's so exciting about these treatment options is they were specifically studied based on the understanding that we have of the physiology of thermoregulation and sleep," Cansino said.
The medications work by blocking certain chemical messengers in the part of the brain that regulates body temperature and manages sleep/wake cycles, according to the guidance.
About 2 million women begin menopause each year. The average age of a woman experiencing menopause is 49.9 years, according to the guidelines. However, symptoms of menopause can begin years before a woman's final menstrual period.
The new recommendations support the use of systemic hormone replacement therapy, or HRT, with a combination of estrogen and progestogen in women with a uterus who have no contraindications to hormones.
Reasons to avoid hormone therapy include undiagnosed abnormal genital bleeding, and current or past histories of certain gynecologic cancers, blood clots, stroke, heart attack, liver disease or a known or suspected pregnancy.
The reason progestogen is recommended in women with a uterus is because estrogen can stimulate growth of the uterine lining and increase the risk of endometrial cancer. Progestogen therapy helps mitigate that risk, Cansino explained.
Around half a million women have hysterectomies each year, and for women without a uterus, ACOG recommends estrogen alone .
As an alternative to estrogen-progestogen therapy, ACOG also recommends a pill, sold under the brand name Duavee, that combines estrogen and a drug called bazedoxifene. Bazedoxifene is a "selective estrogen receptor modulator," which blocks the estrogen from working in certain areas of the body, such as breast tissue, while mimicking estrogen's benefit for bone density, for instance.
Another drug recommended in the new guideline is gabapentin, an anticonvulsant typically used to treat seizures. It can also manage menopause symptoms for people who can't tolerate hormones or the other new medicines.
Cognitive behavioral therapy, mindfulness-based interventions, exercise, clinical hypnosis, and acupuncture can all improve some symptoms, ACOG says, however the guidelines also note that the evidence for these interventions is weaker than the evidence for HRT.
Still, patients may have their own preferences and goals, Cansino said.
"I live in California, and I have a practice where many patients don't necessarily want pharmacologic therapy," Cansino said. So, she tends to have a lot of conversations about non-pharmacologic treatment options with her patients.
"A healthy diet and regular physical exercise is going to go a long way. So let's start with that," and then discuss what other interventions to add to the regimen, she said.
Asked, in a follow-up email, whether Cansino recommended one medication or tool over another, she warned against "over-simplifying treatment based on tiers."
Just like with contraception, she noted that patients may choose a certain method, knowing that it's less effective. "As long as they understand the pros and cons, such a decision is perfectly OK."
Meanwhile, demand for HRT is already rising. Last year, the FDA scrapped the " black-box warning " on labels for certain estrogen therapies.
In recent months, estrogen products like transdermal patches have been hard for pharmacies to keep in stock.
"I think the shortage of transdermal estrogen therapy highlights the fact that we have all of this attention about hormone therapy, and not necessarily enough about other treatment options," Cansino told NPR.
She also stressed the need for patients to talk to trusted clinicians about the pros and cons of treatments and to avoid having "tunnel vision" about a single option.
The level of care that OB/GYNs provide by helping individual patients find the right treatment is one of the most important aspects of the new guidance, Cansino said.
"There's a lot of misinformation out there and exaggerated claims about hormone therapy, and so some people end up taking risks when they shouldn't," she added.

articles.title_orig: Sean 'Diddy' Combs moves from New Jersey prison to facility in Pennsylvania
articles.title_zh: Sean 'Diddy' Combs moves from New Jersey prison to facility in Pennsylvania
articles.content_orig:
Sean "Diddy" Combs has been transferred from a New Jersey correctional facility to a prison in Pennsylvania, the US Federal Bureau of Prisons says.
The rap mogul was moved to FCI Allenwood Low on Friday, a prison official said, but declined to discuss why he was moved, citing privacy, safety, and security reasons.
"His transfer from one low-security facility to another is an important distinction," Combs' spokesman told the BBC, adding that the move "is consistent with a decision made with safety and security in mind".
Combs, 56, who was sentenced to 50 months behind bars, has asked an appeals court to release him from prison and overturn his conviction on two prostitution-related crimes.
Combs' spokesman, Juda S Engelmayer, did not comment on an Associated Press report that Combs had been living a "luxury lifestyle" behind bars in New Jersey or on reports swirling about his health and treatment in lockup.
The move comes about two weeks after NBC News reported that the Bad Boy Records co-founder had access to mobile phones, liquor and other contraband at Fort Dix, as well as allegations that he had paid inmates to cook, clean and make his bed for him, and give him massages. He was also involved in two fights, according to NBC.
"It's because of the disruptive behaviour," Jose Rojas, union secretary for local federal prison employees,  told NBC News of the move. "He's been causing too much trouble over there."
NBC reported Combs was stripped of 41 days for good conduct, pushing back his scheduled release date, which is now listed in the prison's online records as 2 March 2028. He was originally expected to be released in January 2028.
Engelmayer said he appreciates that the Federal Bureau of Prisons is "taking the safety and security of Sean and everyone involved seriously" and "we are grateful for the attention being given to his well-being and hope he can continue serving his time without unnecessary disruption".
The Federal Bureau of Prisons declined to comment on the reports.
"For privacy, safety, and security reasons, we do not comment on the conditions of confinement for any incarcerated individual, including whether a particular individual is the subject of allegations, investigations, or disciplinary sanctions," spokesman Donald Murphy said.
FCI Allenwood Low is a low-security federal correctional institution for male offenders that is about 155 miles (250 km) west of New York City.
The facility houses about 1,044 inmates, according to its website, a significantly smaller population than the one at Combs' previous facility, Fort Dix, of more than 4,200 inmates across two campuses. Allenwood also has medium and maximum security facilities nearby.
Federal prosecutors in New York have accused Combs of using his money, power, and the threat of violence to coerce women into unwanted sexual encounters.
After a high-profile jury trial in New York last year, two of Combs' ex-girlfriends testified that he abused them and forced them to participate in so-called "freak-offs" with male escorts.
In July 2025, Combs was convicted on two counts of transportation to engage in prostitution. They jury acquitted him of two more serious charges, sex trafficking and racketeering conspiracy, and he was sentenced to more than four years in prison that October.
Later that month, Combs was transferred to the federal correctional institution at Fort Dix in New Jersey, where he had been serving out his sentence until his transfer on Friday.
In April, a US appeals court heard arguments to overturn his prison sentence but has not yet issued a decision.
