articles.title_orig: New York City college student dead after being drugged with fentanyl and raped in her dorm room, prosecutors say
articles.title_zh: New York City college student dead after being drugged with fentanyl and raped in her dorm room, prosecutors say
articles.content_orig:
A college student died after she was drugged with fentanyl and raped in a New York City college dorm room, federal prosecutors announced on Thursday.
The student, who prosecutors did not name, and another unnamed student were drugged in a college residence hall in Manhattan in March, according to a press release by the U.S. Attorney’s Office Southern District of New York. The other student survived the incident, prosecutors said.
Court documents show the women went to the Fashion Institute of Technology, which has not returned NBC News requests for comment on the case.
Two men were arrested and indicted in connection with the alleged crime, according to prosecutors.
Moises Freire, 19, of the Bronx, was charged with distribution of a controlled substance with intent to commit rape, distribution of narcotics resulting in death and conspiracy, according to an indictment. Brian Peralta Cabrera, 18, of Queens, was charged with conspiracy to distribute narcotics resulting in death and serious bodily injury.
Both have pleaded not guilty. Lawyers for the two men did not immediately return requests for comment.
On March 18, Freire supplied one of the women with what he told her was “pure cocaine” from Mexico and “falsely” assured her that the drug he was providing did not contain any fentanyl, according the indictment.
Prosecutors say that Freire knew that the drug, which he acquired from Cabrera, was fentanyl and had previously described it as “fake” and “poison.”
Freire encouraged the two women to consume the drug upon arriving to the residence hall, according to the indictment.
Both women “immediately” fell unconscious, according to the indictment. Prosecutors say Freire then raped one of the women while she was overdosing on fentanyl as the other woman lie unconscious several feet away.
After raping the unconscious woman, he took naked photos of her and sent them to his friends, according to the indictment.
Prosecutors say Freire waited about 45 minutes before he contacted campus security, telling them the women were unconscious because they had too much to drink.
Campus security found the women and rendered emergency medical services before they were transported to a nearby hospital, according to the indictment.
Only one of the women regained consciousness. The woman who was raped died “from complications from acute fentanyl intoxication” a few days later, according to the indictment.
“College should be a place where young people can learn, grow, and pursue their dreams, not a place where predators exploit their vulnerability,” said Christopher Roberts, who is the special agent in charge of the Drug Enforcement Administration New York Task Force Division.
“Every student deserves to feel safe, whether walking across campus, sitting in a classroom, or inside their own dorm room,” Roberts said.
The announcement of the alleged crimes and arrests come amid a national reckoning over sexual misconduct on college campuses.
Last month, a woman sued Cornell University , her former sorority, her sorority, Tri Delta; a fraternity, Chi Phi; and seven former Chi Phi members after alleging that she was gang raped. And this week, a 21-year-old woman reported to police that she was sexually assaulted at a fraternity party near another elite academic institution, the University of Chicago .
I’m a reporter on NBC News’ breaking news team, covering crime, extreme weather, pop culture and more. I recently covered Hurricane Milton, which devastated the Tampa, Florida, metropolitan area, and the student-led protests at Columbia University.

articles.title_orig: Apple TV 4K and HomePod Mini Price Increases 'Much More Striking' Than New Features
articles.title_zh: Apple TV 4K and HomePod Mini Price Increases 'Much More Striking' Than New Features
articles.content_orig:
Daring Fireball 's John Gruber shared his first impressions of the new Apple TV 4K and HomePod mini 2 this week, and he concluded that the price increases the devices received are "much more striking" than any of the new features introduced.
Prior to receiving price increases in late June , the previous Apple TV 4K started at $129 in the U.S., while the previous HomePod mini was priced at $99. The new Apple TV and the HomePod mini 2 are priced at $299 and $149, respectively, so both devices are now significantly more expensive than they were just four months ago.
Since the new Apple TV is only available in a single configuration with 128GB of storage and an Ethernet port, it is more fair to compare it to the equivalent previous-generation 128GB model, which was initially $149 and went up to $249 in late June. This means the new model is technically only $50 more expensive, but the reality is that the minimum you can spend on a new Apple TV 4K is now $299, up significantly from $129.
The price increases stack up if you want to use a pair of HomePod mini speakers as the default audio output on an Apple TV 4K. As noted by Gruber, it now costs nearly $600 to buy all of those devices, up from nearly $350 before late June.
"At the old pre-June prices, you could buy a 128 GB Apple TV and a pair of HomePod Minis for $350 ($150 + $100 + $100)," said Gruber. "Four short months later, with today's new models, that combination would cost $600 ($300 + $150 + $150). That price difference is much more striking than any of the new and improved features in the products."
To be clear, Gruber said he still thinks the new Apple TV 4K is "worth it" to him at its current price, and he believes the HomePod mini 2's price is "reasonable." However, he acknowledges that the "general consumer market thought the old prices were too high," and now Apple has made even more price increases on top.

articles.title_orig: Brent oil touches $110 as Iran escalates Hormuz attacks, Ukraine vows to hit Russian refineries
articles.title_zh: Brent oil touches $110 as Iran escalates Hormuz attacks, Ukraine vows to hit Russian refineries
articles.content_orig:
Crude oil prices rose sharply Friday as Iran escalated attacks in the Strait of Hormuz, Houthi militants fired missiles at Saudi Arabia and Ukraine vowed to keep striking Russian refineries.
Brent futures hit a session high of $110 per barrel for the first time since May before easing slightly to close at $109.86, a gain of 3.7%.
U.S. West Texas Intermediate rose 3.5% to settle at $101.41 per barrel. WTI added more than 10% this week while Brent advanced nearly 5%.
Saudi Arabia intercepted several missiles fired over the Red Sea on Friday, including one that was heading toward the oil export terminal Yanbu, a military spokesman said. Three drones were also destroyed in the kingdom's Riyadh and southern regions, the military said.
Iran-allied Houthi militants in Yemen have repeatedly fired at Saudi Arabia this week. Oil giant Aramco came under attack when one of its administrative buildings in Dhahran was hit Tuesday, the kingdom's energy ministry said .
The Houthis attacked Riyadh's international airport on Oct. 10, killing 12 and injuring more than 300.
In the Strait of Hormuz, at least nine tankers and cargo ships have come under attack since Sunday as Iran tries to choke off oil exports through the waterway. Iran sank the container ship GFS Pride on Wednesday, U.S. Central Command said. The crew of the Singapore-registered ship was safely evacuated, according to Singapore's maritime authority.
The attacks have left three seafarers injured and two missing this week, according to the International Maritime Organization .
Crude exports through Hormuz have pulled back after touching prewar levels in September. Shipments  stood at 9.4 million barrels per day for the week ended Wednesday, about 70% of the average before the Iran war, according to data provided by the energy researcher Kpler.
Meanwhile, the " energy ceasefire " that President Donald Trump tried to broker between Ukraine and Russia has quickly unraveled. The Kremlin continued attacking Ukrainian infrastructure despite the supposed truce. President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Kyiv would resume strikes on Russian refineries in retaliation.
Diesel prices have surged this year due to Ukraine's attacks on Russian refineries and Iranian strikes on energy infrastructure in the Middle East. The fuel cost an average of $6.33 a gallon in the U.S. Friday, more than 70% above the same period last year, according to AAA data.
U.S. crude oil prices were also driven higher by a big decline of more than 8 million barrels for the week ended Oct. 9 in commercial inventories due to production shut-ins on the Gulf Coast from Hurricane Isaias, according to the Energy Information Administration.

articles.title_orig: Don’t ignore faith when confronting global problems, says LDS President Dallin Oaks
articles.title_zh: Don’t ignore faith when confronting global problems, says LDS President Dallin Oaks
articles.content_orig:
(The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints) President Dallin H. Oaks, right, greets Mohammad Abdulkarim Al-Issa, secretary-general of the Muslim World League, during the opening ceremony of the 2026 G20 Interfaith Forum in the Tabernacle in Salt Lake City on Thursday, Oct. 15, 2026.
Bringing his plea for peacemaking and compromise for the common good before an audience of global leaders Thursday evening, President Dallin H. Oaks emphasized the need for religion in healing a troubled world.
“Faith-informed perspectives have a meaningful place in global policymaking,” Oaks, leader of The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints, said in a welcoming speech to the G20 Interfaith Forum . “But the key to this whole effort is to bring us all together to address common problems.”
The three-day conference , which draws religious leaders, scholars, humanitarian advocates and civic officials from around the world, began with an opening ceremony at the historic Tabernacle in downtown Salt Lake City and will continue at the University of Utah’s Institute of Religion through Saturday.
(The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints) People arrive for the opening ceremony of the 2026 G20 Interfaith Forum in the Tabernacle in Salt Lake City on Thursday, Oct. 15, 2026.
“People of goodwill, compassion, and a desire to understand and help one another — without demanding a compromise of distinctive commitments — are at the core of peacemaking,” said Oaks, who praised the attendees as “peacemakers in today’s world.”
“We want to be part of your efforts,” he added, “and invoke the Lord’s blessings on all of us as we go forward.”
Hundreds of people gathered in the Tabernacle to hear messages about collaborating on issues ranging from “disagreeing better” to artificial intelligence.
The 2026 forum — centered on the theme “Resilient Hope, Shared Future” — kicked off with a panel discussion featuring Utah Gov. Spencer Cox, former South Carolina Gov. David Beasley and Martin Luther King III, a son of civil rights legend Martin Luther King Jr.. The three discussed the importance of retaining dialogue across political and religious lines.
(The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints) From left, Deseret News Editor Sarah Jane Weaver leads a discussion with Utah Gov. Spencer Cox, Martin Luther King III and former South Carolina Gov. David Beasley at the opening session of the 2026 G20 Interfaith Forum in the Tabernacle in Salt Lake City on Thursday, Oct. 15, 2026.
Cox said the answer to many of the political divisions in the world can be found by creating community.
“We’re all worried about things beyond our control,” he said. “But we don’t know who our next-door neighbor is.”
These gaps can be closed, Cox said, “one conversation, one disagreement, one neighbor, one act of service at a time.”
Beasley said he has discovered during his travels that contempt was hard to hold onto when getting to know those with whom you disagree.
“When you break bread with someone,” Beasley said, “it’s hard to hate them.”
King echoed both sentiments and recalled that his “mom and dad understood that we could disagree without being disagreeable.”
The main ceremony included performances by The Tabernacle Choir at Temple Square and addresses from faith leaders representing Muslim, Catholic, Orthodox Christian, Hindu, Jewish and other faith traditions.
(The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints) Mohammad Abdulkarim Al-Issa, secretary-general of the Muslim World League, speaks during the opening ceremony of the 2026 G20 Interfaith Forum in the Tabernacle in Salt Lake City on Thursday, Oct. 15, 2026.
Mohammed bin Abdulkarim Al-Issa, secretary-general of the Muslim World League, focused on how religious communities can work together to promote peace and human dignity.
“Our natural difference should not be a threat, nor an incitement to clash and conflict,” Al-Issa said. “It’s a part of the diversities that God intended for humanity through his universal predestined wisdom.”
Sadhvi Bhagawati Saraswati, a Hindu spiritual leader from Los Angeles, expressed how faith should propel its adherents to action instead of waiting for the world to change.
(The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints) Sadhvi Bhagawati Saraswati, a Hindu spiritual leader and author, speaks during the opening ceremony of the 2026 G20 Interfaith Forum in the Tabernacle in Salt Lake City on Thursday, Oct. 15, 2026.
“Our faith gives us an inner, resounding yes — yes to life, yes to love, yes to peace, yes to human dignity, yes to hope,” she said. “But faith must also give us an equally resounding inner no — no to environmental destruction, no to poverty, no to oppression and exploitation — and mostly no to violence in the name of God.”
“Hope,” she added, “is not a mood we wait for. It is a capacity we build.”
The forum will conclude Saturday at the Cathedral of the Madeleine in the heart of Salt Lake City.

articles.title_orig: Warsh signals steady Fed outlook despite inflation jump
articles.title_zh: Warsh signals steady Fed outlook despite inflation jump
articles.content_orig:
BANGKOK — Federal Reserve Chairman Kevin Warsh refrained from signaling whether there will be another interest rate hike again this month, while acknowledging a "synchronous tightening" by central banks around the world.
"I don't prejudge meetings. I don't believe in saying now what I might do at the meetings that we have in the balance of this year," Warsh said, reiterating his opposition to the use of forward guidance for markets that should rely on interpreting data.
He also acknowledged that stance may disappoint anyone who had hoped for a steer ahead of the central bank meeting later this month. "It's a new chapter at the Fed [and] we're not in that business anymore," he said.
Warsh spoke at a fireside chat with the International Monetary Fund's managing director, Kristalina Georgieva, as part of the weeklong IMF-World Bank Annual Meetings in Bangkok on Friday.
"Alongside other recent comments from FOMC participants, Warsh's comments indicate that the FOMC is set to pause in October," Goldman Sachs economists led by Jan Hatzius wrote in a note. "We continue to expect a second and final hike in December."
S&P 500 and Nasdaq futures edged higher following the speech, while stock market indexes in Asia and Treasury yields were largely stable.
Warsh described the global shift toward tighter monetary policy as a common fight on prices. Central banks made their own choices under their own mandates, he said, but the result was "a synchronous tightening in monetary policy in most places around the world," which means "there's no free riders."
Surging energy costs stemming from the Iran war and artificial intelligence investment boom are stoking inflation and pushing up borrowing costs around the world, just as global public debt is on pace to exceed 100% of the world's GDP, a level last breached in the aftermath of World War II.
The U.S. government has insisted that strong growth would be the best way to grow out of its rising debt pile, dismissing IMF's warning that the plans of relying solely on growth won't work as something that needs to be taken "with a grain of salt."
Warsh also expressed optimism about how AI will make economies that use it well more productive and wealthier, while warning the road there may be "very bumpy," and its near-term effect on employment is still uncertain.
"I want you to hear from me optimism, but optimism leavened by the seriousness of purpose," Warsh said.
A decade from now, he said, people will look back on the developments and "say this was hugely consequential."
The Fed raised rates to a range of 3.75% to 4% last month, its first hike since 2023 . Traders see a 72.3% chance for the Fed to keep the interest rate unchanged at the Oct. 27-28 meeting, according to CME FedWatch, while the majority expect a 25 basis point hike at the December meeting.

articles.title_orig: CoreWeave stock, bond set for weekly plunge as rate-hike fears hit AI bet
articles.title_zh: CoreWeave stock, bond set for weekly plunge as rate-hike fears hit AI bet
articles.content_orig:
In Austin Powers: International Man of Mystery , a Virtuocon guard famously stands in front of a commandeered steamroller, screaming "No!!" three times before being run over. The joke, of course, is that the hazard moved so slowly he had ample time to step out of the way.
For months, equity traders holding CoreWeave (CRWV) have played that guard. Despite credit markets flashing warnings, equity holders essentially just stood there. Now, after a shocking 27.5% drop from last Friday's close to this Thursday morning's 52-week lows, followed by a whiplash 17% rebound, equity investors, if not squashed like Dr. Evil's henchman, are dazed and confused. Shares are down another 5% today.
With earnings just a few weeks away, massive leverage, a heavily split sell-side, and 15.4% short interest, the stock remains primed for explosive volatility.
The hazard approaching CRWV equity wasn't hidden. The AI cloud infrastructure platform essentially didn't exist five years ago and has accumulated $51.6 billion in debt (~$46 billion net of cash) against a backdrop of zero historical profitability. That was well known, but the CEO's comments that the company aspired to be investment grade so it could borrow "unlimited sums", even as investors already anticipated nearly another $60 billion in debt in the next 18months, spooked folks. (Trick or Treat!) Especially since the debt issued only in June had already fallen 20% since.
From an options trader's point of view, it was hard to reconcile deteriorating credit and rising leverage with falling options premia; as recently as last week, they were in the 6th percentile, 1.5 standard deviations below the one-year mean. At 72%, options weren't cheap in absolute terms, but given everything going on, they should have been higher. The stock also looked somewhat complacent, with the equity chopping around historical support levels dating back to May 2025. The credit side was on tilt:
Because CRWV is levered by more than 2:1, a 10% move in enterprise value translates to a nearly 22% swing in equity value.
Despite the dire credit picture, equity sentiment remains fiercely divided, driving this week's 17% bounce from the lows. For example, HSBC maintains a Sell rating with a $39 price target, essentially calling for the stock to be cut in half. Conversely, banks like BNP and Cantor Fitzgerald (my former employer) suggest these fears are overblown and the stock should more than double from here.
It's not just bankers defending the company either. Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang downplayed systemic concerns, and ARK Investment stepped in to buy 192,000 shares. BofA argues that CRWV's ability to bring active power online at scale, combined with higher pricing from Nvidia's upcoming Vera Rubin deployments, will drive faster-than-expected revenue growth. They described execution risk as a bigger concern than financing; I'm not sure those who bought the 2032 8 1/2s at par would agree.
With CRWV's credit heavily distressed but its equity heavily defended by high-profile dip-buyers, going outright long or short into earnings carries excessive directional risk. A November/January Call Diagonal , currently trading for just under $6 per spread. Almost 9% of the current stock price. Normally, that's a lot, but given this stock has fallen 27.5% and then gained 17% in the past 5 sessions, it isn't.

articles.title_orig: Elon Musk reveals ‘world’s first flying car’ at Tesla event
articles.title_zh: Elon Musk reveals ‘world’s first flying car’ at Tesla event
articles.content_orig:
The Tesla Roadster 2 drove up a curved ramp before using SpaceX rocket thrusters to fly, flip and land
Elon Musk has revealed Tesla’s latest model, which he claims will be the world’s first flying car, using technology from his aerospace company SpaceX to “basically fly like a rocket”.
The billionaire, who hosted a demonstration of the Tesla Roadster 2 at the SpaceX rocket development and testing facility in Texas, said the sports car could go from 0 to 60mph in a record time of less than a second and had thrusters.
A video of the event shows the Roadster, which he said was controlled remotely “to make sure we don’t kill anyone”, driving up a curved ramp using suction to grip upside down, before using thrusters to flip, fly and land .
Later in the demonstration the Roadster is seen using the jets to leap over a line of Tesla’s existing models and then accelerate to 60mph in record time.
“Turns out the future does have flying cars,” Musk said in a post on his social media site, X, accompanying a video from the event.
Speaking at the event on Thursday, Musk said: “Flying cars are real. It’s got altitude controls, thrusters and main thrusters in the rear. So it can basically fly like a rocket, it can do rolls, crazy gymnastics.”
“I’m not sure it’s necessarily legal in all jurisdictions,” Musk said, adding that the prototype was “not necessarily a safety optimised car but it takes the fun meter to 11”.
In 2014 Musk expressed his scepticism about a future with flying vehicles .
However, three years later he announced the development of the Roadster 2, which will go into production in 2028 and is priced in excess of $200,000, (£150,000), to create an electric sports car “to give a hardcore smackdown to gasoline cars”.
after newsletter promotion
After the event, a Tesla reservation website for expressing interest in the two-seater Roadster 2 showed that a “performance” version of the vehicle would require a £50,000 deposit. A “thrust” version would require a $250,000 deposit.
Meanwhile, a one-seater “rocket” variant with “full flight system” was labelled as being available only by invitation. The car company added that flying it was not permitted on public roads.

articles.title_orig: Galaxy S27 reportedly skips Snapdragon 8 Elite Extreme Gen 6 due to overheating
articles.title_zh: Galaxy S27 reportedly skips Snapdragon 8 Elite Extreme Gen 6 due to overheating
articles.content_orig:
According to a new report, Samsung’s Galaxy S27 series might not use the latest Snapdragon chipset due to overheating problems.
The Snapdragon vs Exynos debate has been around for years, with Samsung often mixing its two flagship chipset choices, but also occasionally going all in on one or the other. Snapdragon is almost exclusively used in the US, with the last time Samsung used Exynos entirely in the States being the Galaxy S6 over a decade ago. That was due to overheating problems with Qualcomm’s flagship chip at the time, and it seems we’re in for a case of deja vu.
Seoul Economic Daily reports that Samsung has “informed Qualcomm of the overheating issue” with the Snapdragon 8 Elite Extreme Gen 6 and is looking at Exynos 2700 as an alternative. The report claims:
Samsung is in talks with Qualcomm to resolve the heat issue within this month, according to sources. If Qualcomm meets the required performance, Samsung will adopt Snapdragon as originally planned; if not, it will have little choice but to consider the Exynos 2700 as an alternative, weighing performance stability and mass-production timelines.
Qualcomm announced its latest flagship chips in September and the top-tier Elite Extreme Gen 6 features a 2nm process and two 5GHz cores. Qualcomm claims a 13% boost in CPU performance over the Gen 5 chip, 44% improvement in GPU performance, and boosts to AI processing and power efficiency.
There have already been a few phones announced with the chip, including the US-bound Motorola Signature 27 , but it’s too early to tell if overheating issues are going to be widespread.
Update: Qualcomm, in a statement sent to 9to5Google , says that the report is “inaccurate.”
Recent reporting about thermal issues related to Snapdragon 8 Elite Extreme Gen 6 is inaccurate. We are proud of the innovation and strong momentum behind our next-generation flagship platform and continue to work closely with global OEMs to deliver premium user experiences.

articles.title_orig: L.A. County reports first death from opioid called more potent than fentanyl
articles.title_zh: L.A. County reports first death from opioid called more potent than fentanyl
articles.content_orig:
A warning spreading among students at Colorado State University has put an unfamiliar name in front of people who may already know the danger posed by fentanyl: cychlorphine.
The synthetic opioid has not been detected by the Drug Enforcement Administration in Colorado or the other states covered by its Rocky Mountain Division, the agency told FOX31 . The division said the closest reported cases it was aware of were in Texas and Oklahoma.
That has not stopped concern from reaching Colorado. Students told the station they were sharing warnings because cychlorphine can turn up in drugs without the person taking them knowing it is there.
The national evidence behind those warnings has been building for months. Cychlorphine, also called N-propionitrile chlorphine, is an emerging synthetic opioid from a group known as orphine analogues. Forensic researchers began seeing a sharp increase in detections in fatal overdose cases in late 2025 and early 2026.
The often-repeated claim that cychlorphine is roughly 10 times more potent than fentanyl comes from laboratory pharmacology rather than studies of human dosing. The Center for Forensic Science Research and Education reported in January that in-vitro data suggested that level of potency while warning that detections of the drug were rising quickly.
Embedded media follows; please allow a moment to load.
CFSRE said it had identified cychlorphine in 25 blood specimens from fatal overdoses, with most submitted during late 2025 and early 2026. It was the only opioid detected in 11 of those 25 cases. Another laboratory had tentatively identified it in more than 100 toxicology cases.
Federal data released later showed a wider footprint. An August Federal Register notice said cychlorphine had been confirmed in 225 law-enforcement encounters across 19 U.S. jurisdictions and had been associated with at least 55 fatalities in the United States as of early 2026.
The DEA had already issued a nationwide public safety advisory in May about illicit fentanyl being mixed with cychlorphine, nitazenes, xylazine, medetomidine and other emerging substances. The agency described cychlorphine and nitazenes as potent synthetic opioids and warned that some overdoses involving them may require repeated doses of naloxone.
Federal officials took another step in August, temporarily placing cychlorphine and three related synthetic opioids into Schedule I under the Controlled Substances Act. Temporary scheduling can be used when the DEA determines that controlling a substance is necessary to avoid an imminent hazard to public safety.
The drug has already surfaced in criminal investigations.
In Oklahoma, two men pleaded guilty in federal court to distributing cychlorphine that ultimately resulted in another person's death. Court records cited by the DEA showed pills containing the drug changed hands in December 2025 before being resold to the person who died.
A separate investigation in San Francisco began after a 16-year-old was found dead in April. The San Francisco Police Department said the medical examiner determined that the teenager died from a combination of drugs that included cychlorphine.
Police later arrested four people and seized more than 20,000 suspected counterfeit pills during searches in September. The pills included substances represented as Xanax, oxycodone and other drugs. Police said testing of pills from earlier investigations had detected cychlorphine, while additional testing was underway on pills seized in the September operation.
The case illustrates one of the concerns surrounding emerging synthetic opioids: what a pill looks like does not establish what is actually inside it.
That uncertainty also extends to testing.
Cychlorphine is not detected by fentanyl test strips simply because those strips are designed to identify fentanyl, not every opioid that may be present in an illicit drug supply. Specialized laboratory testing may be needed to identify newer synthetic substances.
Colorado health officials told FOX31 that the state had not recorded an overdose death specifically involving cychlorphine. They also cautioned that the drug is not part of standard post-mortem toxicology panels and could be missed unless a coroner specifically requests testing for it.
That distinction matters when interpreting the available numbers. A lack of identified cases does not necessarily establish that the substance has never been present.
The Colorado Department of Public Health and Environment said naloxone remains appropriate for overdoses involving synthetic opioids such as cychlorphine. Because cychlorphine acts on opioid receptors, naloxone can reverse its opioid effects, although repeated doses and emergency medical care may be necessary in a severe overdose.
For now, the DEA's Rocky Mountain Division says it has not encountered cychlorphine within Colorado, Montana, Utah or Wyoming. The warning circulating among CSU students is arriving before a confirmed local detection — not after one.

articles.title_orig: Astronomers say they’ve discovered the first green star
articles.title_zh: Astronomers say they’ve discovered the first green star
articles.content_orig:
Astronomers analyzing white dwarf stars have for the first time found a star that would appear green to human eyes, according to a new study.
While for most stars, color is temperature-dependent and limited to a few hues, white dwarfs, which are the dense remnants of sun-like stars that have died, can glow in an incredible range of colors, said lead study author Mark Hollands, an astrophysicist at the University of Warwick, England, on Thursday.
“The colors that normal stars can have are pretty much only orange, white or blue,” Hollands told CNN.
“What we found is, for most white dwarfs, that’s the same as well. But there are some special cases where the physics in the outer layers of these stars are sufficiently strange that it causes actually quite big deviations in terms of their spectrum,” he said.
These deviations are due to the interaction between the helium in their atmosphere and traces of other elements, which vary between white dwarfs, depending on what material has interacted with the star over the course of its lifetime.
For instance, iron, magnesium and sodium, elements commonly found in rocks, can be found on the surface — potential evidence of a nearby former planetary system, or from “something like an asteroid that ventures too close to the white dwarf,” Hollands explained.
“It gets shredded up into dust, and then those rocky bits of dust and debris fall onto the white dwarf,” he said.
“And then that gets mixed into the outer layers, and then you can actually use that to measure what the rocky stuff was made off,” Hollands said.
“So we can actually use the white dwarf as a sort of diagnostic tool to actually measure the chemistry of planetary material,” he added.
“The white dwarf is taking apart the planets, and we’re able to see what was actually inside that planet — the proportion of the different elements — and that gives us clues in how these planets were formed,” said Adam Burgasser, a professor of astronomy and astrophysics at the University of California San Diego. “It is a crime scene, and we’re kind of piecing through the evidence that we have left available to us, and that’s allowing us to kind of piece the story of what the planet was and how it was made way, way, way back in in history.”
For this study, Hollands looked at the 151 known white dwarf stars that are within 20 parsecs, or around 65 light years, of Earth.
As for the green star, the main elements present are calcium, sodium and lithium, Hollands said.
“It kind of stimulated interest in me in looking more at that object and why it has so much material being accreted onto it,” said Burgasser, who was not involved in the study. “It can excite the public as well as the scientists in learning more about some of the more, I would say, extreme objects in this sample.”
Another notable star was “almost like a salmon pink,” due to the presence of a high density of carbon molecules, Hollands added.
While no white dwarf stars can be seen directly from Earth, Hollands was able to calculate their color using star spectrum data, which a statement from the researchers defines as “the ‘fingerprint’ produced when starlight is split apart by wavelength, much like a prism splits sunlight into a rainbow.”
Hollands explained that the research has also brought these space objects much closer to home.
“It gives you a nice human connection to these very distant things that are so far away that sometimes even as a researcher you feel quite disconnected from these objects that you study,” he said. “But then you can sort of add a human element into it and it feels a lot more tangible.”
The observations about the green star are based on existing data and may not shed new understandings about white dwarfs, but the study does offer an intriguing approach and view of these celestial bodies, said Agnès Kim, an astrophysicist and professor of physics at Penn State Scranton, who was not involved in the work.
“Doing a study that goes from spectrum to what the human eye would see is a cool intersection of physics and biology to me,” Kim wrote in an email. “I love that some would look green to us if they were close enough for us to see them, and even more fun that some would look pink.”
Burgasser added that the study’s categorization scheme using temperatures and atmospheric properties can be useful for the field moving forward.
“Some things are kind of purplish pink, and some other things were greenish and blue — and that kind of classification, which by the way we do all the time in astronomy, is classify things, allows us to focus on: why are these types of objects these colors, and are they related to each other based on their composition?” Burgasser said. “We have that information in other forms, but I think this is maybe a simplified way of organizing that data.”
Next, Hollands is planning to keep analyzing more white dwarf star spectra, with advances in scientific techniques meaning that researchers will be able to look at a new tranche of stars that are even farther away from Earth.
“We know of white dwarfs that we don’t have spectra for,” he said, “but that’s all about to change because there’s quite a few spectroscopic surveys” that are going to start delivering data.
“We’ll be getting a tenfold increase in the number of white dwarfs that have spectra,” Hollands said. “And so maybe if we’re lucky, we’ll go from one or maybe two green white dwarfs to 10 or 20.”
The study was published in the journal RAS Techniques and Instruments, or RASTI.

articles.title_orig: Pope speaks with Putin, denouncing recent attacks as he shows recovery from lung surgery progressing
articles.title_zh: Pope speaks with Putin, denouncing recent attacks as he shows recovery from lung surgery progressing
articles.content_orig:
The Vatican released new photos of Pope Leo XIV — the first since his lung cancer surgery — showing him celebrating Mass at the hospital in Rome.
The photos, released Friday, show the American-born pope standing at an altar in green vestments, celebrating Mass at a small chapel in Gemelli Hospital.
Vatican spokesman Matteo Bruni said in a statement that the pontiff presided alone over the liturgy, distributed Communion to medical personnel and Vatican gendarmes present and delivered a homily.
In his homily, Leo thanked the medical personnel for their service and their closeness to those who are fragile, and for the way they have taken care of him.
The 71-year-old pope had a portion of his right lung removed and received a diagnosis of lung cancer earlier this week . He is expected to remain at Gemelli Hospital until Oct. 20.
On Thursday, he resumed "a little bit of work activity, " including reading documents, and co-celebrated Mass, Vatican officials said. He also met with Archbishop Paolo Rudelli, undersecretary of state.
Doctors said Friday that tests confirmed "steady improvement" in his recovery.
"His post-operative recovery allows him to carry out his normal daily activities completely on his own," said a medical update signed by Leo's personal physician, Dr. Luigi Carbone, and the head of thoracic surgery at Gemelli Hospital, Dr. Stefano Margaritora.
The Vatican said Leo spoke with Russian President Vladimir Putin over the phone on Friday, during which he "expressed his deep concern about the grave humanitarian situation in the city of Oleshky" in Ukraine . Leo also called for a ceasefire to allow for food and medical assistance to be distributed in the region, as well as the safe evacuation of civilians.
"The Holy Father reaffirmed the Holy See's commitment to promoting dialogue and peace," the Vatican said.
The pope also held separate meetings with Cardinal Luis Antonio Tagle, the dean of the College of Cardinals, and Cardinal Baldassare Reina, the vicar general of the Diocese of Rome.
The Vatican said Leo will make his first public appearance on Sunday to deliver the traditional noontime prayer. Past popes who have been hospitalized have recited the Angelus from the balcony on the 10th floor of Gemelli Hospital.
Leo is scheduled to travel to South America next month. His ability to make the trip has been in question since his diagnosis, and the Vatican can change plans at any time.
However, on Friday, the Vatican published the names of journalists accredited to fly on the pope's plane with him during his Nov. 6-17 trip to Uruguay, Argentina and Peru.
Posting the media list signaled that, at least organizationally, the trip was going ahead.
The Vatican also released photos of some get-well notes that had been sent to Leo from patients at Gemelli's pediatric oncology ward.
One, from 7-year-old Angelo, told Leo that he had been on the 10th floor for 36 days. "My mother and I pray for you every night. Get well soon," he wrote, with little hearts at the bottom.
Giorgia, a university-aged student, wrote to Leo in his native English, saying she had long loved learning and practicing the language.
"When I heard on the news about you and your situation, I felt it a thousand times harder, because in some ways we're going through the same thing, and it made me feel closer to you," she wrote. "I pray to God that we both heal and I ask you to pray for me, too."
Anna  Matranga contributed to this report.

articles.title_orig: KFC is replacing Pepsi with Coca-Cola at US restaurants
articles.title_zh: KFC is replacing Pepsi with Coca-Cola at US restaurants
articles.content_orig:
KFC's U.S. restaurants will ditch PepsiCo and switch to Coca-Cola beverages next year, marking the first time in decades that the Yum Brands chain has changed its drink supplier, the restaurant company said Thursday.
Some of KFC's international markets serve Coke products, but the chain's U.S. restaurants have stuck with PepsiCo drinks ever since Pepsi bought KFC in 1986. At the time of the acquisition, KFC was Coke's second-largest fountain account, trailing only McDonald's. Pepsi later spun off KFC, along with sister chains Pizza Hut and Taco Bell — but even as the combined Yum Brands, the company stayed loyal to its previous owner. Without Pepsi, Taco Bell would not serve its iconic Mountain Dew Baja Blast.
The change comes as KFC aims to win back U.S. diners, who have ditched the fried chicken chain for rivals such as Chick-fil-A or Popeyes.
"This decision is a critical step in the Kentucky Fried Comeback," KFC U.S. President Catherine Tan-Gillespie wrote in a memo to franchisees and employees obtained by CNBC. "A new beverage offering, with a new partner in Coca-Cola, gives us a platform to innovate, meet changing tastes and give customers more reasons to choose us."
For many fast-food chains, beverages have become a critical way to attract consumers. A number of restaurants, including McDonald's and Taco Bell, have broadened their drink offerings with options such as refreshers or "dirty soda." For its part, KFC recently unveiled new drinks, including iced coffees and shakes, at Open House , its innovation restaurant in McKinney, Texas.
Coke told CNBC earlier this year that the company has helped many of its restaurant partners create new drinks.
KFC expects to be pouring Coke beverages in all of its U.S. restaurants by the end of the first quarter of 2027, Tan-Gillespie said.
Tan-Gillespie also said that Pepsi remains an important partner for KFC's parent company and the chain's international markets.
For decades, Coke and Pepsi have tussled over important restaurant partners, which represent both a sales opportunity and the chance to grow the visibility of their beverage brands.
It is unusual for large restaurant chains to switch beverage providers, but not unprecedented. In 2024, Pepsi poached Subway , the largest U.S. restaurant chain by number of locations, from Coke. Besides KFC, Coke has wooed away a number of notable Pepsi customers in recent years, including Culver's, Arby's and Panda Express.

articles.title_orig: China’s Proposed AI Export Controls and New Temporary Export Registration Requirements: Initial Thoughts
articles.title_zh: China’s Proposed AI Export Controls and New Temporary Export Registration Requirements: Initial Thoughts
articles.content_orig:
In the past, one of the concerns frequently raised by China’s technology industry was that regulations targeting emerging technologies and applications sometimes came too quickly. When confronted with new technological risks, regulators occasionally tended to regulate an entire area first and then make adjustments as they gained a better understanding of the situation. There were understandable reasons for this approach, particularly concerns about national security, public interests, and emerging risks. In practice, regulators often made considerable efforts to balance security and development during implementation. Nevertheless, the initial introduction of some policies did create uncertainty in the market and sometimes led to misunderstandings, or even deliberate misrepresentations, abroad.
This time, MOFCOM has taken a somewhat different approach: introducing a pre-export registration requirement first, rather than immediately placing the relevant technologies on the prohibited or restricted export lists, while continuing to seek public feedback. Specifically, from October 16, when the announcement was issued, until the revised Catalogue formally takes effect, companies intending to export technologies covered by the announcement must first register the proposed transactions through MOFCOM’s online system. The information required includes the technology being exported, the exporter and recipient, the destination country or region, the intended end use, and the transaction value. Companies are responsible for determining whether their technologies fall within the registration requirements. Even transactions that have already begun must be registered if they have not yet been completed. Importantly, registration is not limited to outright sales of technology. It also covers licensing technology for use overseas, as well as changes that result in the ownership or actual control of domestically held technology being transferred to a foreign entity.
By introducing mandatory pre-export registration, China is effectively establishing a preliminary administrative step ahead of any formal export licensing requirements. Companies can continue conducting legitimate technology exports, while the government gains a clearer picture of what technologies are being exported, where they are going, and what companies actually need in terms of international technology cooperation. This should provide a stronger factual basis for the eventual revision of the Catalogue. At the same time, if a particular transaction raises national security concerns or could affect China’s technological and industrial competitiveness, MOFCOM may seek additional information or, where legally authorized, take further measures, potentially including temporary restrictions.
In its official Q&A, MOFCOM also explained that the government had already conducted extensive assessments with research institutions and industry associations, consulted major companies, and taken into account the development needs of industries both in China and internationally. MOFCOM specifically emphasized that China’s longstanding policy of supporting companies in international business operations and technology cooperation remains unchanged. To me, this approach is somewhat like letting the dust settle before making a final decision : first gather information, understand actual business needs, and listen to stakeholders, then decide which technologies really need to be controlled and how restrictive those controls should be. It reflects an effort to balance security and development while paying greater attention to industry needs and the international competitive environment.
The legal basis for this temporary registration system is also interesting. From my initial reading, the revised Foreign Trade Law , which entered into force on March 1, 2026, added the phrase “or take other necessary measures” to Article 18. This appears to provide a clearer legal basis for regulatory measures beyond outright prohibitions and restrictions. MOFCOM specifically cited Article 18 when explaining the temporary registration requirement. The arrangement also bears some resemblance to the export certificate mechanism under China’s 2024 Regulations on Export Control of Dual-Use Items . Under that system, certain eligible exports can proceed after exporters submit the required information and obtain an export certificate, providing a simplified procedure for lower-risk transactions already subject to export controls. There are somewhat similar precedents in the United States. Around 2010, the US Department of Commerce’s Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) revised its export procedures for certain encryption products, allowing eligible products to obtain export authorization through simplified electronic registration procedures rather than undergoing the previous technical review process in every case.
Earlier media reports suggesting that China might introduce export restrictions on open-source AI models had raised concerns about whether Beijing was changing its position on open-source AI. Based on MOFCOM’s announcement, the proposed revisions clarify that releasing model technology as open source can constitute a form of technology export. If the relevant model technology falls into the prohibited category, it generally cannot be released through overseas open-source channels. If it falls into the restricted category, publishing it on an overseas open-source platform would require an export licence. However, MOFCOM has also made clear that open-source releases of restricted technologies will be eligible for simplified procedures, including automatic licensing. In other words, although the new framework may introduce a formal licensing requirement for releasing new versions of certain advanced open-source models, the practical approval process is expected to be relatively quick, with limited compliance costs for companies. For Chinese open-source model developers, this is certainly reassuring news.
MOFCOM has also clarified that technologies already lawfully placed in the public domain through open-source releases, academic publications, or other means will not fall within the scope of these controls. This means that if the relevant technology behind a model has already been lawfully disclosed, the publicly available technology would generally not become subject to new export licensing requirements simply because it meets the technical thresholds in the revised Catalogue. This treatment of publicly available technology is broadly similar to the approach taken under US export control rules, which also provide exclusions for certain published technology and software.
Overall, I think the proposed arrangements for open-source models are largely in line with expectations and consistent with China’s longstanding policy of supporting open-source AI development and broader technology sharing. Chinese AI companies have built considerable international influence through open-source models in recent years, attracting developers around the world and creating new commercial opportunities. As long as the eventual licensing procedures are sufficiently simple, transparent, and predictable, these revisions need not significantly undermine the global development of China’s open-source AI ecosystem.
One of the most important aspects of the announcement is the proposed expansion of controls on AI technology exports. The technologies covered include foundation models, AI agents, cybersecurity, chip design, and large-scale AI computing clusters. Broadly speaking, the proposal divides them into two categories: prohibited technologies, which generally cannot be transferred overseas, and restricted technologies, which require export licences.
There are four main categories.

articles.title_orig: American beef still stalled in China, but a new powerhouse market is emerging
articles.title_zh: American beef still stalled in China, but a new powerhouse market is emerging
articles.content_orig:
With China’s long running roadblocks for U.S. beef exports still taking a heavy toll on shipments, there are new bright spots in Asian markets.
According to the U.S. Meat Export Federation ( USMEF ), near-record performance for beef exports to Taiwan and a rebound in South Korea helped beef exports increase year-over-year in August — the most recent month with data available.
U.S. beef exports reached 86,362 metric tons (mt) in August, up 4% from a year ago, while export value climbed 13% to $785.9 million.
“I cannot say enough about the outstanding demand in Taiwan, which has truly been a star performer for U.S. beef in 2026,” said USMEF President and CEO Dan Halstrom.
With U.S. beef largely absent from China, Taiwan is mounting a strong challenge to Canada’s position as the fourth-highest value destination for U.S. beef in 2026. August beef exports to Taiwan reached the second highest value on record at $85.5 million, up 35% from a year ago and just short of the April 2022 record of $86.1 million.
Meanwhile, exports to Korea — the leading value destination for U.S. beef — reached 19,195 mt in August, up 14% from a year ago and above year-ago levels for the first time since January.
August beef exports to China increased from minimal levels the previous year, reaching 2,781 mt, valued at $25.6 million.
The increase reflects renewed eligibility for some U.S. plants, after China agreed in May to renew U.S. establishment registrations that Chinese regulators had allowed to expire. But USMEF said many U.S. plants remain suspended, and most others remain reluctant to ship to China until clarity is achieved regarding residue testing.
While beef exports to China were up slightly, Halstrom said the increase was “just a fraction” of what would be possible in that market.
“China still needs to relist suspended facilities and the U.S. industry needs further clarity on technical requirements before beef exports to China will significantly rebound,” Halstrom added.
For January through August, beef exports were down 7% year-over-year in volume (721,150 mt) but were just 1% lower in value, at $6.32 billion. USMEF said that decline is largely attributable to lower exports to China compared to the early months of 2025 — before market access obstacles began to heavily impact U.S. exports.
When excluding China from the January-August results, beef exports were 1% below last year in volume but 6% higher in value.
Beef export value equated to $436.11 per head of fed slaughter in August, up 17% from a year ago. The January-August average was $430.97 per head, up 8%. Exports accounted for 12.7% of total August beef production, up from 12.1% a year ago.

articles.title_orig: U.S. presses China on Mastercard, Citigroup market access in bilateral Bangkok talks, official says
articles.title_zh: U.S. presses China on Mastercard, Citigroup market access in bilateral Bangkok talks, official says
articles.content_orig:
BANGKOK – U.S. officials pressed Beijing on market access issues for Mastercard Inc and Citigroup Inc during at least two bilateral meetings with Chinese counterparts in Bangkok this week, according to a U.S. Treasury official.
The Treasury delegation, led by Deputy Secretary Francis Brooke, held bilateral meetings with officials from the People's Bank of China and the finance ministry on the sidelines of the Group of 20 finance meetings and the IMF-World Bank annual gathering this week, the official said, speaking on condition of anonymity to discuss the closed-door meetings.
The talks included market access for U.S. companies, including Mastercard, Visa and Citigroup, the official said, adding that regulatory approval was part of the agreement reached during the meeting between Presidents Donald Trump and Xi Jinping during the latter's state visit in Washington last month.
The sideline meetings in Bangkok continued discussions on implementing these deals, the official said.
The PBOC, China's National Financial Regulatory Administration, China Securities Regulatory Commission, Chinese embassies in Singapore and Thailand, the U.S. Treasury Department press office and Visa did not immediately respond to CNBC's request for comment. Citigroup and Mastercard declined to comment.
The progress follows China's Oct. 13 approval for Visa Inc. to begin preparing a wholly owned domestic card-clearing business . Visa has up to a year to prepare before it applies for an operating license, the PBOC has said .
China has opened much of its financial sector to foreign firms since 2018, gradually lifting foreign ownership caps on services such as securities, futures and fund management. It still limits cross-border capital flows and has kept state-backed domestic players dominant in payments.
Mastercard currently operates yuan card payments in China through a local joint venture with NetsUnion Clearing Corp., which began operating in 2024. The pending approval would allow it to operate as an independent entity, the person said.
Citigroup — which has hired several dozen employees for its China unit — is seeking a wholly owned securities license to conduct A-share brokerage, underwriting, research and principal trading businesses in the onshore market, two people familiar with the industry said, requesting anonymity for discussing private matters.
One of the two people close to Citigroup said the bank planned to increase its China securities staff to about 100.
The bank applied in late 2021, and Reuters reported last month that approval could come soon.
Trump and Xi are expected to meet in person for the third time this year in Shenzhen, China, for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in November.
"The move suggests the US-China trade environment remains benign, and Beijing is keen to keep up the momentum," said Dan Wang, China director at Eurasia Group.
Licensing U.S. financial firms is a "limited concession" on market access, she said, though it signals China is continuing to open up, and "this should marginally bolster investor confidence in Chinese assets."

articles.title_orig: HomePod is about to get free upgrade with these new features
articles.title_zh: HomePod is about to get free upgrade with these new features
articles.content_orig:
Apple unveiled three new Home products this week: HomeView , HomePod mini 2 , and a new Apple TV 4K . While there’s no new full-size HomePod launching, Apple did announce three features coming to the existing HomePod 2 via a free software update.
If you have an Apple Intelligence-compatible iPhone, your HomePod will get the new Sound Glow feature that’s also coming to HomePod mini 2.
Per Apple’s webpage for HomePod (2nd generation): “with Sound Glow, the top of your HomePod lights up with colors that match your album artwork, pulsing in tune with the music.”
The HomePod mini 2 announcement adds more details, which hopefully will be the same on the larger HomePod:
With Sound Glow, the top of HomePod mini transforms into a visual canvas that glows and pulses in sync with the music, reacting in real time to bass and treble. The song’s album artwork from Now Playing generates a color-matched light experience that’s unique to every song, and users can pick a soundscape like rain to trigger bespoke animations for a soothing atmosphere.
Apple has long let you use a HomePod as a speaker for your Mac via AirPlay. But soon, you’ll be able to set HomePod as the default Mac speaker for a more seamless, reliable connection.
Like Sound Glow, Apple announced this feature for HomePod mini 2, but its fine print says :
Compatible with HomePod mini 2 and HomePod (2nd generation) with support on all Mac desktops and laptops with Wi-Fi 6E or later.
So if you want to upgrade your Mac speaker setup with the HomePod, or a stereo pair of HomePods, that will soon be easier than ever.
If you want the best, all-Apple home theater experience, a new surround sound feature for HomePod and Apple TV 4K will deliver that.
Exclusive to the new Apple TV 4K (4th gen) , users can set up four HomePods—two as front speakers, two as rear—for a more immersive audio experience.
From Apple’s press release :
Home theater surround sound requires four HomePod mini 2 or HomePod (2nd generation) speakers in matching pairs (front and rear), paired with Apple TV 4K (4th generation) running the latest operating system software.
Apple hasn’t yet confirmed when these new features are launching on HomePod, but they’re expected to debut with iOS 27.2 and HomePod 27.2 later this month .
Are you planning to use any of the HomePod’s new features? Let us know in the comments.
FTC: We use income earning auto affiliate links. More.
Check out 9to5Mac on YouTube for more Apple news:
HomePod is Apple’s effort to “reinvent home …
Ryan got his start in journalism as an Editor at MacStories, where he worked for four years covering Apple news, writing app reviews, and more. For two years he co-hosted the Adapt podcast on Relay FM, which focused entirely on the iPad. As a result, it should come as no surprise that his favorite Apple device is the iPad Pro.

articles.title_orig: Starlink access still not fully restored for Ukraine’s military, says Zelenskyy
articles.title_zh: Starlink access still not fully restored for Ukraine’s military, says Zelenskyy
articles.content_orig:
Ukrainian president says US limiting access was a ‘dangerous and unpleasant surprise’, amid reports the order came from inside White House
Volodymyr Zelenskyy has said the Ukrainian military’s access to the Starlink satellite internet service has not yet been fully restored, as media reports suggested the order to throttle the service had come from within the White House.
Zelenskyy met European leaders on Friday in Brussels, where he asked the EU for another €70bn (£60bn) next year to fund Ukraine’s defence against Russia.
The meeting offered an important opportunity for Zelenskyy and Europe to align their strategies, as Zelenskyy once again found himself embroiled in a major quarrel with the US president, Donald Trump .
Hours earlier, Trump had called Ukraine’s renewed strikes on Russian oil refineries “a disgrace” and criticised ⁠Zelenskyy, after a purported “energy ceasefire” between Russia and Ukraine failed to take hold.
“All he’s doing is making the world oil price higher,” Trump told the Newsmax television channel. “Well, I think that’s a disgrace.”
Energy analysts told the BBC that the US-Israeli war on Iran was having the biggest impact on diesel export volumes , although the Ukraine war was also significant.
Trump’s administration is suspected of withholding intelligence from Ukraine on incoming Russian ballistic missile strikes, and of throttling Starshield, the military version of the Starlink satellite internet network, to prevent it from being used on drones flying faster than 100mph. Neither has officially been confirmed.
Speaking after meeting EU leaders on Friday, Zelenskyy said that Starshield had not yet returned to normal.
“Our defence ministry is in touch and my partners, they told me that there were signals from the White House that they would return these capabilities,” Zelenskyy said. “Have they returned to the previous speed limits? No. But is it coming back now? Yes.”
Reuters on Friday reported that the order to throttle Starshield had come from inside the White House, according to two US officials and a western official briefed on the matter. They did not identify the White House official who had made the decision, but said the Pentagon had been informed that the SpaceX Starshield service for the Ukrainian military had to be slowed.
Zelenskyy called it a “very dangerous and unpleasant surprise” that speeds had been reduced on Starlink, which Ukraine uses to support its most effective air defence systems against Russian jet-powered drones.
Starlink is produced by Elon Musk’s SpaceX, but controlled by the US government .
When Zelenskyy arrived for talks with EU leaders, he was applauded by the heads of state and government of the bloc’s 27 countries. Zelenskyy later said he had heard “only support”, when asked about reports that European leaders had asked him to dial down his criticism of Trump.
According to a transcript of his remarks, he told EU leaders that the war would cost €155bn in 2027. “And we need at least €70bn more from you – for defence, for weapons, and for our resilience,” he said. “This is a realistic amount.”
The European Commission president, Ursula von der Leyen, agreed with Zelenskyy that “it is clear that we have a gap of €70bn that has to be covered” for 2027, although she expected Ukraine’s other partners – which she did not name – to cover part of the sum.
The EU is currently giving Ukraine regular payments from a €90bn funding plan agreed last December that was intended to cover two-thirds of Kyiv’s civilian and military needs for 2026-27. The remaining third was to be filled by other “international partners”, such as the UK, Canada, Norway and Japan.
The realisation that Kyiv again risks a financial crunch has put Russia’s €210bn assets frozen inside the EU back on the table. The EU takes the profits from those assets to support Ukraine, but last year decided against using the funds themselves, instead opting for an EU-backed €90bn loan.
Belgium, which hosts the vast majority of the Russian funds, remains strongly opposed to using the frozen assets, fearing it will be left to carry the financial burden if the plan goes wrong. But Zelenskyy said there could be an alternative.
“We need something like a special EU-controlled custodian to reduce the risk of them being unfrozen and divided up among those who clearly do not want what is best for Europe or an end to this war,” he said.
The European Commission, a strong backer of last year’s rejected frozen assets plan, has been reluctant to propose new variants – such as an EU-controlled custodian – because it fears running into same opposition from Belgium and other sceptical member states.
Before the summit, Belgium’s prime minister, Bart De Wever, said Zelenskyy would “probably look everybody straight in the eye and say: thank you for the €90bn, but that money is going to run out because a war is a very costly thing”.
Von der Leyen said the EU had supported Trump’s energy ceasefire “but we have seen that Russia did not respect it, not a single minute” and instead had escalated its attacks. She said the EU intended to increase pressure on Russia, promising a 22nd round of sanctions and adding: “We will not lift any sanctions unless Russia stops the war.”

articles.title_orig: Trump Cancels Planned Execution Livestream of Nidal Hasan, Fort Hood Shooter
articles.title_zh: Trump Cancels Planned Execution Livestream of Nidal Hasan, Fort Hood Shooter
articles.content_orig:
Americans are backing President Donald Trump's announcement that Nidal Hasan's execution will not be publicly livestreamed. (Credit: Nicholas Ballasy for Fox News Digital)
Americans interviewed by Fox News Digital were overwhelmingly pleased with President Donald Trump's decision to call off livestreaming the Fort Hood shooter’s planned firing squad execution after the Pentagon had announced it would be livestreamed for public viewing.
"I'm really glad that he called it off, because I feel like it's not really a deterrent, it's more like a shock effect," Sylvia from Arizona told Fox News Digital. "I don't think we really need that in this country right now."
"The only other countries that really do that are like North Korea," David from Arizona said. "We don't want to be North Korea."
AMERICANS DRAW THE LINE AT LIVESTREAMING ‘SPECTACLE’ OF FORT HOOD SHOOTER'S EXECUTION: ‘IT’S AN ABOMINATION’
President Donald Trump and North Korea's leader Kim Jong-un talk before a meeting in the Demilitarized Zone on June 30, 2019, in Panmunjom, Korea. (Brendan Smialowski/AFP via Getty Images)
"I never approved of the idea of it being public in the first place," Nate from Virginia said. "I think it's just ridiculous to make a spectacle out of an execution, especially in 2026 of all time."
War Secretary Pete Hegseth announced earlier this month that Nidal Hasan’s execution, set for Dec. 3, would be publicly available via livestream.
Trump took to Truth Social on Thursday to announce that while livestreaming the execution could serve as a deterrent to terrorism , the execution would not be available for public viewing as he acknowledged that many Americans would rather not witness Hasan's death.
"He will die, as scheduled, by firing squad, but this event will not be streamed," Trump wrote on Truth Social.
FORT HOOD SURVIVORS PRAISE TRUMP FOR SCRAPPING HASAN EXECUTION LIVESTREAM: ‘WE’RE NOT BARBARIC’
President Donald Trump announced that the execution of convicted Fort Hood shooter Nidal Hasan would not be livestreamed, reversing an earlier Pentagon announcement that the execution would be livestreamed to the public. (Aaron Schwartz/Getty Images; Bell County Sheriff's Office via Getty Images)
Despite the execution not being publicly available, Trump confirmed that the family members of the victims who died in the 2009 shooting "deserve to witness JUSTICE" and will be permitted to attend in person.
"Well, maybe he has a conscience now," one person said about Trump’s reversal of the Pentagon’s decision to livestream the execution.
Some Americans who spoke with Fox News Digital argued that Trump’s decision to call off the livestreaming was to save face after criticism of the proposal was circulating, with many arguing that livestreaming the execution would turn it into a spectacle and could easily be exposed to children.
"I think it was trying to save his image," Ivy from Georgia said.
"He doesn't wanna look like a bad person, but at the end of the day, we all know who he really is — a piece of s---," Ivy said.
"I think it was just so clearly an unpopular thing to do that he realized it would probably do more harm to his public image than good," Nate said.
Hasan, an Army psychiatrist at the time of the shooting, killed 13 and injured 32 people when he shouted "Allahu Akbar" and opened fire at a military base in Texas. The mass killer is now 56 years old and uses a wheelchair after he was left partially paralyzed from being shot by police officers during his arrest almost 17 years ago.
TRUMP CLEARS WAY FOR FORT HOOD TERRORIST TO FACE ARMY FIRING SQUAD NEARLY 17 YEARS AFTER MASSACRE
Major Nidal Malik Hasan, the U.S. Army doctor identified by authorities as the mass shooter at the U.S. Army post in Fort Hood, Texas, is seen in this undated handout photo from a PDF file of the U.S. Government Uniformed Services University of the Health Sciences downloaded on Nov. 6, 2009. (Reuters/Uniformed Services University of the Health Sciences/Handout)
Only one person who spoke with Fox News Digital argued that livestreaming the execution would have been a good idea, even adding that he would have watched the livestream himself.
"Yeah, I would watch," Daniel from Virginia said. "Because I wouldn't want somebody to kill another person, you know what I mean? That person should be held wrong for what he's done."

Hasan was sentenced to death during his 2013 military trial after being found guilty on all 42 counts. His execution is set to be the first U.S. military execution in over six decades.

articles.title_orig: 'Doomsday Glacier' Could Contribute Twice as Much to Sea-Level Rise by 2100, Scientists Warn
articles.title_zh: 'Doomsday Glacier' Could Contribute Twice as Much to Sea-Level Rise by 2100, Scientists Warn
articles.content_orig:
Global warming is melting the polar ice caps and glaciers of the planet, but there is a particularly significant freezing mass that, by itself, can make sea level rise very important. It is the Thwaites glacier, in Antarctica, known as the ‘Glass of Judgment glaciar’.
Thwaites glacier has been losing ice for decades. Now there are concerns of rapidly accelerating loss.

articles.title_orig: 'We're not moving fast enough': World falling short of promised 30% land and water goals ahead of UN biodiversity summit
articles.title_zh: 'We're not moving fast enough': World falling short of promised 30% land and water goals ahead of UN biodiversity summit
articles.content_orig:
Efforts to raise hundreds of billions of dollars to preserve the world’s oceans, forests, rivers, lakes and other parts of the natural world have fallen short ahead of a key U.N. summit on biodiversity.
The yawning gap between the stated ambition of nations to protect biodiversity and what money has been raised will be a central topic in Yerevan, Armenia, when the biodiversity conference, known as COP17, gets started on Monday. The nearly two-week event, scheduled to end Oct. 30, is a chance for nearly 200 countries that are part of the treaty to take stock of their progress on 23 global targets after agreeing to a historic deal crafted in Montreal in 2022. The United States is not a party to the treaty.
Countries in Montreal committed to protect 30% of land and water considered important for biodiversity by 2030, a goal known as 30×30.
They also promised to raise $200 billion a year by 2030 for biodiversity and begin phasing out or reforming subsidies that could provide another $500 billion for nature. There were also commitments to increase to $20 billion annually by 2025 money that went to poor countries. That number would increase to $30 billion each year by 2030.
“We’re not moving fast enough,” convention executive secretary Astrid Schomaker told The Associated Press, before a U.N. progress report released Thursday found fewer than half of parties’ biodiversity targets are on track and that current commitments would only protect 26% of land and only 12% of sea by 2030.
Data from the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development showed countries were raising between $75 billion and $92 billion each year from 2023 to 2025 — less than half the 2030 goal. Commitments to reduce $500 billion in harmful subsidies — government support and funding for sectors like fisheries and agriculture — have gained little traction, with few countries identifying which subsidies they would cut.
Countries were on track to provide the $20 billion to poor countries by 2025. The latest data showed $19 billion had been raised in 2024. But a drop in foreign aid raises questions over whether the upward trend will continue.
“Do we have enough money actually to finance the commitments that countries have made? And how do we get more finance to flow toward biodiversity positive outcomes?” Schomaker said. “That is the crucial question for the COP.”
The campaign to protect biodiversity, which first garnered global attention with the Rio Earth Summit in 1992, has often seemed like a losing battle.
In a bid to grow their economies and support increasing populations, countries have converted forests into farm land, overfished their waters and reduced habitats of many plants and animals through unchecked development. Climate change , at the same time, has created the conditions for widespread wildfires and prolonged droughts that have decimated ecosystems.
As a result, three-quarters of the world’s land has been “severely altered” by humans and a million of the world’s plants and animals are threatened with extinction, according to a 2019 U.N. report . Wildlife populations have also plummeted, according to the WWF’s 2026 Living Planet Report released this month. They have declined on average by 73% between 1970 and 2022.
“We are losing everything that matters for us as humans on this planet,” Schomaker said.
Meanwhile, there are some signs that countries are protecting more biodiversity. Countries have announced over 5,000 initiatives tied to the treaty.
A report from the Campaign for Nature, a global initiative which has spearheaded the 30×30 effort, found that countries in Latin America have already committed to protecting 29% of their land while those in Oceania have promised to preserve 41% of their seas. Last year, the Philippines created a marine protected area where catching rays and sharks is prohibited, according to the Wildlife Conservation Society. In 2023, Cambodia set aside almost 100,00 acres (40,000 hectares) of flooded grassland habitat for protection while Argentina created a national park in 2024.
Brian O’Donnell, director of the Campaign for Nature, said where and what we need to protect is clear, as are the methods to do so.
“What is now needed is an upswing in political ambition and determination,” said O’Donnell.
O’Donnell said an international agreement reached last year to protect marine diversity on the high seas — the High Seas Treaty — would help but more was needed.
Many expected conference attendees are hoping countries, the private sector and philanthropies use the meeting next week to announce major biodiversity funding initiatives.
Susan Lieberman, the vice president for international policy for WCS, said that protecting important biodiversity required money and expertise.
“You can’t just say, OK, there’s a line on the map. You need to do the science,” she said. “You need to know if it’s in the right place. If you’re going to establish a park, you better have management of the park, governance, infrastructure.”
That is especially true in poorer countries, according to Dorothy Maseke, head of the African Natural Capital Alliance Secretariat, an African-led initiative to integrate nature into financial decision-making. Many developing countries with significant biodiversity are not able to finance protecting and conserving it, as governments are trying to also pay to finance healthcare, education, infrastructure and public services.
Daniel Mukubi, the biodiversity negotiator for Congo, agreed it was “not possible to scale up protected and conserved areas” without sufficient financial help. He lamented that overseas development assistance, including from the United States, has dropped significantly. That has resulted in “weakened law enforcement and eco-guards patrolling critical habitat” including at several of the country’s UNESCO World Heritage sites.
“If these valuable ecosystems collapse because international funding fails to secure them, the resulting economic damages will cost the global market tens of trillions of dollars,” Mukubi said. “So, investing in the Congo basin is not an expenditure. It is the most cost-effective insurance policy the West can buy.”
Another topic expected to be big is how to get governments to reduce an estimated $7.3 trillion in subsidies and redirect that money into nature. That is about 30 times more than what was invested in nature-based solutions in 2023, according to the Campaign for Nature.
“Every year, trillions of dollars go into subsidies that harm nature, even as funding to protect it falls far short of what’s needed,” Patricia Zurita, Conservation International’s executive director, said in a statement. “We can’t reverse biodiversity loss while continuing to finance the activities that drive deforestation, overfishing, pollution and more.”
Associated Press reporter Sibi Arasu in Bengaluru, India, contributed to this report.
