articles.title_orig: Deadly School Roof Collapse in Pakistan Raises Questions Over Regulation
articles.title_zh: Deadly School Roof Collapse in Pakistan Raises Questions Over Regulation
articles.content_orig:
ISLAMABAD, Oct 15 (Reuters) - At least 34 schoolchildren and a female teacher were killed on Thursday when the roof of a school collapsed during morning classes in the northwestern Pakistani city of Peshawar, police and rescue officials said.
As panicked ‌parents and relatives thronged the school site to search for their loved ones, rescue workers spent hours pulling children from ‌the rubble of the privately run Al-Khair Education Center.
Most of the victims were under 13 and from low-income households.
At least 45 children suffered injuries, ranging from minor wounds to ​severe trauma, said Arif Khattak, regional director of the Rescue Department.
Television footage showed rescuers clawing through debris with their bare hands and carrying bloodied children to waiting ambulances as residents crowded the narrow alley where the school stood.
POLICE CHIEF SAYS BUILDING STRUCTURE WAS WEAK
A higher-floor roof collapsed onto classrooms below, crumpling two storeys of the building, a rescue official said.
"The fatalities include 12 girl students and a female teacher," Lady Reading Hospital spokesperson ‌Mohammad Asim said.
Three children remained in critical condition ⁠with head injuries, while most of the injured taken to the hospital had been treated and discharged, he added.
The incident took place at 8:48 a.m. local time (0348 GMT) and the rescue operation lasted for four to ⁠five hours, Khattak said.
"It was a weak building structure," Peshawar police chief Mian Saeed said. "Its roof was overloaded with construction on a weak structure, which caused the collapse."
Saeed said the school's owner had been arrested and an investigation launched. A total of 110 students were attending lessons in three classrooms when ​the ​roof caved in.
'MAKE AN EXAMPLE OF THEM', BEREAVED RELATIVE SAYS
Distraught relatives accused the ​school of ignoring concerns about the building's condition and ‌demanded accountability.
"Make an example of them, a lesson for all, so that no one dares open a school just to make money without providing facilities," said Mohammad Zaman, who lost two nephews in the collapse.
The school was located in a poor, crowded neighbourhood of Peshawar, capital of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa where Pakistan's president imposed a state of emergency on Sunday saying the provincial government had failed to tackle Islamist militancy from neighbouring Afghanistan, an allegation it denied.
Pakistan spends less than 1% of its nearly $450 billion GDP on education, leaving many families dependent on low-cost ‌private schools.
Many of them operate from poorly maintained rented buildings with limited oversight, ​contributing to recurring safety concerns. In June, at least 14 children died when the ​roof of a tutoring centre housed in a dilapidated building ​collapsed in the eastern city of Lahore.
There was no immediate comment from school officials.
Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif expressed ‌sorrow over the tragedy and offered condolences to the victims' ​families, his office said.
Jawad Ahmad, whose ​son and daughter attended the school and survived, said the news left him devastated.
"It felt as if someone had shot me in the chest when I learned that the school building had collapsed," he said.
The province, governed for years by the party ​of jailed former Prime Minister Imran Khan, has ‌frequently been at odds with the federal administration. President Asif Ali Zardari imposed a new governor on the province when ​he declared the state of emergency on Sunday, sharpening the tensions.
(Reporting by Islamabad bureau; Writing by Hritam Mukherjee, YP ​Rajesh and Shilpa Jamkhandikar; Editing by Clarence Fernandez, Ros Russell, Philippa Fletcher)

articles.title_orig: CoreWeave Drops. Even Jensen Huang and Cathie Wood Can’t Buoy the Stock.
articles.title_zh: CoreWeave Drops. Even Jensen Huang and Cathie Wood Can’t Buoy the Stock.
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
Neocloud stocks like CoreWeave ( CRWV ) and Nebius ( NBIS ) are poised to cap off a horrible week in their relatively short time in public markets.
CoreWeave and Nebius stocks are both down about 15% just in the past five days.
While concerns about CoreWeave's financial health are being blamed for the neocloud stock routs, the reality is that it's not just a CoreWeave issue. The overall financial health of the AI economic system build-out is being more closely scrutinized in a land of higher-for-longer interest rates.
Goldman Sachs explained the pressure quite well in a new note on Friday.
US dollar high-yield AI-related debt spreads widened by 25 basis points between Oct. 13 and 14, reaching a new high of 360 basis points over Treasurys. By contrast, non-AI-related debt spreads were only two basis points wider and remain below their March peak, Goldman Sachs pointed out (see charts below).
Within AI-related debt issuers, the widening has been concentrated in AI-related corporate bonds and data center project finance.
"While some softer AI-related sentiment can move datacenter bonds wider, especially if there is a reassessment around off-taker credit risk, we view AI-related corporate bonds, from either neoclouds or firms with significant frontier lab exposure, as being at the epicenter of the funding cost debate," Goldman Sachs strategist Amanda Lynam explained. "Further removed AI-adjacent Energy and Utilities have been more resilient, in our view partly reflecting more diversified revenue streams and a relatively defensive earnings profile. We think the widening reflects a reassessment of the economics of the AI buildout, particularly for lower-rated borrowers that are more exposed to higher-for-longer rates and potential energy-cost pressures."
Lynam sees "some near-term reversal" of the recent sell-off in US high-yield debt tied to AI. But she acknowledges that "dispersion across AI-related issuers is likely to remain high."

articles.title_orig: Young Voters Say They Are Turning Their Backs on Trump and His Party
articles.title_zh: Young Voters Say They Are Turning Their Backs on Trump and His Party
articles.content_orig:
President Trump speaks at a campaign rally in San Antonio on Oct. 7. Trump made big inroads with young voters in 2024, but some of that support appears to be waning. Mandel Ngan/AFP via Getty Images hide caption
📲 Follow the midterms & more in the NPR App .
Gen Z Americans were a key part of President Trump's winning coalition in 2024. Nearly two years later — and with early voting underway in multiple states for the midterms — some of that youth support has faded.
That sentiment was on display in a focus group, conducted last week, of eight Generation Z Trump voters, who reported varying degrees of unhappiness and disappointment over the state of politics, with some going as far as to say they regret supporting Trump in 2024.
The conversation was conducted virtually by Navigator Research , a left-leaning polling group. Participants ranged in age from 20 to 29 and spanned five states: Florida, Mississippi, Ohio, Texas and South Carolina — places Trump won by double digits in the last election. Two of those states, Texas and Ohio , are home to competitive races that could be key to control of the Senate .
For participants who now regret their vote for Trump, much of their frustration centers on what they see as a string of failed promises. When asked to give the president's job performance a letter grade, a majority of participants, 6 out of 8, assigned him a grade of either D or F, while two selected C.
"I just feel like nothing went correctly. I just feel like everything got worse," said John, a 29-year-old Black man from Florida. (Participants agreed to be part of the focus group on the condition that they be identified by only their first names.)
John, who identifies as a Republican and has voted for Trump since 2016, gave the president an F and said he now plans to support Democratic candidates this fall, in large part because of the strain he has felt from rising costs.
"I'm willing to give the other side a chance," he added. "I don't think they're going to make a total change. But things are just horrible right now for me. So I feel like even if they make one or two small changes, it will probably benefit me."
Though the focus group is not a nationally representative survey, the frustrations shared by participants echoed polling conducted by Navigator this month, which found that more than a third of Gen Zers — those under age 30 — regret voting for Trump, higher than older generations do.
Trump's rising unpopularity among young voters isn't in a vacuum. He has also lost ground with other key groups that shifted right in 2024, notably independents and Latino voters — and in a year when the Republican Party is facing political headwinds, it's unclear whether that expanded coalition from two years ago can show up at the same strength now.
While some voters, like John in Florida, do feel compelled to vote blue this cycle in response to Trump, 4 of the 8 who took part in the focus group said they still planned to back Republicans this year. Three said they'd vote for Democrats; one participant said she was still deciding.
Matthew, a 25-year-old Black man living in Texas, said he doesn't regret his support for the president and gave him a C grade.
"I feel like he's done a really good job closing the border," he said. "I also do appreciate his efforts in trying to end some of the conflicts that began under the last administration, besides the fact that the Iran conflict hasn't really worked the best, from my perspective."
He plans to vote in the midterm elections and argued that Trump will be able to carry out more of his agenda if Republicans can secure a larger majority in both the House of Representatives and the Senate, although national polls indicate that the GOP is more likely to lose seats.
But enthusiasm is a different question.
Courtney, a 20-year-old white woman based in South Carolina, said she doesn't regret her vote for Trump in 2024 and overall aligns with Republicans, but she did admit she has grown more distrustful of both major political parties, particularly on foreign policy.
"I just really do feel like we would be in this situation either way. … Education, the economy, everything else would be so much better if we weren't pumping money out into other countries that aren't ours," she said, referring to U.S. aid for Israel and the decision to go to war with Iran.
"I don't think it matters what side you vote on — that's why I voted red, because I agree with those policies more — but at the end of the day, what we do in the Middle East is going to be not at all up to [the] party [in power]," she said during the focus group.
That sense of political disaffection may underscore a growing challenge for both Republicans and Democrats moving forward as both try to repair ties with this generation.
"As we see people regret their vote for Trump, sour on the Republican Party and Republican policies, that doesn't necessarily mean that they're swinging right over to Democrats," said Melissa Toufanian, the managing director at Navigator.
Toufanian points to Navigator's own polling , which has found that even as the GOP has lost trust on economic issues, "it's not a one-for-one with Democrats gaining that trust."
"A lot of people are moving to this middle, this category that 'I don't trust either party,'" she said. "We are seeing people who are becoming increasingly pessimistic about our political parties and our political system, and they're not feeling strongly that either party can really deliver for them."

articles.title_orig: Zelenskyy warns 20M Ukrainians could flee to Europe if Russia wins war
articles.title_zh: Zelenskyy warns 20M Ukrainians could flee to Europe if Russia wins war
articles.content_orig:
BRUSSELS — Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy warned Friday that as many as 20 million Ukrainians could be forced to flee to Europe if his country falls to Russia.
“Russia is killing us,” Zelenskyy told reporters at a press conference on Friday during a summit of European Union leaders, adding Ukrainians were being “pushed” out of their country. “They [Russia] don’t want to stop.”
In the early days of Russia’s full-scale invasion, millions of Ukrainians fled their homes in Europe’s fastest and largest refugee crisis since World War II. Today, over 4 million Ukrainians live in EU countries under temporary protection status, with the largest populations in Germany, Poland and Czechia, according to Eurostat .
Zelenskyy’s stark warning comes as Ukraine heads into a brutal fifth wartime winter under Russian bombardment. Kyiv faces a budget shortfall of $30 to $35 million next year, according to projections from the International Monetary Fund — even accounting for a €90 billion loan Brussels agreed to provide last year.
The Ukrainian president traveled to Brussels to meet with European leaders and shore up financial support for his embattled country. While the EU is Ukraine’s staunchest backer, the bloc’s list of priorities is stacked with rising energy costs, looming elections, geopolitical crises and an impasse over its €2 trillion budget.

articles.title_orig: YORK | ‘Digger’: Making Art in a Hopeless World
articles.title_zh: YORK | ‘Digger’: Making Art in a Hopeless World
articles.content_orig:
Digger is not what I expected. The latest from Alejandro González Iñárritu, whose recent films (notably Birdman and The Revenant ) have been Oscar players, advertised itself accordingly. When the marketing campaign kicked off with a teaser that felt more like an ode to its lead actor’s filmography, it seemed obvious that this film was a Tom Cruise vehicle meant to earn him his first competitive Academy Award. I expected another film like 2021’s Don’t Look Up , which did well at the Oscars, but fell a little short for me. This false advertising was intentional: What Digger is doing is much more interesting and part of what makes the film work is its subversion of expectations. All of this makes it feel nearly impossible to review Digger , which is better experienced with no background knowledge at all, but it feels equally important to write about what might just be the most important film of the year.
Digger follows Tom Cruise’s Digger Rockwell, the cartoonishly evil owner of an oil company whose rig explodes, creating an environmental disaster. As an ice shelf dislodged by the explosion hurtles towards Europe, threatening to flood Norway, Digger must work with environmental expert Dr. Nirav Ganesh (Riz Ahmed) and U.S. President Compson (John Goodman) to decide what comes next. The film isn’t really about an environmental crisis, though climate change is clearly on Iñárritu’s mind. What Digger gets at is the power of storytelling and the different ways it can be utilized. After hearing of the explosion, Digger is fairly uninterested in stopping the ice shelf from colliding. He has no control over nature, as Dr. Ganesh constantly reminds him. What he can control, however, is the narrative, and in the age of modern technology, Digger finds it easy to shape the story that the public begins to tell.
Some might scoff at Iñárritu’s hyper-contemporary setting: Like Ari Aster’s controversial Eddington from last year, Digger directly addresses the effects of social media, short form content and even AI chatbots on our culture. I find this extremely effective — when Digger and Compson discuss deploying a firewall to track and prevent any mention of the incoming ice shelf on social media, rather than warning Norway ahead of time, the audience becomes aware of how our own internet activity can easily be monitored and censored. Even more strikingly, when Iñárritu abruptly cuts from a 10-minute long take to an insert shot of someone’s Instagram live footage, he pulls the audience out of the massive aspect ratio to the vertical smartphone screen. This juxtaposition takes viewers out of the flow of the film, making it suddenly seem much more personal. Digger constantly reminds you that this is not something to watch from a distance, it is a story that must be taken seriously and acted upon: or else the same thing will happen in our own world.
Digger is not just criticizing the rich and powerful, but forces all of us to look within ourselves. In this moment, when Iñárritu switches from VistaVision camera to phone, he also exposes how the audience uses their technology as a shield. In the scene, Digger is monologuing to an audience of politicians and representatives, turning their attacks back onto them. As they blame him for environmental collapse, Digger reminds his audience that the very phones they use to film him require the oil he digs up for energy. Still, his audience watches him only through their screens. Throughout the film, Iñárritu constantly turns his critique back onto the audience, and even onto himself. No one is guiltless in the collapse of our planet and to watch a film like Digger , or any of its predecessors mentioned above, laugh at the antics of the out-of-touch elite, and return to our normal lives without another thought is not a neutral act.
Some have said that Digger seems to hate its own existence, but I see something much more hopeful in its message. There’s a power in storytelling that can be harnessed by all, whether its by the rich and powerful, who use it to censor and control us, by satirists, who find no other choice in times such as these but to laugh, or by audiences, who find comfort in worlds far from our own that make us forget our own problems. Digger questions what it means to create art when it feels like the world is falling apart, probing at the ethics of accepting funding from corrupt corporations, the interplay between artmaking and activism and, ultimately, the communal experiences that art makes possible. Ultimately, while Digger doesn’t pretend to have any answers to the questions it presents, it makes it impossible to watch idly without thinking deeply about the film’s narrative. While some audiences may not connect with the film, I still think it’s worth seeing Digger in the theatre and letting yourself sit in the discomfort.
‘Projections’ is a column focused on reviewing recent film releases.

articles.title_zh: National newspaper supplements mark World Mental Health Day 2026 in Bangladesh
articles.content_orig:
To mark World Mental Health Day 2026, special
newspaper supplements were published across nine national newspapers in
Bangladesh, helping bring mental health messages to readers across the country.
The supplements appeared in seven
Bangla-language and two English-language newspapers: Bangladesh Pratidin,
Bhorer Akash, Jaijaidin, Jugantor, Kalbela, Dainik Amader Shomoy, Prothom Alo,
New Age and The Daily Star .
Published on 10 October, the supplements
highlighted Bangladesh’s ongoing efforts to strengthen mental health services,
promote mental well-being and raise awareness of the importance of mental
health. By reaching audiences through some of the country’s major national
newspapers, the initiative helped bring mental health into wider public
discussion and reinforce its importance as a national health and social
priority.
The supplements featured messages from national
leaders, senior government officials and health-sector representatives,
reflecting broad engagement with the mental health agenda. Contributors
included the President and Prime Minister of the People’s Republic of
Bangladesh; the Vice President of the Ziaur Rahman Foundation (ZRF) ; the
Ministers responsible for Health and Family Welfare, Social Welfare, and Women
and Children Affairs; the Special Assistant on Health Affairs to the Prime
Minister; the State Minister for Health and Family Welfare; and the Secretary
of the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare.
Messages were also contributed by the WHO
Representative to Bangladesh, the Director General of the Directorate General
of Health Services, and the Director of the National Institute of Mental
Health.
Together, the supplements underscored the
importance of sustained attention to mental health, strengthening accessible
and responsive services, and continuing efforts to reduce stigma and increase
public understanding of mental health conditions.
World Mental Health Day provides an opportunity
each year to raise awareness, strengthen commitment and encourage action to
ensure that mental health is recognized as an essential part of health and
well-being. The nationwide publication of the supplements provided an
opportunity to extend these messages beyond the health sector and reach people
in communities across Bangladesh.

articles.title_orig: Ranked: The World’s Biggest Carbon Emitters
articles.title_zh: Ranked: The World’s Biggest Carbon Emitters
articles.content_orig:
China is the world’s largest greenhouse gas emitter by a wide margin, but how do other major economies compare?
This graphic ranks countries by their share of global greenhouse gas emissions in 2025, using data from the European Commission’s Emissions Database for Global Atmospheric Research ( EDGAR ). Global shares exclude international aviation and shipping.
China leads the ranking with nearly 16 billion metric tons of greenhouse gas emissions in 2025, roughly 2.7 times the U.S. total. India ranks third, followed by Russia and Indonesia.
Together, the five largest emitters account for nearly 58% of global emissions, highlighting how much of the world’s total comes from a small number of economies.
Note: Some entries combine multiple geographic areas, as reported in the source data.
Population helps explain emissions totals, but energy consumption and industrial activity also play major roles.
Saudi Arabia, for example, produces more greenhouse gases than Pakistan despite having a much smaller population. Australia also generates more than twice Bangladesh’s emissions, even though its population is less than one-sixth as large.
These differences reflect factors such as fossil fuel dependence, energy-intensive industries, and each country’s energy mix .
Despite their large shares of global emissions, some of the world’s biggest emitters are beginning to see declines.
In 2025, China’s energy-related CO₂ emissions fell by around 0.5% , helped by expanding renewable and nuclear power generation. India’s energy-related CO₂ emissions also declined in 2025, helped by renewable power growth and cooler weather.
Europe has seen more sustained reductions. Emissions in Italy, Germany, and the UK have fallen by double-digit percentages over the past decade. Across the EU, greenhouse gas emissions have declined 40% since 1990, even as its economy grew by more than 70%.
These trends highlight how emissions can decline even as economies continue to grow, although global emissions remain heavily concentrated among a handful of countries.
To learn more about this topic, explore this graphic breaking down global greenhouse gas emissions by sector.

California is America’s largest agricultural economy, but the Midwest as a region produces nearly half of U.S. agricultural production value.
California may be better known for Silicon Valley and Hollywood, but it’s also America’s largest agricultural producer, ahead of traditional farming powerhouses like Iowa, Texas, and Nebraska.
This graphic ranks all 50 states by the value of their agricultural production in 2025, using data from the U.S. Department of Agriculture . The measure includes crops, livestock, farm services, and forestry in current dollars, before costs, reflecting the scale of agricultural output rather than farm profits.
California’s agricultural production was worth more than the combined output of Iowa and Wisconsin in 2025. The state also generated nearly half (48%) of all agricultural production value in the Western U.S.
California’s lead rests on crops. Its crop production alone was worth $46.8 billion, accounting for 68% of its total and 2.7 times the next-highest state crop total (Illinois, $17.3 billion). California produces more than 400 commodities and grows nearly half of the country’s vegetables and over three-quarters of its fruits and nuts.
The table below ranks all 50 states by agricultural production value in 2025, along with each state’s share of the U.S. total:
The Midwest led all regions with $273.6 billion in agricultural production value across 12 states, ahead of the South (27.2% of the U.S. total), the West (23.4%), and the Northeast (4.3%).
The Midwest’s dominance reflects both its fertile prairie soils and its massive livestock industry. The region’s dark prairie soils are among the most productive agricultural soils in the world, supporting the corn and soybean production that helps feed its livestock. Iowa alone had 25.3 million hogs at the end of 2025, roughly one-third of the U.S. total .
America’s agricultural economy generates more production value from livestock than crops. In 2025, livestock and livestock products generated $303.6 billion nationwide, or 50.1% of the total, compared with $238.2 billion (39.3%) from crops. Farm services and forestry accounted for the remaining 10.6%.
While corn was the top commodity by production value in just four states in 2024, cattle held the top spot in 18 states.
The table below breaks down agricultural production value across the 10 largest state farm economies by crops, livestock, and services and forestry in 2025:
Livestock generated more value than crops in several leading agricultural states, including Iowa ($23.7 billion vs. $16.8 billion), Nebraska ($23.2 billion vs. $12.1 billion), and Kansas ($19.0 billion vs. $8.7 billion). In Texas, livestock accounted for 65% of total agricultural production value.
Illinois stands out as a crop-heavy exception, with crops generating $17.3 billion, or 71% of its agricultural production value. Across the Midwest as a whole, livestock accounted for 49% of production value, compared with 42% for crops.

Environmental quality by city in 2026: See which cities lead and lag across air quality, emissions, and environmental risk.
Where do the world’s cities rank when it comes to environmental quality?
This visualization ranks the world’s best- and worst-performing cities using data from the Oxford Economics Global Cities Index 2026 , which evaluates 1,000 cities worldwide.
The environmental index measures factors including air quality, emissions intensity, natural-disaster risk, and temperature and rainfall anomalies. Scores range from 0 to 100, with higher scores indicating stronger environmental performance.
Honolulu tops the environmental ranking with a score of 100, the highest possible value on the index. Fortaleza, Brazil, follows at 96.9, while Bergen, Norway, ranks third at 96.4.
Ocean winds can help disperse air pollution in coastal cities, potentially contributing to Honolulu’s strong environmental performance. The city also benefits from relatively clean air compared with many large urban centers.
However, a top environmental score does not mean a city is free from climate-related risks. Oʻahu remains exposed to flooding, hurricanes, coastal erosion, and other hazards, and the city has adopted climate action and resilience plans aimed at reducing emissions and preparing for these threats.
Fortaleza leads Brazil’s nine entries with a score of 96.9, followed by Aracaju at 92.5. Teresina, Recife, Natal, João Pessoa, Belém, Maceió, and Salvador also make the list.
Several of these cities are located along Brazil’s northeastern Atlantic coast, where persistent trade winds can help disperse air pollutants. Rainfall can also help remove particulate matter from the atmosphere.
Compared with Brazil’s more heavily industrialized South and Southeast, the Northeast has historically had a lower concentration of heavy industry, potentially limiting some sources of urban air pollution. However, the index also incorporates climate and natural-disaster measures, so no single factor explains these cities’ high scores.
Bokaro, India, ranks last with a score of zero. Shahjahanpur and Bhilai Nagar, also in India, follow with scores of 6.7 and 11.7, respectively.
Chinese cities account for 23 of the bottom 30 positions, including Dezhou, Huangshi, Liaocheng, Anqing, and Anyang. Five Indian cities also appear in the bottom 30, alongside Kerman

articles.title_orig: Crowds throng New Delhi and wave Indian flags amid escalating protests
articles.title_zh: Crowds throng New Delhi and wave Indian flags amid escalating protests
articles.content_orig:
Prominent student leader Neha Bora, center, shouts slogans as she is detained by the police during a youth demonstration demanding the resignation of the country's election chief Gyanesh Kumar, in New Delhi, India, Friday, Oct. 16, 2026. Vipin/AP hide caption
NEW DELHI — Thousands of Indians thronged a bustling thoroughfare in the heart of the capital, waving the national flag and demanding the resignation of the country's election chief, the latest show of public dissent against Prime Minister Narendra Modi's government.
The protesters rallied in Connaught Place, one of New Delhi's busiest commercial districts, responding to a call by the youth "Cockroach" movement, whose leader Abhijeet Dipke was detained by police ahead of the demonstration. Protesters spanning generations joined the rally, reflecting broad public anger and intensifying pressure on the country's top election official.
Protests by the youth and opposition parties have intensified over an ongoing review of voter lists that has removed more than 130 million names since last year. Critics say the exercise is politically motivated, threatens to disenfranchise millions more, and has disproportionately affected minorities, particularly Muslims. They have demanded the resignation of election chief Gyanesh Kumar.
Student activist Neha Bora, center, shouts slogans during a youth demonstration demanding the resignation of the country's election chief Gyanesh Kumar, in New Delhi, India, Friday, Oct. 16, 2026. Prabhat Mehrotra/AP hide caption
The Election Commission and Prime Minister Narendra Modi's administration deny the allegations and say the revision is intended to remove duplicate and ineligible entries.
Friday's protest was part of a growing campaign that has put Modi's government under pressure and comes a week after a police crackdown on protesters in New Delhi.
The demonstrators vastly outnumbered the security personnel lining the road, while columns of riot police stood watch.
Police had earlier asked people not to join the rally and offered to let a small group gather to wave the national flag and sing the national anthem. In anticipation of the protests, authorities also closed Central Park, a green space surrounded by Connaught Place's white colonial-era buildings, on Friday and Saturday.
Modi has not publicly commented on the protests. Some of his party leaders have dismissed the demonstrators as "anarchists" and suggested, without offering evidence, that they are backed by foreign powers.
Police detained Dipke, the founder of the "Cockroach" movement, ahead of the demonstrations. He had urged supporters unable to travel to New Delhi to raise the flag and demonstrate in their own communities.
Security personnel patrol ahead of a  tricolor (Indian flag) waving protest called by the youth "Cockroach" movement demanding the resignation of India's election chief in central New Delhi, India, Friday, Oct. 16, 2026. Channi Anand/AP Photo/Channi Anand/AP hide caption
A live video posted on the movement's Instagram account showed Dipke leaving a house and heading toward the street, where police officers intercepted him. After a brief exchange, officers hauled him into a police vehicle and drove away.
"Waving the tricolor (Indian flag) is not a crime," he told reporters Thursday.
The "Cockroach" movement began as an online satirical campaign this summer after India's chief justice compared unemployed young people to parasites. Many young Indians embraced the remark, adopting the cockroach as a symbol of resilience. It has since expanded into a nationwide protest movement of young people. Protests led by the group forced the resignation of Modi's education minister in July, a rare setback for the prime minister, who has been in power for more than 12 years.
It remains unclear whether the protests will grow into a wider political movement. Modi's government remains electorally strong, and anger over voter lists may not necessarily translate into support for the opposition, which has used the issue to criticize his Hindu nationalist government.

articles.title_orig: President Oaks welcomes world religious leaders to G20 Interfaith Forum
articles.title_zh: President Oaks welcomes world religious leaders to G20 Interfaith Forum
articles.content_orig:
President Dallin H. Oaks welcomed religious and civic leaders, scholars and others to the Tabernacle on Temple Square on Thursday, Oct. 15, at the 2026 G20 Interfaith Forum.
The President of The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints thanked the forum’s attendees for their work to bring people from different backgrounds and beliefs together to form stronger communities.
“People of goodwill, compassion and a desire to understand and help one another — without demanding a compromise of distinctive commitments — are at the core of peacemaking,” President Oaks said. “I commend you for your efforts to be peacemakers in today’s world.”
The forum’s theme this year is “Resilient Hope, Shared Future.” Speaking in the opening ceremony of the three-day forum, President Oaks said the gathering is the “most prominent constellation” of religious leaders to convene in Salt Lake City’s history.
“We are profoundly grateful for your demonstration that faith-inspired insights and initiatives can contribute to meaningful and scalable worldwide solutions,” he said.
President Oaks said the efforts of participants in the G20 Interfaith Forum demonstrate how individuals and groups can come together outside of political motivations and regardless of shared or dissimilar beliefs.
“Your record demonstrates that faith-informed perspectives have a meaningful place in global policymaking,” he said. “But the key to this whole effort is to bring us all together to address common problems.”
At the Church’s April 2026 general conference , President Oaks reiterated the Savior’s teaching to love everyone — including those who do not have the same beliefs as Latter-day Saints.
“Today we might say that we are commanded to love our adversaries,” he said . “All mortals are beloved children of God.”
President Oaks was preceded at the gathering by Sheikh Mohammad bin Abdulkarim Al-Issa, the secretary-general of the Muslim World League, and Archbishop Gabriele Caccia, the apostolic nuncio — or ambassador — of the Holy See to the United States. The Holy See serves as the central governing body of the Catholic Church and is led by Pope Leo XIV.
Al-Issa described his definitions of optimism and hope, saying that hope is not just a feeling but a “faith-based endeavor.”
“Optimism waits for things to improve on their own. Hope, however, is a decision of people with a living conscience,” he said.
Caccia shared a message from Pope Leo XIV.
“His Holiness prays that your fraternal gathering may be a shining example of the solidarity of the human family and promote the dedication of the human family to religious freedom and the common good,” he read.
Other speakers at the event included the interfaith forum’s president and vice president, W. Cole Durham and Katherine Marshall, respectively.
Imam Allahshukur Pashazadeh, chief imam of the Caucasus Region, came from Azerbaijan and expressed urgency for the work of the forum.
“Joint efforts of religious and secular groups matter more than ever,” he said.
Elder Metropolitan Emmanuel of Chalcedon from the Ecumenical Patriarchate in Türkiye also spoke.
Emmanuel said the root Greek word for “share” is also the root for the words “community” and “communion.” He explained that shared beliefs and spaces do not mean individuals are the same.
He pointed to the Tabernacle Choir seated in the choir seats behind him as an example. He said that sopranos and basses are part of the same choir singing the same song, but they don’t sing the same notes. They instead sing in harmony with one another.
Pujya Sadhvi Bhagawati Saraswati, the secretary-general of the Global Interfaith WASH Alliance of India; Rabbi Mark Dratch, executive vice president emeritus of the Rabbinical Council of America; and Dr. Francis Kuria Kagema, the secretary-general of Religions for Peace, also spoke in the event.
The opening ceremony was conducted by President Michael O. Leavitt , president of The Tabernacle Choir and Orchestra at Temple Square. President Leavitt drew on his combined experience as former governor of Utah and former secretary of the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services in sharing an anecdote regarding the intertwined nature of governments and religions.
“A government can use taxes to build a clinic,” he said. “But it often takes the voice of a trusted faith leader to walk through the door.”
Policy recommendations established at the interfaith forum are shared with G20 heads of state ahead of their leaders summit in Miami, Florida, on Dec. 14-15. The Salt Lake City event was sponsored by Georgetown University’s Berkley Center for Religion, Peace and World Affairs and Brigham Young University’s International Center for Law and Religion Studies.

articles.title_orig: No one better connects Boston to the world: Delta announces new route to Iceland
articles.title_zh: No one better connects Boston to the world: Delta announces new route to Iceland
articles.content_orig:
New nonstop service from Boston to Reykjavík joins Boston-Venice, Detroit-Athens and Austin-Paris as new additions to Delta’s 2027 transatlantic season.
Editor's note: This story, originally published on Sept. 25, 2026, has been edited to include information about Delta's new service from Boston to Reykjavík.
Exploration awaits, and Delta is adding more ways to discover all of the natural beauty and adventure that Iceland has to offer.
Delta’s new daily nonstop service between Boston and Reykjavík (KEF) begins April 12, 2027, with flights operating through Oct. 30.
Reykjavík will become Delta’s 14th unique long-haul destination from Boston during the peak summer season and its 16 th international destination.
As Boston’s No. 1 carrier, Delta continues to expand the city’s role as a gateway to Europe. Boston is Delta’s closest U.S. hub to Europe, making it ideally positioned to connect customers across the United States with destinations across the Atlantic.
Delta’s history in Iceland dates back to June 2011, when the airline launched nonstop service between New York-JFK and Reykjavík (KEF), marking the first time a U.S. carrier offered scheduled nonstop flights to Iceland. Delta’s new Boston service builds on that legacy, expanding access to one of the North Atlantic’s most sought-after destinations while offering New England travelers a convenient new gateway to Iceland.
The route will be operated aboard a Boeing 757-200 featuring Delta Premium Select, Delta Comfort and Delta Main.
New nonstop service from Detroit to Athens and Boston to Venice will join Delta’s previously announced route from Austin to Paris. The airline is also extending its transatlantic season, with several popular routes starting earlier in the spring or continuing deeper into the fall and winter.
"Customers continue to seek more flexibility, convenience and choice when traveling to Europe, whether they are planning a spring escape, a summer vacation or a fall getaway,” said Jeff Arinder, Delta’s Vice President of International Network Planning. “By adding new European destinations from Detroit and Boston, establishing Austin as a new gateway to Europe and extending service on several popular routes, we're giving customers more choice, greater flexibility and more opportunities to travel when and how they want.”
In addition to Delta's nonstop destinations, partnerships with Air France, KLM, Virgin Atlantic and other airline partners give customers access to hundreds of destinations across Europe through a seamless travel experience.
Delta will also add four-times-weekly nonstop service between Boston and Venice beginning May 7, 2027, with flights operating through Oct. 29.
“Italy continues to be an incredibly popular destination for New England travelers, and we are excited to add Venice to our growing list of international destinations,” said Sharon Williams, Massport’s Executive Director of Aviation. “This new service provides our passengers with another opportunity to experience Italy’s incredible culture, history and tourism while strengthening the ties between our two regions. We’re grateful to Delta for continuing to invest in Boston and expand choices for our passengers.”
Venice will become Delta’s 13th unique long-haul destination from Boston during the peak summer season and its 12th destination in continental Europe. Boston will also become Delta’s third U.S. gateway to Venice, offering connections to nearly 20 destinations across the United States. In addition, service from Boston to Milan will increase to daily in 2027.
The new route further strengthens Delta’s leading service to Italy, with up to 17 peak-day departures from the U.S. and more than 30,000 nonstop seats to Italy each week.
The route will be operated aboard an Airbus A330-300 featuring Delta One, Delta Premium Select, Delta Comfort and Delta Main.
Beginning June 8, 2027, Delta will launch three-times-weekly nonstop service between Detroit and Athens , operating through Oct. 28.
“For the first time at DTW, travelers in Southeast Michigan will have nonstop access to Athens, one of the world’s most iconic destinations,” said Wayne County Airport Authority CEO Chad Newton. “We appreciate Delta Air Lines’ continued investment in Detroit and are excited about the new opportunities this service will create for tourism, business and cultural connections.”
Athens will become Delta’s 12th unique long-haul destination from Detroit during the peak summer season, as well as its seventh destination in continental Europe. The new flight will also make Detroit Delta’s fourth U.S. gateway to the Greek capital.
With connections available to more than 40 U.S. destinations through Detroit, the route will open a convenient new path to Greece for customers across Delta’s network.
Flights will operate aboard an Airbus A330-200 featuring Delta One, Delta Premium Select, Delta Comfort and Delta Main experiences.
The two new routes join Delta’s previously announced daily service from Austin to Paris, launching March 27, 2027. It will be Austin’s first-ever nonstop service to Paris and will give customers one-stop access to nearly 70 destinations across Europe, India and Africa through Delta’s partnership with Air France-KLM.
Daily summer-season service will operate between Austin (AUS) and Paris-Charles de Gaulle (CDG) starting March 27, 2027, on Delta's Airbus A330-900.
The daily flight will operate aboard an Airbus A330-900neo featuring Delta One, Delta Premium Select, Delta Comfort and Delta Main.
Delta is also extending the European travel season in 2027, giving customers more opportunities to visit popular destinations and more flexibility to travel during the spring and fall months.
Seasonal service from Minneapolis-St. Paul and Detroit to Rome will begin in early March, followed by Seattle-Rome in April. Flights from New York-JFK to Catania , Porto , Prague and Copenhagen will also return earlier, as will service connecting Boston and Seattle with Barcelona and Atlanta with Edinburgh.
Several routes will feature increased or extended service as well. Detroit-Rome and New York-JFK-Copenhagen will operate daily when they resume, while Cincinnati-Paris service will continue three times weekly from January through March.
With new routes and an extended transatlantic season, Delta is giving customers more options, greater flexibility and easier access to destinations across Europe.

articles.title_orig: Technics EAH-A1000 Review: Superior Sound And Excellent ANC In A Premium Package
articles.title_zh: Technics EAH-A1000 Review: Superior Sound And Excellent ANC In A Premium Package
articles.content_orig:
The company's flagship over-ear wireless headphones are light on compromises, but enter a competitive market.
When Technics announced the EAH-A1000 over-ear Bluetooth headphones, everything seemed fairly ordinary. Another set of premium cans entering an already crowded category . Sure, they have a few standout features on the spec sheet — magnetic fluid drivers and three-device multipoint Bluetooth, for example. At $450, they are directly taking on Sony's popular WH-1000XM6 , and almost enter the same territory as Sennheiser's audiophile-friendly HDB 630 .
It's a confident move from Technics, to place its flag in the lucrative, but risky, territory between high-end consumer and "affordable" specialist headphones. I've had the A1000 on the testing bench (a.k.a. my head) for a couple of weeks and my initial assessment of how "ordinary" they are might have been a little hasty.
The feature Technics is making the most noise about is the "Magnetic Fluid" technology, but it's not new to the A1000. The AZ100 true wireless earbuds also use it, but these are the first over-ears from Technics to include it. The idea is that it reduces unwanted vibrations in the driver, in turn reducing distortion.
One other feature that stands out is the three-device multipoint Bluetooth. Seamless connection with your phone and PC can now include one more device, like a gaming console or TV. There is a slight limitation here: If you listen via LDAC (which the A1000 also supports), that will limit you to two devices maximum.
Of course there's adaptive active noise cancellation (ANC) coupled with a beamforming microphone for clearer phone calls. Other features you'd expect at this price point, such as Dolby Atmos with headtracking, wear detection, EQ/app control, a healthy 45-hour battery life (with ANC on) and lossless playback via USB-C and 3.5mm cables (both provided) are all present and correct. Cosmetically, the A1000 offers smooth lines and a stylish, but understated, design. They could pass for a Sony or Bose model at a glance.
Headphone marketing materials are like gourmet menus: There are a lot of decorative adjectives to describe beef. Or, in the case of headphones, 40mm drivers. I can't put my hand on my heart and say that the magnetic fluid technology Technics mentions is making a difference, but I was immediately impressed when I first put the A1000 on and pressed play on Spotify.
My music tastes skew electronic, so bass really matters. On the A1000, the low frequencies are some of the tightest I've heard. That's the best word I can find for it. The bass is present, I can feel it, but it's not vibrating in my eardrums at all. It sounds like it's firmly attached to the song with glue, in a good way. Kick drums in dance music offer a gentle thwack, in turn providing a good sense of space and dynamic range in the mix.
Pop and rock genres do a good job at exposing the mid and high frequencies. BTS' Dynamite , for example, sounds much more robust and balanced in the A1000 than it does in my car on the school run when I'm trying to animate the kids. I even heard parts of the bassline I barely knew existed. If there's a minor criticism, it's at the higher end. Listening to AC/DC or the Arctic Monkeys, the guitars sound authentic, but my ears wanted a teeny-tiny bit more sizzle out of them.
I regularly use the Sennheiser HDB 630 and the Technics A1000 surprised me with a slightly bigger sense of space and soundstage. The tight balance and well-rounded bass make them one of the strongest pairs I've tried for a long time.
The stellar sound wasn't the first thing I noticed when I put them on, the adaptive ANC is also extremely good. I'm a little fussy with noise cancellation; it's a feature I appreciate but I prefer good audio chops over superior ANC if I have to choose. With the A1000, that's not really an issue. The noise cancellation is effective for both steady sounds like fans, yet it's adaptive enough that I can't hear people talking when my spouse has guests and I'm working. I prefer it to the ANC on the HDB 630 and I'd say it's good enough to be in the same room with Sony and Bose.
I have a folder on my phone that's a graveyard of unused headphone apps. Technics Connect hasn't made it there, yet. As control apps go, it's easy to navigate and you'll find extra settings like choosing between LDAC compatible multipoint Bluetooth (remember: max two connections) or even turning it off. There's the aforementioned EQ section, the option to choose how long before the headphones auto-turn off and a toggle to disable wear detection, among other fine helpful tools.
A note on the multipoint feature: I've never really had a good experience with it on any headphones, with my Mac usually connecting via the hands-free profile. That was my experience with the A1000, too. Even switching between my phone and my Windows laptop was unreliable. I can't confidently blame these headphones, but I didn't have much luck with two devices, let alone three.
There are no touch controls on the A1000, instead you get two buttons and a clickable volume rocker. Despite everything being on the right earcup, it doesn't feel cramped. The volume rocker is easy to find, but you click "back" for volume up, which feels counter intuitive to me. Media controls are navigated by multiple clicks on the same rocker. It's practical and works, but sometimes the button lightly sticks, turning three clicks into two, which is the difference between a skip forward and skip back.
The $449 pits the A1000 directly against Sony's WH-1000XM6 , and I do think it competes well on sound quality and ANC. The choice will come down to secondary details like design and battery life and app features, with the latter being where Sony really stacks the deck. I'll come right out and say that I personally prefer the A1000 to the $500 Sennheiser HDB 630. Technics might not quite beat them on sound, but it's really close. For ANC, comfort and build quality, for me Technics takes the win. Sonos' Ace Ultra matches the A1000 for price, and Engadget rated them highly, in part for their compatibility with Sonos speakers.
For a legacy hi-fi brand, Technics has taken the long road when it comes to consumer headphones. The true wireless AZ100 made a big impression, thanks in part to those Magnetic Fluid drivers, and the A1000 builds on that success with equally impressive sound. Truly, they're a joy to wear and to listen to. There are also enough extra details, like a beam-forming microphone that destroys background noise with what feels like witchcraft (even if the mic itself is just so-so).
The sticking point for some will be the price. Sennheiser can ask more for the HDB 630 thanks to its long, unbroken record with good consumer headphones. You also get the $60 BTD 700 dongle thrown in. Meanwhile, Sony has built a steady reputation with its 1000X line over the last few years. Technics doesn't have the same recent pedigree, yet, but the A1000 does a really good job at kicking that off.

articles.title_orig: USC scientists discover how to create a never-ending supply of cancer-fighting cells
articles.title_zh: USC scientists discover how to create a never-ending supply of cancer-fighting cells
articles.content_orig:
Scientists at the University of Southern California (USC) have discovered a way to produce a potentially renewable supply of cancer-fighting immune cells, opening a promising new direction for cancer treatment. By working with immature cells that can develop into powerful immune defenders, the researchers have created a system capable of generating large numbers of genetically engineered cells that recognize tumors and help activate the body's natural defenses.
The breakthrough, described in a study published in Cell , could help overcome some of the biggest obstacles facing cancer immunotherapy, including the difficulty of manufacturing enough immune cells and keeping them active in the body. In experiments involving mice, the engineered cells established themselves in bone marrow, produced new immune cells, and slowed the progression of both blood cancers and solid tumors.
The USC Stem Cell-led team focused on a type of immature immune cell called granulocyte-monocyte progenitors (GMPs). These cells normally develop into macrophages and other immune cells that protect the body from infections and participate in immune responses. The researchers found that GMPs could be grown extensively in the laboratory while retaining their ability to develop into functioning immune cells. They could also be genetically modified to recognize specific cancer markers and strengthen broader immune responses.
"The study establishes a scalable and engineerable GMP platform for cellular immunotherapy and introduces concepts that we believe could have broad implications for both cancer immunotherapy and stem cell biology," said the paper's corresponding author Qi-Long Ying, MD, PhD, professor of stem cell biology and regenerative medicine at the Keck School of Medicine of USC.
Scientists Discover a Surprising Ability in Immune Cell Precursors
Beyond its potential applications in cancer treatment, the discovery challenges a long-standing understanding of how blood and immune cells develop.
Stem cells are known for their ability to self-renew, meaning they can repeatedly divide while maintaining their original properties. In the blood-forming system, this ability has traditionally been associated primarily with hematopoietic stem cells, which can produce all the major types of blood and immune cells.
Progenitor cells, by contrast, are further along in development and are already committed to producing a more limited range of cells. They are generally thought to have less capacity for long-term self-renewal.
The USC researchers demonstrated that GMPs can retain this ability under carefully controlled laboratory conditions. Rather than quickly maturing into other cell types, the progenitors continued multiplying while preserving their identity and their capacity to generate functional immune cells.
"The prevailing view has been that long-term self-renewal in the blood system is primarily a property of the hematopoietic stem cells that can generate any type of blood or immune cell," said Ying. "We found that, under the right conditions, GMPs can also self-renew, dividing extensively while keeping their identity and ability to produce functional immune cells. That gives us a scalable starting point for engineering cell therapies for cancer, infectious disease and potentially many other conditions."
This finding could be especially important for developing treatments that require large, reliable supplies of genetically engineered immune cells.
Why Macrophages Could Be Powerful Weapons Against Cancer
Macrophages are among the immune system's most versatile defenders. Their name comes from Greek words meaning "big eaters," reflecting their ability to surround and engulf bacteria, damaged cells, and other unwanted material.
They also help coordinate immune responses by sending signals that influence the behavior of other immune cells. Some macrophages can enter tumors and attack cancer cells, making them attractive candidates for cancer immunotherapy.
One particularly promising application involves solid tumors, which include cancers that form masses in organs and tissues. Existing therapies based on engineered T cells have achieved their greatest successes against certain blood cancers, but treating solid tumors has proven more difficult.
Macrophages offer a potentially different approach because they naturally migrate into tissues and can penetrate tumors. However, turning them into practical treatments presents several challenges.
Once macrophages have fully matured, they are difficult to multiply in large quantities outside the body. They are also challenging to modify genetically and can be damaged during freezing and storage, complicating the production and distribution of cell therapies.
Another problem occurs after administration. Mature macrophages often collect in organs such as the lungs and liver instead of spreading widely throughout the body. Their relatively rapid disappearance can also limit how long a treatment remains effective.
To work around these limitations, the scientists decided to begin at an earlier stage of immune cell development.
Creating a Renewable Supply of Cancer-Fighting Immune Cells
Rather than trying to manufacture large numbers of mature macrophages, first author Shi Yue, MD, of Ying's laboratory and his colleagues concentrated on GMPs, the progenitor cells that can produce macrophages.
The researchers developed a precisely defined mixture of chemicals that allowed GMPs to survive and multiply for extended periods in the laboratory. The mixture prevented the cells from prematurely developing into mature immune cells, preserving a renewable population of progenitors.
Even after extensive laboratory expansion, the GMPs maintained the molecular characteristics that defined them. Importantly, they also retained the ability to develop into functional macrophages and other related immune cells when needed.
This approach could make it possible to manufacture large numbers of engineered immune cells from a starting population that can be continually expanded, instead of repeatedly collecting and preparing mature cells.
To confirm that the method could be reproduced, collaborators in the laboratory of Ravi Majeti, MD, PhD, at Stanford University independently demonstrated that GMPs could be maintained for extended periods and genetically engineered. Their results provided additional support for the reliability of the technique and its potential use in future cell therapies.
Majeti, Director of the Institute for Stem Cell Biology and Regenerative Medicine at Stanford University, noted: "This method for the expansion and engineering of GMPs opens the door to numerous translational applications, much like T cell expansion and engineering. We have already demonstrated engineering of these cells to drive multiple potent functions, and there is a lot more to be explored."
Engineering Immune Cells to Recognize and Attack Tumors
The team next investigated whether these expandable progenitor cells could be programmed to fight cancer.
They genetically engineered GMPs to carry a chimeric antigen receptor, or CAR. This engineered receptor allows immune cells to identify a particular molecular marker on the surface of cancer cells, helping direct their activity toward tumors.
CAR technology is already an important part of cancer immunotherapy, particularly in treatments that modify a patient's T cells to recognize and attack cancer. The USC researchers explored whether a similar strategy could be applied to GMPs, allowing them to generate engineered macrophages and other immune cells.
The scientists also equipped some of the progenitor cells with an additional immune-activating signal. This modification was designed to recruit and stimulate nearby immune cells, including T cells, which can help mount a stronger attack against cancer.

articles.title_orig: Man found shot in the head and stuffed in a barrel in Lake Mead has been identified
articles.title_zh: Man found shot in the head and stuffed in a barrel in Lake Mead has been identified
articles.content_orig:
LAS VEGAS -- The remains of a man who was shot in the head and stuffed into a rusted barrel found on the shore of Lake Mead after the water level dropped were identified Thursday as an Arkansas man whose decades-old killing remains unsolved.
Edward Lelburian Jackson was in his mid- to late 50s when he died, Clark County Coroner Melanie Rouse said. Authorities are looking for people to come forward to help solve Jackson's killing.
There was no evidence directly linking the killing to organized crime in nearby Las Vegas despite longstanding speculation, although a connection hasn't been ruled out, police said. An expert on mob activity in the city said the case bears the "earmarks" of a mob hit and that questions still linger.
Jackson was identified with the help of a bone sample sent for genealogy profiling, along with three angles of a composite face and clothing Jackson was wearing when he died, Rouse said.
"We were able to confirm that the remains were in fact Edward Jackson," she said.
The discovery of the barrel by boaters in May 2022 sparked memories of the city's mob era, which lasted from the 1940s to the mid-1980s. Organized crime helped build up Las Vegas, and a body stuffed in a barrel was known to signify a mob killing.
Jackson, believed to be from Hot Springs, Arkansas, had a brief criminal history in the early 1980s in Salt Lake City, Utah, which included one charge of aggravated arson and conspiracy to commit fraud, said Robert Price, a Las Vegas Metropolitan Police Department homicide lieutenant.
Price said there is nothing to tie the killing to organized crime. He added, however, that it hasn't been ruled out.
Jackson's family told investigators that he liked to travel and detectives found records of him in California, where he lived with his wife in the early '70s. His family said they last saw him in Arkansas in the early '80s, and it is unclear why he was in Las Vegas. Homicide detectives will continue working to figure out what happened to him, said Price.
"It will never be closed until we solve it," he said.
Authorities had already said the man was shot, and they estimate he was killed in the early 1980s.
The man had been wearing a button-down short-sleeve shirt, light blue jeans, a silver wristwatch and blue-and-white tennis shoes.
Price said the family didn't report him missing.
"They knew that he had traveled the country, would show up when he showed up, just to say hi. But they didn't think anything other than that. They just figured he was out and about," he said.
Jackson was married for a short period of time and had no known children, Price said.
Geoff Schumacher, vice president of research, collections and programs at The Mob Museum in Las Vegas, said there are still many questions about who Jackson was and what he was involved in that "earned him a trip in a barrel into the lake."
Members of organized crime were involved in the Las Vegas casino industry from the 1940s to the mid-1980s, both behind the scenes and through shadow ownerships of casinos, Schumacher said.
He said the case had all the "earmarks of a mob hit," mirroring another case from 1976 when Italian mobster John Roselli was killed and stuffed in a barrel and dumped into a bay outside of Miami Beach.
Schumacher said he and Mob Museum staff will comb their records to try to help solve the case.
"I think this story is not over," he said.
Las Vegas historian Michael Green said whoever committed the crime probably thought the body would "never come near the surface." In the early 1980s, the lake levels were so high that the spillways flooded at Hoover Dam, he said.
Now, Lake Mead is at a historic low due to years of overuse, longstanding drought and increasing temperatures. The water level of the 90-year-old reservoir has dropped, exposing areas that were previously underwater.
Several other sets of remains were found at Lake Mead in 2022. Another set of skeletal remains was discovered that May, and they were identified as a drowning victim from 2002. Skeletal remains found in August were identified as a 52-year-old Las Vegas resident who disappeared in 1998. A set of remains found in October 2022 were determined to be an accidental drowning from 1974, according to Clark County.
In August 2026, more human remains were discovered.
Lake Mead and the upstream Lake Powell are the largest human-made reservoirs in the U.S., part of a system that provides Colorado River water to people across the U.S. Southwest and Mexico.
In 2022, Lake Mead's dropping level exposed Las Vegas' uppermost drinking water intake. That forced authorities to switch to a deeper intake to keep serving the city's 2.4 million residents.
Golden reported from Seattle.

articles.title_orig: Trump says Ukraine resuming strikes on Russian oil sites is a ‘disgrace’
articles.title_zh: Trump says Ukraine resuming strikes on Russian oil sites is a ‘disgrace’
articles.content_orig:
President Donald Trump has labeled Ukraine’s resumption of strikes on Russian oil refineries a “disgrace,” the latest salvo in his campaign to pressure the U.S. ally over rising gas prices that could cost Republicans in next month’s midterm elections .
Kyiv said Thursday that it would no longer abide by Trump’s “energy ceasefire,” citing Russia’s refusal to halt its own attacks on Ukraine’s power grid. President Volodymyr Zelenskyy angrily accused the U.S. of costing civilian lives by striking deals with Moscow and withdrawing support that is crucial to Kyiv’s defense against the invasion launched by President Vladimir Putin.
Ukrainian officials had raised alarm after gaps in intelligence sharing left Kyiv vulnerable to Russian attacks and restrictions on the Starlink satellite service disrupted military operations.  Zelenskyy said Friday that the technology was still not fully restored.
With Ukraine defying his demands to halt strikes, Trump responded late Thursday.
“If you tell me that Zelenskyy is again shooting at refineries, all he’s doing is making the world oil price higher,” Trump told Newsmax’s Rob Finnerty. “I think that’s a disgrace. There’s plenty of other targets; they don’t have to hit,” Trump said.
“Zelenskyy is not a good guy for us to deal with” on the war, he said, adding that “I think they actually both would like to see it end, but I think I find Zelenskyy to be more difficult to deal with than Putin.”
As his clash escalated with Trump, Zelenskyy was in Brussels on Friday to shore up support from European allies, whom he called “real leaders” as they gathered for a crucial summit.
Ukraine hit a Russian oil refinery Thursday after Zelenskyy said he was “done” with the truce, which Trump had announced to the apparent surprise of both sides in the war. Neither Moscow nor Kyiv reported any new strikes on Russian refineries Friday.
Trump has sought to blame Ukraine’s strikes for destabilizing the price of diesel globally, despite the impact of his own war with Iran .
But this campaign of attacks deep inside enemy territory has given Ukraine crucial leverage, sparking a major fuel crisis inside Russia .
Kyiv hoped this would give it a stronger hand at the negotiating table, but as Washington pushes for an end to the conflict it has taken a series of steps that have caused surprise and alarm among Ukraine and its backers in Europe.
Last week, Trump announced a deal to buy diesel from Russia, an apparent attempt to relieve pressure at the pump for American consumers ahead of the midterm elections but which reversed years of U.S. policy. Trump then called for Kyiv to stop all strikes on Russian oil infrastructure and said Zelenskyy had to be replaced as Ukraine’s leader.
It comes amid mounting questions about whether the U.S. is still sharing critical military intelligence with Ukraine after a pair of major strikes earlier this week that Kyiv said came without a usual advance warning from its partners.
Ukraine also reported a slowing down of the Starlink satellite terminals , which are critical for its army’s communications, drone missions and aerial defenses.
Kyiv said that Starshield, the military version of the technology that is used by Ukraine’s troops, had been limited without any warning.
SpaceX chief Elon Musk, the billionaire Trump ally, said that such decisions were up to the U.S. military and ultimately Trump.
After repeated requests for comment about Musk’s statement, a senior U.S. official told NBC News that “no such request was ever made by the president.” Trump has also denied restricting military intelligence for Ukraine.
Kyiv said Thursday the Starshield service was being restored, but the episode only added to the mounting suspicion in Ukraine that the U.S. was willing to cut it off from battlefield support in order to exert pressure for a peace deal. Asked about the service on Friday, Zelenskyy said that issues were ongoing. “Has the speed been fully restored to what it was? No. Is the speed returning? Yes,” he told reporters in Brussels.
European and Ukrainian officials told NBC News they believed that the moves, coming only days after Trump eased sanctions on Russia’s diesel exports and railed against Zelenskyy, were most likely aimed at pressuring Kyiv into making concessions at the negotiating table amid the stalemate in peace talks.
The Kremlin agreed with Trump on Friday, with spokesman Dmitry Peskov saying it was clear that “Zelenskyy doesn’t want to take responsibility and move toward a peaceful resolution.”
Russia has always stated it’s open to a peace settlement but only on its own hard-line terms, which would see Ukraine ceding significant territory.
Yuliya Talmazan is a reporter for NBC News Digital, based in London.

articles.title_orig: The Surface Laptop Ultra delivers on most of Microsoft’s promises
articles.title_zh: The Surface Laptop Ultra delivers on most of Microsoft’s promises
articles.content_orig:
Over the past week, the laptop Microsoft sent me has been summarizing books and movies, generating images from my imagination, and running a 70-billion-parameter AI model that would be a stretch to fit on most laptops. It also played AAA games at a speed and fidelity I would have thought impossible on an ARM system just a year ago. Microsoft wants to sell you one computer for all of your needs, and for once that doesn’t feel like total marketing fluff. Mostly.
Microsoft is throwing both arms around the new Nvidia RTX Spark platform with the Surface Laptop Ultra—and setting its sights on the would-be MacBook Pro buyer, or as the company called it, “a high performance audience.” The bet is that rather than a gaming desktop for fun and a development laptop for work, buyers will pay more for one machine that does both.
The Surface Laptop Ultra arrives at a strange time in personal computing. Recent industry numbers showed a 20 percent drop in total PC shipments year over year in the third quarter of 2026. That’s not just consumer purchasing either—that’s across the board. Between the RAMpocalypse that has exploded consumer prices and an industry fixated on enterprise money, there hasn’t been much new hardware to excite PC enthusiasts.
Microsoft isn’t the only one debuting an RTX-chipped laptop. Dell’s XPS 16 Creator Edition and Asus’s ProArt series (our own Ryan Whitwam ‘s review should be appearing on the front page soon) are betting on the chipset as well. The question when reviewing the Surface Laptop Ultra isn’t whether it can achieve the things that it claims competently, but whether there’s finally a compelling reason for power users to switch to an ARM system, and whether their daily workloads can still be achieved without hiccups when compared to a more traditional x86 offering, or the biggest competitor within the segment, the MacBook Pro.
With a starting price of $2,599, this is not a budget alternative to Apple silicon. This is bleeding-edge hardware, and you’re going to be paying a premium for it. Depending on your selected processor and memory options, MSRP can reach as high as $5,899 . Prospective buyers should note that the lower-specced 24GB unified memory model ships with Windows 11 Home, while the rest of the fleet arrives with Windows 11 Pro. I received the 64GB model for testing, and I think that would probably be the sweet spot for a lot of users to align cost and performance.
I really have to wonder if 24GB is enough to go around when we know that Windows 11 is memory-hungry on its own. When you have to assign a significant portion of that 24GB of unified memory to VRAM for gaming, does performance suffer? An audience question inside the Surface Laptop Ultra review information session asked about the usefulness of the base model, and didn’t get much back other than a vague “useful for smaller models locally” answer. Microsoft may have a more definitive answer to that question a few months from now when software and drivers catch up with hardware.
So has the Microsoft and Nvidia team-up created the ultimate all-in-one laptop? Or is this the industry once again putting the hardware hype cart before the finished-software horse?
The 15-inch mini-LED display might not be enough to get folks to run to the Ultra on its own, but it’s a compelling reason to add it to the list. The 3270×2180 native resolution looks simply stunning whether you’re watching a 4K video, playing games, or just staring at a desktop spreadsheet. I preferred the Enhanced color profile, but Vivid and sRGB modes looked fantastic as well.
Blacks stayed deep against bright, vivid subjects without any sort of visible blooming. I wish I could say the same for my TV. While I can’t quantify how it stacks side by side with the latest MacBook Pro Retina display, I can say that this is a damn nice screen. Viewing angles are superb, colors are punchy, and the 2,000-nit peak brightness kept things legible even in a room flooded with natural sunlight. My only gripe is that in bright rooms, there is glare to contend with. The glossy glass looks fantastic at lower light levels but can act a bit mirror-like in direct sunlight. It hindered my ability to photograph the screen more than it did my ability to use the computer. Still, if you’re looking for a matte-screen laptop, you might want to keep that in mind.
The keyboard on the Surface Laptop Ultra is exactly what you’d expect on a premium machine like this. It’s excellent, if unremarkable. The keys have a shallow but satisfying press, the spacing makes sense for my hands, and the whole package delivers a very comfortable typing experience. I don’t have a whole bunch of laptops lying around to compare it to, but unsurprisingly, the closest would be my 2020 MacBook Pro. Microsoft knows what market it’s going after here, and I don’t mind them lifting direct inspiration from Apple in this department.
The trackpad is similarly competent. It’s absolutely huge, measuring 5.5 inches long by 3.5 inches tall, with excellent tracking accuracy throughout my testing time. Normally, one of the first things I do when plugging in a laptop to work from is to attach an external mouse, but over days of testing, I never reached for the mouse drawer. Microsoft made a point to emphasize the trackpad’s haptic feedback capabilities in native programs during the review information session. I’m not sure if there are still updates left to come that I haven’t received yet, but I can’t recall a time when I noticed additional mouse haptics had kicked in when I opened MS Office or anything. As it stands, the trackpad isn’t groundbreaking, but it is premium enough to be part of an “ultra” laptop.
Microsoft describes the included magnetic charging connection and port as being “the world’s first built-in magnetic USB-C charging experience.” It’s difficult to get upset about the marketing department doing their jobs, but this claim struck me as more of a technical truth than engineering feat. Apple’s MagSafe charging debuted on the original MacBook Pro all the way back in 2006 . The concept of a breakaway magnetic charger isn’t anything new, but technically Microsoft’s assertion holds water in that it is the first USB-C connector on a laptop with a matching magnetic port, rather than a proprietary connector.
Marketing claims aside, the magnetic connection does work well. The port and charger naturally guide themselves together, as magnets do, and made plugging the laptop in to charge in a dark room hassle-free. Normally I’d be holding the cord in one hand while trying to fumble around in the dark for the phone in my pocket and remember the gesture to quickly turn on the flashlight. Now I just have to get the cable within the vicinity, and the magnets do the rest. Perfect for when all I want to do is plug the PC in and go to bed.
What’s perhaps the larger selling point for magnetic charging is the cable’s ability to break away if yanked from the PC. Nothing will ruin your day faster than watching a new laptop fly off the counter. With the breakaway cable, you’re getting peace of mind that your laptop shouldn’t meet the floor should a startled cat or curious toddler come into contact with the cable. I’ve never had it happen with one of my laptops, but that doesn’t mean accidents don’t occur. I simulated a few ‘accidental disconnects’ with modest force, and the cable disconnected dutifully as it should.
While I won’t say that it’s a must-have, it’s certainly a nice-to-have. And in this package it’s certainly the type of premium accessory you’d expect, but it’s not going to move units on its own—not at these price tiers.
According to Nvidia, the RTX Spark N1X is a Grace CPU fused to a Blackwell GPU. Unlike chipsets like AMD’s Ryzen AI and Intel’s Core Ultra series, the N1X has no dedicated NPU—instead it leans on unified memory and the heavy-duty Blackwell GPU for AI work.
