articles.title_orig: Hot, windy weather stokes brush fires in Southern California; power turned off for many
articles.title_zh: Hot, windy weather stokes brush fires in Southern California; power turned off for many
articles.content_orig:
This is read by an automated voice. Please report any issues or inconsistencies here .
See more from the L.A. Times in Google Search. Set us as preferred
Fire crews across Southern California were on full alert Friday as they braced for the most extreme window of Santa Ana winds forecast in the ongoing red flag event.
Crews continued to battle two fires that ignited Thursday. The Bryson fire in Malibu was 146 acres and 17% contained by Friday morning, while at Camp Pendleton in northern San Diego County the Henderson fire had burned 1,404 acres.
At least 100,000 customers served by Southern California Edison — including around 35,000 Los Angeles County households — were without electricity as the utility initiated public safety power outages to lessen the risk of its equipment sparking a fire.
At a Friday morning news conference, L.A. County Fire Chief Anthony Marrone praised the “great progress” crews made on the Bryson fire overnight.
“There has been no reported structure loss or damage, and only minor injuries to our firefighting personnel,” he said.
The blaze erupted shortly before 5 p.m. Thursday, sparking evacuation orders for the Encinal Canyon area near Trancas Canyon and placing a larger swath of Malibu under an evacuation warning. On Friday morning, 414 personnel and multiple aerial resources were assigned to the incident, with a focus on ensuring flames do not jump over Ensignal Canyon Road, which would place a much larger hillside area under threat, Marrone said.
A red flag warning remains in effect for parts of Los Angeles and Ventura counties through 8 p.m. Saturday.
“This morning through this afternoon is our most critical period of time during this red flag event: strong winds and very dry conditions will continue to cause fire starts to spread rapidly,” said Kevin McGowan, director of the county office of emergency management. “We’re urging everyone to remain vigilant and ready to act.”
Wind speeds Friday are forecast to be about 10 mph greater than on Thursday, said meteorologist Mike Wofford with the National Weather Service in Oxnard. Downed trees and power lines are also a danger.
“High wind warnings and strong wind advisories look good for much of Ventura and Los Angeles Counties with peak winds likely in the 50 to 70 mph range through late morning or early afternoon before gradually weakening,” the National Weather Service said in its Friday morning forecast .
Even areas that don’t typically see a lot of wind during the Sana Anas may see wind gusts between 25 and 45 mph Friday, the forecast said.
On Thursday, windy areas of San Diego saw peak gusts ranging from 60 to 78 mph, according to the National Weather Service. The Henderson fire ignited around 2:30 p.m. Thursday in a dry, brushy area of Camp Pendleton, prompting a temporary closure of the 5 Freeway.
Mayor Karen Bass said Thursday that Los Angeles fire officials were pre-deploying personnel and resources to potential fire hot spots including the San Fernando Valley, Santa Monica Mountains and Hollywood in anticipation of the red flag conditions.
Reviews of the Los Angeles Fire Department response to the January 2025 firestorm revealed critical failures to pre-stage resources . In particular, fire officials drew heat for failing to pre-deploy engines to Pacific Palisades, despite forecasters warning of extreme fire weather conditions.
At Friday’s news conference, officials projected confidence that they were better prepared to respond to the ongoing fire danger.
Marrone said that “the county family is always improving” and that agencies are implementing changes recommend in after-action reports of last year’s wildfire’s.
“The Jan. 7, 2025, wildfires were very unique in that we had two wildfire-initiated community conflagrations eight hours apart,” he said. “No other jurisdiction in the United States ever fought the fires that we fought on Jan. 7.”
Thursday’s red flag alert was one step below the rare “particularly dangerous situation” warning that was issued in advance of the Palisades fire. Nonetheless, there was a noted effort to ensure fire equipment and personnel are ready to respond to any potential ignitions in high-fire-hazard zones across the county.
In addition to the pre-deployed L.A. Fire teams, the L.A. County Fire Department has bolstered its on-duty staff by about 100 personnel, and additional firefighting crews have been sent to Southern California by the governor’s Office of Emergency Services.
L.A. County Sheriff Robert Luna said the department has augmented its patrol officers in areas impacted by evacuations and public safety power outages.
“If you think you’re going to come in and take advantage of these poor folks who have been asked to evacuate or don’t have power,” he said, “you’re going to run into probably deputies who aren’t in uniform and who are just out there specifically looking for that challenge.”
On Friday, Los Angeles County Supervisor Lindsey Horvath highlighted the $77 million and 44 new positions funneled into the county’s Office of Emergency Management. A review of the Eaton fire found county agencies struggled to monitor rapidly unfolding events and operated with unclear policies for sending evacuation orders.
“We will continue to make those investments,” said Horvath. “We will continue to support our departments and make sure that emergency preparedness remains a top priority for the county.”
Rong-Gong Lin II and Hannah Fry contributed to this report.

articles.title_orig: Alaska Senate candidates clash over the Iran war, high prices and their times in office
articles.title_zh: Alaska Senate candidates clash over the Iran war, high prices and their times in office
articles.content_orig:
BREAKING: Katie Zacharia is out as White House press secretary after just 5 days on the job
The two major candidates vying for an Alaska Senate seat squared off Thursday night over issues ranging from the war with Iran to controversies during the Democratic nominee’s time in Congress in a debate that at times flared into personal attacks.
Republican incumbent Dan Sullivan described Democratic challenger Mary Peltola as someone who sought a lobbying paycheck after her time serving in the House ended in 2025, pointing to recent reporting on the tumult in her congressional office during her tenure.
Peltola sought to tie Sullivan’s support for the war in Iran to the increase in the cost of living at home, pointing out Sullivan’s own increase in wealth while in office.
The race between Sullivan and Peltola, which NBC News rates as a toss-up , is one of a handful that could determine control of the Senate in November. Democrats have targeted the seat as one of five potential pickup opportunities, despite the fact that Donald Trump carried Alaska by double digits in 2024.
When asked what he thought of the White House’s recent announcement that it would allow the release of Russian diesel fuel onto the global market, Sullivan drew a distinction between himself and the Trump administration, a tack other Republicans in tight races have taken in recent debates.
“I just led the effort on a Russia sanctions act that passed the Congress, so I’m opposed to that,” Sullivan said.
The senator then pivoted to his opposition to the Pentagon’s now withdrawn announcement that it would livestream the execution of convicted terrorist Nidal Hasan.
“Certainly he needs to be executed, but if you have a livestreaming of this terrorist, you are going to create more terrorists,” Sullivan said.
Asked about the war with Iran, both candidates said the conflict should end soon.
Peltola attributed the increase in prices at home to the ongoing conflict — issues that polling has shown have become a drag on Republicans heading into the midterms.
“There does not appear to be a peace deal on the horizon, and I think it’s so important that our military be removed and protected,” Peltola said when asked whether she would support ending the war without a peace deal.
Sullivan said he supported President Donald Trump ’s war powers in Iran because “the largest state sponsor of terrorism should not have nuclear weapons.”
“But it needs to end soon. The energy costs from this war are too high,” Sullivan continued, adding that boosting domestic energy production would bring down costs.
In another exchange, Sullivan leveled criticism of Peltola’s lobbying work after losing her the state’s at-large House seat in 2024.
“Mary, you’re walking through the revolving door so much you must be getting dizzy up here,” Sullivan said.
Peltola responded by noting the increase in Sullivan’s net worth during his two terms as a senator.
“Dan’s been in D.C. for 12 years and has gotten richer every single one of those years,” Peltola said.
Sullivan shot back, referring to a recent New York Times article that described turmoil in her congressional office and campaign, including angry outbursts and offensive language.
“Twenty-five staffers quit on Mary Peltola because she abused them physically and emotionally, and then she slanders every other group, African Americans, special needs individuals. It is a character flaw on my opponent,” Sullivan said, referring to the Times’ reporting on her time on Capitol Hill.
Peltola was later asked directly about the Times’ reporting.
“I don’t think this election is about me on my worst day,” Peltola said, calling the stories “allegations” and “mass exaggerations of the truth.”
Thursday’s debate comes just days after Trump visited Wasilla, Alaska, to hold a rally in support of Sullivan amid his multistate blitz to shore up Republican candidates, and Vice President JD Vance visited Fairbanks earlier this month.
The subject of Trump, however, was largely absent from Thursday’s debate, a departure from other high-profile races.
Alaska last elected a Democrat to the Senate in 2008, when Sen. Mark Begich ousted incumbent Republican Ted Stevens.
Peltola finished ahead of Sullivan in August’s all-party primary, with Peltola receiving 49.5% of the vote and Sullivan taking 41.4%.
A second Republican candidate also named Dan Sullivan — who has denied Republican accusations of being a ploy to confuse voters — received only 2.5% of the vote. Dan J. Sullivan did not participate in Thursday night’s debate, although he will be on the ballot in November.
Casey Wooten is a breaking news editor for the politics team at NBC News.

articles.title_orig: What this bankruptcy says about AI startups
articles.title_zh: What this bankruptcy says about AI startups
articles.content_orig:
You're reading a newsletter from The Indicator from Planet Money. Once a week, we curate our favorite stories and insights on business, finance, economics and why they matter. Subscribe here to get it in your inbox every Friday.
After you win the economics Nobel, what would your first act be? Buy a Corvette? Gloat to your childhood bully? For co-winner Michael Woodford, his first act was … proctor an exam . The DAY that Columbia professor Michael Woodford found out that he and Robert Hall won the economics Nobel, he returned to his class with the pithy title "Cognitive Mechanisms and Economic Behavior" to administer an exam. He was welcomed to the classroom with cheers and applause. He held up his arms in triumph.
Michael Woodford, Columbia University professor and winner of the 2026 Sveriges Riksbank Prize in Economic Sciences in Memory of Alfred Nobel. Andrew Harrer/Bloomberg via Getty Images hide caption
What to know: Character.ai is a company that allows you to speak with a "companion" — an AI-powered fictional character, historical figure, or whatever you decide to build. It came out just before ChatGPT and quickly went viral in part thanks to its adoption on TikTok. It hit 28 million monthly active users at its peak.
Character.ai had a lot of engagement, a big customer base, lots of talent … and Google promptly picked 'em up for $2.7 billion back in 2024. But Google didn't buy the company and absorb it! No, that traditional " acquihire " model would require all sorts of legal and regulatory approvals. Instead, they hired away the founders (and other big hitters on the team) and bought the nonexclusive license to the technology, leaving the company itself behind. That's called a "reverse acquihire," and it's happened at least six times in the past two years with AI startups. Now this week, Character.ai is filing for Chapter 11 bankruptcy.
Some of the "Characters" available to users Gabby Jones/Bloomberg via Getty Images hide caption
Why it matters: A "reverse acquihire" doesn't leave a company in the greatest position. After the Google deal, Character.ai had to change its business model away from the quite costly LLM training and toward developing AI characters. Its founders were gone. Sure, the shrunken company had $2.7 billion in the bank, but leadership was still looking to raise money as they struggled to monetize their user base.
So is the "reverse acquihire" what caused the pain? Or was it a symptom of a larger issue? Character.ai faced a mountain of litigation over alleged harm to minors plus copyright concerns from Disney. So what's left behind? A once very promising company, which Disney is very excited to pick over for parts of it for $20 million.
What's going on: President Trump signed a deal last week to get diesel from Russia in an effort to lower fuel prices ahead of the midterms. Two weeks ago, we talked in the newsletter about the potential of a diesel export ban to lower prices. It didn't happen. One week ago, we talked again about Trump issuing an executive order to defer a tax from diesel. Now, this!
It's safe to say people were surprised by the move, given Trump signed a Russian sanctions law just last month that looked to tamp down on their energy revenues. Beyond surprise, a bipartisan group of senators is openly calling for the president to rescind the deal. They said it gives Putin the funds to power his war machine and "enables Russia to continue its brutal attacks on Ukrainian civilians."
Will this do anything? The same bipartisan group of senators said this deal will mean "limited to no relief to Americans." Goldman Sachs estimated the release of Russian oil would affect wholesale prices by $1 to $2 per barrel. The price of a barrel of diesel is around $200. So a $1 to $2 impact? Neil Atkinson, an independent energy analyst, says, "Frankly, [it's] a rounding error. It makes no fundamental difference to the global diesel market."
What's weirder to Atkinson, though … Russia hasn't really been exporting diesel. Its refineries have been damaged, and it's literally been importing diesel to make up for shortfalls. " So where these barrels of Russian diesel are going to come from to go either to the United States or elsewhere in the global market is a bit of a mystery," said Atkinson.
If you HAVEN'T listened: Reporter Greg Rosalsky opens the piece describing WHAT exactly Michael Woodford and Robert Hall won the economics Nobel for. They helped shape what's known as NEW Keynesian economics by bringing microeconomic principles to the traditional models of John Maynard Keynes. BUT THEN, Greg goes on to explain that the Nobel Prize did not initially include an economics award. No, that changed when the Swedish Central Bank, the oldest central bank in the world, wanted to celebrate its 300th anniversary with a bang. They would fund a new award for economics. It's a fascinating story which you can listen to below.
If you HAVE listened: A leading philosophy of John Maynard Keynes is that governments could fight recessions by boosting spending, and deal with inflation by holding spending back. In the initial draft that didn't make it into the final episode, Greg touched on how STAGFLATION was a central thorn in the side of this concept. Specifically, back in the 1970s, during the Arab oil embargo, the U.S. dealt with the one-two punch of high unemployment and high inflation, bringing about stagflation. It challenged the Keynesian idea that when lots of people are out of work and spending less, inflation comes down. Because at that point, unemployment and inflation rose together. Isn't that nice? Greg Rosalsky writes Planet Money's newsletter … you can catch that here .
Producer Cooper Katz McKim is reading The AGI Chronicles
Man oh man, this is the page-turniest nonfiction book I've read in a while. Kevin Roose, co-host of the upcoming NPR podcast Machine Gods , formerly The New York Times ' Hard Fork , tracks the handful of characters racing to make AI a commercial reality. It is far from a clear-cut story. There's no one character who came up with the idea and executed it … the existence of AI today comes down to many papers, many individual discoveries, and a whole lot of obsession. I didn't realize how much progress had been made in AI prior to 2020 and how concerned many industry leaders were about even creating AI (looking at you, Amodei ) for fear of creating a super-intelligence that moves outside of human control. It's gossip-y, it's matter of fact … I would recommend.

articles.title_zh: GOP senators press Pentagon over Ukraine’s loss of Starshield data
articles.content_orig:
Ukraine is bracing for a difficult winter as restrictions on military applications of Starlink have emboldened Russia to intensify attacks on civilian and energy targets, a senior Ukrainian official told CNBC on Friday.
Serhiy Derkach, Ukraine's first deputy minister for recovery, infrastructure and transport, said Russian forces had stepped up strikes on bridges in Kyiv, threatening to isolate nearly 2 million residents on the eastern bank of the Dnipro River, while also targeting railway networks and border crossings in an effort to disrupt transport and sow panic among civilians.
"With U.S. limiting the use of Starlinks on the battlefield, Russia feels that this is their moment to try and inflict even more pain and suffering on Ukraine's civilian infrastructure," Derkach said.
"We are definitely moving towards very harsh weeks and months and need our partners' support now more than ever," he said, adding that Ukrainians already experience blackouts lasting 4-12 hours per day.
His warning came as President Volodymyr Zelenskyy on Friday called for support from European leaders in Brussels to help Ukraine prepare a winter support package, including energy assistance, air defenses and funding.
Zelenskyy praised Europe's "real leaders" for standing by Kyiv on Friday, as his strained relationship with U.S. President Donald Trump clouds a summit focused on securing further support for Ukraine.
"I'm so thankful that we have such huge support from EU Council Commission and leaders – real leaders," Zelenskyy said, emphasizing Europe's backing since the beginning of the war.
His remarks come as tensions between the U.S. and Ukraine have flared up after SpaceX's Starlink service was restricted in Ukraine earlier this week, slowing down the connectivity Ukraine relies on to defend against Russian attacks.
Zelenskyy is also reportedly facing increasing pressure to tone down public criticism of Trump.
Three officials familiar with the EU summit preparations told the Financial Times that they plan to privately urge Zelenskyy to tone down his rhetoric when they meet him in Brussels on Friday.
According to Politico , some EU leaders are also concerned about Zelenskyy's handling of his strained relationship with Trump, with one EU diplomat saying Zelenskyy's public criticism of the president was "not helpful."
"We want to end this war as quick as possible. We don't see now signals from Russia side that they are ready for this to end this war," Zelenskyy told reporters in Brussels on Friday after he on Wednesday lamented that Russia didn't respect the "energy ceasefire" announced by Trump.
Trump last week surprised both Russian and Ukrainian officials by announcing the countries had agreed to stop attacking each other's power infrastructure, in an apparent attempt to ease prices of oil and diesel ahead of the U.S. midterm elections in November.
Zelenskyy later welcomed the proposal and said Ukraine had held off strikes on Russian energy targets for three days to abide by Washington's wishes, but he described the deal with Russia to supply diesel to global markets as "weak."
Russia hasn't confirmed it agreed to an energy ceasefire, saying only that talks are "ongoing." Russian authorities didn't respond to multiple CNBC requests for comment.
— CNBC's George Bextor contributed to this report

articles.title_orig: New dinosaur species discovered in London museum after 100 years
articles.title_zh: New dinosaur species discovered in London museum after 100 years
articles.content_orig:
A dinosaur fossil that spent almost a century in the collections of London’s Natural History Museum has been identified as a new species.
The skull fragment belonged to Invictibellatrix amberina , a previously unknown carnivorous dinosaur that lived around 120 million years ago. It’s also the first confirmed evidence of a megaraptoran dinosaur in Europe.
The fossil was originally discovered at the foot of a cliff on the southwest coast of the Isle of Wight by amateur fossil hunter Reginald Walter Tooley. After his death in 1924, the Natural History Museum acquired more than 1,000 specimens from his collection, including the fragment.
Although scientists knew it belonged to a dinosaur, exactly which one remained a mystery for decades.
Now, researchers have taken another look at the fossil using CT scanning technology, allowing them to examine its internal structure and create a 3D model. Their full findings were published in the journal Royal Society Open Science .
Professor Paul Barrett, the study’s senior author from the Natural History Museum, says, "Despite over 200 years of collecting, the Isle of Wight continues to surprise us with new dinosaur species, and finds of carnivorous dinosaurs, such as Invictibellatrix, have been particularly elusive."
"Work like this shows the exceptional value of working with historical museum collections where there are still many discoveries to be made," he added.
Despite their name, megaraptorans were not the small, bird-like dinosaurs we commonly associate with the word "raptor". They were larger predators, more closely related to tyrannosaurs, with "slender heads", "large arms" and "giant curved claws", according to the Natural History Museum.
Invictibellatrix amberina is estimated to have measured between 3 and 4 metres (10 and 13 feet) in length and stood around 1.5 metres (5 feet) tall. It lived during the Early Cretaceous period, when dinosaurs dominated terrestrial ecosystems.
Researchers have also suggested that it may have had feathers, although its exact appearance still remains uncertain.
According to Dr Cassius Morrison, a researcher at the University College London's (UCL) Earth Sciences department, the species would have eaten small dinosaurs, lizards and mammals - similar to the role in the food chain a hyena holds today.
"It was not the apex predator of its time, but for humans this dinosaur would have been more dangerous than a T. rex. We would have been perfectly sized prey, about a third of their body weight. They definitely would have chased us. A T. rex would not have bothered, as we would have been too small," explains Dr Cassius Morrison, who led the study.
The discovery is particularly exciting because megaraptorans have previously been identified in Asia, Australia and South America, but never conclusively in Europe.

articles.title_orig: Zelensky praises ‘real leaders’ in Europe as his relationship with Trump deteriorates
articles.title_zh: Zelensky praises ‘real leaders’ in Europe as his relationship with Trump deteriorates
articles.content_orig:
Ukraine’s President Volodymyr Zelensky praised “real leaders” in Europe at a summit in Belgium on Friday, taking a veiled swipe at US President Donald Trump amid testy relations between Kyiv and Washington.
European leaders are rallying around Zelensky after the White House heaped pressure on Ukraine to halt strikes on Russian oil facilities, even as Russia’s attacks on Ukrainian energy infrastructure continue unabated.
Ukraine halted strikes on Russian oil refineries for three days after Trump’s surprise announcement on Sunday of an “energy ceasefire” between the two countries, but has since resumed attacks given Russia did not reciprocate.
Trump, who is desperate for soaring global diesel prices to ease ahead of next month’s midterm elections , blindsided European leaders last week when he struck a deal allowing Russian diesel exports – a move Zelensky said had left him feeling betrayed.
The US president has blamed the rise in fuel prices on the Ukraine-Russia war, eager to deflect attention from his war in Iran which remains deeply unpopular with voters.
On Thursday, Trump once again lashed out at Zelensky in an interview with Newsmax, saying he found him “more difficult to deal with than Putin.”
As Zelensky arrived at Friday’s summit in Brussels, flanked by the European Union’s top leaders, he didn’t mention the deterioration in US relations, but was keen to emphasize the strength of his relationship with the EU.
“I’m so thankful that we have such huge support from (the) EU Council, Commission and leaders – real leaders – so that they stay with us from the very beginning of this war,” Zelensky said as he walked into the summit.
Difficulties for Kyiv have mounted this week, with the country reporting restrictions on Starshield, the military-grade version of Elon Musk’s Starlink internet service.
Zelensky said on Friday that the Starlink operations had improved but had not yet been fully restored.
“They disrupted logistics and compromised the protection of the civilian population. That’s why this is very troubling,” Zelensky said, noting the military relied on Starlink-equipped drones, which need to move at a high speed, to deliver food and water to troops on the frontline.
“Have we fully restored the speed we had before? No. Is the speed coming back? Yes,” he added.
Trump on Friday said he was not behind the Starlink disruption , telling reporters at the White House, “I didn’t do that. No, we didn’t do that at all.
“It wasn’t me, and I don’t think it was Elon (Musk). And from what I understand, it’s the same as it’s always been,” he said.
Trump added that he wasn’t sure there were any speed restrictions on Ukraine’s use of Starshield.“I don’t even think it was slowed down. But from what I understand… We didn’t slow it down at all. And I think it’s probably functioning,” Trump said.
Musk said earlier this week that any decision to limit Starshield was up to the US president. A senior US official told CNN that Trump had made no such request.
The Ukrainian government said on Tuesday that it had not received its usual early warning from the US before a Russian ballistic missile struck a major power plant in Kyiv and damaged a residential building .
But Trump insisted that the United States had not stopped sharing intelligence with Ukraine.
Exclusive: Ukraine runs out of Patriot interceptor missiles as Zelensky and Trump clash over war
Amid a challenging week diplomatically, Ukraine has also run out of missiles for the US-made Patriot air defense system, a source familiar with the situation told CNN on Thursday.
“It’s an open secret that we are not a priority destination for these missiles now,” Zelensky told Friday’s news conference, noting that most Patriot interceptors were now being sent to the Middle East. But he added that Ukraine was grateful to the Europeans “who are financing all of this,” as well as to NATO and to the White House.
When a reporter asked whether he thought Trump was treating Ukraine as a scapegoat for his own problems given high fuel prices and the ongoing Iran war, Zelensky paused for a full 15 seconds. With a smile, he told the silent room: “This is my answer.”
Earlier the Ukrainian president said his team was in constant contact with US negotiators and would arrange a meeting in the coming days.
“We will keep living, fighting, and most importantly, living with dignity,” he added. “When the quality of life is so terrible during wartime, maintaining dignity is a very important thing.”
EU leaders said they were preparing a new package of sanctions against Russia – the 22nd package since its full-scale invasion of Ukraine. In contrast with the Trump administration, they were keen to stress that sanctions against Moscow would be strengthened unless Putin stops the war.
“We supported President Trump’s energy ceasefire, but we’ve seen that Russia did not respect it – not a single minute. Instead, Russia escalated, and therefore we have to increase the pressure on Russia,” European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said.
Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov said on Friday that Zelensky has “no desire” for a peaceful resolution, adding “on that point, we are in complete agreement with President Trump.”
In a visit to a military command post in an undisclosed location, Putin vowed to continue the war.
“In response to strikes by the Kyiv authorities against our industrial and fuel-and-energy sector facilities, the Russian Armed Forces continue to carry out strikes against Ukraine’s military-industrial complex and infrastructure facilities,” Putin said, according to a video released by the Kremlin on Friday.
The video shows Putin wearing military uniform and greeting senior Russian commanders.
CNN’s Victoria Butenko, Anna Chernova and Kit Maher contributed to this report.

articles.title_orig: 'Well, it worked': Elon Musk unveils new Tesla Roadster that can fly
articles.title_zh: 'Well, it worked': Elon Musk unveils new Tesla Roadster that can fly
articles.content_orig:
Houston — Tesla CEO Elon Musk unveiled what he described as a "flying" car, equipped with thrusters, during a livestreamed event at his SpaceX rocket company's facility on Thursday.
Technical and regulatory challenges have so far prevented the much-hyped flying car sector from getting off the ground.
Musk revealed Tesla 's new Roadster sports car during a launch event at a SpaceX test facility in Texas.
During the demo, which was livestreamed on Tesla's X account, the car launched from a ramp that curled over so the vehicle was upside down, appearing to defy gravity by clinging to the surface before flying off the end, and then rolled over 180 degrees midair to land on its wheels.
"Flying cars are real," Musk said during the event, adding that the vehicle's "success is not guaranteed" but "it will probably work."
Musk said the car was equipped with "ultra high-pressure air tanks" to propel itself into the air.
The tech billionaire described the development as "what happens when you have a collaboration with the world's best car company and the world's best rocket company," referring to Tesla and SpaceX.
The vehicle would go into production in 2028, he said.
American aviation pioneer Glenn Curtiss debuted the first flying car prototype in 1917.
But successful designs have become more seriously contemplated only in recent years as electric motors and high-performance batteries have advanced.
Musk, who has appeared to have a close but sometimes tumultuous relationship with President Trump, has thrust his companies to the forefront of several major industries, and he continues pushing into new ones.
SpaceX announced a week ago that it had agreed to buy licenses for radio airwaves that will enable its Starlink Mobile satellite business to provide cellular service inside buildings, a move the company said would allow it to "become a major mobile carrier in the U.S."
"This is the last critical piece of the spectrum puzzle needed for SpaceX to provide complete phone coverage in America," Musk said in an Oct. 8 social media post .

articles.title_orig: 'Everything got worse': Gen Z express frustration, regret after Trump vote
articles.title_zh: 'Everything got worse': Gen Z express frustration, regret after Trump vote
articles.content_orig:
President Trump speaks at a campaign rally in San Antonio on Oct. 7. Trump made big inroads with young voters in 2024, but some of that support appears to be waning. Mandel Ngan/AFP via Getty Images hide caption
📲 Follow the midterms & more in the NPR App .
Gen Z Americans were a key part of President Trump's winning coalition in 2024. Nearly two years later — and with early voting underway in multiple states for the midterms — some of that youth support has faded.
That sentiment was on display in a focus group, conducted last week, of eight Generation Z Trump voters, who reported varying degrees of unhappiness and disappointment over the state of politics, with some going as far as to say they regret supporting Trump in 2024.
The conversation was conducted virtually by Navigator Research , a left-leaning polling group. Participants ranged in age from 20 to 29 and spanned five states: Florida, Mississippi, Ohio, Texas and South Carolina — places Trump won by double digits in the last election. Two of those states, Texas and Ohio , are home to competitive races that could be key to control of the Senate .
For participants who now regret their vote for Trump, much of their frustration centers on what they see as a string of failed promises. When asked to give the president's job performance a letter grade, a majority of participants, 6 out of 8, assigned him a grade of either D or F, while two selected C.
"I just feel like nothing went correctly. I just feel like everything got worse," said John, a 29-year-old Black man from Florida. (Participants agreed to be part of the focus group on the condition that they be identified by only their first names.)
John, who identifies as a Republican and has voted for Trump since 2016, gave the president an F and said he now plans to support Democratic candidates this fall, in large part because of the strain he has felt from rising costs.
"I'm willing to give the other side a chance," he added. "I don't think they're going to make a total change. But things are just horrible right now for me. So I feel like even if they make one or two small changes, it will probably benefit me."
Though the focus group is not a nationally representative survey, the frustrations shared by participants echoed polling conducted by Navigator this month, which found that more than a third of Gen Zers — those under age 30 — regret voting for Trump, higher than older generations do.
Trump's rising unpopularity among young voters isn't in a vacuum. He has also lost ground with other key groups that shifted right in 2024, notably independents and Latino voters — and in a year when the Republican Party is facing political headwinds, it's unclear whether that expanded coalition from two years ago can show up at the same strength now.
While some voters, like John in Florida, do feel compelled to vote blue this cycle in response to Trump, 4 of the 8 who took part in the focus group said they still planned to back Republicans this year. Three said they'd vote for Democrats; one participant said she was still deciding.
Matthew, a 25-year-old Black man living in Texas, said he doesn't regret his support for the president and gave him a C grade.
"I feel like he's done a really good job closing the border," he said. "I also do appreciate his efforts in trying to end some of the conflicts that began under the last administration, besides the fact that the Iran conflict hasn't really worked the best, from my perspective."
He plans to vote in the midterm elections and argued that Trump will be able to carry out more of his agenda if Republicans can secure a larger majority in both the House of Representatives and the Senate, although national polls indicate that the GOP is more likely to lose seats.
But enthusiasm is a different question.
Courtney, a 20-year-old white woman based in South Carolina, said she doesn't regret her vote for Trump in 2024 and overall aligns with Republicans, but she did admit she has grown more distrustful of both major political parties, particularly on foreign policy.
"I just really do feel like we would be in this situation either way. … Education, the economy, everything else would be so much better if we weren't pumping money out into other countries that aren't ours," she said, referring to U.S. aid for Israel and the decision to go to war with Iran.
"I don't think it matters what side you vote on — that's why I voted red, because I agree with those policies more — but at the end of the day, what we do in the Middle East is going to be not at all up to [the] party [in power]," she said during the focus group.
That sense of political disaffection may underscore a growing challenge for both Republicans and Democrats moving forward as both try to repair ties with this generation.
"As we see people regret their vote for Trump, sour on the Republican Party and Republican policies, that doesn't necessarily mean that they're swinging right over to Democrats," said Melissa Toufanian, the managing director at Navigator.
Toufanian points to Navigator's own polling , which has found that even as the GOP has lost trust on economic issues, "it's not a one-for-one with Democrats gaining that trust."
"A lot of people are moving to this middle, this category that 'I don't trust either party,'" she said. "We are seeing people who are becoming increasingly pessimistic about our political parties and our political system, and they're not feeling strongly that either party can really deliver for them."

articles.title_orig: Net FDI hits highest H1 in four years
articles.title_zh: Net FDI hits highest H1 in four years
articles.content_orig:
Inflow’s strong results reflect growing confidence among foreign investors
Net foreign direct investment inflows into China reached the highest first-half level in four years, reflecting growing foreign investor confidence as the Chinese economy shifts toward more resilient growth driven by innovation and domestic demand, according to an official, experts and executives.
China recorded net FDI inflows of $60.9 billion in the first half of 2026, up 81 percent year-on-year, according to the latest balance of payments data released by the State Administration of Foreign Exchange.
An administration official confirmed that the figure was the highest for the corresponding period in four years.
“In the first half of 2026, foreign direct equity investment totaled $63.8 billion, up 55 percent year-on-year, indicating that FDI inflows into China are stabilizing and gaining momentum,” the administration official said.
Within foreign direct equity investment, inflows of new capital, which reflect long-term investment intentions, rose 10 percent to $43.1 billion in the first half, the official said.
Furthermore, reinvestment of earnings by foreign-invested enterprises in China increased 31 percent, indicating that they were using more of their earnings to expand investment with a stable willingness to invest and operate here, the official said, adding that “China’s steady expansion of institutional opening-up and improvements to its foreign investment services have helped create a favorable development environment for foreign investors to invest and operate in China”.
“Combined with its vast market, comprehensive industrial system and strong supporting capabilities, these advantages have enabled foreign-invested enterprises to earn relatively high returns, consistently ranking among the highest across major economies,” the official said.
According to the first-half balance of payments data released by the administration, FDI returns in China came in at $179.8 billion in the first half of 2026, remaining stable compared with the same period last year.
Amid persistent global economic and geopolitical uncertainties, executives said that China’s relatively stable growth and pursuit of high-quality development have provided foreign companies with sources of confidence and opportunity, citing the nation’s role as an innovation hub and the growth opportunities offered by its vast domestic market.
Australian wine company Treasury Wine Estates said it will continue to deepen its focus on the Chinese market as its flagship Penfolds brand gains momentum in China.
“The Chinese mainland is one of the world’s most dynamic luxury beverage markets,” said Wu Mingfeng, managing director for China at Treasury Wine Estates.
Iris Cui, vice-president of Asia procurement and operations at Apple, said that more than 80 percent of Apple’s 200 major suppliers worldwide operate manufacturing facilities in China, while work on its newest product — the iPhone Duo — was carried out exclusively in China, from early-stage product development to final assembly.
New capital contributions by foreign direct investors into high-tech services and high-tech manufacturing saw a 61 percent year-on-year increase in the first half, the State Administration of Foreign Exchange said in the latest balance of payments report, indicating that foreign investors are shifting from seeking the cost and scale advantages of “Made in China” to participating in “Created in China”.
Pan Yuanyuan, a researcher at the National Institute for Global Strategy at the Chinese Academy of Social Sciences, underscored the need for drawing on China’s institutional strengths to further provide a predictable business environment for foreign investors.
The administration official said that further measures are planned to facilitate cross-border investment and financing by multinational companies, providing more convenient and efficient services for them.

articles.title_orig: LVMH touts ‘special bond’ with China amid ‘subdued’ sales backdrop
articles.title_zh: LVMH touts ‘special bond’ with China amid ‘subdued’ sales backdrop
articles.content_orig:
Antoine Arnault praises firm’s ‘dialogue with Chinese culture’ during global event after lawsuit backlash and sluggish spending mar results
French luxury giant LVMH Group kicked off a global open-house event showcasing its craftsmanship in Shanghai on Thursday, as the event’s founder Antoine Arnault hailed a “special bond” with Chinese customers at a launch event in Paris.
It came as the group faced pressure from sluggish demand in China and a backlash over a lawsuit against a local tea company.
At the launch event at the Samaritaine department store in central Paris for this year’s Les Journées Particulières, first initiated by Arnault in 2011, he mentioned the Shanghai event, which was the first among 71 venues across 13 countries to open to the public for the three-day event.
“For the first time since the event was created, several LVMH houses have come together in a single venue to share our savoir faire and its dialogue with Chinese culture,” said Arnault, who holds multiple roles within LVMH and is the son of its chairman and CEO Bernard Arnault. “Because we share a special bond with China and our Chinese customers.”

articles.title_orig: Earth from Space: West Antarctica
articles.title_zh: Earth from Space: West Antarctica
articles.content_orig:
You have already liked this page, you can only like it once!
This image over part of West Antarctica was captured by Copernicus Sentinel-3 on 30 September 2026.
Zoom in to explore this image at its full resolution.
At this time of year, winter is coming to an end in the southern hemisphere and the sea ice is at its annual maximum extent. It reaches as far as the tip of the Antarctic Peninsula, visible in the central part of the image, where there is also some cloud coverage.
An area of about 1200 km by 1700 km is shown – this area is on the periphery of the Antarctic continent, which is about 4500 km across its main landmass. Elephant Island, about 50 km in length, is clearly visible against ice-free ocean on the left-hand side of the image. It is about 930 km from the tip of Argentina’s Tierra del Fuego, which is not pictured.
Sea ice for Antarctica’s winter season most likely peaked on 14 September 2026, according to the National Snow and Ice Data Center (NSIDC). This image shows sea ice engulfing the tip of the Antarctic Peninsula as well as part of the Weddell Sea, east of the peninsula.
White cloud covers much of the lower part of the image but sea ice is clearly visible in the upper-right area. A variety of textures reflect the different types of ice, including areas of tightly packed sea ice on the right. Large floes comparable in size to Elephant Island are visible and these progress to much smaller pieces of sea ice that form swirling shapes in the ocean.

articles.title_orig: Trump says he won't use nuclear weapons or send ground troops to Iran
articles.title_zh: Trump says he won't use nuclear weapons or send ground troops to Iran
articles.content_orig:
U.S. President Donald Trump has said he does not intend to use nuclear weapons against Iran or foresee deploying ground troops in the country.
Speaking in an interview with Newsmax, broadcast Thursday evening, he said: "I wouldn't use nuclear. We don't have to. We're the greatest nuclear power in the world."
The right-wing cable outlet asked Trump about reports that Washington was considering using the GBU-43/B Massive Ordnance Air Blast, or MOAB, widely known as the "Mother of All Bombs."
"The mother of all bombs is not nuclear. It's not nuclear at all. This is just an extremely large bomb. It's like a tiny nuclear bomb. But the mother of all bombs is one big bomb, but it's not nuclear," he said, without specifically confirming or denying the reports.
When asked if he would put "troops on the ground," Trump said: "No, I don't see that, I don't see it."
The MOAB is the largest non-nuclear bomb in the U.S. arsenal. It was used in combat in 2017 against ISIS militants in Afghanistan .
Earlier on Thursday , CNN reported that the U.S. military has developed new strike plans to target Iranian energy infrastructure and nuclear sites.
The strikes could take place if Trump orders combat operations to resume, either before or after the midterm elections, the outlet reported. The White House did not immediately respond to CNBC's request for comment.
Trump said on Oct. 8 that he would not order a resumption of military strikes before the Nov. 3 midterm elections.
Merchant shipping through the Strait of Hormuz faces heightened risks after a series of attacks in the critical waterway.
The United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations said that the threat remains "severe" in the Strait of Hormuz, after the Singapore-registered container ship GFS Pride was struck by an unknown projectile, caught fire and later sank.
The UKMTO added that "deliberate hostile action" was highly likely and said it had recorded eight attacks in the critical waterway since Oct. 11.

articles.title_orig: Race Across the World's Kush Burman hopes to help others affected by suicide
articles.title_zh: Race Across the World's Kush Burman hopes to help others affected by suicide
articles.content_orig:
When Kush Burman won BBC's Race Across the World, he wanted to use his new-found platform to help those who had supported him and his family after his dad took his own life.
Burman opened up about his struggles on the popular BBC show following Matt's suicide during the coronavirus lockdown in 2020.
"I had no clue what was going on when I was 14... I had zero indication," said the 20-year-old from Liverpool.
"So it was such a surprise, but I think going through life now I've always got at the back of my mind, just be nice, because you will never know.... you can't know unless someone directly comes to you."
Burman is now an ambassador for Alfie's Squad - a Liverpool-based charity providing support to children and young people just like him.
Race for a Reason - which is in its second year - aims to raise money and awareness of Alfie's Squad as the teams race to different checkpoints across the UK over the next three days.
Kush said he was honoured to be an ambassador of the charity that provided so much help to him, his mum and brothers.
"It's amazing and so to say that I'm an ambassador it does mean a lot," he said.
Kush said his birth father passed away when he was one to lymphoma so he was raised by his stepdad Matt.
"He took his own life in 2020, I was just 14," he said.
"It was the most difficult thing to have to go through in my entire life."
Alfie's Squad was set up by 17-year-old Alfie and his mum after he lost his dad to suicide when he was just eight.
Support groups take place in Liverpool every week.
Kush said Alfie's Squad was "like a family...it's a whole community".
"I think the most valuable aspect I found is that it's not all about the grief, it's about fun and life".
Alfie is doing the race with the former Liverpool goalkeeper and charity patron Chris Kirkland, who said he struggled in the past with his mental health and "not wanting to be here".
"It makes you realise now, when you see these kids and you see the parents that have lost their partner, that could have been my wife and that could have been my daughter - seeing the impact it has.. the devastation... it's why I wanted to get involved," he said.
Thirty teams will travel 650 miles and finish back in Liverpool on Sunday.
None of the teams know anything about the route or the tasks they will have to complete along it.
Kush said he hoped Race for a Reason would allow Alfie's Squad to support more families like his.
"I guess that's my advice for everyone is just be patient with each other and take into consideration what someone might be going through, even if you can't see it," he said.
If you or someone you know are having feelings of despair or are emotionally distressed, the BBC Action Line has advice and support.

articles.title_orig: ‘You got to be the most optimistic human in the world:’ Colorado apple farmers hit hard by devastating April freeze
articles.title_zh: ‘You got to be the most optimistic human in the world:’ Colorado apple farmers hit hard by devastating April freeze
articles.content_orig:
COLORADO SPRINGS, Colo. (KKTV) - Colorado apple farmers are facing devastating losses after an April freeze wiped out crops across the state, and for one Penrose orchard owner, 2026 marks the second straight year of being hit hard.
I spoke with Tony Ferrara, owner of Happy Apple Farm in Penrose, who says he lost his entire apple orchard due to the cold temperatures in spring. He says this is the worst the farm has been impacted since it opened in 1984.
“We lost our crop April 18th. It hit about 22 degrees, and that’s when all the blossoms were on the tree, and uh, it was a total loss.” Ferrara said.
Making matters worse, Ferrara says back-to-back losses are virtually unheard of for the farm.
“2 years in a row and that’s unheard of. The farm has been in the family for 42 years, and I’ve never had back-to-back losses, so it’s not a happy apple farm; it’s a crappy apple farm.” Ferrara said.
The pain extends far beyond one operation. According to Dawn Thilmany, a professor of agriculture and resource economics at Colorado State University, farmers across Colorado have suffered complete or nearly complete losses.
“I would say 90 to 95% of the commercial production is in those handful of counties on the Western slope. Um, there’s about 1400 acres in total, and that is equivalent to about $300 million in production.” Thilmany said.
Despite the losses, Thilmany is urging consumers to support what remains of Colorado’s apple industry.
“We still have a pretty vibrant industry here in Colorado, and we want it to stay, um, so where you do see them, still buy them and support them,”Thilmany said.
For Ferrara, pumpkins are helping keep Happy Apple Farm afloat while he waits for a new crop.
“Luckily we have pumpkins. We do the pumpkins, and we will survive, but it’ll, it’ll be tight until next August, uh, when the new crop will come in, hopefully. There’s no way we can lose them three years in a row, but it’s, it, yeah, financially it’s, it’s a disaster.” Ferrara said.
Ferrara says he is remaining optimistic despite the massive loss and hopes this fall will still be a successful one for the farm. Thilmany says new methods are also being tested to keep crops from freezing in the future, including using solar panels to heat the soil.

articles.title_orig: Megadonors are powering Republicans’ spending advantage
articles.title_zh: Megadonors are powering Republicans’ spending advantage
articles.content_orig:
Elon Musk has spent $158m in a month to back Republicans in midterm races – with his efforts mostly focused on Texas
Tens of millions of dollars are pouring into Texas as Democrats stage an audacious bid to win a US Senate seat in the Republican stronghold.
Elon Musk, the world’s richest person, is among those wading into the closely watched race as November’s midterm elections approach.
In September alone, Musk gave $158m to the Senate Leadership Fund , the primary super political action committee (Pac) backing Republican Senate candidates, Axios first reported. The donation accounted for more than half of the Senate Leadership Fund’s fundraising in the third quarter.
Separately, Musk donated $10m to Lone Star Liberty Pac, the committee dedicated to supporting Ken Paxton , the Republican candidate in Texas, after Alex Latcham, the president of the Senate Leadership Fund, requested the funding.
A source familiar with the matter confirmed Axios’s reporting to the Guardian. The Guardian has also asked representatives for America Pac, the political operation founded by Musk, for comment.
The donations came as Republicans were struggling to keep up with spending by Paxton’s Democratic opponent , James Talarico. Over the summer, Talarico released an ad painting Paxton negatively as a politician with a history of corruption.
Talarico, a young, progressive candidate known for his faith-based messaging, made strides with liberal voters in Texas when he defeated an established Democrat for the Senate nomination earlier this year. Talarico raised $64m – the largest third-quarter fundraising of a Senate candidate in history, just this summer, Politico reported.
“He’s fighting this battle basically alone while Elon Musk and the full weight of the GOP fundraising apparatus outspends him 2:1. This is still an uphill battle,” an unnamed Democratic strategist working in Texas told Politico.
Polls have shown the two candidates are essentially tied, though some have Talarico polling narrowly ahead of Paxton.
The Texas Senate race is one of the most competitive races in the country and was expected to cost millions of dollars because it’s an expensive state to run a campaign.
The Senate Leadership Fund warned, months earlier, that supporting Paxton would cost anywhere from $150m to $200m. But Donald Trump chose Paxton himself to run against Talarico.
When Musk’s team and the Senate Leadership Fund analyzed polling, they found Paxton’s chances of winning dwindling, leading Musk to step in, Axios reported.
after newsletter promotion
In the 2025-2026 election cycle, Musk has donated approximately $366m to federal committees, the New York Times reported earlier this week. That is significantly more than he did during the 2024 election cycle, when he gave about $290m to help Trump.
The increase in spending contradicts a statement Musk made in May 2025 when he predicted : “I think, in terms of political spending, I’m going to do a lot less in the future.”
Andrew Romeo, a spokesperson for America Pac, told the New York Times: “These robust investments have allowed the GOP apparatus to get its message out so Republicans can have a fighting chance to defy history.
“If Democrats take control of Washington and win key gubernatorial and attorney general races this November, then America risks becoming a socialist, woke and borderless country,” Romeo added.

articles.title_orig: Fed's Warsh withholds rate signal, praises recent global tightening with 'no free riders'
articles.title_zh: Fed's Warsh withholds rate signal, praises recent global tightening with 'no free riders'
articles.content_orig:
BANGKOK — Federal Reserve Chairman Kevin Warsh refrained from signaling whether there will be another interest rate hike again this month, while acknowledging a "synchronous tightening" by central banks around the world and there's "no free riders."
"I don't prejudge meetings. I don't believe in saying now what I might do at the meetings that we have in the balance of this year," Warsh said, reiterating his opposition to the use of forward guidance for markets that should rely on interpreting data.
He also acknowledged that stance may disappoint anyone who had hoped for a steer ahead of the central bank meeting later this month. "It's a new chapter at the Fed [and] we're not in that business anymore. But we can go in any direction you'd like," he said.
Warsh spoke at a fireside chat with the International Monetary Fund's managing director, Kristalina Georgieva, as part of the weeklong IMF-World Bank Annual Meetings in Bangkok on Friday.
"Alongside other recent comments from FOMC participants, Warsh's comments indicate that the FOMC is set to pause in October," Goldman Sachs economists led by Jan Hatzius wrote in a note. "We continue to expect a second and final hike in December."
S&P 500 and Nasdaq futures edged higher following the speech, while stock market indexes in Asia and Treasury yields were largely stable.
Warsh described the global shift toward tighter monetary policy as a common fight on prices. Central banks made their own choices under their own mandates, he said, but the result was "a synchronous tightening in monetary policy in most places around the world," which means "there's no free riders."
Surging energy costs stemming from the Iran war and artificial intelligence investment boom are stoking inflation and pushing up borrowing costs around the world, just as global public debt is on pace to exceed 100% of the world's GDP, a level last breached in the aftermath of World War II.
The U.S. government has insisted that strong growth would be the best way to grow out of its rising debt pile, dismissing IMF's warning that the plans of relying solely on growth won't work as something that needs to be taken "with a grain of salt."
Warsh also expressed optimism about how AI will make economies that use it well more productive and wealthier, while warning the road there may be "very bumpy," and its near-term effect on employment is still uncertain.
"I want you to hear from me optimism, but optimism leavened by the seriousness of purpose," Warsh said.
A decade from now, he said, people will look back on the developments and "say this was hugely consequential."
The Fed raised rates to a range of 3.75% to 4% last month, its first hike since 2023 . Traders see a 72.3% chance for the Fed to keep the interest rate unchanged at the Oct. 27-28 meeting, according to CME FedWatch, while the majority expect a 25 basis point hike at the December meeting.

articles.title_orig: Woodbury resident's 'Bob's World' celebrates found family
articles.title_zh: Woodbury resident's 'Bob's World' celebrates found family
articles.content_orig:
Woodbury resident Wisdom Nunn hopes to bring more diverse voices into animation through his YouTube series "Bob's World." As the drummer for the band Nunnabove with his siblings, Nunn already works in a family setting. He brings that same connection into "Bob's World," which follows a pair of teenage bunnies looking for their lost parents and the family of friends they find along the way. FOX 9’s Maury Glover has the story.
WOODBURY, Minn. (FOX 9) - Woodbury resident Wisdom Nunn hopes to bring more diverse voices into animation through his YouTube series "Bob's World."
As the drummer for the band Nunnabove with his siblings, Nunn already works in a family setting. He brings that same connection into "Bob's World," which follows a pair of teenage bunnies looking for their lost parents and the family of friends they find along the way. Nunn said creating the series still feels surreal. "It really is a dream, and I don't think I kind of talk about it enough," said Nunn. He said the show's focus on community and family reflects a big part of his life. "Family is your friends. Family is people that you confide in, people that can talk to, and I think family isn't just blood," said Nunn.
Nunn said the series was inspired by two stuffed animals he and his brother made when they were little. After he taught himself animation, he decided to turn their imaginary adventures into a show. "It's such a wild culmination of things to come together. It warms my heart. I think it's great," said Nunn.
Nunn has completed four episodes of "Bob's World," and each one can take anywhere from eight months to two years to finish. His brother and sisters also help write, voice and score the series, making the project a family effort offstage too. Nunn hopes to complete six more episodes of "Bob's World," but he said that pace will probably take a few years. The show is also up for a regional Emmy. He said getting to illustrate the importance of found family already feels like a win. "I love that the show is about community and family. That's a big theme in my life that I hold very dearly, and I can't wait to see what comes next with it."

articles.title_orig: Europe reckons with a world where Trump is now helping Putin
articles.title_zh: Europe reckons with a world where Trump is now helping Putin
articles.content_orig:
European leaders know they can’t stop courting U.S. President Donald Trump. But as the American leader menaces Ukraine and offers Russian an economic lifeline, they are preparing for a world where he effectively sides with Moscow.
In the span of a week, Trump has trashed years of energy sanctions on the Kremlin, pressured Kyiv to quit bombing Russian oil refineries and suggested Ukraine’s Volodymyr Zelenskyy was an illegitimate leader — echoing Moscow’s propaganda. At one point, Ukraine also lost full access to the Elon Musk-owned Starlink system, leaving it hobbled on the battlefield.
In response, Zelenskyy let rip. He felt betrayed, he said. He called out Trump in public.
